Homage to the illustrious Maheśvara.
The Essence of Ritual Action: The Second Casket.
Now begins the fifth instruction: This *Vyāsasūtra* is a vessel for the nectar-stream of the bliss of Brahman;
for those whose minds are proficient therein, I shall declare the essence of reality.
Through the systematic arrangement of the various codes of conduct (*ācāra*) as primary and subordinate members, Brahman stands established like the head of one entering through a doorway. || 2 ||
Proper conduct is the primary dharma; from that comes prosperity, and from that, victory.
From that comes freedom from anxiety, and from that arises the purity of the mind.
From that, there arises confidence in the scriptures; then, having entered into them, comes thorough study.
From that, firm resolve shall arise, and from that, the continuous flow of certainty.
Through the continuous flow [of practice], by means of the ripening of accumulated future and commenced karmas,
the liberation of the wise takes the form of union (sāyujya) through their identity with Brahman.
Therefore, good conduct is the root; its root is the teacher himself.
One should remain devoted to good conduct by following the path instructed by the teacher.
The Supreme Self is the manifest Guru for those existing within the limitations of time;
the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is directly Maheśvara himself.
The guru alone is the supreme Brahman; therefore, one should follow the guru.
Devoted to virtuous conduct, one should always abide by the words of the guru regarding the universe.
(2) The various types of right conduct have been described by means of authoritative sources;
in brief, there are five kinds of conduct that are without distinction. (9)

Those learned in the scriptures declare that [ritual action] is fivefold: the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the obligatory-occasional (nityanaimittika), and likewise the obligatory-optional (nityakāmya).
The fivefold conduct, along with its specific distinctions, established by the scriptures and characterized by right behavior, has always been respectfully adopted by the Vīraśaivas. (11)

The wise know that [the penance] performed without regard for the end of the body, even when there is danger to life during its interruption, is indistinguishable from [the full penance] accompanied by the prescribed expiation.
The wise know that [an act] which results in the end of the body or a life-threatening severance of the vital breaths is specifically devoid of expiation (prāyaścitta). || 13 ||
The qualified manifestation (saviśeṣa-prapañca) has been adopted in the Vīraśaiva compendium;
however, the unqualified [manifestation] (nirviśeṣa) is either accepted or not by the Vīraśaivas.
Thus, for those who are thus doubting, in order to remove their hesitation and anxiety, I shall explain everything in accordance with the path of reality. 15.
Regarding that which was stated as the fivefold path of ritual (vidhi-mārga) known as the "without-distinction" (nirviśeṣa):
therein, the daily evening fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), the domestic fire-ritual (aupāsana), and so forth [must be performed]. (16)
The eternity [of the Veda], its being enjoined by revelation, and the occurrence of fault in negligence;
furthermore, the rule for expiation (prāyaścitta) for the purpose of removing that fault. (17)
When a solar transit, a lunar eclipse, or a planetary conjunction occurs, the ritual acts prescribed in the Vedas must be performed; such rites are said to depend upon the specific time.
"One offers with curd, one offers with milk," and so forth—
these they call "obligatory-cum-optional" (nityakāmya), for when performed, there is a supreme exaltation.
They declare that the obligatory and occasional rites are prescribed for every rainy season;
and the rite known as the Nirūḍhapaśubandha is performed when a fault arises through negligence.
The performance of virtuous acts again, accompanied by expiatory rites, is declared by the wise to be *kāmya* (optional) action, such as the *pavitreṣṭi* sacrifice and others. (21)
(3) Indeed, for the purpose of removing [doubts], it is exactly the same even in the case of the Smṛtis;
because the Smṛtis are rooted in the Śruti, the injunctions of the Smṛtis are [equivalent to] the injunctions of the Śruti. (22)
Practices such as these are not to be observed by Vīraśaivas;
for if they were not observed, their status as followers of the Vedas would be inconsistent. (23)
If they were to practice this, the state of being a Vīraśaiva would arise; otherwise, that claim of being a follower of the Vedas would then be like the horn of a hare.
Enough of your wandering with such delusive confusion;
you have indeed spoken the truth regarding the Vedic nature of these practices. (25)
What kind of conduct do they require? They do not require anything from those who are qualified.
If there were a requirement in that regard, then the time, the rule, and the sequence would have to be stated. (26)
If there were no dependence [on scripture] at all times and in all actions for everyone, then your status as a follower of the Veda would vanish due to such undifferentiated conduct. (27)
Therefore, you must certainly explain time, the object, and sequence;
if that is so, then determine them through the vision of reality as follows. (28)

For those established in the four stages of life (āśramas), the arrangement of duties according to their respective qualifications is declared by the Śruti; some [of these] pertain to the religious student (brahmacārin). (29)
Specifically for householders and some for forest-dwellers, certain rituals are prescribed; however, for ascetics, no rituals or observances whatsoever have been heard of in the scriptures.
For those established in the supreme stage of life (atyāśrama), ritual actions and observances would no longer exist;
yet, their status as knowers of reality is thus ordained by the very means of valid cognition.

The Vīraśaiva observances are preceded by the state of the ultimate stage (atyāśrama); they are divided into categories such as the Nirābhāra and others, and those who observe them are likewise distinguished.
For them, no sacred ford exists, nor sacrifices, nor even vows;
there is no requirement for the practice of yoga, nor the purification of days.
However, let there be many kinds of observances for those whose minds are disciplined—provided they possess disciplined minds, are dispassionate, and are patient. (34)
But all this is improper for others—those worldly beings whose minds are intent upon sense objects, who possess sons, grandsons, wives, and cattle. (35)
For those wandering in saṃsāra, whose minds are bound by fetters, who long for sense objects, who cling to the body as their identity, and who follow the path of the world; (36)
Or how could there be disregard for the actions that have been proposed? Furthermore, how can it be established here that the accomplishment of the goal does not occur through mere words alone? (37)

If it is argued thus, it is not so; for among Vīraśaivas, there is no such [restriction] regarding their own respective duties, especially for those who are incapable, just as in the case of ascetics and householders. || 38 ||
Just as there is atonement by some particular rite for those who are deficient in the performance of their own duties, so too is there [atonement] for these who are attached to sectarian marks.
Through the fulfillment of one's own duty according to one's respective capacity, liberation and the severance of the bonds may occur by the grace of the true guru. (40)

Surely [merit arises] from bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), from beholding a holy field (kṣetra), during eclipses, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), and at the conjunctions of Pāta and Vaidhṛti. || 41 ||
At the ocean, at the Setubandha, at Kāśī, and in Kurujāṅgala;
and at the rivers headed by the Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī.
From various duties and rituals—through giving gifts, burnt offerings, worship of the gods, fasting, and by means of the kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances for oneself; || 43 ||
If it is the case that the purification of householders as well as of renunciants is described by some in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, how is it [not so] for you? 44.
If it is argued that there is a deficiency in the performance of one's own dharma and that it must be fulfilled, then listen: for them as well, purification of the mind is prescribed. (45)

Through devotion to the Guru, through devotion to Śiva, through worship of Him in the form of the Liṅga, through the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, and through giving gifts according to one's capacity. || 46 ||
For the mind alone is the cause of all merit and demerit;
by means of purity of mind, they attain the supreme goal.
(5) [Objection: In that case, let it be performed by the Vīraśaivas without distinction;
for that action which is without distinction serves to complete any deficiency.
The ascetic, intent on action for the sake of fulfilling his own deficiencies, does not act in this manner; rather, he diligently performs those actions that are non-contradictory [to his goal]. (49)
In the same way, let the Vīraśaivas perform their respective rites without contradicting their own duties; indeed, those [rites] shall be explained by me.
As it is stated in the Śrutis: "Seated upon one's own seat during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should contemplate the chosen deity and then perform the meditation on its name. (51)
By means of the primary practice of cleaning the teeth, as well as through purification with clay,
one attains the purity of the body while casting off both external and internal impurities.
Bathing should be performed according to the purity of one's mind among the ten types of baths;
specifically, even one who has already bathed should perform the ash-bath (bhūtisnāna).
Having performed the daily worship, one should practice one's own respective dharma;
for Śaivas, this much is the daily rite, and now the occasional rite is being described.

Especially on a field of merit, on an auspicious day, at a meritorious time—specifically during a solar transit (saṅkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), at the lunar node (pāta), and during eclipses of the moon and sun. || 55 ||
One should bathe, give the jewel of life, and recite the *Āmocana* mantra;
for the two eyes of Śiva are the moon and the sun, and those two [are likewise] his.
When [the time for] the eclipse has arrived and Rāhu has obscured [the sun or moon], one should perform religious duties there,
provided it does not conflict with one's own regular obligations and one’s mind is fully intent upon the daily rites.
One should pass that time by reciting the Jīvaratna mantra alone, just as one does during the time of the Agnihotra when an eclipse occurs. || 58 ||
He should pass that time either by means of the Agnihotra or by performing a sacrifice, so that no fault arising from its transgression may accrue to him. (59)
In this regard, it should be understood that the non-transgression of the injunctions consists in the performance of obligatory and occasional rites on the occasion of Śivarātri. (60)
The duty that ought to be performed should be understood as being exactly the same for all; however, other religious practices are not desired if they are in contradiction with the Śaiva dharma. (61)
The Śaiva dharma is included within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, just as the Agnihotra is;
therefore, no fault whatsoever exists in its transgression. || 62 ||
But as for their obligatory-optional worship, such as the daily worship and so forth, it is the performance of worship for a certain period of time with a view toward some specific purpose. (63)
Or else, for many others as well, according to the aforementioned analogy,
just as the monthly Agnihotra occurs within the obligatory daily Agnihotra.
The fault arising from its transgression flees far away;
one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites even when a guest has arrived at the home. (65)
Hospitality must be extended there by all means; this is the certain conclusion.
For others besides them, inclusion within that [hospitality] is declared to be easily attained. (66)
That rite, which is both obligatory and optional, should be performed when a mobile liṅga has arrived at one's home;
it is certain that it should especially be done for the duration of a month with various kinds of food and edibles.
Many kinds of optional rites have been declared—bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and austerity;
all of these should be cultivated by the wise man without contradiction.
We do not say that the Śrutis, the Smṛtis, or even the Purāṇas lack authority; rather, we speak of their mutual contradictions.
Having placed non-contradiction foremost, I have described the intended meaning;
for a wise person should not be deluded by the thought that another is mistaken. (70)
Those who perceive the truth should understand, without distinction and in manifold ways, the authority of all scriptures and all means of valid cognition. (71)
But surely, if this were so, it would merely be a bold assertion;
let there be this "beyond-the-stages" (atyāśrama) for those who are dispassionate and have renounced their minds. (72)
Furthermore, for those who are householders, their own specific customs are the primary causes [of merit];
however, the practices belonging to the higher stages of life (āśramas) are not appropriate for them. (73)
Just as a religious student does not have the right to the duties of a householder, so too a householder does not have the right to the duties of an ascetic. (74)

Thus, even those who observe the conduct of the various stages of life (āśramas) and possess the external marks and limbs [of their order], do not deserve to attain steadfastness in the [highest] object, as they are characterized by mental fickleness. (75)

Furthermore, because there would be no performance of even those prescribed rites that ought to be performed, there would be a contradiction with Vīraśaivism; thus, that same defect remains as it was.
To this it is replied: this Vīraśaiva doctrine was proclaimed by Śiva;
therein also there are various divisions, such as the distinction between the Nirābhāra and others. (77)
One who is without support does not deserve distinctions regarding those phenomena;
one who is devoted to the universal [reality] never deserves particularized qualities. (78)
Indeed, the rites proposed by you must be performed exactly as such;
whether it be whatever [is required], or however much, or whatever has been specifically determined. (79)
To the extent that there is the performance [of vows], there is the drying up of the seven oceans;
and as for what was said—that one who observes celibacy is not fit for the householder’s life—[that too is addressed]. (80)
Regarding the statement "and a householder [should perform] the duties of an ascetic," one should understand it in this way:
or rather, [the meaning is that] a householder bathes, whereas one who observes celibacy (brahmacarya) should not bathe. 81.

A householder would not possess qualities such as tranquility and the like that a renunciant possesses; however, if a householder were to practice those duties which are not common [to both], he would indeed be a renunciant. (82)
"No householder whatsoever should renounce [the world]; therefore, your statement is difficult to justify.
Moreover, it is pleasing only at first sight—so let it be; what is the use of further elaboration? (83)

But surely, how could a householder who possesses the marks of [monastic] signs be characterized by the Nirābhāsa and other [stages], just as a celibate student cannot possess the characteristics of a householder? (84)

In this regard, it is said that one who is deficient or excessive in qualification does not deserve rites such as the *aupāsana*; therefore, how could he not likewise be unworthy of his own superior duties? (85)

We shall not declare the eligibility of a student (brahmacārin) for those rites that are to be accomplished by householders; rather, we shall speak again of his eligibility in accordance with his own stage of life (āśrama).
Through the practice of non-contradictory dharma, there is auspiciousness;
thus, let the conduct of those situated in the higher stages of life not be that of a householder. (87)
Furthermore, the status of a Vīraśaiva is not lost for householders by that [marriage];
indeed, what is it other than the state of being without [other] stages of life (anāśramatva), which is the sole fitness for the path to liberation? 88.
And she was seen by the high-souled householder Vāmadeva, as well as by Gārgī; for she was indeed a female ascetic. (89)
Therefore, for the sake of increasing one's spiritual welfare, a Vīraśaiva should perform the prescribed rites without contradicting the principles of Vīraśaivism. (90)
Having resorted to the path of Brahman, he should perform bathing, giving, and the worship of Śiva;
yet, for the prosperity of the kingdom, he should follow the path of the Kṣatriya.
One should have the Vedic rites performed by whomever has the wealth; that result belongs to him.
Then, having summoned those learned in the Vedas, that king [should proceed] in due order from thereon. (92)
Having indeed followed the occupation of a Vaiśya while performing his service, he should bathe; wealth and other such things should be given [to him].
Having obtained a livelihood through the occupation of a Śūdra, the wise man should then desist from it. 93.
Thus, in accordance with my promise, I shall describe the daily obligatory rites (nityakarman) as they are set forth in the Parāśara Purāṇa and expounded in the treatises on Dharma (dharmaśāstra).
Quickly teach me the conduct of the virtuous by which a wise man may conquer the worlds;
likewise, explain dharma and adharma, as well as that which leads to heaven and hell. (95)
One who possesses both Vedic knowledge and Vedic conduct is called a "Brāhmaṇa" by name;
indeed, a Vipra is one endowed with Vedic knowledge and Vedic conduct, while a Dvija is one who possesses even one of these.
A Kṣatriya who serves as a king’s attendant possesses little conduct and little Vedic knowledge;
likewise, a Vaiśya engaged in agriculture and trade possesses only a modicum of conduct. (97)
One who is himself a cultivator is called a "Brāhmaṇa-Śūdra";
one who is envious and malicious toward others is called a "Caṇḍāla-Brāhmaṇa. (98)
The king is the protector of the earth; likewise, others are called Kṣatriyas.
A Vaiśya is one who deals in the purchase and sale of grain and such; others are called Viśas. (99)
One who serves the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is called a Śūdra; the cultivator is to be known as a Vṛṣala, and others are indeed Dasyus. (100)
"For everyone, facing the east at dawn, should contemplate [the deities] beginning with the gods"—in such statements from the Purāṇas, moreover, by means of their qualities... (101)
Names such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are derived from [specific] relationships and not from birth;
because they are Vedic, the practices of the Vīraśaivas are the highest among Vedic traditions. (102)
Now, regarding the morning duties:

having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and seated oneself on one's own seat in a state of purity, one should consider dharma and artha, as well as their afflictions (*kleśas*), income, and expenditure. (103)
Longevity, enmity, death, sin, as well as fortune, disease, prosperity, and peace—these are the fruits of the directions corresponding to the time of rising in the morning. (104)
The final watch of the night and the half-watch of dawn are called the junction (saṃdhi);
having risen at that time, the wise man should void his excrement and urine.
Having gone a long distance from his house, restrained in speech and properly clothed, he should enter facing north; however, if there is an obstruction, he may face another direction.
Now, the procedure for purification:
Facing water, fire, Brahmins, and other deities, one should cover the private organ with the left hand and the mouth with the other hand. (107)
Having discharged the waste and stood up, one should not look at that excrement;
one should perform purification outside the water using only water drawn out [of a vessel]. 108.
Alternatively, even without descending to a sacred ford for the sake of the gods and ancestors,
one should cleanse the anus with earth seven times or three times.
In the penis, [the amount] should be the size of a *karkoṭī* fruit, while for the anus, one *prasṛti* is prescribed.
Then, having risen, one should perform ablutions with water for the feet and hands, and take eight mouthfuls of water for rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*).
With whatever vessel or wooden stick is available, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with cotton fiber outside of the water, avoiding the index finger. 111.
I shall write down, in brief, the words spoken in the divine scriptures:
when two *muhūrtas* remain before the rising of the sun. (112)
Having risen, with his hands and feet washed and having applied the smearing of ashes,
he should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess in his heart as a common initiate (sāmānyasamayin).
The practitioner, who belongs to a distinguished observance and has been initiated into the liberation at the *bindu* on the crown of the head,
should sip water and contemplate Śambhu at the end of the twelve.
One should recite his heart-pleasing names and deeds;
for one who is free from worldly burdens and distinguished should indeed contemplate in this very way. (115)
Having gone to a suitable place, one should void excrement and urine;
facing north during the morning and evening twilights, and facing south at night. (116)
Facing either east or west during the first and second halves of the day, facing north at midday, and facing south during the night. (117)
One should avoid looking at the sky, excrement, urine, the cardinal directions, the moon, the sun, the stars, or fire;
likewise, one should avoid facing a deity, a cow, a sage, a brahmin, or a woman. 118.

One should wipe the anus with grasses that are not parts of a sacrifice and are otherwise useless, or with clods of earth and the like; one should not use excellent leaves, branches, flowers, fruits, or similar items.
Looking downward and holding his private parts with his left hand,
he should approach the water and perform purification with earth and water.
One application of clay is for the penis, five for the anus, ten for the left hand, six or seven for the back and the two feet, and seven applications of clay for both hands. (121)
On an anthill, at the root of a tree, in a house, on a path, in the midst of water, in saline soil, in a place dug up by mice, in a cow-pen, or in a temple; || 122 ||
On the banks of ponds, wells, and tanks; on sandy ground;
on a street; in a cremation ground; or in a place defiled by insects, husks, frost, or charcoal—123.
One should not take earth from a dusty place, from ground strewn with soil intended for the purification of others, from land tilled by a plough, nor from mud, nor from gravelly ground. (124)
On the pure ground, one should dig up the soil and remove the top layer of earth, so that it becomes sufficient for purification, or until nothing remains [of the impurity]. (125)
First, there should be cleansing of the anus; then [the hands] with a measure of one *prasṛti*;
thereafter with half that measure; and after that, with half of that again. (126)
For purification after urination, the amount of earth should be equal to a fresh *āmalaka* fruit;
for semen, it should be double that amount, and for sexual intercourse, three times that amount. 127.
This is the purification for a householder; it is greater than that in the midst of impurity caused by death.
For those such as the student (brahmacārin) and others, however, it is respectively two, three, and four times as much. 128.
Whatever purification is prescribed for someone during the day, half of that is prescribed for him at night;
half of that is said for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey.
Having washed the feet up to the ankles and the hands up to the wrists with earth,
one should afterwards wash them up to the knees or the elbows with water.
One who desires the perfection of purification should not perform ablution with streams of water;
rather, it should be performed with a mere handful of water according to the rule for cleansing the hands. (131)
For the purpose of providing earth and water for purification, two attendants should be appointed;
the earth held in the left hand should be cast into the right hand.
One should perform twelve mouthfuls of rinsing after voiding feces;
one should perform four after urinating, and sixteen at the end of a meal.
One should wash one's feet facing east, and here, the hands facing north;
then, facing either north or east, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Now, the procedure for cleaning the teeth: Then, one should take a tooth-stick provided with bark, using the heart-mantra;
it should be cut level at the tip before the joint, fresh, and with a brush-like tuft at its end.
It should be as thick as the little finger or fine according to the delicacy of one's teeth;
it is eight fingers long for those committed to lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika) and twelve fingers for those seeking worldly enjoyment (bhogin).
For those belonging to the [four] castes, it should be ten, six, eight, or seven finger-breadths;
for those who have renounced the world, six finger-breadths; and for women, four finger-breadths. (137)

[The flowers] produced from the *jambu*, mango, *kakubha*, *aśoka*, and *kapittha* trees, as well as those arising from the *bakula*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *phullāṅghri*, *jāti*, *campaka*, and *śaṅkha*. (138)
One should take atimuktaka, apāmārga arising from the kadamba tree, and [roots] of serpents;
and also this: śairīṣa, cirabilva, and karañjaka. (139)
[One should prepare a paste] from the heartwood of śrīparṇī and nirguṇḍī, or from the khadira group [of trees],
along with akṣa, kṣīrī, dhava, eraṇḍa, vaṭa, aśvattha, and kakudvara.
[One should prepare a paste] from guḍikā, madhuka, śilpī, and those born of the kula-niśigru; and from nākulī, peruvā, nīra, dhātrī, and what arises from kādamba. (141)
[The seats] made from dates and coconuts, from the Palāśa tree, from the Tāla palm and bamboo, from grass, leaves, and Piśāca-wood, and from bricks, charcoal, and ashes; 142.

On the finger, the index finger (tarjanī) is to be avoided, as is [an image] made of gold and the like; likewise, the first, ninth, sixth, and twelfth lunar days constitute the five festival days (parva).
The day of fasting, the three [days] of birth, Saturday, Sunday, Vyatīpāta, an eclipse, and the day of one's birth. (144)
After sunrise, the cleaning of the teeth with a tooth-stick (dantadhāvana) should be avoided;
instead, one should cleanse the teeth with twelve rounds of mouthfuls of water or with [tooth-]twigs.
One should perform the scraping of the tongue for the purpose of purifying the impurities of the tongue;
[one should likewise cleanse] what arises from saliva, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, semen, feces, urine, and the body.
Whatever has come into contact with the hands and feet must all be cleansed;
the nose, ears, eyes, and so forth are purified by washing. (147)
Nails, hair, and other such things are purified with earth, āmalaka, and similar substances;
having thus cleansed away impurities and the like, one should perform the ritual bath of Varuṇa (vāruṇasnāna).

Now, the procedure for bathing: Having paid homage to the deities of the water, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras—a practice that removes all impurities and destroys bad dreams and other such evils. (149)
If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one should pour water reaching the neck, or even the waist, or up to the knees, and perform the mantra-bath.
The wise one should satisfy the gods and others by means of the recitation of the root mantra;
with a pure mind, he should satisfy Śiva, the Goddess, and the hosts of Śiva’s attendants. (151)
Having taken a washed cloth, one should wear it with five folds;
likewise, an upper garment must be worn in all ritual activities. 152.
At bathing places such as rivers and the like, a wise person should pull the bathing garment downward; however, at bathing sites such as ponds, wells, and reservoirs, he should pull it upward. (153)
Whether on stone, wood, or other materials, or even in water or on land, the twice-born man, having purified it, should wring out the cloth for the satisfaction of the ancestors. (154)
A Vīraśaiva, however, would not need to perform libations for the liberation of his ancestors, because they have already attained union with Śiva through the Śāmbhava initiation. 155.
Thus has the ritual of bathing been determined for the Vīraśaivas.

Thus ends the fifth instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭhaśivācārya, who was a knower of the one hundred and one topics constituting the secret essence of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.

The Sixth Instruction: Now, for the sake of the ablution and the wearing of ash by the Vīraśaiva who has already performed the ritual bath with water, the origin of the sacred ash (bhasma) is demonstrated. || 1 ||
Now, for the purpose of smearing with ashes, the authoritative texts that prompt the production of ashes are set forth:
in the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad, the scripture regarding liberation known as the Bṛhajjābāla.

"Grant me your instruction. Then, saying "So be it," from Sadyojāta came the earth; from that, Nivṛtti; from that, Nandā of tawny color; from her cow-dung, Vibhūti was born. From Vāmadeva came water; from that, Pratiṣṭhā; from that, Bhadrā of black color; from her—

From *Gomaya* (the Cow) ash was produced; from *Aghora* fire, and from that, *Vidyā*; she is red-colored and fragrant, and from her cow-dung ash was produced. From *Tatpuruṣa* wind, and from that, *Śānti*;
she is white-colored and of excellent character, and from her cow-dung alkali was produced.

From Īśāna comes space; from that, the Śāntyatītā [Kalā]; from her, the multicolored Sumanā; from her, protection (rakṣā) was born in cow-dung. Vibhūti, bhasita, bhasma, kṣāra, and rakṣā—these are the five names of the sacred ash (bhasman).
It is called *bhūti* because it causes great sovereignty through its five names; *bhasma* because it consumes all sins; *bhasita* because of its brilliance; *kṣāra* because it destroys calamities;
and *rakṣā* because it protects from the fears of ghosts, spirits, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, epilepsy, and worldly existence.

Thus it is said; likewise, in the third Brāhmaṇa: "Then Bhūsuṇḍa said to Kālāgnirudra, 'Please explain the yoga of Vibhūti. He replied: [one should wear] a cow that is deformed-limbed, insane, very wicked, dirty, marked with signs such as those of inauspiciousness, and emaciated."

One should avoid a cow that has lost its calf, one that is not calm, one that does not yield milk, one that lacks its senses, one that has already grazed on grass, one that eats hair, rags, or bones, one that is in heat (*sandhinī*), one that has recently calved, or one afflicted by disease; instead, one should collect excellent cow dung. Regarding this, there are these verses:
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is designated as the "power" (śakti) of all things;
knowledge rests upon the three qualities (guṇas), and that [reality] is the substratum of knowledge.
These three qualities are the cow; knowledge is the auspicious dung, and the Upaniṣads are said to be the urine. From that, one should subsequently prepare the sacred ash.
Its calves are the Smṛtis, and its cow-dung is produced from them;
one should consecrate the cow there with the five-syllabled mantra.
Then, having fasted on either the fourteenth day of the bright or the dark fortnight, the observer of the vow should consume one hundred and eight mouthfuls of water or grass.
Having risen early on the following day, being pure and composed,
having bathed and put on clean clothes, he should release a cow for the sake of milk.
Having raised up the cow with effort, one should collect her urine with the Gāyatrī mantra;
one should hold it in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay.
One should place cow urine in a vessel made of lotus, or of Palāśa wood, or even in a cow-horn; likewise, one should take cow dung with the root mantra.
(15) The householder should take [the vessel] so as not to let it fall to the ground; the wise one should cleanse the cow-dung in the previously mentioned bowl with the eight root mantras. (8)
Having recited the mantra ten times, one should discard the cow-dung from its place;
with the mantra "bhavāya namaḥ," one should pour cow's urine onto the cow-dung.
One should offer fourteen morsels (piṇḍas) with the mantra "Salutation to Śarva," having purified them with the rays [of the mantra] and drawn them forth with the root-mantra of seven syllables.
Then, one should place balls of cow-dung in the previously mentioned vessel and,
having established the fire according to the very procedure taught by Śiva, one should worship it.
One should deposit morsels of food there with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end,
using the syllables of the six-syllabled mantra as they are repeated.
There, one should offer rice-balls to the deity of the [respective] caste with mantras ending in "svāhā";
likewise, one should offer the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) using the root mantra alone. || 13 ||
Then he offers twenty-three oblations into the *nidhanapati* fire;
five oblations named after Brahman are to be offered, [with the mantra] "Obeisance to the auspicious God. (14)
Having thus offered all the oblations with mantras ending in the dative case—
namely Bhava, Śarva, Mṛḍa, Rudra, Hara, Śambhu, and Maheśvara— || 15 ||
The wise one should likewise offer oblations with these, as well as the eightfold root mantra;
there is an oblation of three for Śiva, and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering from the root mantra.
Having thus completed the remainder of the rite, as well as the offering of the full vessel of water, one with a pure mind should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) one hundred and eight times.
One should sprinkle that water on the head with the *pañcabrahma* mantra;
and having recited it ten times, one should scatter the water in all directions. (18)
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Śaivas for the sake of peace, one should collect the hair-roots (pulaka), saying:
"I shall collect [them] for the protection of the ritual acts of all the Śaivas. (19)
"I cover you, who are Jātavedas, with my bristling hairs (pulakas).
With this mantra, one should then cover that fire with the pulakas.
Covering oneself with horripilation for three days is said to be for the sake of remaining within the fire;
one should feed those devoted to Śiva with devotion and eat oneself while restrained in speech.
If one desires an abundance of ashes, one should collect an excess of cow dung,
either over the course of three days or on a single day.
On either the third or the fourth [lunar day], having bathed in the morning, wearing white garments, with a bright white Śaiva thread and anointed with white sacred ash; || 23 ||
Having white teeth and smeared with ashes, the knower of mantras,
having recited this root mantra, should cast off the *pulaka* ashes.
Therein, one should perform the sixteen services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), as well as the vyāhṛtis; then, one should withdraw the fire.
One should take the excellent ashes with the mantra beginning with "sadyojāta," and thereafter wipe them away with the subsequent mantra.
Having mixed [the powder] with fragrant waters or with the urine of a Kapila cow,
one should likewise add moonstone, saffron from Kashmir, uśīra, and sandalwood.
Having finely ground the three types of agallochum (agaru),
one should cast that powder into the ashes while reciting the "Om" syllable, the mantra of Brahman.
Then the wise man should take up large balls [of food] with the Praṇava,
and then with the Aghora mantra, having recited the root mantra ten times.
In the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the acquisition and retention of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*).
Having become pure, [one should approach] a woman with deformed limbs, who is insane, inauspicious, and possesses either deficient or redundant limbs."

Having abandoned a barren woman, one who wears bones or rags, one who eats impure things, or one who is diseased, and having taken the cow-dung of a woman with auspicious marks, one should form it into a ball, dry it thoroughly,
cover it with white purifying substances, and cook it either in the domestic fire, the sacrificial fire, or in a cooking vessel; [it should be placed] in a vessel made of *bilva* wood or earthenware.
Or one should establish it.
In the Bodhāyana-smṛti: "The cow-dung should be taken with the left hand, and one should consecrate it with mantras using the left hand. (1)
One should burn the funeral cake with the Aghora mantra, while it is to be received with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Goddess spoke these words.
"O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me correctly about that ash-bath.
Īśvara said:
"Now, therefore, O fair-eyed one, I shall fully explain the ash-bath."
May longevity, strength, health, prosperity, and nourishment increase accordingly;
for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the complete abundance of all wealth. (4)
For people smeared with ashes, it serves to ward off fever and the fear of Māryā;
the ash may be threefold: pacifying (śāntika), nourishing (pauṣṭika), and the bestower of desires (kāmada).
Cow dung that is fresh from the source, taken directly with the hand and consecrated by the Brahma-mantras, is here called the "pacifying" (śāntika) substance.
Being attentive, one should take cow dung that has fallen from a good cow into the intermediate space, and then burn it with the six-limbed [mantra].
That is declared to be nourishing (pauṣṭika); now hear about that which grants desires (kāmada).
That cow dung which has fallen by chance upon a perfectly pure patch of ground— || 8 ||
One should burn this with the *prāsāda* mantra; this is called the "grantor of desires.
O Goddess of Gods! having risen in the morning, pure and observing a vow of silence, [one should perform this]. || 9 ||
Having gone to a cow-pen and having paid homage to the herd of cows, one should collect auspicious cow dung from those cows whose colors correspond to the desired [deity]. (10)
The cow of a Brāhmaṇa is said to be white, that of a Kṣatriya red, that of a Vaiśya yellow, and that of a Śūdra black. || 11 ||
On the full moon day, the new moon day, or the eighth day, one of purified intellect,
having taken auspicious cow dung with the Prāsāda mantra.
Having formed a ball of cow dung with the heart mantra,
one should heat it in the rays of the sun in a pure and beautiful place.
One should cast [the fire] with husks or even with chaff, or by means of a palace;
one should cause either a forest-born fire or a fire of husks to be used.
One should then install Agni there as Śiva himself through the mantra; then the wise practitioner should burn that [element] from the root (kanda) down to ashes.
Taking up a new vessel, one should deposit [the substances] with a gracious mind:
likewise the ketakī, the pāṭalī, uśīra, and sandalwood.
One should cast [the substance] into its center; it becomes pure immediately by means of the mantra.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, the words of Śrī Rāma are as follows:
"O Yellow Ocean! If you are pleased with me, what indeed is difficult to accomplish? (17)
"Therefore, O best of sages, tell me about the initiation (dīkṣā) of Viraja.
Agastya Muni said:
"On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, or especially on the eighth day," ||| 18 ||
One should begin on the eleventh lunar day, on a Monday, or under the Ārdrā asterism;
[he who is] that which they call Vāta, that which is Rudra, the eternal Supreme Lord.
They say that Śiva is higher than the highest, even higher than the highest;
they call Sadāśiva the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Vāyu.
Having meditated and purified the domestic fire (āvasathya-agni) with that fire,
he should separately restrain the five elements according to the sequence of the rules for the qualities of the measures.
There are five measures and four; then three measures, and after that two. Then there is one measure and the measureless, which is established at the end of the twelve. (22)
Having remained steady and having become immortal, one should observe the Pāśupata vow.
"I shall perform this Pāśupata vow in brief," [he should say]. (23)
Having thus made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) early in the morning and having established the sacred fire, he returned;
being himself fasting, pure, bathed, and wearing white garments.
Then the wise man, smeared with white ashes and possessing white teeth and so forth,
should offer oblations with the Viraja-mantras, beginning with Prāṇa and Apāna.
At the end of the section (anuvāka), with one-pointed concentration, having separately offered fuel-sticks,
clarified butter, and cooked rice, he should internalize the fire within himself by means of the mantra beginning with "te agne" (and others).
Having reflected with the mantras beginning with "bhasmādāyāgniḥ," one should touch the limbs;
this method of *homa* will be demonstrated later.
Likewise, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā as well, the method for performing the Pāśupata vow, preceded by fire-oblations and other rites, is explained in great detail; this too will be set forth further on.
Having taken the dung of a tawny cow that falls from the sky—neither moist, nor too hard, neither foul-smelling, nor stale—[one should use it]. (27)
If it should fall, one should discard what is above and below and pick it up;
having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire or similar [receptacle] while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the uncooked and the overcooked portions, and having taken the white ash and stirred it with water in a cloth, one should deposit it into the receptacle for the ashes.

Having placed it upon a vessel that is well-prepared, very firm, pure, washed, sprinkled, and auspicious, the practitioner of mantra should deposit the ashes into the vessel while reciting the mantra.
One should take the consecrated ashes oneself or have one's attendant take them;
one may place them in the hand of one's own kin, but one must not cast them upon an impure surface.
One should not touch it with the lower parts of the body, nor should one neglect it or step over it;
therefore, having taken the consecrated ashes, one should employ them.
(p. 20) Now, regarding the arrangement for the ash, it is stated in the Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad:
"One should prepare a vessel for the ash that is made of metal, wood, or likewise of clay; otherwise, it should be something else that is beautiful and pure. (33)

For members of the three twice-born classes who are householders, it is that fire born from the *agnihotra*; for those same classes [who are not householders], it is the fire born from the marriage rite (*vivāha-agni*) or the domestic fire (*aupāsana-agni*); for students (*brahmacārins*), it is the fire from the sacred fuel-sticks (*samidh-agni*);

for the dispassionate who have transcended the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramin*), it is the fire born from the *virajā* [sacrifice]; and for *śūdras*, [it is the fire born from the *pākayajña*].

The ash produced from the cooking fire in the house of a *śrotriya* belongs to others; that which arises from a forest fire belongs to [other] ascetics; for those who have transcended the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramin*), it is the same wherever it is found. Even among them, for those who are dispassionate, it is found everywhere. For all, it is said to be found in a temple; for Śiva-yogins, it is the ash born from the fire of Śiva.
Or that linga situated in a temple of Śiva, which has been purified by the consecration of mantras.
In the fifth chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha-laiṅga:
"O great sage, all members of the three twice-born classes must wear ashes produced from the agnihotra fire and from the Virajā fire. (34)
The fire produced from the *aupāsana* rite is distinguished for householders; the fire produced from the *samit* (sacrificial wood) is indeed to be maintained by students (*brahmacārin*s). (35)
For Śūdras, [the fire] produced from the cooking-fire in the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) should be maintained;
for all others as well, that produced from a forest fire (dāvānala) should be maintained.
In the Sūtasamhitā: "With ash produced from the fire of sacrificial fuel, or from the fire of Virajā, or from the Agnihotra fire, and mixed with water... (37)
With the six or seven mantras beginning with "Agni," one should apply it in sequence.
In that very place [it is said]:
"O best of the twice-born, this ash is very little in substance, yet it is proclaimed in many ways. (38)
O best of scholars, O twice-born ones! There is one kind that is Śrauta and another that is Smārta;
the Śrauta ash is declared to be primary, while the Smārta is proclaimed as secondary.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones! Ash is of three kinds: purely worldly, Vedic (śrauta), and traditional (smārta); these are proclaimed specifically for the twice-born. (40)
(21) Furthermore, there is another, worldly ash for all others as well.
In that very same section on the Greatness of Śiva (Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa), it says:
"O best of sages, [this is] again for the sake of attaining the direct knowledge of Śiva. (41)
Having taken with reverence the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice—
as stated in the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad*, beginning with "What is the substance? and concluding with "That substance is the ash pertaining to Agni."
In the Bhāradvāja-smṛti, having introduced the topic with "Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed ācamana," it says: "Taking the white ash produced from the agnihotra fire. (43)
In that very same [text]:
"Ash held in the hand of a Śūdra must never be worn by the twice-born;
ash held in the hand of a Śūdra or an outcaste (antyaja) must never be worn at any time. (44)
Therefore, for the sake of the increase of his merit, a twice-born man should daily apply the Tripuṇḍra with the very ashes produced from the Agnihotra, remaining ever vigilant. (45)
But those who awaken one to the goals of human existence [state]:
"The rule for wearing the *vibhūti* has been taught there;
it is proclaimed by me here [as well], solely to avoid the confusion of practices mentioned therein, and not otherwise. (46)
The ash prepared by Śaiva priests in the presence of Śiva should be accepted with supreme devotion, even after having requested the officiants.
(There, having requested the perfected ash according to the stated path,) if it is given anywhere by worshippers, it should indeed be accepted by those following the Vedic tradition;
likewise, even if unrequested, [it may be taken] from the presence of Mahādeva by the Śaivas. 48.
If worldly ashes are offered, they should indeed be accepted by those who follow the Vedic tradition;
however, they should not be sought after by Tantric worshippers, wherever they may be.
If worldly ash is offered, it must not be accepted by those who follow the Vedic path, nor by Kāpālikas, Śūdras, heretics, or others. (50)
If ash is given by those solely devoted to the Vedas, it must certainly be accepted—even if the giver is a student, an ascetic, or even a Śūdra. (51)
"If that prosperity is always to be accepted, otherwise he is indeed a traitor to me—what is the meaning of this statement of Śiva? If you ask this, [the answer is as follows: 52.
Whether in the house of a Caṇḍāla or in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, one who knows the supreme truth perceives no difference whatsoever regarding what may be eaten or enjoyed.
"Decide for yourself that whatever is the destiny of this [ash], that same is the destiny of him;
as many particles of ash as have fallen upon the earth," (54)
"For so many thousands of years one shall go to the Raurava hell"—thus is the great fault of smearing ashes proclaimed. (55)
"Having become extremely attentive, the wise man should maintain the sacred ash. Thus it is said.

Now, the Virajā-homa, as described in the Padma-purāṇa which supplements the Bṛhajjābāla-upaniṣad, is demonstrated: On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight (or the dark fortnight), the practitioner,
having become pure and having fasted while preceded by a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), [should approach] on that very day a commendable cow.

Having consecrated [the offerings] with the mantra "ā gāvaḥ," he should cause [the cow] to consume grass and water with the mantra "gāvo bhagaḥ. Thus, being observant of the vow on the fourteenth day, having risen early the following morning,
become pure, composed, and having performed his bath and put on clean garments—

Having performed the morning worship of Śiva and other rites preceded by the wearing of the *vibhūti* ashes, one should go to the cow for the sake of milk. At the time when the cow is joined with her calf, [one should collect the milk] into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, clay, horn, or *palāśa* wood, or into a lotus leaf, while reciting the *Gāyatrī*.
One should fetch cow urine. Into the very same vessel mentioned previously, one should fetch cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvāram," taking it as it lies on the ground.
Even if it has fallen on pure ground, one should discard what is at the bottom or on top and fetch what remains in the middle. One should purify the cow dung with the mantra "śrīr me bhavatu."

With the mantra "May misfortune perish for me," one should discard the cow-dung containing sand, seeds, grain, and so forth. With the mantra "I sprinkle you," one should pour cow-urine onto the cow-dung. Immediately thereafter, having thoroughly kneaded the cow-dung with the mantra "Of the five winds... [one should proceed].

One should prepare fourteen *piṇḍas* with fourteen mantras. If there is a desire to produce an abundance of extra wealth, one should prepare the *piṇḍas* silently. Having placed them in a pure vessel, one should dry them with the rays of the sun.

One should place [the offering] in the previously mentioned vessel. Immediately thereafter, having established and ignited the fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā), and having performed the rites beginning with the spreading of the grass mats (paristaraṇa) and the selection of the Brahman priest, up to the throwing of the fuel sticks (idhma), one should subsequently offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). *Oṃ svāhā*.
This is for the Supreme Self, not for me; *svāhā*. This is for Indra, not for me;
*maṃ svāhā*. This is for Rudra, not for me; *śiṃ svāhā*. This is for Viṣṇu; *vāṃ svāhā*. This is for Brahmā; *yaṃ svāhā*. This is for Skanda; *yaṃ svāhā* again; *vāṃ*.
Svāhā! Śiṃ svāhā! Maṃ svāhā! Naṃ svāhā! Oṃ svāhā!
If there is a desire for further prosperity, one should silently cast other morsels into the fire.
Having performed the rites up to the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*:
"Svāhā to the Lord of the Nidhana; to the one near the Lord of the Nidhana; to the Upright One; to the one whose mark is upright;
to the Golden One; to the one whose mark is golden; to the One of Good Color; to the one whose mark is of good color; to the Divine One."
To Divyaliṅga, to Bhava, to Bhavaliṅga, to Śarva, to Śarvaliṅga, to Śiva, to Śivaliṅga, to Jvala, to Jvalaliṅga, to Ātman, to Ātmaliṅga, to Parama, to Paramaliṅga—
this is the mantra for the hand that establishes the universal liṅga of Soma and Sūrya.

Pavitraṃ svāhā! To Soma and the others, this [is mine], not mine. Sadyojātāya svāhā! To Sadyojāta, this [is mine], not mine. Bhave bhave nātibhave bhavasva māṃ bhavodbhavāya svāhā! To Bhavodbhava, this [is mine], not mine. Vāmadevāya svāhā! To Jyeṣṭha...
To the Most Excellent, to Rudra, to Kāla, to Kalavikaraṇa, to Bala, to Balavikaraṇa, to Balapramathana, to Sarvabhūtadamana, to Manonmana— svāhā!
To the Aghoras, to the Ghora ones, to those more terrible than the terrible, to all the Śarvas, to all the Sarva-Śarvas— svāhā!
Salutations be unto you who possess the forms of Rudra; svāhā! We know that Puruṣa—may He impel us;
svāhā! This is for Tatpuruṣa and the others. Īśāna, Sadāśiva, Oṃ, svāhā! This is for Īśa and the others. Or else, [one may offer] with the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.

One should offer five oblations: "Homage to Hiraṇyabāhu, Svāhā! To the one of golden form, the lord of gold, the lord of Ambikā, the lord of Umā, Svāhā! To Paśupati, Svāhā! To Ṛta and Satya, indeed, homage, Svāhā! This is for Ṛta and the others. "Rudra is indeed all; to that Rudra..."
Homage be! Puruṣa indeed is Rudra, the Great Being; homage, homage, svāhā!

This is for Rudra, whose self is all persons. May the universe, the world, and the manifold be svāhā! This is for Rudra, whose self is the beginning of the universe. Homage be to Kadrudra, the wise one!

Svāhā! To Rudra, whose essence is Pracetas—this [is for him]. Svāhā! To him from whom the fuel-stick made of *vaikaṅkata* wood is produced—this [is for him]. Having offered oblations with the three *anājñāta* formulas and the *vyāhṛtis* for the sake of the excellence of what has been offered and not yet offered in this rite, [one performs] the rites beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* and ending with the sprinkling of water around the fire, excluding the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the *jaya* offerings.

Having prepared a full vessel and placed it before him, he should pour in pure water with the mantra: "Thou art full; thou art undecaying; mayest thou not decay for me. Then, having cast water in the various directions starting from the east with the words, "In the eastern direction are the gods," and so forth, he should say: "Amṛta is established among the Brāhmaṇas."

Having poured a little [water] on his head with the mantra beginning "May Jātavedas purify you with Ūrjayantī," he should pour the remaining water on the ground with the mantra "I send you to the ocean. Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin and performed the rites up to the worship of the fire (agnyupasthāna), he should say: "I shall bring [the oblation] for the gods."

"For the protection of all [the practitioner's] actions, I shall cover you, O Jātavedas, with these tufts of wool"—with this mantra, one should cover [the fire-pit] with tufts of wool. One should perform the covering with tufts of wool in such a way that the fire remains established for a period of three days. In the event of a deficiency in the ritual cakes (piṇḍas) or when there is a favorable wind and so forth...

And on the second or third day, if one intends to produce a display of splendor, one should cover the *pulaka* in accordance with that requirement. On the first day, having fed the Brahmins according to one’s capacity, one should eat oneself while maintaining silence. On the second, third, or fourth day, in the morning—
Having bathed and performed the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*), being pure, wearing white garments, clean,
wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), with white teeth, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
his limbs smeared with white ashes, and bearing the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), he should go near the fire and [offer] a single blade of *pālāśa* wood with the mantra "Oṃ tad brahma."

Having discarded the ashes and performed the sixteen services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), one should consign the fire with the mantra "That which is yours, O Agni. Taking the finest ash with the mantra "Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni," and wiping it with the mantra "Thou art Agni," [one should purify it] with the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, or with the urine of a tawny cow (*kapilā*).
Having combined camphor, saffron from Kashmir, saffron (kuṅkuma), ushira, sandalwood, and the two types of agaru,
and having ground them into a fine powder, one should cast it into the ashes while reciting the mantra "Oṃ, Brahman" or simply "Oṃ," and then fashion large pills with the mantra "Aṇoraṇīyān."
Alternatively, the Pāśupata vow is described according to the method stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:

on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, having prepared a site for the fire-oblation (homasthala) in a sacred field of Śiva or an auspicious grove, and having performed thorough purification;
Having performed the ritual bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), and so forth,
and having offered worship and prostrations, he should request permission from the preceptor and perform a special worship of Śiva.
(p. 25) Wearing white garments, with a white sacred thread, and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
seated facing either east or north upon a seat of *darbha* grass and grasping a handful of *darbha*,
he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), meditate upon the God and the Goddess, and [receive] their permission.
Having meditated thus, one should form the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the Pāśupata vow."
Either until the fall of the body, or for twelve years, or half of that, or half of that again, or even for a single month. || 1 ||
Or else, it may be for twelve days, beginning from the time of the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Likewise, at the time of the resolve, one should make the resolve: "For as long as I have the capacity to perform the observance within the aforementioned period, for the sake of pleasing the Lord."

Alternatively, since there exists the statement later on, "Or whoever, anointed with ghee and devoted to the vow, should perform this vow for two, three, or even one day— he too is a *naiṣṭhika*," one should proceed in this manner. Svāhā! To the skin and so forth, this [offering]. "May I become possessed of head, hands, and feet; svāhā! To the head and so forth, this [offering]. "Arise, O Puruṣa! May I become free from passion and free from evil; svāhā! To "Arise" and so forth, this [offering]. "Earth, water, fire... may I become [possessed of these]; svāhā! To earth and so forth, this [offering].

*Śabdasparśabhūyāsaṃ svāhā*. This is for sound and the rest. *Manovākkāya svāhā*. This is for mind and the rest. *Avyaktabhāvairahaṃ jyotirahaṃ virajā vipāpmā bhūyāsaṃ svāhā*. This is for the unmanifest and the rest. *Ātmā me*.

May [my external self] be purified, svāhā! This is for the self (ātman). May my inner self (antarātman) be purified, svāhā! This is for the inner self. May my supreme self (paramātman) be purified, svāhā! This is for the supreme self. To hunger, svāhā! This is for hunger. To hunger and thirst, svāhā!
To hunger and thirst, this. To the science of the Vedas, svāhā! To the science of the Vedas, this. To the ritual application of the *Ṛgveda*, svāhā!

To the ritual application of the *Ṛgveda*, this. To the *pṛṣotkā* [offering], svāhā! To the *pṛṣotkā*, this. I destroy the stain of hunger and thirst, the eldest misfortune; svāhā! To hunger and the others, this.
May you drive away all misfortune and lack of prosperity; may my evil be removed, svāhā!
This is for the deities mentioned in the mantra.
May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified.
"May I become light, stainless, and free from evil; svāhā! (p. 26).

This is for [the self] consisting of food and the others. Thus, there are twenty oblations with food. In the Āndhra recension, there is the sequence of the self consisting of breath, the self consisting of mind, and the self consisting of consciousness. But in the Drāviḍa recension, however—
May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā! The renunciation of the sections is as before.
[May] my speech, mind, sight, hearing, tongue, nose, semen, intellect, intention, and resolve [be purified].

May they be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā! May my head, hands, feet, sides, back, belly, shanks, penis, generative organ, and anus be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā!

May my skin, hide, flesh, blood, fat, bone, and marrow be purified; may I become light, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā! May sound, touch, form, taste, and smell be purified for me; may I become light, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā!
May earth, water, fire, air, and space be purified for me; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā!
May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified for me.
May I become light, stainless, and free from evil; svāhā! To the one who knows all, svāhā!
To the one spoken of as the speckled, svāhā! Arise, O Puruṣa, green, tawny, and red-eyed! Give, give! May my burners be purified;
may I become light, stainless, and free from evil; svāhā! Om.
Svāhā! This is for the Supreme Self (Paramātman). In this manner, eleven oblations each with fuel-sticks (samidh) and clarified butter (ājya) should be performed.

Having performed the Virajā-homa, immediately thereafter the Tattva-homa should be performed. Its procedure is as follows: having established the fire according to the rules for the sake of the Virajā-homa, one should offer oblations with clarified butter, fuel-sticks, and cooked rice (caru) in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
When the *pūrṇāhuti* has been offered, he should again enter into the purification of the principles (*tattvas*) before him,
performing oblations with those very materials— fuel sticks and so forth— using the root mantra.

By the power of the statement, "May these principles (*tattva*) within my body be purified," it is understood as follows: "May the *ākāśa*-principle in me be purified; may I become free from passion (*viraja*) and free from sin (*vipāpman*);
*svāhā*. Oṃ namaḥ śivāya svāhā. The same applies to the subsequent [principles] as well.

"Om, for Śiva, who has the ether of the word *tattva* as His limiting adjunct, let this [oblation] be offered. May my vital air (*vāyu*) be purified; may I become the radiant light, free from passion and free from evil, Svāhā! Om, obeisance to Śiva, Svāhā!
Let this be for Śiva, who has the wind as His limiting adjunct. In the same manner, the dedication of the offering (*uddeśatyāga*) should be inferred for the subsequent stages as well.

p. 27) May my fire be purified, svāhā! May my waters be purified, svāhā! May my earth be purified, svāhā! May my subtle element of sound be purified, svāhā! May my Sadāśiva be purified—*svāhā*. May my Power be purified—*svāhā*. May my Śiva-principle be purified—*svāhā*.
"May I become light, stainless, and free from evil; svāhā! Om, salutation to Śiva, svāhā!

This [offering] is for Śiva, whose limiting adjunct is the Śiva-principle. In this manner, one should offer oblations individually with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*). Regarding this, there are these scriptural statements:
The five elements, the five subtle essences, and the five organs of action—
these fifteen are divided into five groups each, according to the distinction between knowledge and action.

The seven constituents beginning with the skin, the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa, the mind, the ego-sense, intellect, the qualities (guṇas), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa). || 2 ||
Passion (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), and limited agency (kalā), as well as necessity (niyati) and time (kāla), along with illusion (māyā), pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva. (3)
They know the principles (tattvas) in their proper order as Śakti and Śivatattva;
by offering oblations with pure mantras, that sacrificer shall become free from passion (viraja).
Then, having taken cow dung, formed it into a ball, and consecrated it with mantras,
he should place it in the fire, guard it throughout that day, and subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Since it is stated that "having formed a ball [of clay] with this verse, one should consecrate it," one should perform the repetition of the mantra regarding the ball just as one does for the evening and morning milkings on the new moon day (*darśa*). In that regard, first taking excellent cow dung and mixing it with excellent cow urine, one should [proceed] with the hand.
Having performed thorough grinding, having cast out the seeds, small stones, and other debris remaining therein,
having formed them into a mass and placed it in a pure vessel, having dried it thoroughly with the rays of the sun,
and having brought the existing masses along with that vessel and touched them with the hand, [one recites] "ā gāva" and so forth.

One should mutter the mantras: "The cows have come, and they have performed what is auspicious; let them sit in the cow-pen, rejoicing with us. May they be here, prolific and many-formed, milking for Indra throughout many dawns. "The cows are indeed Bhaga; that is true for Indra," and so forth. [And: "Gandhadvārām—Śriyam."

"May Fortune attend me; may Misfortune perish from me. I sprinkle you with the *yajus* for progeny, long life, and wealth. Since [the ritual] exists as being performed by collecting [the materials] and depositing them in the fire with these fourteen mantras, beginning with "I take you for the restraint and support of the five winds," and so forth...

According to the principle that "what is not explicitly stated, provided it is not contradictory, should be understood from other sources," the method of placement within the fire is understood through the mantra itself.
And one should cast the mantras and the *piṇḍas* therein with the *praṇava* at the beginning and end,
using the syllables of the six-syllabled mantra as they are individually repeated.
There, one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to each respective deity with mantras ending in "svāhā."

Since this is stated in the section on questions and answers, one should cast [the offering] into the fire with the initial and final *praṇavas*; then, for the six-syllable mantra, one should offer oblations at the end of each syllable with "svāhā" as the refrain.
This is because of the statement in the *Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad*: "One should offer balls of food to the deity of the letters."
Such is the manner of the oblation: *oṃ svāhā*—this for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). *naṃ svāhā*—this for Indra. *maṃ svāhā*—this for Rudra. *śiṃ svāhā*—this for Viṣṇu.
*vāṃ svāhā*—this for Brahmā. *yaṃ svāhā*—this for Skanda. Again, *yaṃ svāhā*.

Vāṃ svāhā! Śiṃ svāhā! Maṃ svāhā! Naṃ svāhā! Oṃ svāhā! Oṃ svāhā! The others, however, he should cast in silently. "Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda are their presiding deities," so it is stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
Having thus performed the ritual procedure above and having attended upon the fire, I shall bring [the deity] for the protection of the rites of all the gods;
I cover you, O Jātavedas, with my hair-like bristles.

With this mantra, one should cover the fire with *pulaka* grass. One should perform the covering with *pulaka* grass in such a way that the fire remains for up to three days and whiteness appears in the ashes. Because of the statement "on that day, one who eats *haviṣya* [food]," one should eat *haviṣya* food on the thirteenth day.

Having performed the evening rites and having engaged in the five-syllable mantra recitation, meditation on Śiva with the Mother (Ambā), and so forth, he should sleep silently on the ground near the fire during the night.
And at dawn on the fourteenth day, having performed everything previously described,
one should spend the remainder of the day fasting.

According to this statement, even on the fourteenth day, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, performed meditation on the Guru and meditation on Śiva with Ambā, bathed, completed his daily rites (*āhnika*), performed the special worship of Śiva, and performed the *agnimukha* rite, he should perform the *virajā-homa* with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), cooked rice (*anna*), and clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having performed the concluding rite (uttarāṅga) and having protected the sacred fire as on the previous day, one should spend that day fasting, passing the specific period of time through the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, meditation on Śiva accompanied by the Mother (Sāmbaśiva), the reading of Purāṇas, and so forth.
Likewise, having performed [the rites] on a festival day in the morning,
one should diligently take up the ashes from the Rudra-fire at the conclusion of the Homa, after having touched it.

By this statement, on the third day as well, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, performed meditation on the Guru and Śiva, and completed the rites of purification, bathing, and the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*),
one should go near the fire, perform the ritual up to the mouth-offering, and carry out the *virajā-homa* with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having performed the *tattva-homa* as before, and having completed the subsequent subsidiary rites (*uttarāṅga*) beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one should conclude the fire ritual with the verse "yā te agne. The subsidiary rites consist of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering made with the oblation immediately after the principal offerings (*pradhānāhuti*),
followed by the *jaya* and other homas, and the application of the ointment and smearing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

The casting away of the prastara-grass bundle: having consecrated the fire with a mantra, he wipes it on the ground. The casting away of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The offering of the remnants (*saṃsrāva-homa*). The expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-āhuti*). The full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse "Seven are thy [stokes], O Agni. The regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*). The sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*) and the release of the *praṇītā* water.
The dismissal of Brahmā, the worship of the fire, and the mounting of the fire [into the self]— on the third day,
prior even to the withdrawal of the fire, one should recite "Oṃ tad brahma," as this is found in both the Bṛhajjābāla and Padma Purāṇas.
With that mantra, one should discard the ashes of the *paulākyā* [fire]. One should perform worship for it.

Then, since there are sixteen services beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should perform the sixteen services beginning with the invocation for the deity Agni, who is of the nature of Paramaśiva.

Immediately thereafter, one should perform the placing of the fire (*agnisamāropaṇa*). Since it is stated in the present text that "one should carefully take the ashes," one should take that finest ash with the mantra, "Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni," place it in a pure vessel, and wipe it clean with the mantra, "Thou art Agni."
Having mixed [the ashes] with the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers or with the urine of a Kapilā cow,

and having ground camphor, saffron, kuṅkuma, uśīra, sandalwood, and the two types of agaru into a fine powder, one should cast them into the ashes while reciting the mantra "Oṃ, Brahman" or simply "Oṃ," [meditating on him] as subtler than the subtlest.

With this mantra, one should prepare large *vaṭaka* cakes. In the absence of water from the Gaṅgā or other such sources, one should simply place the ashes [on the head] silently. For as many days as the vow has been resolved upon, for that many days one should remain either with matted hair (*jaṭī*), or shaven-headed (*muṇḍī*), or with a single lock of matted hair on the crown (*śikhāmātrajaṭī*).

If it is objected: "How is it that for a householder there is shaving [of the head] but not the cutting off of the top-knot (*śikhā*)?", we say no; because shaving is prescribed even for a householder in specific sacrificial sessions (*satra*) and in specific expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
Here too, since the focus is on the vow (*vrata*), shaving and so forth are prescribed as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the vow. And this is done optionally.

Regarding the subject of the *sattra*: if he is devoid of shame, he may be naked (*digambara*), or else clothed in saffron robes (*kāṣāyavasana*), or else wearing rags (*cīrāmbara*), or a single garment, or clad in bark (*valkalī*); and there is also the alternative [of being] carrying a staff (*daṇḍī*) and wearing a girdle (*mekhalī*).
Or rather, even in the preceding cases concerning matted hair and so forth, as well as concerning garments and so forth, there are fixed alternatives (*vyavasthitavikalpa*).
If he is a householder, he should live with only his top-knot matted, wearing a single garment, carrying a staff, and wearing a girdle,
for the purpose of making it known to the world that he is devoted to his vows and for the sake of receiving honor.
If he belongs to the forest-dweller stage of life (vānaprastha), he should have matted hair, wear bark garments or rags, carry a staff, and wear a girdle.
This applies universally. If he is a renunciant (sannyāsī), he may be shaven-headed, naked, clothed in saffron robes, or observing silence.
If it is argued that this vow is indeed true because a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) lacks the qualification for performing fire-offerings (homa), [the answer is:
True; however, according to the maxim "the disciple is like one's own hands and feet," the performance of homa and other rites is possible through the medium of the disciple.
Alternatively, since the Virajā-homa has already been performed at the very time of renunciation, the Tattva-homa is accomplished by means of recitation (japa).
Because it is possible to accomplish [this], and because it is possible for them to receive gifts from householders.

Alternatively, if one who is a householder becomes dispassionate and proceeds to undertake the Pāśupata vow, he is able to perform everything in due order. For instance: having first performed the *jīvaśrāddha* and so forth, and then having performed the *virajā-homa*, the *tattva-homa*, and the *piṇḍa-homa*.
Having approached the fire, performed the collection of the ritual materials, and uttered the *preṣa* formula, he—

either naked or clothed in saffron robes— goes outside the house and should observe the vow according to the method prescribed in the Atharva Veda at all three times of the day. Performing in this manner...

Practicing the wandering for alms only once a day, he should remain so for the duration of his life. If he seeks knowledge, he should approach a renunciant who is devoted to Śiva and established in Brahman.
In the absence of absolute dispassion, or when possessing only slight dispassion, he should wear matted hair and bark garments, remaining steadfast in the vow of sacred ash.

He should remain so for the duration of his life. In the absence of complete detachment from all things, he should wear his hair in a single tuft (*śikhā*), bathe, and, clad in a single garment, carrying a staff and wearing a girdle, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) after washing his feet; then, having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the five-syllabled mantra, thereafter—

The wearing of sacred ash according to the manner prescribed by the injunctions; the daily worship of Śiva; and subsequently, as an ancillary part of the vow, having procured a crystal liṅga and installed it according to the rules, [one should fashion] a golden lotus inlaid with nine gems, complete with its pericarp, filaments, and petals.
Having prepared [the site], or in its absence having prepared a red lotus or a white lotus,
one should place a very small crystal *liṅga* established upon its pericarp; then,
if one has the means, one should diligently procure whatever materials for the worship of Śiva and so forth are available.

Having worshipped according to one's means, or having performed the worship, one should then contemplate the auspiciousness of the Supreme Lord together with the Goddess; then, having given wealth to the Brahmins according to one's capacity, one should complete the remainder of the rite. Thereafter—

The rule regarding the materials for the previously mentioned worship and means of accomplishment, such as bilva leaves, lotuses, and so forth; the rule regarding their number; immediately thereafter, the particulars concerning the *arghya*, incense, and other offerings; immediately thereafter, the worship of the *āvaraṇas* (retinue deities) prior to the food offering (*naivedya*); immediately thereafter, the great food offering (*mahānaivedya*); immediately thereafter—
Having performed the other royal services beginning with betel-leaf offerings and ending with the lustration rite (*nīrājana*),

having completed the hymns of praise, silent recitation (*japa*), circumambulation, prostrations, and so forth, having caused the deity to face [the worshipper] by means of the *liṅga*, and subsequently having performed the worship of the fire and dismissed the fire;

One should perform the remaining rites. In this very manner, on the days of the vowed observances as previously resolved, the production of fire (*agnyutpādana*), the *virajā-homa*, and the *tattva-homas* must be performed. Subsequently, having taken the *liṅga* worshipped as an integral part of the vow and having constructed a temple for Śiva, one should install the Lord therein.
Immediately following is the propitiation of the destitute through pleasing the Guru, devotion, worship, and so forth.

Immediately following that is the regulation for the patron regarding eating, sleeping, and other matters. All of this is clearly stated in the twenty-ninth chapter of the first part of the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*. That very text is now written down: The Sages:
(32) O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the supreme Pāśupata vow, by performing which even Brahmā and the others are all remembered as Pāśupatas. || 1 ||
Vāyu said: I shall proclaim to you the secret that cuts away all sins—
the Pāśupata vow established in the Atharvaśiras, which is based on the Śruti.
The time is the full moon day of the month of Caitra; the place is a sanctuary of Śiva, or any other auspicious location with favorable characteristics, such as a sacred field or a grove. (3)
There, on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, having bathed well and performed his daily rites,
he should take leave of his own preceptor, worship him, and prostrate before him.
Having first performed the Vaiśeṣika rite, he himself wore white garments;
his limbs were smeared with white ashes, and he was adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Seated upon a seat of darbha grass and holding a handful of darbha,
he should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), facing either the east or the north.
Having meditated upon the God and the Goddess,
and having formed the resolve, "I shall perform this vow" by way of petitioning them, he becomes initiated.
Either until the fall of the body, or for twelve years,
or half of that, or half of that again, or for twelve months.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or even for one month,
