or for twelve days, up to the limit of the formal resolve for the vow.
Having established the sacred fire according to the rules for the purpose of the Virajā-homa,
he offered oblations with clarified butter, sacrificial fuel-sticks, and cooked rice (caru) in the proper sequence.

When the *pūrṇāhuti* has been offered, he should again perform the purification of the principles (*tattvas*) before him, offering oblations with the root mantra using those very same fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other materials.
Meditating thus: "May these principles within my body be purified"—namely, the five gross elements, the pentad of subtle elements, and the sense organs—12.
(33) By the division of knowledge and action, there are five each;
the seven elements beginning with the skin, and the five winds beginning with prāṇa. || 13 ||
Mind, ego-sense, intellect, the qualities, primordial nature, and the spirit; passion, knowledge, limited agency, necessity, and time as well. (14)
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śivatattva—these they know as the principles (tattvas) in their respective order. || 15 ||
Having offered oblations with the Vairaja mantras, that officiant shall become free from passion (viraja).
Then, having taken cow dung, formed it into a ball, and consecrated it with mantras— || 16 ||
Having placed it in the fire and guarded it on that day while eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya),
one should perform everything previously described at dawn on the fourteenth day.
On that day, one should remain without food and complete the remainder of the time;
likewise, on the morning of the festival, having performed the rites up to the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having approached Rudrāgni, one should carefully take the ashes;
thereafter, one may have matted hair, a shaven head, or a single tuft of hair.
Having bathed after having been [so], if he should again become free from shame, he may be a naked ascetic (digambara),
or another wearing saffron robes, or one clad in skins, or even one dressed in Chinese silk.
He should wear a single garment or a bark dress, carry a staff, and wear a girdle;
then, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water twice, he [should purify] his own body.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with that ash produced from the Virajā fire,
one should apply it in due order using the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning with "Agniriti."
Having wiped the limbs from the head down to the feet, one should touch them with those [ashes];
then, in that very same sequence, one should smear oneself with the ashes.
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes using either the Praṇava or the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, one should fashion the Tripuṇḍra known as the "Triple Longevity."
Having attained the state of Śiva, one should practice the conduct of Śiva;
one should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow during the three periods of the day.
This bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśu).
Having abandoned that state of being a bound soul and having performed the Pāśupata vow, [one attains the goal]. || 26 ||
The eternal Mahādeva, whose form is the Liṅga, is worthy of worship.
There is a golden eight-petaled lotus adorned with the nine gems. (27)
One should imagine a seat provided with a pericarp and filaments; according to one's means, or in their absence, it may be red or even white. (28)
In the absence of even that [physical] lotus, one should create a lotus consisting solely of meditative visualization;
having placed a very small liṅga in the center of the pericarp of that lotus, [one should worship it].
Having installed that well-adorned liṅga according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it in due order, expansive and provided with a crystal pedestal.
One should visualize the seat and the form according to the five-faced mode, using the meritorious substances such as the five products of the cow, gathered according to one's means. (31)
One should bathe [the deity] with divine jars prepared in numbers such as a thousand,
using fragrant substances including camphor, sandalwood, and saffron.
Having anointed the *liṅga* with *sāvitraka* paste and adorned it with ornaments, [one should worship] with *bilva* leaves, lotuses, and red, white, or blue water-lilies. || 33 ||
With blue lotuses and other such fragrant flowers, with meritorious, praiseworthy, and variegated offerings such as dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and blossoms. || 34 ||

Having worshipped [the deity] according to one's means through the procedure of the great worship (mahāpūjā), one should especially offer incense, a lamp, the water-offering (arghya), and food-offerings (naivedya). || 35 ||
Having offered his wealth, he should perform auspicious deeds;
specifically, those desirable acts which have been acquired through righteous means.
All substances should be given, especially in this rite for the spirits;
the number of lotus and blue-lotus petals is considered to be one thousand.
Furthermore, there is another specific number for each, namely one hundred and eight;
even in that regard, one should especially not omit the bilva leaf.
They say that a single golden leaf is superior to a thousand lotus petals;
this is likewise true for blue lotuses and the like, as well as for bilva leaves. (39)
There is no fixed rule regarding other flowers; one should worship with whatever is available.
An eight-limbed *arghya* offering is excellent, and incense and ointments are especially so. (40)
One should apply black agallochum to the face called Aghora, realgar to the Sadyojāta face,
sandalwood to the one called Vāmadeva, and yellow orpiment to the Puruṣa face.
Some maintain that in the northeast there is ash as an ointment;
they do not consider it to be incense, because of the prescription for a different kind of incense.
One should place white aloe-wood in the face called Aghora, black aloe-wood again in the Puruṣa face, guggulu resin in the Sadyojāta face, and fragrant substances in the Saumya face.
Furthermore, one should especially offer incense to Īśāna;
specifically, that which is combined with sugar, honey, camphor, and the ghee of a tawny cow.
Sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, and other such substances are prescribed for the left face;
likewise, a series of lamps enriched with camphor, wicks, and ghee should be offered. (45)
Thereafter, the *arghya* and *ācamana* should be offered in due order to each.
In the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha are to be worshipped in sequence. (46)
Then, when the limbs of Brahmā have thus been worshipped in the first enclosure,
the Vidyēśvaras, the sovereign rulers, are to be worshipped in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure are the eight forms beginning with Paścādbhava, as well as the eleven forms beginning with Mahādeva. (48)
In the fourth enclosure, all the lords of the Gaṇas are to be worshipped;
however, in the fifth enclosure, outside the lotus, they are to be worshipped in sequence.
The ten guardians of the directions, along with their weapons and followers, as well as the mind-born sons of Brahmā and all the hosts of luminaries, are likewise to be worshipped.
All the gods and goddesses, all the sky-dwellers, the others who dwell in the netherworld, and even all the hosts of sages— 51.
All the gurus of the yogins, as well as the five Mothers, the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) with his retinue, and all this world of moving and unmoving beings—[all these are present]. 52.
Then, having worshipped the Supreme Lord at the conclusion of the preliminary offerings,
one should devotedly present the oblation— consisting of ghee, side dishes, and heart-pleasing foods.
Having offered mouth-fresheners and the like, as well as betel-leaf with its accompanying snacks,
and having adorned [the deity] once more with various flowers and ornaments, (54)

Having performed the ritual in detail up to the waving of lights (nīrājanā), one should complete the remainder of the worship; then one should offer the cup along with the sacrificial gifts and the bed.
Whatever was suitable for a king and pleasing to the heart, having prepared all that himself and having caused others to prepare it, he performed a formal act of worship.
Having recited the hymn that removes sins, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī-vidyā);
then, having performed circumambulation and prostration, one should offer oneself [to the deity]. || 57 ||
Then, one should worship Guru and Vidya in front of the deity;
having offered the arghya and eight flowers, one should invoke the deity into the liṅga.
Having worshipped the fire with food offerings and having likewise dismissed it according to the rules,
one should perform everything previously described every day after thus generating [the fire] again.
Then, one should offer that linga together with its lotus and all its appurtenances either in one's own home or likewise in a temple of Śiva.
Having honored his gurus and others, especially those observing vows,
he should, if he is able, satisfy his devotees, servants, the poor, and the helpless.
He himself should either practice fasting, subsist on fruits and roots,
observe the milk-vow, live on alms, or likewise eat only one meal a day.
Always eating only at night, sleeping on the ground, abstinent and pure,
he may sleep on ashes, on grass, or on rags or animal skins.
Delighting always in the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya), one should observe this vow on Sundays,
as well as under the constellation Ārdrā and on the fifteenth day of both lunar fortnights.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should also fast if one has the capacity;
[one should avoid] those who follow heretical paths, the fallen, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, and those of the lowest castes.
One should avoid [all that is unwholesome] with every effort through mind, action, and speech;
one should always be characterized by patience, generosity, compassion, truthfulness, and non-violence.
Contented and tranquil, devoted likewise to the recitation of mantras and meditation,
he should perform the three daily ablutions or else the bath with sacred ashes.
One should perform special worship through both action and even the mind;
what need is there to say more? The observer of the vow must not perform anything inauspicious. (68)

But if, through negligence, one has performed such conduct, one should determine its gravity or lightness and perform the appropriate expiation by means of worship, fire-oblations, recitation, and so forth. (69)
Until the completion of the vow, he should act in this manner without negligence;
he should perform the gift of a cow, the rite of releasing a bull, and worship the assemblies.
This general outline of this vow has been told in brief;
now I shall declare the specific details for each month in their proper order.
In Vaiśākha, one should know the vajra-liṅga; in Jyeṣṭha, the auspicious emerald;
in Āṣāḍha, the pearl; and in Śrāvaṇa, that which is fashioned from sapphire.
In the month of Bhādrapada, the excellent ruby is prescribed.
And on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should duly offer an auspicious image made of gomedha stone.
On the full moon of Kārttika, one should worship a liṅga made of coral; on that of Mārgaśīrṣa, one of lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya);
on that of Puṣya, one consisting of topaz (puṣyarāga); and in Māgha, a liṅga of the Sun made of gems.
In the month of Phālguna, it should be made from moonstone; in Māgha, the reverse;
or in all months, in the absence of gems, it may be made of gold alone. (75)
In the absence of gold, [the vessel] may be made of silver, copper, stone, or clay;
or it may be made of whatever is available, or even something else intended for a single occasion.
Or else, at the conclusion of the vow, having performed his daily rites, he should fashion a linga made of all kinds of fragrant substances according to his preference.
Having performed a special worship and offered oblations as before,
he should honor the venerable teachers and especially those who observe the vows.
Permitted by the preceptor, facing either east or north, seated upon a seat of *darbha* grass with *darbha* in hand, and having restrained the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; (79)
Having recited the root mantra according to one's ability and meditated upon the three-eyed Lord together with Ambā,
and having requested permission as before, one should restrain the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Having requested permission from all the wise ones and having paid homage with palms joined, [he said]:
"O Blessed One, by your command, I relinquish this vow. (81)
Having spoken thus and having torn out the root, he should discard the *darbha* grasses to the north;
thereafter, he should also cast away his staff, matted hair, bark garment, girdle, and so forth. (82)
Having sipped water again according to the rule, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra;
he who, having performed the ultimate initiation, remains undisturbed until the end of his body.
One who performs this vow is indeed remembered as a *naiṣṭhika*; he is to be known as one who has transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramī*), as well as a great *Pāśupata*. (84)
He alone is the best among those who shine; he alone is the observer of the great vow.
Among those seeking liberation, there is no one equal to him who has accomplished his purpose.
If an ascetic becomes one who has reached the final goal, they call him the "supreme naiṣṭhika";
he who, being dispassionate, should observe this vow for twelve days.
He too shall be equal to a perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika) because he is called one of "intense vows" (tīvravrata),
provided that he, being devoted to his vow, performs this observance while subsisting on ghee and food.
Whether for two, three, or even one day, that certain person who is steadfast and free from desire, thinking "it is done," should practice this supreme vow. (88)
One who has constantly dedicated his soul to Śiva is never equalled by anyone;
even a learned Brahmin covered in ashes is freed from the consequences of great sins. (89)
One is instantly liberated from sins; indeed, one is liberated, there is no doubt.
That which is the supreme virility of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed as ash.
Therefore, in all worlds, the energetic one who is joined with ashes—
whose very foundation is ash— burns away all defects through contact with the fire of ash.
One whose self is purified by the bath of ashes is known as "established in ashes" (bhasmaniṣṭha).
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, he bears the radiant triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) made of ashes.
The man who lies upon ashes is known as one established in ashes;
[by this,] ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like, as well as diseases and other unbearable afflictions, [are overcome]. (93)
By the mere proximity of one who is devoted to the sacred ash (bhasmaniṣṭha), [all impurities] melt away; of this there is no doubt.
It is called *bhāsita* because it illuminates, and *bhasma* because it consumes all defilements (*kalmaṣa*). 94.
Prosperity is the bringer of prosperity for men, and protection is the supreme provider of protection.
What more need be said here regarding the cause of the greatness of sacred ash? 95.
The practitioner who has bathed with ashes is Maheśvara himself;
this ash is the supreme weapon of the Śaivas and belongs to the Supreme Lord. (96)
Because the interference with the asceticism of Dhaumya’s elder brother was averted, therefore, having performed the Pāśupata vow with every effort, [one attains success]. 97.
Having collected the ash from Dhana, one should be devoted to the bath of ash (*bhasmasnāna*).
In the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who had come to perform penance for the sake of propitiating the Supreme Lord on behalf of his son:
Pratyupamanyu said:
"Welcome to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa! Our ascetic penances have now borne fruit. (98)
Having praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa with these and other verses, the great sage Upamanyu thereafter spoke of the Pāśupata Yoga.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Upamanyu bestowed upon Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, the knowledge of the Pāśupata vow and yoga. (99)
Thus addressed by that best of sages,
the god Madhusūdana likewise propitiated the lord Rudra through his ascetic penance.
With his entire body smeared with ashes and wearing matted hair and bark garments,
he recited the Rudra-Īśāna mantra with his mind solely intent upon Śiva.
Thus it is said. And in this very context, previously in the fourteenth chapter:
"To Śikhaṇḍin was born a son renowned as Suśīla;
he was righteous, endowed with beauty, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. (102)
Having studied the various Vedas and remaining steadfast in austerity according to dharma,
that knower of dharma, through the power of his good fortune, set his mind toward renunciation.
Having performed his service at sacred fords and being established in sacred study and austerity,
he once went to the slopes of the Himalayas, which are frequented by the Siddhas.
There he beheld the forest named Dharmavana, which bestows the attainment of dharma; it is accessible to yogins but inaccessible to those who hate the knowers of Brahman.
There flows the most meritorious, pure river named Mandākinī,
endowed with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, and adorned by the hermitages of the Siddhas.
(40) On its southern bank, filled with joy, he beheld a most meritorious and delightful hermitage frequented by lords of sages and yogis. || 107 ||
Having bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he worshipped Mahādeva with flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies.
Having meditated upon Īśāna situated within the sun and having placed his joined palms over his head,
he gazed at the radiant one and praised the Supreme Lord.
He [should worship] with the Rudrādhyāya, with the life-story of Rudra, the Lord of the Mountains,
and with various other hymns originating from the Vedas and composed by the seers.
Then, in the meantime, the great sage beheld one who had arrived,
named Śvetāśvatara, the most excellent among the great Pāśupatas.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, clad in a loincloth,
his body emaciated by asceticism, and adorned with a garland of rudrākṣa beads.
Having concluded his praise of Śambhu, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he bowed his head at the Lord’s feet and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: ||| 113 ||
I am blessed, I am graced, since today this lord of sages has been seen by me in person—this master of yoga, a yogi, the best among those who know yoga. (114)
"Oh, how great is my fortune! My austerities have borne fruit.
What shall I do? I am your disciple; protect me, O sinless one! (115)
Then, having shown favor to King Suśīla, who was endowed with virtuous conduct and whose impurities had been worn away by austerity, he accepted him as a disciple.
Having caused him to perform the entire rule for the state beyond the stages of life (*atyāśrama*), the wise one bestowed upon him the supreme, divine knowledge as declared in his own Vedic branch.
"That which is the essence of all the Vedas without exception, which effects liberation from the bonds of Paśu, and is known as Atyāśrama, has been practiced by Brahmā and the other gods. (118)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, endowed with austerity and yoga, remain forever with me; from that, you shall attain perfection.
Having spoken thus and meditated upon the god who wields the Pināka bow, the lord of brahmins correctly imparted the great mantra for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. (120)
The meritorious rite beginning with "Agnir" (Agnir iti), which pacifies all sins, is the essence of the Vedas, bestows liberation, and was promulgated by the seers.
At his word, King Suśīla, filled with faith,
became a manifest Pāśupata and devoted himself to the practice of yoga.

"With all his limbs smeared with ashes, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, peaceful, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and engaged in the observances of the highest stage of life"—thus it is said. (123)

In this context, by the statement beginning with "the wise one, having caused him to perform the entire rule for the *atyāśrama*," the vow consisting of the smearing of ashes— which is denoted by terms such as the *pāśupata-atyāśrama* and is prescribed as a means of attaining knowledge— is [enjoined] for the virtuous king who has been accepted as a disciple.

It is understood that the sage named Śvetāśvatara, acting as an auxiliary to that vow and for the purpose of producing the sacred ash (bhasma), caused the king to perform the Virajā-homa and other rites, and further instructed him in the mantras for the application of the vibhūti, beginning with "Agniriti."
Now, one might ask: how is the *virajā-homa* understood by the term "the rule for the highest stage" (*atyāśrama-vidhi*)?

We reply: because the *virajā-homa* is indispensable at the time of initiation into the highest stage (*atyāśrama-dīkṣā*), specifically during the production of the sacred ashes (*vibhūti*) which is well-known as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that rite.

If it is asked, "How can Vīraśaivas have the qualification for performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*) and so forth?", we say no; for they are primarily established as those who have transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramin*). Just like ascetics (*yati*), even in the absence of fire-sacrifices and the like, the performance of the Pāśupata vow is logically possible.

If it is argued that this being the case, the scriptural injunctions prescribing the fire-oblation (*homa*) would become purposeless—since the performance of the *pāśupata* vow is possible even without the oblation—the answer is no;
for the purification of the mind has already been accomplished through the performance of oblations and vows in previous births. Or alternatively:

Since it is established in the *Pūrvatantra* that the recitation of a mantra is purposeful— that is, that the restriction of the performance and its fruit arises from the mantra itself even in an action distinct from a possible [external] object— it is easy to maintain that the goal is accomplished simply through the recitation of the mantra employed for the *pāśupata* vow, in accordance with that principle.
Since the objects revealed by the mantra consist of such qualities as being free from passion (*viraja*) and free from impurity (*vipāpman*),

they are to be accomplished through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and since it is precisely the scripture that governs the Vīraśaiva doctrine which establishes such meanings therein, that alone has been tasted [by us].
It is not that [the offering] has not been consumed at all, for it is observed among the Vedic traditions that the purpose is accomplished by mere smelling;

and because the oblation is considered both offered and unoffered through the recitation of the mantra, there is no contradiction with the Vīraśaiva system. This applies when there is a conflict between two equally authoritative sources.
By the principle "it is a conceptual construction," the established conclusion is that it is a conceptual construction.

In reality, however, since it was established at the very commencement of this treatise that the fulfillment of ritual action occurs precisely through the gross five-syllabled mantra (*sthūla-pañcākṣara*) as the support for the dissolution of all Vedas, everything is consistent.

Thus ends the sixth instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṅgraha* composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭhaśivācārya, who was a knower of the one hundred and one topics concerning the secret essence of the illustrious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
Now begins the seventh instruction.
In this seventh instruction, the wearing of ashes is declared according to the methods set forth by the statements of various Agamas and Purāṇas. (1)
Then Janaka of Videha approached Yājñavalkya and said, "O Blessed One!
Tell us the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Yājñavalkya replied:
"Its measurement is threefold: from the forehead to the eyes, and from the eyes to the middle of the eyebrows. Then Janaka of Videha...

He said: "O Blessed One! That substance which is the ash of burnt cow-dung is of the nature of Agni; having taken it with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, and having consecrated it with the mantra *agnir iti bhasma*, one should apply it to the head, forehead, chest, and shoulders with the seven mantras beginning with *mā nastoke*."

He becomes purified; he becomes liberated. He obtains that fruit which one who recites the *Rudrādhyāya* a hundred times attains. "This is the light of the ashes; this is the light of the ashes," said Yājñavalkya.

Then Janaka of Videha said to Yājñavalkya: "What fruit does one enjoy from the wearing of the ashes? Yājñavalkya replied: "From the wearing of those ashes alone, liberation occurs; from the wearing of those ashes alone, one attains union [with the Divine]. He does not return again."
"He does not return again. This, O Yājñavalkya, is the 'ashes-light'."

(p. 43) Janaka of Videha said to Yājñavalkya: "What fruit does one obtain from the wearing of ashes, or is there none? In this regard, [the tradition of] the Paramahaṃsas—Saṃvartaka, Āruṇi, Śvetaketu, Dūrvāsas, Ṛbhu, Nidāgha, Jaḍabharata, and Dattātreya—[is as follows]:...
Even Raivataka, Bhuśuṇḍa, and others became liberated simply by wearing the sacred ash; that indeed is the "Light of Ashes," so says Yājñavalkya.
Janaka of Videha said to Yājñavalkya: "What is produced by the ash-bath? [He replied:
"As many as there are pores on the body of anyone—be it a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra—so many *liṅgas* (emissaries) become and remain."
Indeed, by means of that retention, one remains established in that very state which possesses the form of this word.
Then Janaka of Videha went with Paippalāda to the world of Prajāpati. Having arrived there, he said: "O, O Prajāpati! Tell me the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
To him, Prajāpati replied: "As is the majesty of the Lord, so too is that of the triple mark."
Prajāpati spoke that greatness to him.

Then Paippalāda went to Vaikuṇṭha and said, "O Viṣṇu, tell me the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). He replied, "As is the majesty of the Lord, so too is the majesty of the triple mark," thus spoke Viṣṇu.

Then Paippalāda approached the Blessed Kālāgnirudra and said: "Teach me, O Blessed One, the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Then Kālāgnirudra said: "I shall declare the procedure for the triple mark. Thereupon—

Dūrvāsas, Bhṛgu, Nidāgha, Jaḍabharata, Dattātreya, and others also approached Bhusuṇḍa and spoke. The great sage Raivataka said to Bhusuṇḍa, "Please explain the procedure for the Tripuṇḍra. Bhusuṇḍa replied, "The procedure for the Tripuṇḍra was not [taught] by me..."

"It can indeed be said that it is true," he replied. Immediately thereafter, having bowed three times to the sages, he said to those sages, "Forgive me. [The sages replied,] "All the sages [forgive you]."

Then Śvetaketu and Jābāla approached the Blessed One, Kālāgnirudra, and spoke; and Hariścandra and Prajāpati also approached Kālāgnirudra and spoke. Then the gods and the sages, having gathered together through mutual emulation, [spoke].
"We shall question Kālāgnirudra."
Then Kālāgnirudra said, "I shall declare the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The gods and the sages listened. Now, one who is covered with ashes is liberated from saṃsāra;
[so too is one] on a bed of ashes.
While lying down, one whose sphere of focus is that Śiva attains union; as a reciter of the Rudrādhyāya, he goes to immortality. This is indeed the "Light of Ashes" (bhasmajyotiḥ).
By wearing the ashes (vibhūti), one attains liberation (kaivalya) and crosses the ocean of saṃsāra.

Merely by wearing the ashes, one becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas). Furthermore, whatever fruit one obtains at Vārāṇasī or at the three holy sites (tristhāna), that fruit one attains. This very thing is the light of the ashes (bhasmajyotis). Of whom...

On the body of someone, the mark of the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) exists: the first is Prajāpati, the second is Viṣṇu, and the third is Sadāśiva. This is indeed the light of the sacred ash (bhasmajyotis).
As many as there are pores on the body of anyone, so many are the Liṅgas that exist in Vārāṇasī.

And they attain the state of being composed of light. This very thing is the ash-light (*bhasmajyotis*). Merely by the contemplation of the ash, one reduces sin to ashes. Indeed, merely by the contemplation of the ash, transgressions and the like perish.
Merely by the contemplation of the ash, one reduces sin to ashes. Merely by the contemplation of the ash...

It effects deliverance from saṃsāra. This is that Bhasmajyotis. By meditation on the ashes, Īśvara becomes meditated upon. From meditation on the ashes, the recollection of the five-syllabled mantra occurs.
Through meditation on the ashes, one attains the state of Sthāṇu. This is that Bhasmajyotis.
Then Paippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra questioned the Blessed Kālāgnirudra: "What will happen as a result of wearing the *vibhūtis*?
Then Kālāgnirudra said, "I shall declare the essence of all the Upaniṣads; he is the Lord of All."

He is the omniscient inner controller; He is the source of all, for He is indeed the origin and dissolution of all beings. He is neither one whose consciousness is directed outward, nor one whose consciousness is directed inward, nor one whose consciousness is directed toward both. He is not unconscious, yet He is not a mass of consciousness. He is invisible, beyond conventional dealings, indefinable, inconceivable, and indescribable.

They consider [Brahman] to be the essence of the realization of the Self within the body, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, and the fourth state (*turīya*). From it comes death—blazing and terrifying—for those who are not its devotees; yet for its own devotees, it is indeed immortality, for it delivers them from death and the very nature of mortality. It is the giver of the Self, the giver of strength, whose command the entire universe worships. Its supreme instruction...

"Whose shadow is immortality, whose [shadow] is death—to which god shall we offer worship with oblation? Thus, by His own majesty, He causes all kings, all gods, all selves, and all beings to blaze; He is caused to blaze, and He causes them to blaze.

Savitṛ, the impeller; the radiant one, shining like a lamp; the blazing one, the blazer; the ascetic; the scorcher, the intensely heating one; the luminous one, the shining one; the beautiful one, the one who shines forth; the auspicious one.
Having beheld His own true nature within Himself, all the gods and all living beings [tremble] with fear.
They flee. He himself does not fear from anything whatsoever. (p. 45) "From fear of him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises;
from fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run away. This is the Great [Fear].

He attains prosperity. The exponents of Brahman deliberate upon this: if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya studies this Bhasmajābāla, he who is not learned in the Vedas becomes learned in the Vedas; he who is uninitiated becomes initiated.
He becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by truth. He...
He becomes purified by all; he is known by all the gods; he is meditated upon by all the gods;
he is as one who has studied all the Vedas; by smearing himself with that ash, he is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas);
by it, he has performed all sacrifices; ten thousand *praṇavas* have been recited by him.

It is so. It purifies even the blind and the outcaste. "It purifies up to the seventh generation of ancestors," said the Blessed One. Kālāgnirudra declared: "Among all forms of yoga and meditation, Śiva alone is the object of meditation, the one who brings auspiciousness. Having abandoned everything else, a twice-born man, having studied this [text],"

Whether one is a forest-dweller, one who is dispassionate, or a sovereign ruler of an empire, one is cleansed from dwelling in a womb—*Oṃ Satyaṃ Oṃ Satyaṃ Ity Oṃ Satyam*. Then Kālāgnirudra spoke: "By reciting this once, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for sacred rites; by reciting it a second time, one attains the status of Gaṇapati."
Having recited the third [mantra], one enters the God alone; thus, "Om, Truth.
Thus ends the Ṛgveda Bhasmajābāla Upaniṣad.

The ash produced from the *agnihotra*, that arising from the *aupāsana* fire, that born from the *virajā* fire, or any other ash— having ascertained which is appropriate for oneself according to the two sections defining the production and application of ash—
one should take that ash, place it in a pure vessel, and perform the washing of the feet.

Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice, and having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he takes the vessel with his right hand while reciting the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta; having poured it into his left hand and touched it with his right hand, [he recites]: "The ash is fire, the ash is wind, the ash is water."

"Bhasma-sthalam" (the place of ash), "bhasma vyoma" (ash is the ether), "bhasma bhasma" (ash, ash), "bhasma sarvam" (all this is indeed ash), and "mana etāni cakṣūṃṣi bhasmāni" (the mind and these eyes are ashes)—one should recite these three times. Immediately thereafter, having touched with the right hand the water contained in a pure vessel, [one recites]: "āpo vā idaṃ sarvam" (water indeed is all this).
All beings are water; the vital breaths are water; cattle are water; food is water; immortality is water; the sovereign ruler (*samrāj*) is water;
the radiant ruler (*virāj*) is water; the self-ruler (*svarāj*) is water; the meters are water; the lights are water; truth is water; all the deities are water.
Having recited the two mantras— "bhūrbhuvaḥ svar āpa oṃ" and "om āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ svaroṃ"— and having visualized that water as being Viṣṇu in form,
one should pour that water into the ashes and perform the mixing with the mantra "mā nastoke."
Having formed it into a single mass, one should meditate upon that ash in the form of the *sāmbara*; then, taking half of it and placing it on the right knee,
one should again divide the *argha* held in the left hand into six parts, and [place] one of those there.
Having taken [the first] portion, one should perform anointing on the head, proceeding clockwise, with the Īśāna mantra.
Again, having taken another portion, one should perform anointing on the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Again, having taken another portion, one should [anoint] the region of the chest and both arms with the Aghora mantra.

One should smear [it]. Taking another portion, one should smear the region of the hips below the navel with the Vāma mantra. Taking another portion, one should smear both the right and left feet with the Sadyojāta mantra. Immediately thereafter, taking the remaining portion,
Having stirred it with both hands while reciting the *praṇava*, one should smear it over all the limbs.

Having washed the hands and performed the two rounds of *ācamana*, one should take the ashes present on the knee; then, having meditated upon that ash as being the very form of Śiva with Ambā and having stirred it with both hands—

With the three fingers— the index, middle, and ring— or with the index, ring, and thumb, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra,
and takes the form of the *gārhapatya* and other sacrificial fires, according to the method described in the *Kālāgnirudropaniṣad*.

Having performed the meditation, one should then apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the head, forehead, chest, and shoulders by repeating the three-syllabled mantra, the Tryambaka mantra, and the six-syllabled mantra.

One should act in this manner during all three periods of the day. Even after the application of the *tripuṇḍra*, one should wash one's hands and perform other ritual acts between the forefinger and the middle finger.
Then, because the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) is of the nature of a bath, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*).
And it is said in the Śivarāghava-saṃvāda:
"The wise one should smear [ashes] on all his limbs with the Praṇava;
having washed his hands, sipped water for purification (ācamana), holding Darbha grass in his hand, and being composed."
One should place [the water] on the head with "Salutation to the All-Self (Sarvātman) for Nīlakaṇṭha," and having then washed both hands, one should perform the sequential ritual practice.

Thus, at the time of applying the *tripuṇḍra* by celibate students (*brahmacārins*), there is the traditional recitation of mantras beginning with "medhāvī": "May I be wise, radiant, glorious, possessed of Vedic luster, long-lived, and may there be well-being. However, for the *paramahaṃsa*, [the application] is performed without mixing water.
At the time of applying the *uddhūlana* ash and the *tripuṇḍra*, the mantra "Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ Haṃsa Haṃsa" is to be used everywhere.
In the Kālāgnirudropaniṣad:
Then Sanatkumāra questioned the blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra:
"Teach me, O Blessed One, the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) along with its true essence. What is the substance? How many are the locations? What..."

"What is the reality? What is the means of knowledge? What is the line? What are the mantras? What is the power? Who is the agent? What is the deity? What is the fruit? To him, the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra said: "Whatever substance there is, that is the ash belonging to Agni."
Having taken it up with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, having consecrated it with the verse beginning with *agnir*,
having lifted it up with the mantra *mānastoke*, and having mixed it with water with the mantra *mā no mahāntam*,
[he should apply it] on the head, forehead, chest, and shoulders with the mantra *triyāyuṣam*.
One should draw three horizontal lines with the *triyāyuṣa*, *tryambaka*, and *triśakti* mantras.
This is the *śāmbhava* vow, which has been declared by the exponents of the Vedas in all the Vedas;
therefore, one who desires liberation should practice it in order to avoid rebirth.
Then Sanatkumāra asked: "What is the measure for this wearing of the Tripuṇḍra?

Having divided it into three lines—on the forehead, up to the eyes, between the eyebrows, and on the crown of the head, and in the middle—what is its first line? It is the Gārhapatya fire, the letter *A*, and *Rajas*."

The earthly realm (bhūloka) is the Self (ātman), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the Ṛgveda, the morning libation (prātassavana), and Maheśvarī as the deity. That which is its second line is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the syllable *ukāra*, the quality of goodness (sattva), the intermediate space (antarikṣa), the inner self (antarātman), the power of will (icchā-śakti), the Yajurveda, and the midday libation (mādhyandina-savana).

Sadāśiva is the deity. That which is his third line is the Āhavanīya fire; the letter *M* is darkness (*tamas*), the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the Sāmaveda, the third pressing (*savana*), and Mahādeva is the deity.
In the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad: "One should smear the region of the head with the Īśāna mantra, the face with the Tatpuruṣa,
the chest with the Aghora, and the private parts with the Vāma."
One should apply [the ash] to the feet with the *sadyojāta* mantra and to all the limbs with the *praṇava*.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Taking a handful of ash consecrated with the *saṃhitā-mantra*..."
The ash-bath from the head down to the feet has been described previously. || 1 ||
One should perform the ritual bath using that very mantra;
one should carefully scatter ashes five times upon the head with the Īśāna mantra.
Four [syllables] are in the mouth with Tatpuruṣa; eightfold in the heart with Aghora;
and thirteen in the secret region with Vāmadeva, according to the division of the locations.
Having diligently smeared the feet eight times with the *sadyojāta* mantra,
one should perform the smearing of all limbs according to the prescribed rule for a member of the royal caste (*rājanya*).

And having wiped away all that [impurity] except for the face, according to the sequential method, during the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), at midnight, as well as at the beginning and the end of the day; (5)

It is indeed described that after sleeping, eating, drinking water, or performing necessary duties such as voiding, one should address a woman as "maiden," a eunuch as "child," and an elder as "grandfather," and so forth.

One observing the vow should not perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) in the presence of gods, fire, gurus, or Brahmins; nor when viewing forbidden sights, nor on impure ground, nor while on a path.
There should be a mixing with conch-water, the root-mantra, and ashes;
or it may be joined with sandalwood paste, or indeed combined with water.
One seeking knowledge should smear oneself with sandalwood paste; that indeed is the powder.
Before midday, it should be mixed with water, but thereafter one should avoid using water.
Then Bhusuṇḍha questioned the Blessed One, Kālāgnirudra, regarding the procedure for the *tripuṇḍra*. On this subject, there are these verses:
"Thereafter, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra*, which consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva."
Having taken [it] with the three middle fingers while reciting the root mantra. || 10 ||
Alternatively, the *tripuṇḍra* may be made with the ring finger, the middle finger, and the thumb;
a Brahmin should smear it on his face, while a Kṣatriya should apply it all around his head.
One should apply [the mantra] to thirty-two places, or else to sixteen places, or likewise to eight places, and also to five places. (12)
On the head, the forehead, the two ears, and likewise the two eyes, as well as on the nose, the chin, the neck, and immediately thereafter on the two shoulders. (13)
At the elbows, at the wrists, at the heart, on both sides, at the navel, at the two private parts, as well as at the thighs, the buttocks, the knees, and the shins; || 14 ||
In the two shanks and the two feet are the thirty-two supreme locations;
[therein reside] the eight Mūrtis and the eight Vidyeśvaras, together with the [eight] directions, time, and the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Anila, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāta—these are declared to be the eight Vasus. (16)
A wise person should wear the *tripuṇḍra* with the name-mantra of these [deities];
being composed, he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* at sixteen locations.
On the head, on the forehead, on the two ears, and also on the two shoulders;
on the elbows, on the wrists, on the heart, and on both sides of the navel. (18)
And having thus established oneself on the back [of the seat], one should recite there the presiding deities:
Śiva, Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, and the one called Rudra. (19)
The nine Śaktis beginning with Vāmā—these are the sixteen deities;
Nāsatya and Dasraka are declared to be the two Aśvins.
Alternatively, [one should place them] on the head, in the hair, in the two ears, as well as in the nostrils;
and likewise in the two arms, in the heart, in the navel, and in the pair of thighs. || 21 ||
In the two knees, the two feet, and the back, there are sixteen [deities]:
Śiva, Indra, the Moon and the Sun, Vighneśa, and Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Śrī is in the heart, and Prajāpati is in the navel;
there are both the Nāgas and the Nāga maidens, as well as the daughters of the sages.
The oceans are remembered as being at the two feet, and the sacred ford (tīrtha) is on the back;
thus, the sixteen locations have been described, and now the eight locations are stated.
The place of the Guru, the forehead, the two ears immediately thereafter, the pair of shoulders, the heart, and the navel shall be the eighth. || 25 ||
Brahmā, the seven ṛṣis, and the deities are proclaimed [as the presiding deities];
or alternatively, [the parts of the body are] the head, the two arms, the heart, and the navel. (26)
Those people who know the reality of the ash have declared these five locations;
one should perform them according to their possibility, taking into account the place, time, and other such factors.
If one is unable even to perform the smearing (uddhūlana), one should apply the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) and so forth on the forehead, the heart, the navel, the throat, and the two wrists. || 28 ||
In the middle of the arms, at the base of the arms, on the back, and on the head;
on the forehead, salutation to Brahmā; in the heart, salutation to Havyavāhana;
at the navel, salutation to Skanda; on the throat, salutation to Pūṣan; at the base of the right arm, salutation to Rudra.

In the middle, salutation to Āditya; at the wrist, salutation to Śacīpati; at the base of the left arm, salutation to Vāmadeva; in the middle, salutation to Prabhañjana; at the wrist, salutation to the Vasus; on the back, salutation to Hara; on the head, salutation to Paramātman.
With these and other mantras, one should thus wear the *tripuṇḍra* on twelve locations.
Three-eyed, the support of the three qualities (guṇas), the progenitor of the three, and auspicious.
Reciting "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark on the forehead;
below the elbows for the ancestors, and likewise above them for Umā and Īśa.
Having said "Obeisance to the two Īśas," one should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the two sides;
and having said "Obeisance to the two Bījas," one should wear it on the two forearms.
Then, one should offer [the oblation] on the back with "To Bhīma," likewise in the cooking pot with "To Śiva," on the head with "To Nīlakaṇṭha," and [finally] with "Salutation to the Soul of All."
One should wear ashes consecrated with the mantra "mā nas toke";
the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is the Sāman, and the middle mark is the Yajus.
The lower mark (adhahpundra) is the Ṛgveda itself; therefore, the puṇḍra is called "triyāyuṣa" (the triple-life).
One should apply these triple-life marks upon the forehead and the two arms.
At the navel, the head, the heart, and the sides, [one should apply it]; thus are the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas [instructed].
In the Jābālopaniṣad:
"Having taken the ashes with the mantra beginning with 'Agni' and so forth, and having rubbed them, one should touch the limbs. Likewise, further on:
And one should wear the Tripuṇḍra mark horizontally.
In the *Atharvaśiras*:
"Having taken ashes with the mantra beginning with 'Agni' and having rubbed them, one should touch the limbs;
therefore, this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu*)."
In this regard, the corroborative statements from the Jābālopaniṣad and other texts are found in the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"With all the mantras beginning with 'Agni' that occur in the Jābālopaniṣad,
one should perform the smearing with ashes mixed with water."

O best of the twice-born, it is taught that the wise, who are righteous and have mastered the Vedas, should wear the triple-threaded cord according to the *triyāyuṣa* mantra, following the sequence for women, men, and eunuchs.
Or else, being wise and observing the vow of celibacy day by day,
one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes mixed with water.
Both the householder and the forest-dweller should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the Tṛyambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the Śiva mantra.
"A mendicant should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the syllable Oṃ uttered three times along with the *saṃhaṃsa* mantra"— this is the Jābāli Śruti.
The wise man should always wear the Tripuṇḍra on the forehead, on both arms, and likewise on the chest; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) has been proclaimed with reverence by the Jābālas as being required for both mantras and stages of life (āśramas), whether performed with a mantra or even without one.
In the Śrī-Bodhāyana-Sūtra:

"Then, having taken that ash, one should consecrate it; having consecrated it again in the reverse order starting from Īśāna, and then in the fivefold order starting from Sadyojāta, [one recites] 'mānastoke tanaye'."
Having taken [the ash] with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, and having silently mixed it with water, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) while reciting "triyāyuṣam."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The Tripuṇḍra made with ashes using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers—that Tripuṇḍra shall be auspicious... and so forth.
Moreover, they cite this:
"A twice-born man, ever vigilant, should wear that sacred ash on his forehead, heart, both arms, throat, belly, and head."
"It is known that one must not be negligent regarding prosperity. Then, with the mantra "tryambaka," he should wipe his entire body; thus he becomes purified.
In the Bodhāyana-smṛti:
"One should perform the bath with the Īśāna-mantra, beginning from the head down to the feet."
In the Bhāradvāja-smṛti: Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed ācamana as before,
he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and then perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Having taken white ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire,
one should scatter them upon one's own head with the *Īśāna* mantra.
Then, having taken that ash, one should apply it to the face with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra,
to the heart with the one called *aghora*, and to the secret parts with the one named *vāmadeva*.
One should sprinkle ashes on both feet with the mantra named Sadyojāta,
and thereafter one should dust the entire body with the Praṇava mantra alone.
This Agneya bath has been proclaimed by the supreme sages;
a wise person should perform it at the outset for the sake of the successful fulfillment of all undertakings.
Then, having washed his hands and other limbs and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
he should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) across his forehead, heart, and throat according to the prescribed method.
"Or else, with the five Brahma-mantras, or with the mantra 'tato'gniḥ'.
And in another Smṛti:
"One should wear the consecrated ash with the mantra 'mā nastoke'."
In the Vāyupurāṇa:
"Then one should fashion the Tripuṇḍra, which is called Tryāyuṣa.
And in the Taittirīya Śruti, within the teaching of Śiva:

"One must not be negligent regarding truth; one must not be negligent regarding dharma; one must not be negligent regarding what is wholesome; one must not be negligent regarding prosperity (*bhūti*); one must not be negligent regarding study and teaching. And so forth. In this context, the word *bhūti* has the meaning of "ashes."

Baudhāyana stated: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) by the twice-born; 'one should not neglect prosperity'—thus it is known. Having begun thus, he continues: "It purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, oneself as the twenty-first, and the row [of guests] as well."

"One attains union with Brahman or residence in the same world as Brahman," so said the venerable Bodhāyana (p. 53). It is thus clearly established that those who do not wear the *tripuṇḍra* possess no Brāhmaṇahood at all. Now, the corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇas*).
The statements of the Smṛtis and Purāṇas are written here:
and the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (supplementary elaboration) is stated in the *Lokākṣi-smṛti*:
"Smearing with ashes and the horizontal triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) are the constant means of practice."
The rejection of [the authority of] the means of valid cognition is heard in the Taittirīyaka.
In the Mahābhārata also:
"One should augment the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa] also:
Indeed, the meaning of the Veda is clearly understood through the Purāṇas alone;
the Veda fears the man who is devoid of the study of the Purāṇas.
In the Sūtasamhitā as well: "In determining the meaning of the Vedas, which depends upon infinite branches [of tradition],
the corroboration provided by the scriptures is indeed weightier than the logic devised by one's own intellect."

Sudarśanācārya also states: "For in the process of determining the meaning of the Vedas, the Purāṇas constitute an auxiliary limb (aṅga); the Smṛtis have as their subject matter those topics of the Vedas that have already been determined."
In the Mānava Purāṇa as well, an expansion of the Śruti is observed:
"One must not swerve from truth, nor from dharma, nor from what is beneficial;
[one should strive] for prosperity arising from the fire, and thereafter the covering of the body."
By wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, the heart, and both arms, one must never,
even through delusion, neglect it at any time.
"Always perform the study of the sacred texts and likewise the recitation [of them].
Also, in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*:
"From truth, from dharma, from skillfulness, and also from the smearing with ashes..."
And by the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), as well as by the study and recitation of the Veda.
"And from divine [rites], from ancestral rites, from good deeds, and from the honoring of mother, father, and others.

Although the author of the *Bhāṣya* has explained the word *bhūti* as referring to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), nevertheless, according to Bodhāyana’s statement, "One must not be negligent regarding prosperity (*bhūti*),"...
Since the Śruti has been cited as the authoritative source for the triple mark of ashes (tripuṇḍra), and since there exist corroborating statements in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas,
it is appropriate that the word *bhūti* refers specifically to ashes.

If it is argued that, since the word *bhūti* has multiple meanings here, let there be a different meaning [than prosperity], we say no; for that would contradict the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*, which states: "One should expand upon the meaning of the Śruti by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas," and from which it is understood that "therefore, one must not be negligent regarding prosperity" (*tasmād bhūtyai na pramaditavyam*). Furthermore—

Furthermore, from the statement in the Vedabhāṣya by Vidyāraṇya— “From truth, from dharma, from the wholesome, and even from the smearing with ashes”— it follows that [the term] in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad refers exclusively to ashes.
"One who seeks liberation should not abandon even through negligence the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra); such is the Vedic revelation."

Since it is stated thus in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, the word *bhūti* refers exclusively to ashes. Even if the word *bhūti* were explained as referring to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) due to its polysemous nature, there would be no contradiction here; provided that such an explanatory text (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) exists, that too should be accepted as an interpretation.
Baudhāyana: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the preparation and wearing of *bhūti* (ashes).

Having become pure, [one should avoid] a woman with deformed limbs, one who is insane, one who is inauspicious, one with deficient or redundant limbs, a barren woman, one who eats bones or rags, and so forth; thus he has set forth everything."
In the Parāśara-smṛti: "A Brāhmaṇa should always wear the tripuṇḍra made of sacred ash produced according to the prescribed rite on his forehead, as a horizontal smearing of ash."
In the *Śrutisārasamuccaya*:
"One who is unable to follow the conventional conduct [of the sect], yet commits sin even in thought,
shall remain eternally pure by wearing the *tripuṇḍra*."
In the *Anuśāsana-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*:
"I am named Paśupati, and those men who are my devotees—
all of them should be known as Pāśupatas, their hair and bodies smeared with ashes."
"For the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification...
and so forth. Also, in the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*:
"With the five mantras beginning with 'tryāyuṣam,' [one should apply the mark] on the forehead, the heart, the right shoulder, and the left."
Then, on the back and on the five [limbs], he applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes;
[he may apply it] to one, two, three, or all of these deities.
In the Mādhyandina Gṛhya-sūtra as well: "With ashes, [one should mark] on the forehead, the neck, the right shoulder, and the heart, with the mantra 'Tryāyuṣam'."
Regarding the phrase "with each mantra," it is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"A Brāhmaṇa who constantly wears the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) in all ritual acts..."
Or with the ashes of the Agnihotra fire, or those produced from the fire of Śiva.
In the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga, Mahādeva said to Vasiṣṭha:

"Know that the sacred ash (bhasma) is the supreme Brahman, which brings about truth, consciousness, and bliss. The wise man knows that the primary [Brahman] is obtained through the knowledge of that ash, while the other is secondary."
O Brahman, best among the knowers of Brahman, know that the secondary [means] is related to fire; it is the instrument of knowledge that destroys ignorance, and it is manifold in its various forms.
O Sage, likewise [the merit] born from the Agnihotra and other rites, that born from the Virajā fire,
that produced from the Aupāsana fire, and that arising from the Samidh fire;
O great sage! All members of the three varṇas must apply ash produced from the agnihotra fire, as well as that born from the virajā fire.
The fire produced from the *aupāsana* rite is specifically for householders; the fire produced from the *samidh* wood is indeed to be maintained by students (*brahmacārin*s).
For Śūdras, fire produced from the cooking fire in the house of a learned Brāhmaṇa should be maintained;
for all others as well, fire produced from a forest conflagration should be maintained.
With the six mantras beginning with "Agni" from the Atharva Veda,
or likewise with the seven Jābāla mantras, one should apply the ashes in their secondary (gauṇa) form.
One should dust one's own body with [ashes], which removes the fear of the mass of sins,
using either the *triyāyuṣa* mantra or the one beginning with "medhāvī."
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be worn with secondary ashes by the religious student (brahmacārin),
using either the Tryambaka mantra or likewise the Satarudriya mantra.
O great sage! [One should apply it] with the five-syllabled mantra joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) on the forehead, the heart, and both arms.
A householder and one in the forest hermitage should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
composed in meditation with the Haṃsa-mantra of the Self or the Praṇava.
One who has entered the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
likewise, a Śūdra who delights in service should do so using the name of Śiva ending in "namaḥ."
O observer of noble vows, one should always perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark with devotion; this applies to all others as well, even without the use of mantras.
"O Sage, the smearing [of ashes] and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be performed with devotion.
Regarding the manner of wearing [the ashes] by students (brahmacārins), Bodhāyana says:
"Having performed the ritual in whichever fire one pays homage, one should take the full amount of ashes from that [fire]."
Having consecrated it silently and touched it, he should take it up with the mantra *mā nas toka* and hold it according to the rule: on the forehead with *tejasvī*, on the right arm with *varcasvī*,
on the left with *brahmavarcasvī*, at the region of the heart with *āyuṣmān*, and on the throat with *bhūyāsaṃ svasti*.
"It adheres everywhere."
In the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa]: "One should not transgress, even in thought, against the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
since these are enjoined by the Śruti, one who abandons them becomes fallen."
In the Mānava-upapurāṇa:
"He who does not wear the triple mark with sacred ash and likewise does not cover his body with it while reciting the mantra shall immediately become fallen."
In the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"One who seeks liberation should perform the smearing with ashes and likewise the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), even through inadvertence; for such is the Vedic revelation."
In the Parāśara Upapurāṇa: "In the beginning, having become a Brāhmaṇa, he wore the Tripuṇḍra with ashes;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should always wear that very Tripuṇḍra."
One should never abandon the application of ash— established by the Vedas— for marking the three lines on the body, nor even the worship of the Linga of Rudra, even if one is struck down.
Believers declare that this wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is the duty of Brāhmaṇas and the duty of all stages of life (āśramas).
In the Sanatkumārasaṃhitā:
"One established in the householder stage of life should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
a mendicant should also always wear it—such is the Jābāli Śruti."
A learned Brāhmaṇa should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
he should wear the triple mark constantly and should not transgress it even in thought.
Since it is enjoined by Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
As stated by Parāśara:
"For those who are solely devoted to the duties of Śruti, the emblem (liṅga) must indeed be that of Śruti alone."
Thus and so forth has been written.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for gods and Brahmins; a circular mark is for kings and Vaiśyas;
a half-moon is for Śūdras; and others [should wear] the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka)."
When the end of the age has arrived, people will out of delusion, yet with faith, wear on their foreheads the vertical *puṇḍra* and other marks that are not based on the Vedas.
In another Smṛti:
"Whatever various treatises are seen in this world that are contrary to Śruti and Smṛti, their foundation is indeed characterized by darkness (tāmasī)."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "Due to the abundance of sins, because of the curse of Dadhīca,
and because of the curse of the sage Gautama, the Vedic liṅga does not please him."
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Due to the curse of the high-souled sage Durvāsas when he was enraged,
and due to the curses of Kaṇva, Bhṛgu, and Upamanyu..."
Due to the curse of the sage Dadhīca and the curse of Gautama,
the minds of the southern Brahmins were afflicted by sin.
"O Śivā, there is not even a slight degree of faith in sacred ash or rudrākṣa beads. Thus it is said.
And in the *Mānava*:
"In former times, all the Brāhmaṇas, well-protected by Gautama,
deliberated together on the matter and prepared to depart for their own country."
"Under the influence of great delusion, those pitiless and base men have falsely cast this calumny upon me, saying that Gaurī was violated by Gautama."
Having heard that, the illustrious sage Gautama, the best of sages,
filled with great wrath, cursed those lowest of brahmins.
In whatever is related to Rudra, you most wicked people are everywhere averse to it;
you are in every way the lowest of Brahmins.
If you are not intent upon private study, the chanting of mantras, and likewise upon teaching them,
you are in every way the lowest of Brahmins.
If you are in every way averse to all matters declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas,
you are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas.
Marked with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, staff, noose, goad, and so forth,
you shall become the lowest of Brahmins through your faith.
Those who bear the marks of a circular emblem, a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, a half-moon, a trident, and so forth,
though endowed with faith, are in every respect the lowest of Brahmins.
Those who have taken refuge in the Buddhist dharma worship a liṅga made of aśvattha leaves;
likewise, there are those in the Pāñcarātra, the Kāpāla, and even the Kālāmukha systems.
O lowest of Brahmins, you have been initiated into the Śākta [tradition],
as well as into the Cārvāka doctrine and the heretical [pāṣaṇḍaka] systems.
"You have been initiated into the Vaiṣṇava [sect]; you are the lowest of Brahmins!
Likewise, you have been initiated with faith into the wicked-minded and other paths that are outside the Vedic tradition; you are the lowest of Brahmins! and so forth.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Having created other Vedic statements at will,
and having fabricated the Purāṇas, you sinners have become the lowest of Brāhmaṇas."
Wearing heated seals and other marks upon the root of the arm, you evil-minded ones have strayed from the path of the Vedas; become the lowest of Brahmins!
Placing Viṣṇu alone at your forefront, you revilers of the path of Śiva—
you, the lowest of Brahmins, shall go to the torments of hell.
O lowest of Brahmins, you are revilers of the true path, utterly deluded by the wicked path alone, and devoted to the teaching of sin.
Having abandoned the path to liberation and following only a crooked path, you who are intent on reviling the Vedas— be, O lowest of Brahmins!
Having abandoned rites such as the Agniṣṭoma,
those who revile the Vedas and become devotees of deities such as Vāyu are the lowest of Brahmins.
The Śaiva systems, such as Vīraśaivism and others, grant liberation as their sole fruit;
yet those who revile them are sinners and the lowest of Brahmins.
Marked with the wheel-sign, yet revilers of the path of Śiva and defilers of their own souls, and acting contrary to the way of Dharma— be such, O lowest of Brāhmaṇas!

Even if you were to fabricate statements from your own intellect regarding the *Bhārata* and other texts, you baseless fools who understand only meanings imagined from your own heads— you, O lowest of Brahmins, would remain as such!

Thus, because they have been struck down by [the aforementioned] curses, those statements fabricated as authoritative for the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and so forth should not be remembered. What is the use of this praise of the irrelevant? Let the elaboration cease.

Thus ends [the section on] the Kriyāsāra within the Nigamāgamasārasaṃgraha composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who was proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secrets of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita Siddhānta.
The Seventh Instruction: The Presentation of the Wearing of Vibhūti and its Measure.
Now, in the Eighth Instruction, there is the supreme praise of the sacred ash (bhasman).
I shall describe the cause of the confusion of castes regarding the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka).
I worship that Lord Īśvara together with Ambā, whom those who have entered into cakras, marks, and sectarian tilakas through mantras taught in the Tantras are unable to cross over his māyā.
I shall briefly proclaim the majesty of wearing the sacred ash, as revealed in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Tantras.

Whether seeking liberation or desiring worldly enjoyment, a preeminent twice-born who is pure in the Vedic way should always wear the sacred ash with reverence, according to the path declared in the Vedas.

A wise man, following the Vedic way, should wear white ash produced from the Agnihotra fire by means of the very mantra prescribed in the Vedas, through the practice of applying the Tripuṇḍra and smearing the body.

Having abandoned all other marks, a follower of the Vedas should never, whether by mistake or otherwise, wear any mark other than the single horizontal *tripuṇḍra*, which is the sole means for attaining the goals of human existence.
If one who is purely Vedic should ever wear a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) that is not prescribed by the Śruti out of delusion, he certainly falls; of this there is no doubt.

(61) Since the application of the horizontal *puṇḍra* mark with clay is prescribed in the *Smṛtis* and other texts, it is not logical to declare that one who wears it has fallen from his status. || 8 ||
The greatness of the vertical *puṇḍra* mark was declared by the high-souled Vyāsa, the foremost knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, and by Satyavrata.
He who bears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Ganges truly bears the form of the sun for the destruction of darkness; this is indeed recorded in the tradition.

He on whose forehead a pure vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made with clay is seen—even if he is an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), he is a pure soul and is certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. (11)
In the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, which is enchanting to all living beings, the greatness of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) has been demonstrated in various places. (12)
Whoever applies the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) using clay from the root of a Tulasī plant, for him there shall be a third eye right there; he should bear a digit of the moon upon his head.
O best of Brahmins, sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors— all these become fruitless if they are devoid of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
The greatness of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), along with its ritual procedure, has been proclaimed by Brahmā out of compassion in the Purāṇa known as the Brahmāṇḍa. 15.

I shall now declare the measurements of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the substances according to the divisions of the fingers, the colors, the mantras, the locations, and the fruits [of these practices].
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, especially in my sacred field,
on the shore of the ocean, at an anthill, or at the root of a Tulasī plant.
These types of clay should be collected, while other kinds of earth should be avoided;
black clay is said to bring about pacification (śānti), and red clay brings about subjugation (vaśya).
They say that yellow brings prosperity, while white is declared to belong to Viṣṇu;
the thumb is said to bestow nourishment, and the middle finger brings long life.
The ring finger always bestows liberation, as does the index finger;
one should perform [the rite] with these various fingers, but never touch [it] with the nails.
Or likewise the shape of a wick-lamp, or similarly the shape of a bamboo leaf,
as well as the form of a lotus bud and that of a water lily.
Alternatively, it may have the shape of a fish or a tortoise, or even the form of a conch shell;
that which measures ten finger-breadths is called the most excellent of the excellent. (22)
The middle [size] should be nine finger-breadths; beyond that, it may be eight finger-breadths.
The middle *puṇḍra* is traditionally remembered as being of three kinds: seven, six, or five [finger-breadths]. (23)
The smallest *puṇḍra* is of three types, being devoid of four, three, or two [of the prescribed] parts.
One should know Keśava or Nārāyaṇa on the forehead. (24)
Having placed Mādhava in the heart, Govinda at the ear and elbow, and Viṣṇu on the right side of the abdomen—thus he is designated. (25)
Beside that, in the middle of the arms, one should worship Madhusūdana;
Trivikrama in the region of the throat, and Vāmana on the left side of the belly.
One should remember Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck, Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the crown of the head.
These twelve names are at the head of Vāsudeva;
one should recite them with a concentrated mind during worship and at the time of the fire-oblation, both evening and morning.
Having uttered the names according to the prescribed rite, one should wear the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*;
even if one is impure, or of improper conduct, or committing sin in thought, [one is purified]. (29)
A man marked with the vertical *puṇḍra* should always remain pure;
wherever a mortal dies while wearing the vertical *puṇḍra*, [he attains liberation]. (30)
"Know that even a dog-cooker (outcaste) is honored in my world;
therefore, do not have any doubt regarding such words as these. (31)
If it is argued that even one who follows the Veda must wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay, [we reply:
for a twice-born man who is solely devoted to the Veda, the vertical mark is indeed based on the Śruti.
By asserting that it is prescribed [by scripture], your scholarship is indeed great;
for if the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) were based on the Vedas, there would have to be a direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti) for it. (33)
In that case, how could the Ekādaśī vow not be considered Śrauta?
If it is argued that there is a Vedic revelation (Śruti) for the Ekādaśī vow which has been inferred, [then...]
Why is there no Vedic authority inferred for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*?
Why has the vow of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī-vrata*) not been prohibited anywhere? (35)
Therefore, there is certainly a scriptural basis for this that has been inferred; of this there is no doubt.
However, the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* has been repeatedly prohibited in the Purāṇas.
Therefore, for this [work], there is no need for inference, nor indeed any doubt regarding its scriptural authority;
it is like the submarine fire that dries up the ocean of doubts arising from all the scriptures. (37)

In the Pārāśara [Smṛti], other types of sectarian marks (puṇḍra) along with their ritual procedures have been thoroughly rejected; likewise, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the trident, the circular, and the square [marks] are forbidden. || 38 ||
One who is devoted to the Vedas and has entered the path of the Vedas, having received his birth-status through birth, should not wear even the shape of a half-moon. || 39 ||
One should never wear a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) on the forehead even by mistake,
nor for the sake of attaining fame, profit, and other such successes, according to the Viṣṇvāgama and other scriptures.
A person learned in the Vedas should never wear any other mark than the horizontal triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra);
for, out of delusion, he might abandon the Vedic tripuṇḍra and adopt another mark.
If a mortal should wear it on his forehead, he surely falls; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, one should not burn [the image], nor should one consume it with weapons and the like.
The king should swiftly banish from his own country anyone who has been branded;
for among those who have fallen [from their status], branding with the foot of a dog and other such marks is indeed most severe.
Therefore, one should not study from those who are impure, nor should one mark oneself as pure during the teaching and learning of the Śrauta and Smārta rites. (44)
One who is not authorized for conversation or social association is marked [as an outcast];
however, even in other circumstances, the wearing of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and so forth belongs to the Vaidika.

It has been proclaimed as a means of avoidance that one should always abandon the horizontal sectarian mark (tiryakpuṇḍra) and adopt another mark prescribed by the Śrutis, for the horizontal mark is a cause of falling [from one's status]. 46.
If one should wear [these marks] out of delusion, he surely falls; of this there is no doubt—[provided his body is not properly marked with the heated conch, discus, and other signs].
The attainment of hell for one who merely looks [at such a person] is demonstrated in the Nāradīya:
"That man whose body is marked with the heated discus and other [weapons]... (48)
That outcaste (caṇḍāla) shall experience all forms of torment for ten million births;
whereas a twice-born man whose body is marked with the heated conch and other [emblems] such as the discus— || 49 ||
Having conversed [with such a person], one goes to the Raurava hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
no one whatsoever should dwell where there is a body marked with the discus.
If such a great sinner were to remain [in that state], he would become equal to a thousand killers of Brahmins,
even if he were devoted to bathing in the Gaṅgā or engaged in horse-sacrifices.
Having seen a body marked with the sign of the wheel, a man should look at the sun and recite the *Puruṣasūkta*;
otherwise, O Lord of Men, he shall go to the Raurava hell.
Having seen one whose body is marked with the wheel-sign, a man should look at the sun and recite the Śatarudrīya; O Lord of Men, otherwise he shall fall [from his status]. (53)
The body of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as the refuge of all the gods;
O King, if that [body] has been tormented, what shall I say of such a great sinner? 54.
O King, one whose body is marked with the discus or even marked with the conch should be known as ineligible for the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and the Smṛtis. (55)
In his own compendium, the compassionate Sūta has, in various places,
prohibited the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and other such sectarian marks, as well as those accompanied by symbols.
The wearing of the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with ashes,
and the wearing of no other mark besides it out of delusion, renders one fallen.
If one who is solely devoted to the path of the Vedas is marked even by delusion, he certainly falls; of this there is no doubt—even [if it occurs] because of another sectarian mark (puṇḍra).
One who has taken refuge in the path of the Vedas should not make a marked body;
nor should he ever apply another sectarian mark on his forehead, even by mistake.
One should not, even out of delusion, make the marks of gods, humans, or others; if one should do so, one falls downward.

(65) A person marked with sectarian signs (lāñchita) can never be a witness for anyone; nor is one marked with such signs qualified for the performance of rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis. (61)
Branded with marks, they shall never be spoken to, nor touched, nor even looked upon; the king should quickly banish them from the country. 62.
People afflicted by heresy will not practice the smearing [of the body] with ashes or the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the very path declared in the Vedas.
People afflicted by heresy will, out of delusion, wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead, as well as circular or half-moon shaped marks. (64)
People afflicted by heresy will, out of sheer delusion, mark their own bodies with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. (65)
But those people, afflicted by heresy, will be marked by the names of men or even by their physical forms. (66)
Because it has been refuted by these and other such statements from the Purāṇas, no Vedic authority can be inferred for the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
If there were a scriptural authority for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), even though it is prohibited by inference,
why would there not be one for such acts as bowing to a shrine (caityavandana) or plucking out the hair (keśolluñchana)?
Since they are not mentioned anywhere in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, it is logical that those Śrutis themselves do not exist. (69)

If it is argued that, because the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is mentioned in the *Smṛtis* and other texts just like other religious duties, it is not reasonable to claim an absence of scriptural authority (*śruti*), and therefore such a scripture must exist as inferred—then [the following is said]: 70.

Merely because it is mentioned in the Smṛtis and other texts, your claim that the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is like other dharmas taught in those sources makes your scholarship appear all the more brilliant. (71)
Would an elephant or a horse become a donkey simply by living in a city? Or would a Śūdra become a Brāhmaṇa merely by standing on a Brāhmaṇa’s street? (72)
