If it is asked, "Why is the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) prescribed in the Smṛtis and other texts if it is not based on the Śruti? then say this: "Why is the creation described by Ātreya mentioned in the Sāṅkhya? (73)
If it is argued that the creation of those [Sāṅkhyas] was proclaimed in the Smṛtis and other texts with reference to the Sāṅkhyas, then [we reply]:
in that case, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is also mentioned here with reference to the Tantric Vaiṣṇavas. (74)
Regarding the inferior [devotees], the Lord has proclaimed in various places in the Pāñcarātra the practice of marking with the vertical *puṇḍra*, the discus, and other signs for the Vaiṣṇavas. (75)
In the Purāṇas as well, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is declared to belong to the Vaiṣṇavas;
having seen that, I have spoken thus according to my own understanding, and not otherwise.
Those who have been initiated with faith according to the path taught in the Viṣṇu Āgamas are proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavas of many kinds, such as the Ekāntins and others. || 77 ||
The vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) is said to be of two kinds: with a central opening and without an opening;
this is both taught in the scriptures and observed in actual practice. (78)
It is further of two kinds: having the appearance of a trident and having the shape of the foot of Hari.
In the middle of a perforated trident, a line is drawn with turmeric.

In the Pañcarātra, the Blessed One [taught] with respect to those who are *sacchidra*, *mukta*, *aikāntin*, and *paramaikāntin*, as well as regarding the deficiency [of others] compared to other Vaiṣṇavas. (80)
The single-minded, highly fortunate, stainless ones who know my true nature should apply sectarian marks (puṇḍra) in the shape of my foot, leaving a space between them.
Even those who are supremely devoted (paramaikāntinaḥ), being solely intent upon my feet, likewise [offer] beautiful [flowers] shaped like spikes and mixed with turmeric powder. (82)
Other Vaiṣṇavas as well should devoutly apply marks that are without gaps,
shaped like the flame of a lamp or a bamboo leaf.
Those who are exclusively devoted to Viṣṇu may make [the rites] either flawless or flawed;
for them, no transgression is found in making them flawless. (84)

For those who are single-mindedly devoted, for those who have taken refuge, and even for those who are supremely single-mindedly devoted, there would be a great transgression in failing to apply the unbroken sectarian mark (puṇḍra). || 85 ||
A twice-born Vaiṣṇava should apply an auspicious vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) in the shape of a staff with a hole in the middle, using the names beginning with Keśava and ending with "namaḥ. (86)
He who makes the upright *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark—with a space between the lines, straight, gentle, with beautiful sides, and very charming—shall become exceedingly dear to me. (87)
The man who applies pure *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks with spaces between them, he builds for me therein a vast temple. (88)
In the middle of the broad and exceedingly beautiful ūrdhvapuṇḍra,
I dwell there in bliss, seated together with Lakṣmī.
That lowest of the twice-born who makes an upward sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) without leaving an interval between its parts indeed drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī who reside therein.
But that person of deluded intellect who applies an upward tilaka (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with gaps shall, by means of that very act, dwell in twenty-one hells in succession.
One should apply straight vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with distinct sides and intervals, resembling a staff, a lotus, a lamp, or a fish.

What is the use of much talk? One should fashion [the tooth-stick] as pleasing to the heart, gentle, beautiful to behold, straight, with well-formed sides and a tip pointing upward, and with a very clear center.
O great sage, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) must be worn by the twice-born just like the topknot and the sacred thread;
for if these are distorted, all ritual acts become fruitless.
Therefore, in all undertakings, it should be worn by a wise Brahmin; it provides protection and destroys malefic planets and inauspicious influences. 95.
Nothing superior to the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) has been seen, known, or heard by me;
one should likewise wear the vertical marks which are dear to Viṣṇu. (96)
Especially through recitation, burnt offerings, worship, meditation, charity, and so forth, all the afflictions of men arising from sin are destroyed. (97)
All desired things shall come to pass through the wearing of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
One should indeed wear thirteen or twelve *ūrdhvapuṇḍras*. (98)
Some desire one, four, six, or even eight [repetitions], using the *praṇava* as well as mantras consisting of six, eight, or twelve syllables. || 99 ||
His body was adorned with twelve auspicious and pleasing vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), fashioned from white clay brought from sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha).
[He beheld] the high-souled Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi and a treasure-house of asceticism, adorned with all his five weapons held in their proper places. (101)
Once, a most excellent sage named Kāśyapa approached, and having paid homage, he stood nearby with his joined palms placed upon his head. (102)
Constantly wearing the upright sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) made of the recommended white clay, and marked with signs such as the conch and discus upon his respective limbs. || 103 ||
One who is endowed with such characteristics is called an Ācārya;
he always wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the tilaka, and [remembers] the twelve names.

One who possesses a praiseworthy and radiant appearance, marked with the conch, the discus, and other such signs, and endowed with qualities such as these, is called a disciple of steady intellect. (105)
With white clay produced from a praiseworthy Vaiṣṇava sacred site,
preceded by the utterance of the names of the forms beginning with Keśava.
The wearing of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts of the body is considered by the best of yogis to be an earth-element bath (pārthiva-snāna).
One who wears purifying lotus seeds as well as the marks of the conch and discus shall never be harmed by the servants [of Yama] and others. || 108 ||
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, or anyone else should mark their own body with the discus and other symbols with supreme joy. (109)
To prevent undesirable things, for the sake of single-minded devotion to the Lord of the World,
and for the successful accomplishment of one's actions, the mark of the discus and other symbols should be worn.
One who possesses the beloved marks of Hari, such as the conch, the discus, and the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
shall attain Acyuta even more than through all other religious duties.
When he perceives himself as having become a servant of the Supreme Self, at that very moment he should mark his body with the conch, the discus, and other [emblems]. (112)
One who is marked on some part of the body with a single wheel alone shall not yet fall under the power of undesirable beings. (113)

Or, having offered oblations and so forth into the fire of Viṣṇu’s sanctuary, or into the fire of the Guru, or even into one's own fire— with the forms [of the deities] heated and worshipped in due order— 114.
One should wear [the marks] with a mantra using the discus, lotus, mace, bow, and sword;
one may be marked with both the conch and the discus, or indeed marked with all of them. (115)
For everything else, such as the mace and so forth, is indeed subordinate to the conch and the discus;
for in the fire-sacrifice and the lotus-discus, all things are of that very nature.
A Brahmin should indeed carry the Sudarśana on his right arm, and he should carry the conch on his left; thus the knowers of Brahman understand.
O Sudarśana of great flames, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
forever show the path to Viṣṇu for me, who am blinded by ignorance.
O Blessed One, Sarvavijaya, Sahasrāra, Aparājita, you who bring prosperity, O Śrīsudarśana, I have come to you for refuge. 119.
O Pāñcajanya, who has destroyed the accumulation of sins by Your own roar, protect me, a sinner fallen into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra! 120.
In ancient times you were born from the ocean and held in the hand by Viṣṇu;
you were saluted by all the gods—O Pāñcajanya, salutations be unto you! 121.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) belongs to the Vaiṣṇavas here, and also in the Vaikhānasa tradition;
however, it is distinct from that [mark made with ash] because of the difference in their ritual systems (tantra) and the difference in their mantras.
Having taken the sacrificial ashes with the white eight-syllable mantra,
one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) after tying a protective cord (pratisara) on the hand.

And to the south, once the oblation has been performed with sacrificial fuel sticks and cow’s ghee, one should have him consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Having taken that ash in one's hand and consecrated it with the mantra itself,
the application of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is indeed the fire-bath (āgneyasnāna).

Taking ashes with the words "Bhūtir bhasme," and having smeared them on the forehead, heart, arms, throat, and other parts with the tips pointing upward while reciting "Ādityaḥ somo namaḥ," and having sprinkled them with water while reciting "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should worship the fire with the mantra "Yatte agne tejas tena" and [the verse] "Udvayam."
With these and other such verses, one should worship the Sun.
By bathing with ashes, one constantly obtains the merit of all sacrifices performed.
"Agni, Māruta, Dhṛti, Āditya, Soma, Namaḥ"—this is the sequence for the branding and the various *puṇḍra* marks of the Tantrikas. (126)
"It is called 'beneficial' by the Compassionate Sūta;
it is prescribed for those who have been initiated into the Viṣṇvāgama and other tantras. (127)
O wise ones, the marking with the conch, discus, and mace does not apply to other embodied beings;
rather, it is for men who have been initiated into the Tantras. 128.
O bulls among sages, the application of other *puṇḍras* by one who has been initiated has been described in the Tantras in due order as being solely for the sake of benefit. (129)
O best of sages, it has been declared in due order that the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) made with clay must be worn by a Brahmin who speaks of Brahman, as it is indeed beneficial. 130.
With the mantra "Uddhṛtāsi," especially that dedicated to Viṣṇu, the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, woman, and likewise others [should perform the rite]. || 131 ||
"One should mark one's own body with the discus and other [emblems] with supreme joy"—by such statements, the marking of other *puṇḍra*s is established as being of primary importance. (132)
Who would not say that the Lord Sūta, the omniscient one, has thus declared this in his own Gītā through the power of his compassion for those belonging to the castes and stages of life? 133.

And he has stated that the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) exist even for the followers of Tantra; furthermore, Śambhu— the omniscient Lord of all gods— declared that for those humans who have fallen from the path of the Vedas, the Guru is the Tantra.
For those devoted to the path of the Vedas, there is no Tantra whatsoever that brings happiness here; everything has been truly stated in its full detail. || 134 ||
The Śruti also proclaimed the duties of the castes for human beings,
and likewise the Supreme Teacher declared them in all the Tantras;
[so too did] the Ocean of Compassion [proclaim] the duties of the castes for those who have strayed from the path of the Śruti.
It should certainly not be resorted to by those devoted to the path of the Vedas. || 135 ||

Just as the stages of life (āśramas) have been declared for those devoted to the path of the Vedas, so too has the Supreme Guru, the Lord of All, described the stages of life for those humans who have strayed from the path of the Vedas. But for each of those...
Hari also spoke to the foremost of sages in his own Tantra: || 136 ||
Even the Creator has declared that the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) pertain only to those men who have strayed from the path of the Vedas;
for those who are devoted to the path of the Vedas, the Tantra is not to be practiced at all.
The path equal to the way of the Vedas—what I have spoken is indeed the truth. || 137 ||
Now, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) described in the Vaikhānasa texts is not for a Vedic practitioner, because it is prescribed with mantras other than those declared in the Śruti. || 138 ||
The distinction between the paths taught in the Śruti and the Tantra arises from the difference in their respective authorities;

just as there are distinctions such as [the mantras] *Sāhaṃsa*, *Tāra*, and *Tryambaka*, so too the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) may be worn with or without a mantra, but it should not be worn by those who follow the Vedic path. 139.
This is because the scriptures specifically prohibit other types of marks (puṇḍra) with reference to those [three lineages],
and especially because they prohibit the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) when made with ashes alone.

In another Smṛti, it is clearly stated that the horizontal mark (tiryakpuṇḍra) is made with clay, while the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is made with ash, and likewise the horizontal mark with clay. (141)
Sages who have mastered the Vedas declare that sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron used without Vedic mantras is equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin. (142)
Those who desire beauty and happiness should wear it in the form of horizontal marks (tiryakpuṇḍra);
since the mark is worn with sandalwood paste and other substances, one should not abandon the sacred ash.
One who abandons the ashes would be consumed by the fire of anger born from the Vedas;
therefore, a wise man should wear the Vedic ashes upon sandalwood and other unguents. (144)
One should not wear worldly substances such as sandalwood paste upon the ashes;
for there is no harm in discarding sandalwood and the like if they are treated as mere ashes. || 145 ||
Therefore, sandalwood and the like are purely worldly; of this there is no doubt.
For when ashes are placed upon sandalwood and such things for the sake of visible beauty and other qualities, [the latter's nature remains unchanged]. (146)
If there were no fruit from wearing a small amount of sandalwood paste and the like, then [there would likewise be none] when white ash is worn over sandalwood and such. (147)

Who could prevent one from obtaining the fruit of attaining the ashes that are the very essence of sandalwood and other such things—[that fruit] which belongs to the twice-born who touches Śiva while wearing the impure stains of a cowherd woman? (148)
He who draws the sectarian mark with ashes alone shall go to an inexhaustible hell along with twenty-one generations of his lineage; one should not draw it with clay or other substances. 149.

"In the absence of ash from the Śrauta fire and so forth, one should take ash from a common (laukika) fire," because of this [rule], there is a prohibition against using Gopīcandana, clay, sandalwood, and the like. (150)

If it is asked how a follower of the Vedas may wear sandalwood paste and the like according to the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, [the answer is that] there is a prohibition regarding the use of *gopīcandana* and clay established within that same *Kūrma Purāṇa*. (151)
This [practice] pertains to all stages of life (āśrama) without distinction;
however, the prohibition of sandalwood and the like does not apply to the householder.
However, the subject regarding ascetics and others is made clear in another Smṛti:
"The use of betel, the application of ointments, and eating from a vessel of bell-metal [are forbidden]. (153)
Having performed [the ritual], the monk should observe the fast while adorned with garlands, perfumes, and other ornaments;
because it is based on Vedic scripture and is not prohibited, the horizontal triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) should be worn.
Because it is not based on the Vedas and because it is prohibited, other types of *puṇḍra* must be abandoned by the twice-born.
What need is there for much speaking on this matter? A follower of the Veda should [abandon them] even out of negligence. (155)
He who wears a sectarian mark other than the triple-line mark (tripuṇḍra) falls downward;
this prohibition of other marks applies specifically to one who follows the singular path of the Vedas. (156)
He is undoubtedly equal to a Tantric Śaiva as well,
according to the Vāyavīya Purāṇa and others that illuminate the practice of the Śaivas.
The circular and other [forms] are proclaimed as being by virtue of Śiva’s teaching. || 157 ||
Having first performed the ritual actions with mantras, one should mark the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead with ashes using fragrant water, making it straight, long, and clearly visible. (158)
Whether circular, square, a dot, or even a half-moon—whatever mark (*puṇḍra*) is drawn on the forehead with white ashes [is prescribed]. (159)
One should draw such [a design] upon the arms, the head, the breasts, and the space between them—square, circular, resembling a linga, a lamp, or a half-moon. (160)

Thus, the sixfold teaching of Śiva, including the *tripuṇḍra*, has been declared; therefore, for the follower of Śiva who is solely devoted to the Veda, there exists no [other] primary authority. (161)
Thus, this teaching of the Lord has been declared as a sign of non-birth (ajāti),
with the intention of expressing the distinctions in the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva.
Every linga, beginning with the circular, is declared to be the teaching of Śiva.
The circular linga and likewise the bindu-linga belong to the devotees of Brahmā. (163)
For Vaiṣṇavas, there is the *liṅga*, the lamp, the square, and the half-moon; for devotees of Śiva, there is the ash, the *liṅga*, and the horizontal triple-mark (*tripuṇḍra*). || 164 ||
While I, Parāśara, was present as the setting sun for the ocean of doubt, the individual liṅgas of the gods and their respective attendants were described one by one. 165.
In the Skanda, Parāśara, Kaurma, Nāradīya, Gāruḍa, Śivadharma, Vāsiṣṭha, Laiṅga, and also in the Kālottara; || 166 ||
Likewise in the Prājāpatya [Purāṇa], in the Mānavīya-saṃhitā,
in the Śivarāghava-saṃvāda, and in the Vāyavīya and Mānava [Purāṇas] (167).
In the Liṅga Purāṇa and the Śivarahasya, as well as in the Mātsya, the Bodhāyana [Purāṇa], in the Smṛti composed by him (Vyāsa), and likewise in the Bharadvāja Smṛti; || 168 ||
In the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*, which is a treasury of the nectar of the essence of Dharma, and in the *Smṛtisārasamuccaya*, known as the *Śrutibhāskara* (The Sun of Revelation). || 169 ||
In the Nāradīya Smṛti within the Bhārata, as spoken by Lokākṣi, the greatness of wearing the sacred ash (bhasma) is proclaimed everywhere. || 170 ||

Throughout this entire work, at various intervals, the proclamation of the fruits such as knowledge is clearly heard as establishing the superiority of the practice of wearing sacred ash (bhasma). 171.
One should always wear the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead, both arms, the neck, the head, and the chest; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (172)

Whether performed with mantras or even without mantras, the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) for all castes and stages of life has been proclaimed by Bādara in the Jābāla [Upaniṣad]. (173)
The best of sages belonging to the Śvetāśvatara branch declare that smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are means of accomplishment as limbs of knowledge. (174)
This is the dharma of the supreme hermitage; for those by whom it is joyfully practiced, there arises the knowledge of Śiva, which is the cause of the destruction of saṃsāra.
The best of sages, established in the Atharvaśiras, prescribe the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the cessation of the bonds of Māyā. (176)
O wise ones, for him by whom the Pāśupata vow has been correctly practiced, knowledge arises; through that, there is liberation from the bonds.
The best of sages, who are the direct branches of the tree of liberation, declare that smearing with ash (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are solely limbs of knowledge. (178)
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the severance of bonds and for the accomplishment of knowledge,
one who desires liberation should properly perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

Since the supreme state transcends truth and the other virtues, one who desires liberation should therefore apply the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍraka) and perform the smearing with ashes for the attainment of knowledge. 180.
"One who seeks liberation must not abandon even through negligence the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra); such indeed is the Vedic revelation. (181)
The Vedic revelation prescribes both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the destruction of great sins.
The Vedic revelation ordains the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the protection of all beings. (183)
The Vedic revelation ordains the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the sake of auspiciousness for all.
The Vedic revelation ordains the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the purification of all. (185)
The Vedic revelation ordains the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the sake of the Liṅga by the devotees of Maheśvara.
The Vedic revelation ordains the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the sake of the spiritual knowledge of all.
The Vedic revelation prescribes for all people the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) as a religious vow.
The Vedic revelation ordains that the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall be regarded as a form of gift for all.
The Vedic revelation ordains that for all people, the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) constitute austerity itself.
The Vedic revelation ordains that both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) constitute a sacrifice for all.
The Vedic revelation ordains for men the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) as being in accordance with all dharma.
The ash was worn by Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and likewise by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra),
as well as by the gods, in the form of the triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of the body.
Umādevī, Lakṣmī, Vāṇī,
and all other women likewise wear the sacred ash in the form of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing of the body.
The ash, worn as the Tripuṇḍra and applied by smearing, has been maintained by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes, as well as by those who speak Apabhraṃśa.
O best of sages, only those who joyfully practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are truly cultured and wise; no others.
Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark with faith have no liberation from saṃsāra even through ten million births. (197)
For those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith,
there is no knowledge of Śiva even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
(76) O Brahmins, even my Guru would not be able to describe the greatness of wearing the sacred ash (bhasmadhāraṇa), even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O lords of sages, even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra,
it is not possible to fully describe the majesty of wearing the sacred ash (bhasma).
Oh, how great is the power of delusion, O lords of sages who discourse on Brahman! For men, having abandoned Brahman, pursue other desired objects. (201)
The Śiva-liṅga is the jewel itself, as is the five-syllabled mantra;
likewise, sacred ash alone is the medicine for men in the rites for attaining liberation and subjugating women.
Wherever one who has smeared his limbs with ashes— whether he be a fool or even a scholar—
eats, there Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, eats together with his consort.
In the Saura-saṃhitā: "The man who follows one whose entire body is covered with ashes is instantly purified, even if he is burdened with every kind of sin."
Just as the Prājāpatya sacrifice is remembered as auspicious among all the Purāṇas,
so is the city of Vārāṇasī auspicious among all cities.
Likewise, among all marks (puṇḍras), the auspicious triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is said to be supreme,
just as Rudra is sung of in all the Vedas as superior to the universe.
Likewise, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is extolled in all the Purāṇas:
"That man who washes the feet of one who wears the triple mark [attains great merit]."
Even a man burdened with every sin is instantly purified merely by the gift of alms to one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Even one burdened with every sin is purified before long;
by him the Veda has been studied, by him it has been mastered, and by him everything has been performed.
By that wise person by whom the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has not been worn on the head with ashes,
what was done remains undone, and what was heard remains unheard.
Whether one has studied the Vedas or not, if the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is worn by him,
his Vedic study is in vain, his sacrifices are in vain, his charity is in vain, and his austerity is in vain.
Vows and fasts are in vain for one who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
likewise, truth, purity, sacrifice, pilgrimage, and the worship of gods and other deities [are fruitless].
All this would be in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra;
even in the lands of Kīkaṭa, wherever one is adorned with sacred ash.
A human being should always dwell there, for that place is indeed equal to the sacred field of Kāśī;
whether he be of bad character or endowed with virtue, or whoever he may be, even if devoid of auspicious marks.
One who is endowed with the ashes and the staff is to be honored like a prince;
so too is one who, even through a disguise, bears the Lord’s ashes and staff.
Even with hundreds of sacrifices, one does not attain that destination which he reaches who,
whether out of association, sport, or even fear, holds [this teaching].
He who possesses the splendor prescribed by the rules is indeed worthy of worship just as I am;
he who bears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of ashes with Vedic mantras.
For one who achieves Brahminhood through diligent effort, it is fully realized;
for those established in the Vedas and Vedāntas, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is made with sacred ash alone.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes while reciting Vedic mantras bestows right knowledge quickly; this is the truth that has been spoken, there is no doubt.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes while reciting Vedic mantras is indeed a fierce sun to the darkness consisting of a multitude of great sins.
The wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with ashes using Vedic mantras is declared to be the remover of all sins; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash while reciting Vedic mantras is the cause of satisfaction for Śiva, Viṣṇu, the gods, and Brahmā.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash while reciting Vedic mantras is the cause of satisfaction for Pārvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and Bhāratī.
Without the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes and Vedic mantras, liberation is not attained by humans or gods. (p. 78)
Without the realization of Vedānta,
the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash using Vedic mantras does not arise for anyone at all.
The wise great sages proclaim that the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes and Vedic mantras constitutes the path of the virtuous.

The great sages proclaim that the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for the sake of protection and for the sake of auspiciousness; whatever man desires liberation while abandoning the wearing of the triple mark, [desires it in vain].
For by drinking poison, he indeed makes himself eternal;
likewise, by smearing himself with ashes according to the path declared in the Vedas.
By the mere wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), perfect knowledge arises through Śiva,
the Supreme Self, who has become one with the Brāhmaṇa.
The ash worn with reverence in the form of the horizontal triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of the body is the dharma of the primordial Brāhmaṇa, consisting of the transverse triple-mark.
A Brāhmaṇa should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) smeared with ashes, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, along the paths established by the Vedas.
The wise declare that the worship of the Rudra-liṅga is the very mouth [of the tradition],
while for those established in all the Āgamas, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) smeared with ash is the crest.
"It is the truth that I have declared: among all emblems, the ash is the most excellent;
it should be used by all who seek the highest good, regardless of the caste they were born into."
The Brahmin should wear the sacred ash in the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and perform the smearing (avakuṇṭhana);
indeed, he who is smeared with white sacred ash alone is truly a Brahmin.
The king should protect that man who is radiant with the lines of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
whose entire body is covered with ashes, and whose head is marked with the triple mark.
The king should punish without hesitation those men who revile [the Vaiṣṇavas];
he should always carry a Vaiṣṇava mark and a water-pot filled with water.
O twice-born ones, the sacred thread, the upper garment, and the application of the triple mark with holy ashes— whatever twice-born man possesses such signs as these, [he is a true Brahmin].
(p. 79) Truth alone has been proclaimed by me: fruitful is the life of him by whom the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) have not been joyfully practiced.
The knowledge of Brahman does not arise for him even in ten million births,
by whom the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) have not been joyfully practiced.
Indeed, the knowledge of Brahman arises for that very person before long;
therefore, one who desires liberation should always be endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and other such virtues.
One should always perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the Śruti,
following the prescribed rules at pure great rivers or in a pond.
Or one should bathe with white ashes for the sake of purifying evil,
using the seven mantras beginning with "Agnis" as spoken by Jābāla.
One should also wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) horizontally upon the forehead;
for even those beings who are endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and other virtues [are purified by it].
They shall by no means be devoid of the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
just as [they are not devoid of it] in their distinguished human birth, in their status as Brahmins, or in their physical form.
The performance of sacrifices, charity, and other rites is difficult for all embodied beings to achieve; likewise, among the Vedic duties, the application of the triple mark with ashes is rare.
Indeed, the worship of the Rudra-linga is difficult for embodied beings to attain,
as is the wearing of the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of the body with sacred ash.
Knowing that it is indeed very difficult to attain, the Lord of All,
the Master of the World— who is free from suffering, stainless, and manifest eternal bliss— acted thus.
Tell me, for what purpose did Śiva act? He is the manifest, untainted one; the Great Lord who is eternally beyond injunction, the eternal agent, and the eternal enjoyer.
Tell me, for what purpose did he perform it? O Sage, having understood that this which was spoken by the practitioner is extremely difficult for men to attain, Maheśvara [acted].
He always performed the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes;
indeed, the wearing of the triple mark and other such rites must be performed by one who has not yet attained perfection.
O best of men, [one should strive] specifically for one's own gain and not for the gain of another;
O believer, even without regard for one's own gain, [one should act] for the sake of removing the misfortunes of others.
Even one who has attained perfection must perform [this rite], just as the Lord of All did;
for in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the Creator, under the guise of creation, proclaimed the excellence of the *tripuṇḍra*.
He indeed created the forehead neither obliquely, nor upwards, nor circular;
for transverse lines appear upon the foreheads of all embodied beings.
Nevertheless, foolish men do not apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
for them there is no meditation, no charity, no knowledge, and no austerity.
Whatever is performed by a Brahmin without the mark of the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra) shall be as if it were performed by a Śūdra, who has no entitlement to the study of the Veda.
Without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), a Brahmin has no authority for the worship of Śiva;
neither by giving gifts, nor by sacrifices, nor by extremely difficult austerities.
The merit that is obtained by the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) cannot be attained by pilgrimage;
O Nārada, [that merit is equal to] charity, sacrifice, dharma, and pilgrimage itself.
Meditation and austerity do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
for just as a king always regards one who bears his own insignia as his own kinsman.
Likewise, Śiva regards one who bears the mark of the triple-tilaka as equal to himself—
whether he be of the twice-born caste or of the lowest caste— by means of the pure white ashes.
He who wears the mark of the triple-tilaka has Rudra brought under his control;
even if he has abandoned the conduct of caste and stage of life, or even if all his ritual actions have been lost.
Even he who wears the triple sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) drawn once across his forehead is worthy of worship;
one should not examine him for knowledge, nor for lineage, nor likewise for religious observances.
O Nārada, he whose forehead is marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra) is indeed worthy of worship;
even Brahmā would not be able to describe the full majesty of the mere presence of sacred ash (śrī-bhūti).
How much less could anyone dare to speak of the ash arising from a conditioned fire?
For there is no mantra superior to the Śiva-mantra, nor is there any reality higher than Śiva.
There is indeed no merit higher than the worship of Śiva, nor any sacred site (tīrtha) superior to the sacred ash (bhasma).
That which is the supreme potency of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed to be that ash.
It is the destruction of all sufferings and the purification of all sins;
whether one is an outcaste or even a low-born person, a fool or even a scholar.
In whatever land he who is endowed with the teachings of prosperity may dwell,
there Śiva, accompanied by Soma and surrounded by hosts of all beings, is ever present.
Endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas), he always maintains his presence in whatever region he dwells, eternally joined with the governance of prosperity.
Even that place would become pure, how much more so his temple!
These are those very ashes, sanctified by the mantras of Śiva and serving as ornaments for the limbs of the one who has consumed desire.
The lines of the Tripuṇḍra applied upon the surface of the forehead erase the ill-fated letters inscribed by destiny.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"Those who are dear to Śiva, devoted to Śiva, intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet,
and who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)— they indeed are the supreme Bhāgavatas."
In the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa]:
"For one who joyfully gives wealth to a person whose body is smeared with ashes, all his sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt."
All the Śrutis, all the Smṛtis, and even all the Purāṇas proclaim the greatness of Bhūti; therefore, a twice-born man should wear it.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"He who applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva."
That which is the supreme virility of Rudra-Agni is proclaimed as ash;
it is the destroyer of all sufferings and the purifier of all sins.
For he who, with his senses restrained, constantly performs at the three junctions of the day the entire ritual bath pertaining to Agni, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall go to the supreme goal;
the bath with ashes possesses innumerable qualities superior to the bath with water.
Therefore, having abandoned the Varuna bath, one should perform the Agneya bath;
whatever merit exists in all sacred fords, and whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords—[that is obtained thereby].
One obtains all that fruit from the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), there is no doubt;
whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or burdened by minor sins (upapātaka).
By means of the ash-bath, one burns away all that [impurity] just as fire consumes fuel;
there exists no purifying bath superior to the ash-bath.
Having spoken thus to the sages and the gods, Lord Śiva himself bathed;
from that time forward, Brahmā and the other sages have been seekers of Śiva.
In all ritual acts, they diligently performed the ash-bath;
therefore, whoever should perform this Agneya bath of Śiva [attains the highest state].
With this very body, he is Rudra; there is no doubt about this. Whether he be of bad conduct or endowed with virtue, whoever he may be, if he seeks the fruit [of his practice], [he shall attain it].
One who is endowed with the teaching of the Bhūti-śāsana is to be honored like a prince.
In the Vāsiṣṭha-laiṅga:
"Listen to the fruit of the merit of him by whom the sacred ash (bhasma) has been worn in this manner."
O tiger among sages, multitudes of great sins as well as other transgressions are destroyed; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
O Sage, it bestows the fruit of Vedic study upon those established in the stage of studentship (brahmacarya),
and it grants all prosperity to all householders.
O best of sages, it constantly bestows merit upon Śūdras and destroys the sins of others for whom the sacred ash has not been worn according to the prescribed path.
Know, O Sage, that the birth of those who become fully satisfied upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash is as fruitless as that of a boar.
Without a doubt, that man who stands with all his limbs covered in ashes is always worthy of worship by the gods, asuras, and the lords of sages.
Upon seeing him, even the King of the Gods will offer salutation to those who consume forbidden food preceded by the smearing of ashes.
O Sage, that alone shall be their food; there is no doubt about this.
He who constantly bathes with ashes after first bathing with water—
Whether he be a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller,
one who performs this with devotion is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme goal.
The fire-related bath with ashes is prescribed for ascetics;
ashes are indeed superior to the wet bath, for from the wet [bath] comes the certain destruction of birth.
One should know that moisture is the primary nature (prakṛti), and they know the primary nature to be bondage.
For the sake of abandoning this primary nature, bathing with ashes is prescribed.
Oh, the greatness of delusion! It cannot be described by me:
that men, having abandoned the means [of liberation] which is like ashes, strive elsewhere.
What is the use of saying much? The wearing of ashes is the destroyer of delusion;
for one who is constantly joined with ashes, knowledge arises without delay.
The sinner shall be liberated from sin, there is no doubt;
there is nothing equal to the Brahman even within the three worlds that is like the sacred ash.

O Sage, for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification, I previously created the sacred ash (bhasma) according to the Śruti; it was indeed given by the beloved of the Goddess.
In the *Kālottara*:
"Therefore, whoever practices this Āgneya-knowledge of Śiva,
being liberated from the fetters of worldly existence, is glorified in the world of Śiva."
Fever-demons, piśācas, asuras, and yātudhānas;
kumāra-grahas, bhūtas, kūśmāṇḍas, and hosts of ḍākinīs.
The foremost among the Brahma-rākṣasas, as well as pūtanās, kuṣṭha, gulma,
all types of fistula-in-ano, and the eighty diseases caused by vāta.
There are sixty-four diseases of bile, seventy-five of phlegm,
as well as the fear of tigers and snakes, and other wild beasts as well.
By means of the ash-bath, [sins] perish like deer and other animals before a lion.
In the Vāyavīya [Saṃhitā]: "The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be made with pure cold water and with ash."
He who maintains the supreme Brahman attains it, without a doubt;
those men whose bodies exist without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) [do not].
Therefore, that which resembles a cremation ground should not be beheld by people who perform meritorious deeds;
shame on a forehead devoid of ashes, and shame on a village that is an abode of inauspiciousness!
Fie upon a birth that does not worship the Lord! Fie upon knowledge that takes refuge in the inauspicious!
Those who revile the *tripuṇḍra* mark revile Śiva himself.
And those who bear [this] with devotion, they also bear Śiva;
what is the use of much speaking here, as it is described again and again?
Apart from the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), there is indeed no other means for liberation;
just as a sacrifice does not shine when devoid of fire.
Worship of Śiva devoid of ash, even if it possesses all other means, is incomplete.
As stated in the *Mānavīya-saṃhitā*:
"The triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) should be applied in the morning, at midday, and in the evening."
One should apply white ashes; he is Rudra—of this there is no doubt.
As stated in the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*:
"By duly maintaining the seed of fire upon the forehead..."
Just as fire consumes what is written on a cloth, it destroys even that which is ordained by fate;
sin committed above the neck is destroyed by wearing the conch-shell mark.
By wearing it on the neck, sins committed by the neck and its parts are purified;
by the arms, sins committed by the arms; and by the chest, those committed by the mind.

By holding [the breath] at the navel, one removes sin committed against the back; by holding it at the back, one removes sin committed against the anus; and by holding it at the sides, O Rāma, one removes the sin born of embracing another's wife and similar acts.
The wearing of that ash is praised; likewise, all three marks represent the wearing of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, as well as the three sacred fires.
By him indeed was performed the upholding of the three worlds and their qualities;
his seat is ashes, his bed is ashes, and his body is smeared with ashes.
By bathing with ashes, they are always liberated from sins; there is no doubt about this.
Elsewhere it is said:
"Having reached the abode of Dadhīci, even one who has entered the jaws of death [is saved]."
Near his wall, however, there was consecrated ash;
the dog fell into this ash, O Māra, and went to death.
Yama, having honored him, bowed down and said: "O most meritorious sage, your presence in my house is not fitting; please go outside."
Having spoken thus, that dog went outside and stood there;
Nārada, having informed Śaṅkara of this, brought him back to that place.
Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods, he then addressed the God:
"O Lord, this devotee of Maheśvara—make him the leader of the Gaṇas."
"So be it," Śiva replied; and the Gaṇa became dog-faced.
As stated in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"A learned twice-born man, though covered in ashes, is freed from the consequences of all sins."
One is immediately freed from defects; one is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, in all worlds, the heroic one is joined with the ashes.
That which is the supreme potency of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed as ash;
for one who is established in ash, defects are burnt away through contact with that fire.
One whose self is purified by the bath of ashes is known as "established in ashes" (bhasmaniṣṭha);
his entire body is smeared with ashes, and he bears the radiant triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made of ashes.
The man who sleeps on ashes is known as one established in ashes;
likewise, ghosts, spirits, and demons, as well as diseases that are exceedingly difficult to endure, [are overcome].
By the mere proximity of one who is devoted to the sacred ash (bhasmaniṣṭha), [all sins] melt away; of this there is no doubt.
It is called *bhasita* because it illuminates (*bhāsana*), and it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities (*kalmaṣabhakṣaṇāt*).
Prosperity that brings prosperity to men, protection that is the supreme means of protection—
what else need be said regarding the cause of the greatness of sacred ash?
By bathing with ashes, the Lord Maheśvara himself is attained;
that ash is the supreme weapon of the Śaivas and belongs to the Supreme Lord.
That the harm intended toward Dhaumya’s elder brother during his ascetic penance was averted—
[for] upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the Bhūtas and Pretas, led by their chiefs, [turn away]. (From the *Mānava*).
Terrified and trembling, they go forth swiftly; of this there is no doubt.
As stated in the *Laiṅga*: "By the mere remembrance of Rudra, even sin is utterly destroyed."
Likewise, by merely wearing it, all his sin is destroyed;
even one who has committed thousands of misdeeds, if he bathes with ashes, [is purified].
Just as fire consumes a forest with its brilliance and turns it all to ashes,
so too does that twice-born man— even if he has committed incomparable sin— burn away everything at the time of death.
One who bathes in ashes shall, in a short time, be somewhat liberated from sins;
with his self purified by the ash-bath, he has conquered anger and subdued his senses.
"Having come into my presence, one does not return again.
In the *Śivarahasya*:
"And Kāśī consists of the multitude of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
Viśveśvara is the supreme among all the gods;
likewise, this *puṇḍra* is the manifestation (*vibhūti*) that is the singular essence of all principles (*tattva*), and this is the *tripuṇḍra*.
A certain man, his life-breath having reached the throat, arrived at the time of death and resembling one already dead,
lies helpless in the cremation ground, slain by the weapons of bandits.
Then, indeed, a certain follower of the Senā-Pulindas,
running with great speed here and there, [stumbled] upon a heap of ashes situated within that [place].
Then, with his foot placed upon the tip of the forehead of the woodcutter who was burning [with grief], he departed;
meanwhile, the followers of Yama, Death and Time, arrived to lead him away.
When he approached that lifeless one who had come there,
at that very moment the leaders of the Gaṇas raised various weapons.
There, in the celestial chariot, throngs of apsarases surrounded him;
then the messengers of Dharmarāja, having seen the cause of his being marked with ashes, [approached].
Remembering that cremation ground of Śambhu and abandoning the wearer of the sectarian mark, they fled terrified in all directions; meanwhile, the Gaṇas led him to the city of Śiva.
In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "What is the use of sacrifices? What is the use of disputes over numerous sacred fords? What is the use of the toil of reciting the Vedas?
What is the use of various formidable and stainless austerities? What is the use of mantras, tantras, and the chanting of prayers?"
What is the use of meditations, what use for the multitude of various gifts, and what use for the delusions of Sāṅkhya and Yoga?
One who is wise and skilled in seeking liberation should instead apply the triple mark with white ashes.
In the Bodhāyana-sūtra it is known: "One must not be negligent regarding prosperity. Likewise, they cite:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with ashes using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers..."

"In that regard, the white *tripuṇḍra* shall be the destroyer of great sins. Thus it is said. Then, one should rub [the ashes] over all the limbs with the mantra "Tryambakam. One becomes purified; one purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, oneself as the twenty-first, and the entire row.
"One attains union with Brahman or residence in the same world as Brahman," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
In the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*:
"One should take up cow-dung with the right hand, but consecrate it with the left."
One should burn the piṇḍa with the Aghora mantra, but it should be taken up with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.

One should perform the bath with the mantra ending in "Īśāna," starting from the crown of the head down to the feet; having sipped water (ācamana) and being seated on a four-legged seat, one should become Śiva and recite the Śiva-mantra.
Bharadvāja: Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before,
he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and then perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Having taken white ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire,
one should scatter them upon one's own head with the *īśāna* mantra.
Then, having taken that ash, one should apply it to the face with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra,
to the heart with the one called *Aghora*, and to the secret parts with the one named *Vāmadeva*.

One should sprinkle ashes on both feet with the mantra named Sadyojāta; thereafter, one should smear the entire body with the Praṇava mantra alone. This is declared by the supreme sages to be the Āgneya bath.
A wise person should perform this at the outset for the sake of the successful accomplishment of all activities.
Then, having washed his hands and other limbs and performed the ritual sipping of water according to the rules,
he should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) across the forehead, the heart, and the throat according to the prescribed method.
With a serene mind, one should apply either the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire or the sacred ash (*bhasita*) prepared with the five *brahman*-mantras.
This triple mark (tripuṇḍra), when worn, is purifying in all rites;
one should wear the triple mark constantly for the purification of all sins.
The twice-born and others must never wear ashes held in the hand of a Śūdra;
nor should the ashes ever be worn by Śūdras when held in the hand of an outcaste (antyaja).
Therefore, for the increase of his merit, a twice-born man should daily and without negligence apply the Tripuṇḍra mark using the very ashes produced from the Agnihotra fire.
Otherwise, all ritual acts never bear fruit.
As stated in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*:
"That triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) which is applied on the forehead with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb..."
In that regard, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is auspicious and the destroyer of great sins.
In the *Dharmasārasudhānidhi*:
"One should always apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) with ashes purified by mantras, according to the procedure declared in the Vedas; thus one shall attain union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*)."
In the *Smṛtibhāskara*: "When the moon has entered the forest (the new moon), one whose body is smeared with ashes,
upon seeing Śaṅkara worshipped, is liberated from all sins."

It is called *bhāsita* because it shines; it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities. It is *bhūti* because it brings prosperity to men, and it is the supreme *rakṣā* because it provides protection.
In the *Śrutisārasamuccaya*: "Whether one is impure or lacks proper conduct, and even if one should commit sin with the mind,
one shall always remain pure by the wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*)."
In the Śrī Mahābhārata:
"O King, a man who desires long life, or one who desires prosperity,
or indeed a twice-born who desires liberation, should always wear sacred ash."
In the *Nāradīya-smṛti*:
"The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) is supremely meritorious and consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Those terrible *rākṣasas*, *pretas*, and other lowly creatures [are repelled by it]."
Upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they flee without a doubt—
even after drinking liquor, approaching the wife of a guru,
committing theft, or having committed the murder of a Brahmin.
One who is covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes,
and reciting the Rudrādhyāya is liberated from all sins.
Truthfulness, purity, recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and other deities—
all of this is in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra.
In the *Lokākṣismṛti*:
"The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) made on the forehead with ash using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is praised as the destroyer of great sins."
Whoever, with a mind deeply bowed in devotion to Śiva, wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
by that great-souled one the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar— are sustained.
The excellent Brahmin who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), who bears rudrākṣa beads, and who is pure, destroys diseases, evils, ailments, famine, and thieves.
He who proceeds to the supreme Brahman from which he does not return again—
he is a purifier of the assembly, pure, and worthy of worship even by the Brahmins and the gods.
Kātyāyana says: "In the Śrāddha, sacrifice, recitation, fire-oblation, Vaiśvadeva rite, and worship of the gods,
a man who has applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes purified in soul and conquers death."
Whatever rite one performs without wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), that is in vain;
smearing with ashes and the horizontal triple mark are the daily practice.
The rejection of negligence is heard in the *Taittirīyaka*:
"One must not be negligent regarding prosperity.
In his own *Saṃhitā*, Romaharṣaṇa, the foremost knower of the meaning of the Vedas, [states this].
The foremost of those devoted to the ash has clearly explained the meaning of the word "bhūti."
From truth, from dharma, and from virtue; even from smearing oneself with ashes, from wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and from the study and recitation of the Vedas.
And from rites for the gods and the ancestors, from the worship of mother, father, and others,
as well as from all other ritual acts likewise.
If one who desires liberation does not constantly fall away from the practices taught in the Smṛtis,
and is endowed with the aforementioned means, he indeed proceeds from bathing to the sacred ash.

The supreme nature of Śiva is remembered as *bhasman* (ashes) because of its luminosity; that very same [nature] appears within the phenomenal world arising from His own *māyā*, like the sun reflected in water.
That ash which has entered into that very form is declared to be Śaiva; by even a trace of that ash, the Lord of Gods is present as a reflection.
Śiva is indeed independent, the embodiment of the image, eternally smeared with ashes;
that God is to be worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the highest of the gods.
In the *Atharvaśiras*, which illuminates the two types of sacred ash, there is heard a proclamation of the fruits that establishes the desire to wear the ash.
This is also clearly heard in the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad, beginning with the words "Agni...
[and so on], stating that one should rub ashes over the limbs while touching them.
This Pāśupata vow, which effects liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu),
was declared at that time by the Jābāla Upaniṣad itself.
With the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should wipe away the ashes and touch the limbs;
likewise, the wise person should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark both above and across.
In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, this is respectfully referred to by the term "beyond the stages of life" (*atyāśrama*).
The wearing of ashes is prescribed as a means for attaining knowledge.
Seated on a comfortable seat in a secluded place, pure, with his neck, head, and body held straight,
and abiding beyond the stages of life (atyāśrama), he [should restrain] all the sense organs.
Having ceased [all other thoughts], he bowed to his own guru with devotion.
In the Śvetāśvatara branch as well,
the wearing of ashes is prescribed as a means for attaining knowledge by means of the term "atyāśrama."
Then the wise Śvetāśvatara, through the power of his austerity and by the grace of the gods, correctly proclaimed to those who have transcended the stages of life this supreme purifier,
which is cherished by the assembly of sages.

The meaning of the state beyond the stages of life (*atyāśrama-pada*) has been proclaimed in the *Saṃhitā* by the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), who is devoted to the great ash while possessing only a small amount of ash.
The wise declare that the smearing with ashes using the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," as well as the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra, constitutes the Atyāśrama.
I worship that Śiva, known as Mahābhasma, who is always smeared with ashes and reflected in the image of Īśa, together with Ambā.
In this work, within the third part, the third chapter has been proclaimed— the medicine for the disease of sin caused by the most terrible curse of the six lords of sages.
To Śiva, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the unliberated,
who is liberation itself and whose nature is consciousness, I offer this meditation within my inner self.
I worship Him who is adorned with ashes, for whom the vow known as Pāśupata was proclaimed in the Atharvaśiras as a means to attaining knowledge.
For the sake of achieving the complete performance of the foremost Śrauta and Pāśupata rites, know that the wearing of the sacred ashes (vibhūti) is required; I shall explain it to you in brief.
Or else, [the ash] produced from the Agnihotra fire, or that arising from the Viraja fire,
or that produced from the Aupāsana fire, or that arising from the Samidha fire.
Having respectfully taken it up and placed it in a pure vessel,
he should wash his feet and hands, perform the ceremonial sipping of water twice, and remain composed in mind.
Having taken that ash into his hand with the five Brahma-mantras,
he should slowly perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) and then consecrate it with the mantra "Agnir iti."
Having consecrated that [water] three times with those same seven mantras,
and having recited "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" and meditated upon Viṣṇu as the lord of the waters;
Having mixed water with ashes using the mantras beginning with "agniriti," and having wiped [the body] while meditating on Śiva along with Ambā, one should smear [the ashes] from head to foot.
By means of that meditation, having become one with Brahman through white ashes,
[he should apply them] upon his forehead, chest, and shoulders with the mantra prescribed for his own stage of life (āśrama).
One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion at the three times of day, using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, both in the forward and reverse order.
This Pāśupata vow is devoid of the sacrificial staff, matted hair, and [the wearing of] snakes;
following the sprinkling of ashes as a form of bathing, one should thereafter wash both hands.
One should sip water twice at the end of wearing the *tripuṇḍra*,
likewise at the end of smearing oneself with ashes, and likewise at the end of the *tripuṇḍra*.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, the clear procedure for sipping water (ācamana) was declared:
the wise one should sprinkle all his limbs with the Praṇava.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, with darbha grass in hand and composed in mind,
he should offer salutation to the All-Self, saying "Obeisance to Nīlakaṇṭha," upon his head.
Then, having washed both hands, one should perform the sequential practice—
that which is certain, namely the Pāśupata and Śāmbhava Atyāśrama.
The vow proclaimed in the Kaivalya, Atharvaśiras, and Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣads,
which is joined with the Virajā oblation, matted hair, the staff, and so forth.
Those who know the meaning of the Vedas declare that [the Vedic tradition] is of two kinds:
that which is devoid of this [practice], and that which involves the adoption of conduct such as non-scriptural marks, sectarian signs (*puṇḍra*), and other such observances.
If you ask what the reason for the abandonment of the sacred ashes and other such items is, [the answer is]:
"Sin, the confusion of births, and conflict arising from the curse of a sage."
Furthermore, the curse upon the lotus-born Brahmā arising from Viṣṇu’s wrath is also a cause here;
all this is [explained] by Parāśara as the sun within the lotus-heart of the wise.

(p. 94) It has been demonstrated by the omniscient sage named Parāśara that in those men who possess great sins, hatred arises toward Maheśvara, who is established by the Vedas, as well as toward the application of the *tripuṇḍra* and the smearing of ashes (*uddhūlana*).
In ancient times, not realizing the superiority of Rudra, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa engaged in battle out of delusion, each thinking, "I am Brahman" and "I am [the Supreme]."
Filled with great wrath, Brahmā, the lord of the entire world,
being utterly deluded, cursed Viṣṇu, saying, "Become one dwelling within a womb."
Your devotees, the Brahmins, would constantly turn their faces away from the ash-marked Tripuṇḍra, even though Maheśvara is established in the Vedas.
The twice-born practitioners of Tantra should always be devoted to the *puṇḍra* marks, whether they be triangular, quadrangular, or shaped like a bamboo leaf.
The twice-born are marked with their own weapons, such as the conch, the discus, and others.
Due to great delusion, they may become heated by fire on both their shoulders.
There are many such curses. Now, the sixth chapter of the *Atharvaśikhopaniṣad* is written: "This is the conduct of Rudra; for this God indeed [pervades] all the directions."
For he was born first; he is within the womb. He is the one already born, he is the one yet to be born;

facing all directions, he stands with faces on every side. With eyes on every side, indeed with faces on every side, with hands on every side, and with feet on every side, he blows forth with his two arms and...

The one God, generating heaven and earth with his wings—that is what should be meditated upon. They call that the "internal grasping" (*antargrahaṇa*). This is the path extended upward, by which the gods, by which the seers, and by which the ancestors reach the supreme station, the ultimate goal.
In the center of the heart, [resides] that which is the size of a hair-tip— the universal Veda, the Jātavedas, the most excellent.
The wise who perceive that Self (sthaṃ) as such—
For them there is eternal peace, but not for others.
He who, being one, presides over every womb,
by whom all this is filled with the Puruṣa— him, the Lord, the giver of boons, the adorable God...
One should meditate upon that Supreme; one attains ultimate peace.
(95) They say that within the vital breaths is the mark of the mind—
that wherein there is anger, as well as thirst and hunger.
Having abandoned craving, the root of the web of causes, and having established that which was accumulated by the intellect within Rudra;

Rudra is indeed the oneness; for Rudra is eternal, ancient, the restrainer through food, vigor, and austerity. This is the Pāśupata vow: "Fire is ash" (wind is ash), "water is ash," "earth is ash," "space is ash"; indeed, all this is ash.

"Manas"—these are the eyes; "Bhasma"—with these words, having taken ashes with [the mantra] beginning with "Agni," one should rub them and touch the limbs. Therefore, this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu). The Brāhmaṇa who constantly recites the Arthavaśira [Upaniṣad]...

He becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by the sun; he becomes purified by Soma; he becomes purified by all; he becomes purified by truth; he becomes known by all the gods; he becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords; he [becomes purified] in all...
He becomes one who has studied the Vedas; he becomes meditated upon by all; he becomes one who has practiced the observances and conducts prescribed by all the Vedas;

he becomes one who has performed all sacrifices and rituals. By him, hundreds of thousands of recitations of the *Rudras* from the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* have been performed; [and] a hundred thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī*.

It becomes recited; ten thousand *praṇavas* have been recited. In every form, it purifies ten ancestors; it purifies ten descendants up to the sixth generation, even beyond the range of sight—so said the Blessed One, the *Atharvaśiras*. Having recited it once, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for ritual action.

It comes to pass. Having recited it a second time, one attains the state of Gaṇapati. Having recited it a third time, one enters into the very God—Oṃ, Truth! To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is within the waters, who has entered into the herbs and the plants, who has fashioned all these worlds—to that Rudra [be homage].

Homage be! Today Atharvan’s head shall be shattered, as he drives upward from the brain, blowing away the heart. Thus the Atharvaśiras, the treasury of the Veda, has been established. May Prāṇa protect it—its prosperity, its food, and its mind.
Prosperity is food, and then the mind; knowledge is food, and then the mind;
liberation is food, and then the mind; the *liṅga* is food, and then the mind; the *liṅga* is food, and then the mind. Thus: "Oṃ, Truth. This is the Upaniṣad.
The Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad is complete.
Now, for the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad: Saṃvartaka Agni is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda);
the illustrious Rudra in his universal form (viśvarūpī) is the deity (devatā); and its application (viniyoga) is in recitation (japa) for the purpose of pleasing Rudra. Now...

Sanatkumāra questioned the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra: "Teach me, O Blessed One, the true nature of the rite of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra): what is the substance, what is the location, what is the measurement, how many lines are there, what is the power, what is the presiding deity, who is the performer, and what is the fruit? He said to him:
The Blessed One Kālāgnirudra has said that whatever substance is [used], that is the fire-born ash (*bhasma*);

having taken it with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta*, or having consecrated it with the mantra "Agni is ash" (*agniriti bhasma*), one should lift it up with the mantra *Mā nastoke*, mix it with water, and apply it to the head with the mantra *Triyāyuṣam*.

One should draw three horizontal lines on the forehead, the chest, and the shoulders with the *tryāyuṣa*, *tryambaka*, and *triśakti* formulas. This is the *Śāmbhava* vow, which has been declared by the exponents of the Vedas in all the Vedas.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice it in order to avoid rebirth. Now, Sanatkumāra said:
The authority for this wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) is that there are three lines:
from the forehead to the eyes, from the eyes to the eyebrows, and from the eyebrows to the top of the head; and one from the middle of the eyes.
Of these, the first line is the *gārhapatya* fire, the letter *a*, the *rajas* quality, the *bhūrloka*, and the individual self (*ātman*).

The power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is the *Ṛgveda*, the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), and Maheśvara as the deity. That which is its second line is the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*), the syllable *ukāra*, the quality of goodness (*sattva*), the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the inner self (*antarātman*), the power of will (*icchāśakti*), the *Yajurveda*, the midday libation (*mādhyandinasavana*), and Sadāśiva as the deity. That which is its...

The third line is the Āhavanīya fire, the letter *M*, darkness, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the Sāmaveda, the third extraction (*savana*), and Śiva as the deity. Thus, the wise man— whether a student (*brahmacārī*), a householder (*gṛhī*), a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), or an ascetic (*yati*)— applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with sacred ash.

He becomes purified from all major and minor sins (*mahāpātaka* and *upapātaka*). He has bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). He has meditated upon all the gods. He is a constant reciter (*jāpī*) of the Rudra-mantras.
Having enjoyed all pleasures and cast off the body, he attains union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*). And not...
"He returns once more," said the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra. "Whoever hears and studies this Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad becomes exactly like that—Om, this is the truth.
Thus it is stated in the Jñānayogakhaṇḍa of the Sūtasamhitā.
Regarding the student (*brahmacārin*), it is said that he is a learned twice-born (*dvija*) who has been initiated:
"With ashes produced from the *samidh* fire, or from the fire of the *virajā* [rite],
or from the *agnihotra* fire, mixed with water..."
Having wiped all the limbs in sequence with the six or seven mantras beginning with "Agnis" and so forth, one should thereafter thoroughly dust them off.
Having become pure, one should apply three horizontal lines on the chest, the forehead, and the neck with ashes from the hands and other parts, while meditating upon Śiva and Śivā.
"A Brāhmaṇa should always wear [the sacred thread] with the mantras beginning with 'medhāvī'. Thus it is said.
In this very section, [it says]: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the householder's stage of life," referring to the gṛhasthāśrama.
Having introduced the subject—
One should perform the smearing with ashes once, according to the path taught in all the Vedas,
using the *Tryambaka* mantra together with the *Satarī* Śiva mantra.
One who has entered the stage of a householder should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
by that, everything has been studied and heard, and by that, everything has been performed.
By that Brahmin who has worn the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his head with ashes—
one should wear the triple mark with devotion and not transgress it even in thought.
"Because it is enjoined by Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
Thus, having introduced the subject with "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha)," [it continues]:
"A householder should perform the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes according to the path prescribed for himself."
Now, therefore, having introduced the subject with "I shall fully explain the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa)," it continues immediately thereafter:
"O best of sages, mendicants (bhikṣus) are to be known as fourfold according to the difference in their modes of life (vṛtti): the Kuṭīcaka, and likewise the Bahūdaka."
"The Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa—of these I shall tell you the conduct.
Having said this, and having described certain duties beginning with "The Kuṭīcaka, having renounced... and ending with "...one should constantly recite the Gāyatrī," [the text continues:]
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes alone during the three junctions of the day,
and one should worship the Śivaliṅga with faith every single day.
Having said this, and subsequently having described certain duties of the Bahūdaka— from the words "Bahūdaka" onwards up to "the earthen spade and the small sword"—
[he states] the smearing of all limbs with ashes and the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

Thus it has been stated that one should indeed maintain [these]. Immediately thereafter, by means of the passage beginning with "The *haṃsa* [should carry] a water-pot" and ending with "one should always respectfully carry a single bamboo staff," the author describes certain duties of the *haṃsa* as well.
"One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and smear ashes (uddhūlana), worship the Śiva-liṅga, eat only eight morsels once a day, and wear the hair in a topknot (saśikha). Thus it is said.

Immediately after that, having stated the duties to be abandoned by means of the passage beginning with "The Paramahaṃsa [should abandon] the triple staff," and so forth, and having subsequently stated the duties to be adopted by means of the passage beginning with "A loincloth for covering, a patched garment," and ending with "an unblemished bamboo staff," he says:

"One should joyfully perform the smearing with ashes using the mantras beginning with 'Agniriti' (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.37), and having uttered 'Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ,' one should apply the Tripuṇḍra along with the Haṃsa-mantra. Thus it has been stated.
In the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
For all mendicants, there must be tranquility, self-control, endurance,
ritual bathing, purity, non-violence, and the avoidance of false speech.
The constant smearing with ashes using the mantras beginning with "Agniriti" and the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra are directly identical in essence to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"The worship of Śiva at the *liṅga* is declared by the eternal ones to be the constant duty.
By this statement,
[the right of] *uddhūlana* for the *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa* [ascetics is established].
The necessity of always wearing the *tripuṇḍra* and the fact that the *tripuṇḍra* consists of the three deities (*trimūrti*) have been stated. In that very same [text]:
"Worship of Śiva at the *liṅga* and the wearing of *rudrākṣa* beads..."
With the mantras beginning with "Agni" and the seven [verses] spoken by Jābāla.
"Indeed, there is the smearing of all the limbs as well as the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

In this regard, because the wearing of ashes is a means for the accomplishment of mantras, it is understood from the indicative mark (liṅga) that it is a duty of the religious stages of life (āśramadharma). In that very same [text]:
Meditation on Śiva, knowledge of Śiva, as well as the chanting of the word "Śiva," and the smearing with ashes using the mantras beginning with "Agniriti."
"99) The wearing of rudrākṣas with devotion and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
as well as renunciation (saṃnyāsa), are a most great expiation for sins.
Here too, on account of the previously mentioned indicative marks and because of the injunction regarding renunciation, these constitute the duties of the [fourth] stage of life (āśrama-dharma).
In the Sūtasamhitā: "Both the householder and the forest-dweller should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) with the Tryambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the Śiva-mantra."
"Or even by the words beginning with 'the wise one,' the student (brahmacārī) should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) day after day with ashes mixed with water.
In this very statement, repetition (vīpsā) is also shown.
Now, regarding its permanence, the Sūta-saṃhitā states:
"One who has entered the householder stage of life should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) constantly;
a mendicant should also wear it constantly—such is the Jābāli Śruti."
In that very same [text]:
"The best among the believers, being ever vigilant, should likewise perform the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) daily."
O sinless ones, I have told you everything; one should especially be devoted to the realization of Śaṅkara.
In the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga:
"A householder and one in the forest-dwelling stage of life should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
one who has entered the stage of renunciation should also always wear the triple mark."
One should always perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
In the Mānava [Smṛti]: "One should always perform the smearing with holy ashes (bhūti) and the wearing of the triple mark."
Since it is superior to all dharmas, one should therefore practice it constantly.
This is the excellence of the sacred ash: that it should always be worn.
As stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"Those by whom smearing with ash (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) have always been joyfully practiced..."
They alone are the cultured and the wise, and not others, O best of sages.
Now, regarding its inviolability: "One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion; one should not transgress it even in thought.
Since it is enjoined by the Śruti, he who abandons it becomes fallen."
In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"The virtuous should always wear sacred ash in the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and smearing (uddhūlana);
one should not transgress against this smearing and the triple mark even in thought."
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "A learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) even in his mind;
since it is enjoined by the Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen."
Now, regarding the quality of being never to be abandoned: "One must not be negligent toward prosperity," so it is stated in the *Taittirīyaka*.
And in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"From truth, from dharma, from skill, and also from the smearing with ashes..."
By the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and also by the study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāya).
Whether from rites pertaining to the gods or the ancestors, from the worship of mother, father,
and others, or likewise from all other Śrauta rituals;
"And if one desires liberation, one should never fall away from the practices prescribed by tradition.
Regarding this very point, it is said:
"The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and the smearing with ash, established by the Vedas..."
One should not abandon the worship of the Rudra-linga, even if it is done out of delusion.
In the Parāśara [Smṛti]:
"One should not, even through delusion, abandon the smearing of the body with ash established by the Vedas as the *tripuṇḍra*, nor the worship of the *rudraliṅga*."

(p. 101) Now, regarding the fault in abandoning [the practice]: In the Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad—“Those men who perform ritual actions while omitting the wearing of ashes have no liberation from saṃsāra, even after ten million births.”
O wise ones, for those burdened by great sins throughout all their births, a very firm aversion toward the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing of ashes arises from every side.
O Brahmin, those who feel aversion upon seeing the ashes on [one's] forehead should be inferred by the wise to be of mixed birth.
Those men who, upon seeing one who wears ashes, revile him with their speech—
their origin from a Śūdra should be inferred by a wise man.
O Sage, it is certain that for those who always lack faith in the Vedic revelation,
there are no purificatory rites such as the conception ceremony (*garbhādhāna*) and the rest.
Those who revile the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself;
those who wear it with devotion wear him himself.
In the Sūtasaṃhitā, the words of a twice-born man named Suśīla addressed to a king named Bhujabala:
"O protector of the earth, he whose intellect is fixed upon the sacred ash, or even upon its wearing..."
The fortune of that sinful person is not born; it perishes at that very moment.
Poverty shall befall him, and likewise diseases arise;
for the sinner, deficient limbs shall occur—of this there is no doubt.
