Now, the scriptural statements establishing its capacity to fulfill desires are recorded: regarding its bestowal of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*),
the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad* states, beginning with "The knower thus goes," that having enjoyed every enjoyment,
at the end of the body one attains union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*) and does not return again.
In the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"The wise man should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, the two arms, and likewise on the chest; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
The person who maintains this consecrated ash according to the prescribed rite finds that his desires are fulfilled and even his misdeeds are destroyed.
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"The twice-born should wear [the sacred thread] with the six mantras beginning with 'Agni' in due order;
having wiped the limbs, they should touch them starting from the head down to the feet."
Then, having likewise smeared himself with ashes in that same sequence,
he should perform the smearing of all his limbs with the Praṇava and with the Śiva-mantra.
Then, having assumed the state of Śiva, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* known as the "Triple Longevity" (*triyāyuṣa*) and practice the yoga of Śiva.
One should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow during the three junctions of the day;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva).
Having abandoned that state of being a bound animal (paśu) and having performed the Pāśupata vow,
Mahādeva, Sadāśiva in the form of the Liṅga, is to be worshipped.
In the Śrī Mahābhārata:
"O King, whether a man desires long life, or prosperity,
or even liberation, a twice-born man should indeed always wear the sacred ash."

Now, regarding its purpose for liberation: in the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad* it is said—“One should draw three horizontal lines; this is the Śāmbhava vow, which has been declared by the exponents of the Vedas in all the Vedas. Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice that for the sake of non-rebirth. This is also seen in the *Atharvaśiras*.
By means of [the mantra] beginning with "Agni," etc.
In the Jābālopaniṣad,
the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra declares: "The fourfold ash cuts away sin and bestows liberation."
In the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"The best of sages, established in the Atharvaśiras, prescribe the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the purpose of removing the bond of Māyā."
In the *Kātyāyana-smṛti*:
"He who wears the *tripuṇḍra* mark with pure cold water and sacred ash attains the Supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt."
In the *Parāśaropapurāṇa*:
"By all who seek the highest good, and by those who have attained their caste through birth,
the application of ash in the form of the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* and the smearing (*avakuṇṭhana*) with ash [should be performed]."
The wearing of rudrākṣas should be performed by men seeking all forms of spiritual welfare.
As stated in the Kālottara:
"Therefore, whoever should perform this fiery ablution of Śiva..."
And being liberated from the fetters of existence, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Now, regarding its being an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñānāṅgatva*), the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* states: "To those who are performers of action, learned in the Vedas, steadfast in ritual, offering oblations themselves with faith— only to them should one impart this knowledge of Brahman, provided they have observed the vow of the head-shaving."
And that which has been practiced according to the injunctions—
in that very context:
"Furthermore, by one desiring liberation through an excellence of dispassion alone..."
Having cast aside all ritual actions and become tranquil through the desire for liberation.
Having taken the ash produced from the fire of the *virajā* plant, or that produced from the *agnihotra* fire,
one should apply it in sequence with the six Atharvan mantras beginning with "Agni."
Having respectfully rubbed his limbs from the head down to the feet,
and having thoroughly dusted them, he should prostrate before the true teacher with the knowledge of the Self.
"I shall cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra by means of my own self.
In the Parāśara Upapurāṇa:
"For those established in the Vedas and Vedānta, there is the smearing [of the body] with sacred ash alone."
It bestows right knowledge quickly; this truth has been spoken, there is no doubt.
In that very same [text]:
"For one by whom the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) have been joyfully performed,
the realization of Brahman indeed arises before long."

Therefore, one who desires liberation should always and constantly perform the ritual smearing with ashes and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), which are prescribed by the Vedas, together with tranquility, self-restraint, and other such virtues.
In the Sūtasamhitā:
"Compared to all the ancillaries of knowledge, white ash alone is superior;
for those steadfast in the wearing of ash, ash itself is directly named Śiva."
"Just as the supreme and transcendent reality shines forth through tranquility, so too [is it revealed].
Thus, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"The smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are respectfully regarded as limbs of knowledge."
The best of sages, the followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch, declare this.
"The best of sages, established in the *Atharvaśiras*, declare that smearing [the body with ashes] and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) are the complete destruction of ignorance.
O wise ones, by whomsoever the Pāśupata vow has been properly observed..."
"His knowledge shall arise, which dispels dense ignorance.
Thus it is said in the *Saurasaṃhitā*:
"Now, therefore, by the power of my compassion, I shall proclaim this to you."
The means to knowledge has been shown in brief by the Veda itself.
Peace, self-restraint, renunciation, and that which is called the "supreme swan" (parahaṃsa).
"Endurance of dualities and the like, one-pointedness of mind, smearing with ashes,
wearing the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra), and faith in the worship of Rudra.
Thus it is stated in that very same [text].
In all the branches [of the Veda], there is one single reality called Śiva, who is the mass of pure existence and consciousness;
likewise, there is knowledge concerning that [reality], and likewise the Śirovrata.
But he who chooses the knowledge of reality heard from all the scriptures should especially and constantly perform the head-vow with devotion.

One who is devoid of the *śirovrata*, even if endowed with all other dharmas, has no qualification for the knowledge of the Self as Brahman; of this there is no doubt. This *śirovrata* is the burner of the entire wilderness of sins.
Therefore, one should properly perform the practice (sādhana) of the Śiva-vidyā;
for the subtle Atharvaṇa Śruti reveals the most subtle meaning.
One should always properly perform that vow which he spoke out of affection,
using pure ashes and the six mantras beginning with "Agniriti."
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes, which is called the "Head Vow" (śirovrata);
one should respectfully observe this Head Vow during the periods of the twilight rituals.
As long as knowledge has not arisen, that [ignorance] is indeed his supreme knowledge.
Now, regarding its preeminence, the Sūta-saṃhitā says:
"Therefore, I shall state this in brief."
Śiva alone is the supreme authority of the Vedas;
he is declared the most excellent, and the smearing of pure white ashes as well as pure knowledge (viśuddhavidyā) are nothing other than him.
In the Parāśara Upapurāṇa: "For those established in all the Āgamas, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) smeared with ashes is superior to all other liṅgas; this truth has been declared by me."
For all beings indeed, the scriptural mark is unsurpassed;
one should apply the triple line (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with white ashes.
In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"Just as the majesty of the Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, is difficult to comprehend,
so too has that of the sacred ash been declared by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas."
In the Bṛhannāradīya:
"Those who are dear to Śiva, devoted to Śiva, intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet,
and who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)— they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas."
In the Saurasaṃhitā it is said:
"The smearing with ashes, the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and the worship of Śiva—
these indeed the Purāṇas proclaim with reverence as being of primary importance."
The vow known as the Pāśupata, which is called the "Beyond-the-Āśramas," is the most essential and supreme among all the Vedāntas.

"Especially for a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to dharma, there is the duty of smearing [the body] with holy ashes and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). And so it is said. Furthermore, regarding its power to destroy sin, the Kālāgnirudropaniṣad states:
The wise man—whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—who applies the triple mark with ashes becomes purified from all major and minor sins;
he is as one who has meditated upon all the gods; he is as one who constantly recites the Rudra-mantra.
In the *Bhāradvāja-smṛti*,

after beginning with "Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed *ācamana* as before," and having explained the methods for smearing ashes (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), it concludes as follows:
All this constitutes the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which is purifying in Vedic rites;
one should wear the triple mark constantly for the purification of all sins.
In the Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad:
"Having slept, having eaten, having drunk water, or having performed the necessary bodily functions such as voiding;
[one should not look at] a woman, a eunuch, a vulture, a cat, a crane, or a mouse."
Having touched others of such a kind, one should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
In that very same [text]:
"He who has abandoned the conduct of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), even though all his ritual actions have been lost..."
By wearing even a single horizontal triple-tilaka mark, he too is liberated.
In the Parāśara Upapurāṇa:
"One should always sleep on ashes, be covered with ashes, and wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
one should constantly recite the Rudrādhyāya for one month without indolence."
One should constantly and always recite either the *praṇava* or the five-syllabled mantra;
this shall be the expiation, for it is a secret—of this there is no doubt.
In the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga:
"O Sage, for those who consume forbidden food while preceded by the wearing of ashes, that very [forbidden] food becomes permissible for them; there is no doubt about this."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or burdened by all sins,
by resorting to the bath of ashes, one is liberated from all sins."
In the Vāsiṣṭha-laiṅga: "Listen to the fruit of merit for him by whom the sacred ash is thus worn:
even the multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) and other sins as well [are destroyed]."
They perish, O tiger among sages; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
As it is said in that very [text]:
"He who daily bathes with ashes after having first bathed in water..."
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, or a forest-dweller, he should practice with diligence.
Freed from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal;
what is the use of much speaking? The wearing of ashes is the means to liberation.
For one who is constantly engaged with the sacred ash, knowledge arises before long;
such a sinner shall be liberated from sin, of this there is no doubt.
In the Nāradīya-smṛti:
"Out of the power of my compassion, I shall briefly declare to you the means for the purification of all sins without effort."
Even a man who has fallen away from his caste and stage of life is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes, according to the very path prescribed in the Vedas.
A man who has abandoned fire-sacrifices and avoided ancestral rites is purified merely by wearing the triple mark with ashes.
Even a man who approaches another's wife, who commits treachery against others, or who steals the property of others,
is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes.
A heretic, a slanderer, one who is difficult to endure, or a man who commits offenses against his wife—
a person is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark with sacred ash.
A man who sells oil, betel, oil-cakes, perfumes, women,
and other such goods is purified merely by wearing the triple mark with sacred ash.
Even a man who reviles the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others,
is purified merely by wearing the triple mark with sacred ash.
A man who violates established boundaries, who defiles sacred fords, or who eats from a broken vessel,
is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes.
One who bears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the goad, the leaf of the holy fig tree, the circle, and the thunderbolt—
by the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes, a person is purified.
A person marked on the body with the conch, discus, and other weapons of the deity,
is purified merely by wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made of sacred ash.
A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed—
a man is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes.

The wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* in ashes does not only remove the sins of one who is devoted to the ashes; rather, it removes them for the worshiper of the one devoted to the ashes as well. As stated in another *Saṃhitā*:
"That man who washes the feet of one who wears the *tripuṇḍra*..."
Even a man burdened with every kind of sin is instantly purified.
In the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]: "Elementals, ghosts, piśācas, and other such beings, as well as diseases that are exceedingly difficult to endure,
flee without a doubt from the mere presence of one who is established in the sacred ash."
In the Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad: "Vibhūti, bhasita, bhasma, kṣāra, and rakṣā—
these are the five names of the self (ātman), corresponding intensely to the five channels."
It is called *bhūti* because it is the cause of sovereignty; *bhasma* because it consumes all sins;
*bhasita* because it shines; and *kṣāra* because it destroys calamities.
"Because it protects from the great terrors of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, and *apasmāras*, it is called 'Rakṣā' (Protection). In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Having spoken thus, the great sage Upamanyu bestowed this knowledge."
This Pāśupata yoga [he taught] to Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
Thus addressed by that best of sages,
the god Madhusūdana likewise propitiated the lord Rudra through his ascetic penance.
"With all his limbs smeared with ashes and endowed with matted hair and bark garments.
Regarding this, it is said: "In former times, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Senses, the Soul of the Universe, and the Son of Devakī, dwelt for one year always observing the Pāśupata vow."
"With all his limbs smeared with ashes, solely intent on the meditation of Rudra, Hari worshipped Śambhu, having undertaken the Pāśupata vow. Thus it is said.
And in the Padma Purāṇa:
Then, on the auspicious Ramagiri at the bank of the Godavari,
Rama installed a Shiva-linga and underwent initiation according to the prescribed rites.
With all his limbs adorned with ashes and equipped with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads,
he was consecrated with the holy waters originating from the confluence of the Gautamī and the Sindhu.
Having worshipped him likewise with wild flowers and wild fruits,
he remained seated upon a tiger-skin seat, covered in ashes and sleeping upon ashes.
In the *Saurasaṃhitā*, introducing the world of Rudra:
"Right there, the deities presiding over the syllables beginning with *praṇava* worship Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods, who bears the moon upon his crest."
The Praṇava is the support of all mantras and the designator of the Supreme Self;
it is matted, pure, and its form is smeared with ashes.
Adorned with armlets and bracelets, and resplendent with three sectarian marks (puṇḍra),
the Supreme Goddess Vyāhṛti is especially the bestower of liberation.
Radiant with rows of triple marks (*tripuṇḍra*) and smeared with sacred ash,
the highly fortunate Sāvitrī was adorned with two earrings.
She has a serene face, is divine, and bears a beautiful mass of matted hair;
her body is smeared with ashes and adorned with three sectarian marks.
And all other Vedic mantras that grant many desires [become effective] for those whose entire bodies are covered with ashes and whose foreheads are marked with the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra).
Adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa beads and joyfully wearing a mass of matted hair;
as stated in the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"In the meantime, the illustrious one, the most excellent among the supremely compassionate..."
He wore a black antelope skin as an upper garment and was adorned with the Āṣāḍha staff.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, wearing a pure horizontal *tripuṇḍra*,
and adorned with a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads, he joyfully recited the five-syllabled mantra.
"Accompanied by such disciples, the Great-Souled One has come in person.
Having introduced the topic with "prepared for the conclusion of the sacrificial session," at the point of describing the sages, [it says]:
"The sages are gentle, self-abiding, and free from all pairs of opposites."
Adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa beads and smeared with white ashes.
"Blazing with rows of triple-marks (tripuṇḍra), endowed with matted hair and bark garments,
they were constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga of Śiva, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Thus, having introduced the sages known as the Kāvaṣeyas as seekers of distinguished dharma:
Having gone to the side of the Himalayas, they performed their ablutions at the three periods of the day;
with all their limbs smeared with sacred ash, their foreheads were marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra).
"Adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa beads, wearing matted hair and bark garments—
thus were the sages, the best of munis, beginning with Śveta and ending with Ṛṣya,
numbering one hundred and twelve."

"And these [devotees] have their limbs smeared with ashes, their foreheads marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra), and they wear ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, being intent upon the worship of Rudra. Thus it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta* (p. 111).
This ash produced from the perpetual *agnihotra* sacrifice should always be worn by the Vedic practitioners upon the surface of the forehead, the chest, and the head,
as well as on the two arms in the form of horizontal *puṇḍra*s, accompanied by mantras; by doing so, they have effectively performed a hundred sacrifices.
Bathing in ten million times a thousand sacred fords and the gift of the entire, faultless earth [are not equal to this].
One should not wear a trident that is circular, facing upwards, or otherwise shaped like a lamp, a half-moon, or a four-pointed star;
nor should one maintain the sacred ash with water or other substances.
Falling into tens of thousands of hells.
A twice-born man should not have his own body branded with the marks of a trident, a wheel, a conch, or a thunderbolt;
for by doing so, he becomes fit for recitation and ritual performance, but unfit for conversation.
With his body thus marked, he goes to the terrible Mahāraurava hell along with those who performed the branding.
Even while censuring this wearing of ashes and maintaining a sense of rivalry toward it, he nevertheless wears the ashes.
The bodies of the Brahmins are entirely inhabited by hosts of gods on all sides;
those [bodies] which have been heated, struck from all sides, afflicted, cut, or pierced—
by these [acts], the gods indeed slay them, as they are utterly agitated by pain, with their whole being.
The king should expel from his own domain anyone who causes suffering to such a person.
It is proper to apply ash horizontally and clay vertically; if these two are reversed, there is total ruin.
Furthermore, even ash must be worn [in its proper place];
otherwise, if one applies ash over another substance out of delusion, it falls downward.
Furthermore, even sandalwood, saffron, and the like would become merely worldly clay.

The Brahmin, moreover, taking this sandalwood and saffron, as well as the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire, those born from the domestic (*gṛhya*) fire, those born from the *viraja* fire, and further those born from the sacrificial wood-fire,
applied them with reverence along with the mantras, while moving them horizontally in due order.
The sage Dhanika stated that there are seventy-four [syllables] in the *uṣṇih* meter, including the ploughshare, the shoulder, and the chest.

The white ash arising from the fire of the Śrauta ritual, which is free from passion (viraja); that produced from the fire of the domestic (gṛhya) rite for the householder who maintains the sacred fuel;
and the various kinds of ash belonging to those who have attained liberation, which invariably dispel the emergence of delusion—[all these are the same].
Having received everything from a truly virtuous guru, one must retain it; otherwise, one will be a partaker of suffering.
Having performed the smearing with ashes in the manner prescribed by the mantras, he who harbors neither attachment nor aversion toward those two [ashes and the body] is not a sinner;
he has been consumed by falling into the fire of Gautama’s curse. No one else is as stainless as Śiva.
A man who hates the rudrākṣa, devotion to Śiva, discourse on the Lord, or sacred ash, [is lost].
Enraged, the eminent sage named Gautama cursed a brahmin who, scorched by his harsh words, had placed ashes and rudrākṣas upon the site of Śiva’s temple during the rite of worshipping Śiva,
and who was engaged in conversation and stories praising Śiva among the devotees of Maheśvara.
They hate the king who knows Brahman in many ways, for the word of the virtuous is indeed never in vain.

A wise man should not perform that which has been declared as pleasing by sages, recorded in the Smṛtis, arisen from tradition, practiced in due order, and even performed by virtuous men as dharma, if it has been abandoned [by others]. Indeed,
whatever local custom is appropriate for a particular region should be observed, even if it is not accepted by others.
Therefore, based on the words of the Śruti, ash should be worn by those born of all countries and families.
Keeping the hair and beard, wrapping the head, covering the breasts, likewise for women on the road, carrying earthenware vessels,
renouncing paternal property, crossing the ocean, [and having intercourse with] the husband's brother— these are [forbidden].
Furthermore, in the Kali age, one should avoid procreating sons and marriage that does not involve physical injury [to the woman].

In the Kali age, the Gomedha, Naramedha, and Hayamedha sacrifices, as well as the departure for a pilgrimage, the highest stage of forest-dwelling, and the state of perpetual celibacy, are all to be avoided by followers of the Vedas.
Those established in Yoga who have conquered their senses [should instead pursue] the supreme goal declared in the assembly of the Upanishads (the crest-jewels of the Vedas).
Having propitiated Śiva with devotion, one should proceed while wearing Rudrākṣa beads and sacred ash on one's own body.
The sacred ash worn upon the surface of the forehead produces the vision [of Śiva];
it extends the crescent moon upon the head, the dark mark upon the throat,
the woman at the side, the deer on the arms, and the trident upon the body.
At the end, one should worship the tiger, the elephant, the lion, the mountain, and the bull with invincible offerings.

The *liṅga* is the divine jewel; the white ash is the perfected medicine; the Vedic mantra consisting of five syllables, preceded by the *praṇava*, is the supreme mantra of the *manus* that grants the fruits sought;
it is skillful in the act of subjugating the woman who is liberation. Yet, he himself is attached to her.
One should never abandon it until, by necessity, it becomes eternal.
Wherever that best of men, Bhasma Śrautamahodaya, resides, there Lord Śaṅkara is worshipped daily by Gaurī as he offers Him that [ash];
whatever is given to him becomes inexhaustible, for he is indeed the supreme, faultless, and liberated one.
Even if born for a thousand lifetimes, one who possesses neither ashes nor the sacred thread shall never attain liberation.
For the welfare of the worlds, Śiva bestowed upon the Goddess the supreme virility arising from the fire of Rudra, as well as pure ash for the sake of protection and preservation;
it instantly destroys the venom of spirits, piśācas, rākṣasas, hosts of pretas, serpents, and scorpions.
The ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) pacifies death caused by insects, tigers, phlegm, or heat; it bestows all prosperity and auspiciousness. It pacifies manifold sins and is superior to bathing in water.
By performing it, it effects both external and internal purification and utterly destroys the fear of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Skilled in removing all diseases and impurities,
it was borne upon the heads of Śiva, Agni, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and others, as something irreproachable.
Having taken pure ash from the sacrificial fire, produced from the fire of the *viraja* rite kindled with fuel-sticks,
and originating from the domestic (*aupāsana*) fire, which is likewise purified;
One should keep [the alms] in a wooden bowl or a cloth bag.
Having washed his feet and wiped them with water, holding the *pavitra* in his hand and being well-composed,
he should then sit upon *darbha* grass facing the east.
Facing north, having placed the ashes in his hand.

Then one should mutter the Pañcabrahma-mantra three times while restraining the vital breaths (prāṇas); then, with all [the mantras] beginning with Agni, one should consecrate [the water] seven times.
Having joined it with water by reciting "Oṃ āpaḥ," one should sprinkle oneself with the [mantras] beginning with Agni while muttering them.
Meditating upon Śiva accompanied by Ambā, [he offered] even his two arms from his head down to his feet.
(114) Having first performed the smearing with ashes, which removes sin and is like a bath, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
that white ash-water [is purified] by means of fire and the other elements.
Or else, the measurement of the eyes is made with the middle fingers.
With the ring finger, thumb, and middle finger,
one should write with five-colored powders while reciting the Tryambaka mantra ten thousand times,
following the natural direction on the forehead.
Or, one may apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rule, either in reverse order or in the correct order.
Just as [the mantra] consisting of Brahmā, Hari, and Īśvara resides on the forehead, the heart, the belly, and the two excellent arms,
so too does this [mantra] belong to the householder who has gone to the forest.
Furthermore, the rule for those belonging to the [student] stages of life is stated.
The fire produced from fuel-sticks, the stainless fire-born fire, and the sacrificial fire belong only to those belonging to the [four] stages of life (varṇin), and not to others;
[one should apply] the previously mentioned mantras to ashes mixed with water.
It should be worn specifically for the sake of the threefold life-span.
A monk should apply the *puṇḍra* crosswise with his own mantra joined with three *oṃ*s and the *haṃsa*;
a *śūdra* should do so with the mantra of Śiva ending in *namaḥ*.
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and perform the smearing with ashes (paridhūlana).
The white ash produced by the cooking fire of true Vedic scholars, constantly shaken from their garments, [is pure];
whereas that born of a forest fire belongs to those beyond the Śūdra class.
They declare that the ashes should be worn accompanied by mantras.

They say that for maidens and noble women, having meditated upon Śiva with the five-syllabled mantra, the application of ashes and the smearing [of the body] should be performed while visualizing Him as accompanied by Ambā;
this is to be done solely for the sake of attaining liberation.
The ash used in the Śrauta rite is from sacrificial wood; in the Laukika rite, it is of two kinds.

(115) For Brahmins, it is prescribed that the ash should be maintained with water at all three times of the day; for women and mendicants, it is without water; for those living in vows or in the forest, it is of various kinds;
and for men who have not received initiation, it is traditionally held to be accompanied by water until midday.
Other virtuous people say that this is equal for all, and that there is no prescribed method to be known.
Having discarded that which is most closely bound, namely the over-ripened [body], one should place that excellent, pale ash— smeared upon it—
in a superior vessel made of wood, stone, clay, or metal, or in a fine cloth, so that not even a single atom of it falls upon the ground.
If it falls upon the ground, it leads only to fault; if held upon the head, it bestows liberation.

Having bathed and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should place the sacred ash in the hand; consecrated by the Sadyojāta and other mantras, one should then perform the smearing (uddhūlana). Thereafter, one should wipe the head with the Īśāna mantra, the face with the Tatpuruṣa, the heart with the Aghora, the navel with the Vāmadeva, and the feet with the Sadyojāta.
This smearing of all the limbs with *sadyojāta* and the other [mantras] is the *āgneya* bath.
Having then taken up pure milk, one should touch another cloth twice;
bathing in this [milk] removes the great sins of men.
And for one who is unable [to perform other rites], water also brings about purification.
Furthermore, the Sūtras and the Śrutis proclaim the greatness of this sacred ash.
Having taken up the ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should rub them and touch the limbs.
This is praised by the passage starting from "This is the Pāśupata vow" and ending with "Thus spoke the Blessed Kālāgnirudra."
Even a hundred [other merits] are not equal to the majesty of the sacred ash; thus it has been sung by the sages, and even as it is being proclaimed,
O faultless one, may I never again return to this shore today.
The greatness of Śivagiri is indeed the direct manifestation of divine power itself.
The greatness and merit of sacred ash, the destruction of sins by the rudrākṣa,
as well as the [merit] of uttering the name of Śiva and of the Śaiva vow.
The majesty of Śiva’s merit, the non-committal of offense against the Lord,
the majesty of the worship of Śiva, and the splendor of Śiva-yoga.
O best of the twice-born, all this greatness of the knowledge of Śiva was taught by Skanda of immeasurable splendor to Agastya.
By the power of my compassion, I shall today explain that to you as it truly is:
ash is traditionally known to be of three kinds, distinguished as the Kalpa, Anukalpa, and Upakalpa.
Because it burns away all sins and because it is the remembrance of the Lord, it is called *bhasma*; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The person who maintains this consecrated ash according to the prescribed rite will have his desires fulfilled and even his misdeeds destroyed.
Just as the majesty of the Lord of Pārvatī cannot be fully known,
so too has the nature of sacred ash been described by those who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāntas.
Truth, knowledge, compassion, faith, fire, wind, water, earth,
and all the elements beginning with space— these, O twice-born ones, are indeed ashes.
By the gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, by the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others of mixed castes.
This ash, which is exceedingly dear to Śiva, should indeed be worn by women;
through its wearing with the mantra, the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvaryāṇi) are accomplished.

those seized by the evil influence of a malignant gaze are [subdued] by consecrated ashes alone.
In this world, one sees that happiness is easily attained;
yet, due to the defect of one's vision, it is not perceived as such, even when treated with clay, charcoal, and vermilion.
O wise ones, observe for yourselves how people in this world are liberated from the bondage of the ear-ornament (kautuka),
whether it be that which is prescribed by the Śruti, the Smṛti, or even ordinary custom.
Indeed, all the authors of Gṛhya-sūtras, as well as Tryambaka,
have prescribed that one should perform the rite of sprinkling with white sacred ash alone.
Moreover, people on earth who have been consumed by curses revile the sacred ash;
therefore, those born of the lineage of Buddha who disparage it are disparagers of the Vedas.
Those of great sin, fallen from their duties due to their actions,
were cursed by sages such as Gautama and others, and reduced to ashes by Śambhu.
The supreme understanding regarding the rudrākṣa does not arise in those sinners;
these wicked sinners, branded with the heated seal, are untouchable by the devotees of Śambhu.
Those most wicked people are not to be spoken to, nor are they even to be looked upon;
yet in that land, sinful men are seen again by the devotees of Śiva.
To eliminate those defects, one initiated into the Śiva-dīkṣā should either recite the five-syllabled mantra or gaze at the sun.
Through such words and others, as well as through prohibition,
faith in the sacred ash arises by the power of merit for those of meritorious deeds.

Thus ends the eighth instruction, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sacred Ashes," in the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, composed by the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who was proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secrets of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
The Ninth Instruction:
In this ninth instruction, the origin of the rudrākṣa is described as it is recounted in the first half of the Kiraṇāgama, the Purāṇas, and other such texts.
Formerly, during the destruction of Tripura, the first sweat that fell upon the earth from [Śiva’s] eye was of four kinds and golden in form;
from that there arose a great tree, which is called by the name Rudrākṣa.
(p. 134) Then Bhusuṇṭha questioned the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra:

"How did the Rudrākṣa originate, and what is the fruit from wearing it? The Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra said to him: "In ancient times, for the purpose of slaying Tripura, my eyes were opened wide. From them..."
Drops of water fell upon the earth; they became rudrākṣas for the sake of bestowing grace upon all.
By the mere utterance of their names, the fruit of giving away ten cows is obtained.
Through seeing and touching them, double the fruit is obtained. Beyond this, it is not possible to speak further.
I am able [to explain]. Regarding this, there are these verses:
"From what is it born? What is its name? Or how is it sustained by men?"
How many faces do they have here, by which mantras are they sustained, and how?
For thousands of divine years my eyes have been opened;
from both of them, with their beautiful lashes, drops of water have fallen. (2)
There, the drops of tears became great rudrākṣa trees, having attained the state of stationary beings for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees. (3)
Through devotion, it removes the sin committed at night during the day, and that committed during the day at night;
from seeing it, a hundred thousandfold merit arises, and from touching it, ten millionfold merit is produced.
A person who upholds it obtains a hundred crore merits,
as well as thousands of lakṣa-crores and hundreds of lakṣa-crores.
A person obtains merit from the recitation of that [mantra] by wearing rudrākṣa beads;
indeed, by wearing auspicious rudrākṣas, there shall be a great fruit.
That which is the size of an āmalaka fruit is declared by the wise to be the best; that which is the size of a jujube fruit is called the middling.
The lowest [caste] shall be the size of a chickpea; this system is now declared by me.
By the command of Śiva, there are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Trees born upon the earth are of that same nature as auspicious eyes;
those that are white are to be known as Brāhmaṇas, while those of red color are Kṣatriyas.
Yellow ones are to be known as Vaiśyas, while black ones are declared to be Śūdras. A Brāhmaṇa should wear white ones, but a king should wear red ones. (10)
A Vaiśya should wear yellow [beads], while a Śūdra should wear black ones;
those that are copper-colored, glossy, firm, thick, and provided with thorns are auspicious.
One should avoid six types of rudrākṣas: those bitten by insects, those that are split or broken, those devoid of thorns, those covered with sores, and those that are not round.
A rudrākṣa that has its own opening formed naturally is considered the best in this world;
however, that which is produced through human effort would be mediocre.
A wise person should fasten the rings—which are equal, smooth, firm, and round—with a linen thread, ensuring they are symmetrical across all parts of the body. 14.
That rosary on which a line is clearly visible, like a streak of gold upon a touchstone, should be known as the most excellent; it is to be worn by the worshippers of Śiva. (15)
One should wear a single rudrākṣa on the topknot, thirty on the head,
thirty-six on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms.
One may also wear twelve beads on the wrist; one should carry five hundred on the shoulder, and one should employ a rosary of one hundred and eight beads for the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
One should wear two strings, or three strings, or five strings,
or even seven strings, around the region of the neck.
On the crown, the earrings, the ear-ornaments, and the necklaces; on the armlets, the bracelets, and especially on the waistband. (19)
A man should always wear rudrākṣas while sleeping or drinking;
three hundred are said to be the lowest number, and five hundred are called the middling.
A thousand [recitations] are declared to be the highest; one should thus maintain them according to their divisions:
with the Īśāna mantra on the head, and with the Tatpuruṣa mantra on the throat. (21)
It should be worn on the neck with the Aghora mantra, and likewise on the heart;
the wise one should wear it on both hands with the mantra known as Aghora.
(136) One should place the mantra "vyomavyāpin" along with fifty syllables on the belly;
the three garlands consist of five, seven, and five [syllables], accompanied by the five Brahmans and the ancillaries (aṅgas). 23.
Alternatively, one may wear all the beads with the root mantra.
Then Bhusuṇṭha questioned the blessed Kālāgnirudra regarding the different types of faces of the Rudrākṣas, what the nature of each bead is, and what its fruit is.

"Tell me that which is endowed with the nature of its own essence, which destroys misfortune, and bestows the desired fruit. Kālāgnirudra said: "I shall speak that by hearing which there is immediate liberation for listeners and the grace of Śiva; listen with an attentive mind," he said.
The single-faced rudrākṣa, however, has the nature of the supreme reality (paratattva).
By wearing that, one who has conquered the senses merges into the supreme reality.
Furthermore, there is the two-faced rudrākṣa, which is of the nature of Ardhanārīśvara. (25)
By wearing it, Ardhanārīśvara is eternally pleased with him;
and the three-faced Fire himself directly consumes the sin of killing a woman in an instant.
The three-faced rudrākṣa is declared to be the triad of fires;
by wearing it, the consumer of oblations (Agni) is pleased and clearly grants all desires. (27)
The four-faced rudrākṣa is declared to be the form of Brahmā;
the five-faced rudrākṣa, however, has the nature of the five Brahmās.
Brahmā himself, who possesses five faces, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
Sadāśiva is always pleased merely by its wearing. (29)
The wise declare that the six-faced rudrākṣa has Kārttikeya as its presiding deity, and it also has Vināyaka as its presiding deity. (30)
The seven-faced rudrākṣa has the sevenfold garland as its presiding deity;
by wearing it, there shall be great prosperity, supreme health,
and a vast abundance of knowledge, and one remains eternally pure through its wearing.
The eight-faced rudrākṣa has the eight Vasus as its presiding deities;
it is dear to the eight Vasus, brings pleasure to Gaṅgā, and is auspicious. (31)
By wearing that, these speakers of truth shall become pleased. The nine-faced rudrākṣa, however, has the nine śaktis as its presiding deity.
Merely by wearing it, the nine Śaktis are pleased.
The ten-faced Rudrākṣa is declared to have Yama as its presiding deity. (33)
It generates joy in the ten directions when worn; of this there is no doubt.
It has eleven faces, possesses eyes, and has the eleven Rudras as its deities.
They say that this twelve-faced rudrākṣa, which has Indra as its presiding deity and is the very form of Mahāviṣṇu, always increases good fortune. (35)
Devoted to that indeed, he maintains the twelve [eyes] presided over by the Ādityas;
and the thirteenth eye, which is auspicious, bestows desires and grants purity. (36)
By the mere retention of this, Kāmadeva becomes propitious;
it is the fourteen-faced eye, born from the eye of Rudra. (37)
It removes all diseases, and one shall always obtain good health;
[one should avoid] liquor, meat, garlic, onion, and even the śigru plant. (38)
A man who avoids the śleṣmātaka fruit, village pigs, and other forbidden foods during an eclipse, at the equinoxes, and also at the solstices [attains great merit]. (39)
On the new moon day, on the full moon day, and on auspicious days,
one is immediately liberated from all sins by wearing rudrākṣa beads.
The root of that rudrākṣa is Brahmā; its stalk is said to be Viṣṇu;
its mouth they call Rudra; and its dot (bindu) is all the deities.

Whether a child, a youth, or an old man, whoever studies this Upaniṣad becomes Śiva. He becomes a teacher of all mantras for everyone. With these very [mantras] one should perform the fire-oblation (homa), and likewise with these one should perform worship. This [Upaniṣad] of the Guru destroys demons and delivers one from death.
Having obtained it, bind it around the neck, the arm, or the topknot.
One should not even conceive of the earth, consisting of the seven continents, as a fee for the purpose of a sacrificial gift. || 41 ||

Therefore, whatever cow one gives with faith, that becomes the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). A Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who studies this Upaniṣad in the evening destroys the evil committed during the day; by studying it at midday, he destroys the evil committed during the six months.
It destroys [evil].
(Studying in the evening destroys the evil committed during a year.
Studying both in the evening and in the morning destroys the evil committed over many lifetimes. He who...
The Brāhmaṇa who is a Vīraśaiva studies this Upaniṣad;

he obtains the fruit of one who has performed six million and five hundred thousand recitations of the Pañcākṣara mantra. He becomes purified from the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. He becomes purified from the drinking of liquor. He becomes purified from the theft of gold.

One becomes purified from eating forbidden food; one becomes purified from association with such persons. One becomes consecrated for all sacrifices; one becomes bathed at all sacred fords. One becomes purified from consuming what should not be eaten; one becomes purified from approaching women who should not be approached; one becomes purified from violating the bed of a guru.
By conversing with one who has fallen [from his caste], he becomes purified; he purifies a hundred thousand lines [of ancestors];
he attains union with Śiva. He does not return again, he does not return again. Om, this is the truth.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "The greatness of the rudrākṣa seed, which is identical with Śiva, has now been correctly described through its full majesty."
Tell me in detail according to the rules:
what is it like, by whom, and when should it be worn?
Nāthaśarman:
In ancient times, there was a famous Daitya named Tripura, who was invincible against all those of faultless character.
By him the gods were slain, the wielder of the discus conquered Viriñca, and the lords of the quarters were defeated.
Giriśa was praised for a thousand autumns by those who remained after the slaughter and were utterly terrified; being pleased,
he reflected, desiring to strike back at him.
A weapon difficult to obtain even for the entire host of immortals.
Opening their eyes for a thousand autumns for the protection of the world— [eyes] which emit sparks, possess the brilliance of the sun, and destroy all that is inauspicious.
The Maghorama weapon for the purpose of destroying enemies.
Then his three eyes became agitated, and tears fell from them;
they became *rudrākṣa* trees with their branches.
By the command of Śiva, for the welfare of the entire world.
The Rudrākṣa trees born from the sun’s eye are twelvefold, distinguished by their tawny varieties;
those born from the moon’s eye are sixteenfold and white in color.
The ten black ones are born from the fire-eyed one.
The Brahmin seed is white, endowed with the color of Kapila;
the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are both of a dual nature;
they declare the Śūdra seed to be black.
The various species originate from the rudrākṣa seed.
The single-faced seed-syllable of Rudrākṣa is Śaṅkara himself manifest; it destroys the sin of killing.
The two-wheeled seed-syllable destroys the sin of slaughtering many cows.
It is the deity of the Lord of Gods, unattainable for the eyes.
May that [deity] whose three faces are said to be fiery, which instantly destroys the killing of women,
and which possesses four faces worthy of being gazed upon by the four-faced one, protect you.
It destroys the sin of killing a human being in an instant.
Indeed, when one holds in hand the Skanda Purāṇa, which contains the Kālāgnirudra with its five faces,
the destroyer of the sins of consuming forbidden food and associating with the wicked,
and which possesses six faces;
It should be worn on the right hand by a Brahmin for the sake of purification from the sin of killing a twice-born.
Indeed, the Lord of Serpents, Ananta, bestows immediate purification from theft and other sins upon the seven-faced [image];
likewise, the eight-faced golden image of Gaṇeśa does so.
It is clear that [this practice] destroys sins such as approaching the wife of one's guru.
The nine-faced Bhairava himself is the deity;
holding it in his left hand, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, possessing power equal to that of Śiva.
It destroys even ten million times the sins of those who have committed murder.
Hari himself is the seed-syllable of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa),
and [the subduer] of piśācas, bhūtas, grahas, and rakṣasas,
as well as of all vetālas and adversaries— the lion among warriors.
It swiftly destroys the ferocity of tigers and other such beasts.
One should wear upon the crest, according to the faultless rite, the eleven-faced [form] with ten fierce eyes;
[it yields the merit of] ten thousand human sacrifices, horse sacrifices, and Vājapeyas.
It is equal to a thousand gifts of a thousand cows.

That which is spoken by the twenty mouths is known as the *Bhāskariya*; it abides in the letters, brings satisfaction to the Sun, and, when recited twice, is equal in merit to the sins of two hundred horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*).
Everything is accomplished, including all enjoyments and fortunes, [as well as the welfare of] the fetus, the noble ones, the mother, and the father.
One is purified from the killing of a brother or a woman by giving [the flesh of] a dadhna; there is nothing superior to this.
One should wear a single rudrākṣa on the head,
place a garland of thirty-six on the crown,
and wear thirty-two around the neck.
And it should be worn on the heart, fashioned with fifty [beads].
A rosary of beads should be worn on the two arms by those who possess artistic skill, while a rosary of beads should be held at the limit of the wrist;
alternatively, the garland may consist of one hundred and eight beads.
For a garland made with half that [number] is indeed half of it.
He by whom a rosary of eight hundred rudrākṣas is fashioned and always worn around the neck, having recited [the mantra] while holding it, shall obtain the merit of a thousand sacrifices.
Oh, by merely wearing them around one's neck, one instantly obtains merit greater than that of great sacrifices;
for even a donkey, though dead, became like Rudra on Mount Vindhya by carrying a load of rudrākṣas, and Hāhā became a faultless attendant of the Lord for a hundred kalpas on Kailāsa.

White, red, yellow, or even black— these colors of the rudrākṣa are traditionally assigned to the brahmins and the other castes respectively. One should wear this [rudrākṣa] accordingly on the crest-lock,
in the hand, around the neck, on the pair of ears, as a sacred thread, or on the heart, having bound it with silver or other materials.
One who is liberated by means of the mantras known as the five-syllabled Praṇava becomes unknowable.

Whether during bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, the performance of vows, worship of the deities, giving gifts, initiation, ancestral rites, or sacrifice, one who possesses a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads should perform all Vedic rituals while wearing them;
then the fruit of those actions shall become inexhaustible.
If it were not so, this [effort] would be in vain; alas, this evil one is certainly guilty of a faultless [deed].

Some do not place a garland on their chest during birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), death-impurity (*śāva*), the voiding of water or excrement, or when in contact with a woman, thinking that their own life-span would be diminished.
One should apply the venerable [garland] to the face; one who is like [the Lord] in face [should wear it] with pearls, coral, and black [stones].
A mortal who offers honey and fruit with golden jewels shall become irreproachable.
If even a dog, having died while bearing a rudrākṣa upon its body, becomes liberated and goes to the city of Śiva within a single muhūrta, it shall not be born again;
what need is there for many words? One who always wears this [rudrākṣa] upon one's own limb along with the mantra [attains this].
O faultless one, I shall tell you how a person does not enter into saṃsāra again.
By the touch of the wind that has brushed against the flowers, sprouts, and buds of the Rudrākṣa tree,
even distant trees, grasses, and creepers attain imperishable fruit.
May a man constantly wear that jewel, which bears the characteristic mark born from that meritorious tree.
"He would release one from the bonds of saṃsāra"—is this not something truly wonderful, O beloved?
Having thus learned of the origin of the rudrākṣa with reverence through these words,
the wise and illustrious person who wears it shall attain union [with the Divine] at the end.

Thus ends the ninth instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, the knower of the one hundred and one stages of the secret doctrine of the illustrious Viśiṣṭādvaita school.
The Tenth Instruction:
In this tenth instruction, the wearing of rudrākṣas is set forth, as declared by the Śaiva doctrine obtained through traditional practice. (1)
"Beginning with the words, 'I shall describe to you the greatness of wearing rudrākṣas,' this is set forth in the Skanda-bhāsvat-purāṇa. (2)
It removes all sins and is meritorious for those who read it or even listen to it;
whether one is devoid of devotion or devoted, whether a fool or even a greater fool—(3).
Whoever wears a rudrākṣa is liberated from sins;
the sages who perceive the truth call this the "Great Vow" (mahāvrata). || 4 ||
With what indeed could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared?
He who, firm in his vows, wears a thousand rudrākṣas— || 5 ||
The gods and asuras bow down to him; he is just like Rudra.
In the absence of a thousand [arms], however, there are sixteen on each side.
One [syllable] on the crest-lock, twelve on each of the two hands,
thirty-two in the region of the throat, and six on each of the two ears.
He who wears one hundred and eight Rudrākṣas on his chest and forty on his head is indeed worshipped like Rudra himself.
He who wears Rudrākṣas made of pearl, coral, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, or gold is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. (9)
Even he who wears only rudrākṣas and the mudrās of Rudra is not touched by sins, just as darkness does not touch the sun.

A mantra recited with a rosary of Rudrākṣas bestows infinite fruit; (the recitation of men without Rudrākṣas yields only that much fruit). Even a single Rudrākṣa upon one's body bestows great merit. (11)
The birth of that man would be as meaningless as a forehead devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
for the wise man who bathes after placing a rudrākṣa upon his head.
The fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him; there is no doubt in this—provided he worships the rudrākṣa after performing its consecration with water.
One certainly attains that very same fruit which results from the worship of the Liṅga;
[whether one has] one face, five faces, or likewise eleven faces. || 14 ||
Certain rudrākṣas with fourteen faces are honored by the world;
even a poor mortal who worships them with devotion shall obtain prosperity. || 15 ||
Listen with attention, O Brahmins, to these meritorious narratives.
Formerly, in the village of Nandigrāma, there was a woman well-known as Mahānandā.
There was a courtesan beautiful in every limb;
her parasol resembled the full moon, and her vehicle was resplendent with jewels. (17)
She has fly-whisks with beautiful handles, golden sandals, variegated garments, and couches resembling the luster of the moon. (18)
There were hundreds of cows and buffaloes, and garments in great numbers;
this was his anointing with perfumes, saffron, camphor, and musk. (19)
She wore most excellent ornaments and possessed wealth numbering ten million;
she was constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Always intent on stories of Śiva and eager for the chanting of Śiva’s names,
she would always bow with joy upon seeing people who were devotees of Śiva.
p. 144) For the sake of diversion, that courtesan [placed] a single monkey and a cock, adorned with rudrākṣa beads, in the middle of the dance pavilion. || 22 ||
She herself constantly causes [them] to dance with hand-claps and songs;
then, surrounded by her companions, she laughs loudly. (23)
Adorned with armlets, neck-ornaments, and earrings made of rudrākṣa beads,
the monkey dances before her like a child, following her instruction.
With rudrākṣa beads tied to the tip of his crest, the cock, together with the monkey, being a knower of reality after dancing for a long time, brought wonder to those who watched. (25)
In due time, these two, the monkey and the cock, met their death at the hands of the king named Bhadrasena, the ruler of the realm of Kaśmīra.
The son of Markaṭa was indeed Sudharma by name;
and the son of that minister Kukkuṭa was named Tāraka. (27)
Both those princes, exceedingly affectionate and beautiful in form, being young boys devoted to the study of sciences, engaged in play together. (28)
Both of them had Rudrākṣas for ornaments on all their limbs,
adorned with necklaces, armlets, crowns, earrings, and other such decorations.
Having set aside their ornaments made of gold and jewels, the two of them wore rudrākṣas;
they were constantly garlanded with rudrākṣas and adorned with excellent rudrākṣa bracelets.
With rudrākṣa beads as their neck-ornaments and always wearing rudrākṣa earrings, those two, born into a noble family, enjoyed all desired pleasures. (31)
Through their former practice, endowed with faith and devotion toward the rudrākṣa,
they attained in time the supremely auspicious state of Śambhu.
Also in the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad: Then Sanatkumāra questioned the blessed Kālāgnirudra, saying, "Teach me, O Blessed One; tell me the procedure for wearing Rudrākṣa beads."
At that time, Nidāgha, Jaḍabharata, Dattātreya, Kātyāyana, Bharadvāja, Kapila, Vasiṣṭha, Pippalāda,
and others approached Kālāgnirudra and said: "Now, Kālāgnirudra, for what purpose..."
"Regarding your arrival," they said, "we all wish to hear the ritual procedure for wearing the rudrākṣa beads. Then Kālāgnirudra spoke:
"It is well known in the world that rudrākṣas were produced from the eye of Rudra; or else..."

Sadāśiva, having performed the act of withdrawal at the time of dissolution, closes his eye of withdrawal; it is explained that the rudrākṣas were born from that eye, and therefore they possess the nature of rudrākṣa— so declared Kālāgnirudra.

When that Rudrākṣa is made an object of speech, one enjoys that fruit which is obtained by the gift of ten cows. "This very Rudrākṣa is Bhasmajyotis," he said. Desiring to touch that Rudrākṣa with the hand, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a hundred cows.

By the mere wearing of that rudrākṣa, the fruit of giving away a thousand cows is obtained. When that rudrākṣa is worn on the two hands, the fruit of giving away two thousand cows is obtained. When the rudrākṣa is worn on the neck, the fruit of giving away three thousand cows is obtained. [When it is] worn on the two ears...
The fruit is equal to that of giving away eleven thousand cows; or one attains the state of the eleven Rudras.
When it is worn on the head, the fruit is equal to the gift of ten million cows. Regarding these locations, he said:
"It is impossible to describe the fruit for [wearing it] on the two ears."
Then Sanatkumāra asked: "Is there indeed a fruit for the gift of Rudrākṣas?

Then Kālāgnirudra replied: "By giving one hundred and eight Rudrākṣas and wearing one hundred and eight Rudrākṣas, one obtains that same fruit which is obtained by the gift of the entire circle of the earth."

He enjoys the fruit. "This indeed is the light, the Rudrākṣa," he said. Then Sanatkumāra questioned the blessed Kālāgnirudra: "Is it possible to wear a thousand Rudrākṣas in succession? Then Kālāgnirudra replied: "Regarding the wearing of Rudrākṣas..."

Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration (*adhivāsa*) and ending with the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should wear *rudrākṣa* beads for one year; one attains the state of Brahmā. One should wear two thousand *rudrākṣas* for two years;
one attains the state of Viṣṇu. One should wear three thousand *rudrākṣas* for three years.
He attains the state of Sadāśiva. He does not return again; he does not return again. "He alone is the light, Rudrākṣa," so it was said. Then Sanatkumāra questioned the blessed Kālāgnirudra.
"Tell me the essence of all the Upanishads and the fruit of its retention. Then Kālāgnirudra spoke:
"I shall tell you the essence of all the Upanishads; listen attentively. On this point, there is this verse.
Thus it is said.

The Tenth Instruction, titled "Description of the Wearing of Rudrākṣa," from the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who was proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secret of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
The Eleventh Instruction:
In this eleventh instruction, there is the praise of rudrākṣas; all the statements seen in the Vedas and Āgamas are presented here in their entirety and in proper sequence. (1)
Formerly, there was a king of the Puṣkara region named Saumya;
he was always devoted to evil ways and was constantly fond of delighting in courtesans.
His wife was Vasumatī, endowed with beauty and youth;
seeing that the king was visiting courtesans and was dissatisfied with her own self, she [acted].
Then, with a mind overcome by grief, he went before his wife named Satyavratā and spoke these continuous words of lamentation.
Having informed the king of his misconduct and the cause of his own suffering, [he asked:
"By what reason could there be a lack of delight for him in his own [kingdom]? (5)
When she had asked this, she replied to her once more:

"O sovereign of brahmins, there is no one like you in this entire world. (199)
"O virtuous one, since you wear this purified Rudrākṣa around your neck, you are blessed, O great being of steady mind and firm vows! (200)
"You are indeed Rudra, of this there is no doubt, and you are worthy of worship by the best of the gods.
Choose a boon, O meritorious soul; I shall grant you whatever you desire. (201)
Having heard these words of Kālī, Śāntika then said to her:
"If a boon is to be granted to me, and if you have affection for me as well. (202)
O Goddess, let this human sacrifice not take place for you every year;
rather, with a satisfied mind, grant whatever this king desires.
Having heard those words of his and having likewise granted him that boon, the Goddess, looking at the king, spoke these words again: (204)
O King, always worship him who is adorned with the excellent Rudrākṣa beads;
having heard these words of Rudra, you ought to abide by them. 205.
"Give your daughter to him according to the rite of marriage;
if this is done, all your desires will be fulfilled. (206)
O King, because they brought him forward for the sake of the sacrificial offering,
he was truly slain by that very fault in your presence.
"O Lord of the Earth, his son has also died today, and his blameless wife has likewise died;
moreover, his great house has been consumed by fire. (208)
Those brothers and fathers who hate him are extremely sinful;
they have their wealth stolen by thieves and are tormented by diseases such as leprosy. || 209 ||
Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, without food and without shelter,
they wander from country to country, submerged in an ocean of suffering.
Those who worship this one wearing rudrākṣas like Maheśvara, having their sins eternally burnt away, rejoice upon the earth like gods. (211)
Having heard these words of Kālī, the king, filled with joy,
caused his daughter’s resplendent hand to be taken according to the prescribed rites.
Having constructed for him a dwelling adorned with various jewels,
the king gave it to the twice-born man and, beholding him, honored him as if he were Lord Śiva himself.
Even Śāntika, having considered such a fruit as resulting from wearing a single rudrākṣa on the neck,
the arms, the shoulders, the wrists, and even the head, [proceeded accordingly].
He indeed wore Rudrākṣas numbering more than a thousand;
accompanied by his wife, he remained in the palace, sporting with joy.
Having heard this entire account, his paternal uncles and brothers,
concluding that he was indeed their own, quickly reached that region.
Having seen them—those who had abandoned the conduct of the twice-born and whose bodies were drenched with wounds—he joyfully brought them into his exceedingly beautiful home. (217)
Having quickly bathed them with oil and provided divine garments,
this observer of vows adorned them all with rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
Through the greatness of the rudrākṣa, they too were freed from diseases such as leprosy;
they constantly wore divine garments and were adorned with celestial ornaments.
Having enjoyed pure pleasures together with this Śāntika,
they reached the incomparable Kailāsa, filled with supreme joy.
O Great-minded One, it is indeed heard that even though he did not know it, Rudrākṣa was worn by him at that time under the mistaken impression that it was a jewel; its fruit is truly complete.

Who indeed among the wise could know the fruit obtained here by those who, having recognized Rudrākṣa as the supreme ornament of Śiva that bestows both heaven and liberation, joyfully and properly wear it upon their own bodies according to the prescribed rite, thereby burning away their own sins?
Having abandoned Śaṅkara, Ambikā, and Gaṇapati, truth has been proclaimed by me. || 222 ||
Having heard the words of Supradīpa, they were filled with wonder;
from that time forward, they have worn the rudrākṣa, which is the ornament of Rudra.
Having burned away the flood of his sins and abandoned the bondage of his own karma, the lord of sages quickly attained the state of a Śiva-yogin through the grace of Śiva alone. || 224 ||

He attained liberation through the knowledge of Śiva, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to achieve. From that time forward, the king also shone, adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads.
Having ruled an entire kingdom free from enemies for many ages, and having enjoyed vast pleasures endowed with human bliss, [he passed away]. (226)
O twice-born ones, having entrusted the kingdom to his son,
Supradīka also departed for the world of Śiva after describing the greatness of the rudrākṣa.
Having reached his own home, he enjoyed various kinds of pleasures for many years with great joy, resplendent and accompanied by his sons and grandsons. || 228 ||
Accompanied by his disciples, grand-disciples, kinsmen, and his wife, he ascended a divine celestial chariot adorned with divine women. (229)
He was surrounded by the sounds of celestial drums and high-flying showers of flowers,
with hosts of divine sages walking ahead of him.
Having sent the Kalpavṛkṣa tree and likewise the ornament, which were dispatched by Indra,
he presented them to Mahākāla Maheśa in Ujjayinī.
Then, together with this very cat, she went to the world of Śiva;
thereafter, in the course of time, she attained union (sāyujya) with the Supreme Lord.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, you have previously described the greatness of the sacred ash (bhasman), and you have also described the greatness of the rudrākṣa, which is esteemed by all. (233)
"By the mere wearing of ashes, all desired objects are fully attained.
O Tāpaseśvara, if that is so, for what purpose should the rudrākṣa be worn?"
O expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, sever this doubt of ours;
there is no other scholar besides you who can resolve this uncertainty.
O ascetic, when great beings such as you are present as listeners,
there is nothing that should not be spoken, even the supreme secret that purifies.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Sūta, the best of those learned in the Purāṇas,
spoke with a deep voice, his lotus-like face graced by a gentle smile.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages who are now free from sin;
even a mere smearing of ashes with a single drop of water has been performed by him.
O Brahmins, if fear arises for embodied beings due to rain, bathing, contact with people, and other such causes; || 239 ||
For spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, as well as rākṣasas, predatory beasts, thieves, tigers, lions, and the like—all of whom always seek to pierce one's vital spots—[are kept at bay by this]. (240)
The gods on earth (brāhmaṇas) treat with contempt one who lacks ash and rudrākṣa;
therefore, one should constantly wear rudrākṣa on the ears, the neck, the hands, and so forth. (241)
One who desires his own welfare should wear it together with the ashes;
O Brahmins, this [ash] is not like ordinary ash, nor is it subject to decay by water or other such means.
Neither ghosts, spirits, nor piśācas, nor even rākṣasas harm him;
and serpents do not bite one who wears ashes and rudrākṣa beads. (243)
O twice-born ones, this rudrākṣa should be strung with a thread made of gold, silver, or copper, and worn around the neck and other parts of the body.
Or else, O twice-born ones, one should always wear a single sacred thread (yajñopavīta) smeared with ashes;
therefore, with every effort, one should be adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads.
He does not fear his enemies and remains truly fearless;
regarding this, O brāhmaṇas, I shall relate a supreme ancient history.
In the land known as Savitṛ, there was a certain great ruler named Sindhusena, residing in the beautiful and glorious city of Sūrapura. (247)
But that one of great strength, having conquered in battle his enemy, King Siṃhābha—the lord of the Vindhya region and ruler of the city named Kākalā—[returned]. || 248 ||
O best of Brahmins, he caused [the enemy] to flee with his own army in that great forest;
meanwhile, that lion, having lived in that forest for a long time, [returned] once again.
Having propitiated Govinda, the destroyer of all enemies, through ascetic penance,
he obtained a very great discus that brings about the destruction of foes.
At the time of the offering of the discus, Mādhava was then pleased;
performed five times, this incomparable rite shall be the destroyer of enemies. (251)
"O Lord of the Earth, thereafter he will come into my presence";
having spoken thus and bestowed this wonder, the god vanished in an instant. (252)
Having obtained that [opportunity], the powerful king Mahīpāla emerged from the forest in an instant and suddenly surrounded Sindhusena along with his army.
Having fought again, he engaged the terrifying discus;
that discus suddenly struck down the entire army, leaving nothing behind except him.
(166) Again, he encountered his most terrifying hand;
this Sindhusena, all alone, entered the exceedingly fearsome forest. || 255 ||
While wandering there, O gods, he reached the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
having seen Vasiṣṭha there along with himself, Gautama, and others. (256)
Having prostrated before Kauśika, Nārada, and the other great sages, he said:
"O sages, endowed with supreme knowledge and firm in your vows! (257)
"Let the wise know me as the Lord of this entire region;
yet here I am, defeated in battle by an enemy of equal splendor. (258)
Now, having sought refuge through the weight of your merit, may I achieve sufficient victory by some means or other. (259)
"O Blessed Ones, O lords of sages, please tell him that means.
Having heard these words of his, all those best of ascetics [spoke].
Having deliberated upon the supreme means for victory, the prosecutor took with his own army ashes and Rudrākṣa beads that bestow victory. (261)
If battle is waged, victory will surely follow; of this there is no doubt.
(And all your armies shall be devoid of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads. Indeed, all armies are destroyed by the absence of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads. || 262 ||
"O best of ascetics, thus has it been said by you; from that [statement] arises doubt. Having considered these words of his, some of the foremost among those who practice austerity [spoke]. (263)
O King, because you have worn the ash and the victory-bestowing rudrākṣa,
it is certain that the discus has emerged from you, leaving you behind for this very reason.
The King said: "Even by me, having applied sacred ash and wearing rudrākṣa beads, was this battle fought;
yet I am smeared with musk and sandalwood paste and adorned with necklaces of pearls. (265)
"O best of ascetics, I only know this much: that I entered the battle adorned with blue gems and pearls. (266)
"Nevertheless, having released me and struck down the army, the discus has departed.
Hearing these words of the king, the sages of rigid vows [spoke]. (267)
"Cleanse now here the pearl necklaces and the other garland as well. Having said this, they quickly began to cleanse the pearl necklace.
There, having seen a single rudrākṣa, they showed it to him;
upon seeing this, they were overcome with wonder and likewise trembling with fear.
"O King, by whom was this given, and from what point has it been worn?
Having reflected upon this, tell us today in our presence exactly as it is. (270)
The King said: "When I set out from my home in haste, fully prepared for battle, a certain merchant then gave me this as an offering. (271)
Having seized this with the speed of his hand, he advanced upon the field of battle;
yet, due to the confusion of the fray, this pearl necklace was not cleaned. || 272 ||
Having heard these words of his, those sages were greatly amazed; "O King, you have been restored to life by his majesty—of this there is no doubt. (273)
Defeated and his strength destroyed, he made an effort to kill [him] once [the arrow] had emerged;
thereafter, you took hold of ashes and the most excellent rudrākṣa beads. (274)
He was surrounded by his forces, who bore ashes and rudrākṣa beads;
if he emerges for battle, victory will certainly be his.
"There is no other means for victory superior to the sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Having heard these words of theirs and having resolved that it was so, he [acted accordingly].
Having applied sacred ash and wearing rudrākṣa beads, and having resolved to fight,
he set out alone from the forest, taking up his excellent bow.
At that time, some of his armed soldiers gathered together;
having given them sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, he made this supreme effort.
He quickly besieged the city of Siṃha along with his own forces;
Siṃha, too, having emerged swiftly with his troops, raised a great clamor.
He dispatched that discus, the destroyer of all enemies;
with a great roar, that discus reached the enemy army. (280)
Having seen them wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads and possessing the splendor of Rudra,
he bowed with supreme devotion and performed circumambulation of them.
O brahmins, as soon as he saw that the hand had withdrawn from the performer, he became utterly terrified and fled quickly to the forest, broken and defeated.
O twice-born ones, having heard this account, the exceedingly wise Siṃhaka performed very great penance, directed toward Varuṇa.
When the Lord of aquatic creatures was pleased, she requested an excellent boon:
"O Lord, Master of aquatic creatures, whenever rain is required by me," (284)
"If you would be pleased in every way, may it happen very quickly.
Having said, "So be it," Varuṇa departed swiftly toward his own abode. || 285 ||
Having thus obtained the boon, Siṃha, having raised a clamorous din, summoned Sindhusena for battle on the following day.
Sindhusena accepted that lion who was arrogant in battle;
then, even at midday, that lion called upon Varuṇa.
Then the Lord of Waters arrived with great speed in the form of water;
by that rain, the armies of both sides were thoroughly drenched at that time.
Among the armies of Sindhusena, those warriors who were mere wearers of ashes had their own splendors wiped away by that great rain.
Then, assuming a terrifying form as a lion, he of incomparable prowess took up his discus and joined the army of Sindhuseṇa.
Having suddenly assailed that great army of Sindhusena,
he surrounded it with ashes and [slew] many soldiers who were devoid of Rudrākṣas.
Having quickly killed and released the king, who was wearing rudrākṣa beads,
he swiftly placed his hand into the mouth of that highly powerful lion.
Sindhusena, being accompanied by only a few soldiers adorned with rudrākṣa beads, reached the forest in great distress. (293)
Having seen the ancient sages there, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, he bowed to them;
and having taken up sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, he associated with those who wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
O ascetics, having heard your words, Bala entered the field of battle;
he quickly joined his discus with it and [struck] our [warriors].
Having suddenly assailed that wheel and slain my brave warriors,
he left three or four of us behind and retreated toward the great [city].
Having observed him, he spoke thus to the sages, overcome with extreme fear;
having heard what was said by the king,
they reflected upon it within their own hearts at that very moment.
O Lord of the Earth, he who constantly bears this upon his body does not meet death by the weapons of enemies.
Having heard these words of theirs, he spoke again to the sages.
Having taken up sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, some were smeared with ash;
others engaged in battle, after which a torrential rain fell.
Then, when both armies were thoroughly drenched by the rain,
this lion released his discus, the destroyer of enemies.
"By that terrible one, my ascetic armies have been slain.
Having heard these words of the king, the sages there [sought] the cause.
Having observed the king and reflected in their minds, those gods on earth (the Brahmins) said:
"O protector of the earth, the most purifying ashes of those [who wear them] have been washed away by the rain. (302)
Those very same ones who were slain in battle, being devoid of the rudrākṣa,
have come back to life along with you, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣas.
O King, in ancient times, there was no fear even of the great gods for the Daityas of Tripura, who wore ashes and rudrākṣa beads. (304)
The gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, having raised up terrifying spirits through the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra), dispatched them swiftly. || 305 ||
O King, having suddenly seen all of them adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, those [beings] fled in terror. (306)
Furthermore, having rendered them averse to the sacred ashes and rudrākṣa beads,
the gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, caused them to be slain by Śiva.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads,
should fearlessly put your enemies to flight in battle along with your own soldiers.
A rudrākṣa, the supreme ornament, should be worn together with sacred ash;
for ash alone is certainly washed away by rain and other such elements. (309)
O King, the Rudrākṣa beads are not defiled by rain or other such elements;
however, those who merely wear ashes are dead even while alive. || 310 ||
"It is truly said that those ashes were washed away by a great rain.
Having heard these words of theirs, the king became free from anxiety. || 311 ||
Saying "So be it," he quickly bowed to them; having taken the rudrākṣa along with the sacred ash, he gave a rudrākṣa to the soldiers together with the ash.
Accompanied by all his soldiers of immeasurable valor, whose every limb was adorned with ashes and decorated with rudrākṣa ornaments, he went forth. || 313 ||
O twice-born ones, he quickly challenged that lion, who was like a śarabha to a lion;
then the great lion, whose weapon is the discus, set out for battle.
Then a tumultuous battle indeed took place between those two;
thereafter, Siṃha, uttering cries of "kila-kila," hurled his discus.
Beholding that entire circle adorned with ashes and rudrākṣas,
he performed three circumambulations, prostrated, and departed in haste.
Then, out of anger, he remembered Varuṇa, the remover of his own distress;
and at that time, O twice-born ones, there was a heavy rain upon both armies.
The ashes of those followers of Sindhusena were scattered;
observing that, O twice-born ones, he once again employed his discus.
O best of the twice-born, having seen these soldiers—though their ashes were smeared away—adorned with excellent rudrākṣa ornaments, he fled out of fear, thinking them to be Cakrin. (319)
O best of Brahmins, having seen this, the lion, along with his army, suddenly took to flight toward the forest out of great fear.
Sindhusena, too, having suddenly raised a great clamor,
captured his city and established his own territory.
Having given sacred ash and rudrākṣas to those residing in his own country, that high-minded one caused them to become wearers of sacred ash and rudrākṣas.
Having recollected the majesty of the sacred ash and the rudrākṣa beads, he himself resided there;
having dwelt for a long time and enjoyed pleasures according to his desire.
Accompanied by all the people residing in his own country as well as his beloved kinsmen,
he ascended an incomparable celestial chariot and reached Kailāsa.
