The lords of the Brāhmaṇas gradually attained liberation and freedom from misfortune;
and that lion, too, having abandoned passion and hatred through dispassion, [attained the same].
Having worn sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and having remained for a long time in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta),
he attained at the end of his body's life that liberation which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should wear the rudrākṣa together with the sacred ash.
O brahmins, it is celebrated as "rudrākṣa" because it is the eye (akṣi) of Rudra. || 327 ||
Śambhu bestows his full and gracious glance upon those who wear rudrākṣas;
all who wear rudrākṣas are proclaimed to be of the very form of Rudra. || 328 ||
Those men who hear, read, or cause others to hear the majesty of this rudrākṣa are indeed the very embodiment of Rudra himself. || 329 ||
Having obtained long life, health, sovereignty, sons, and grandsons,
those wise ones attain union with Śiva in the end.
Therefore, a twice-born man should be encircled by rosaries of rudrākṣa beads;
for him whose birth is supreme, the wearing of rudrākṣas is essential.
In the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) as well as in the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), there shall be supreme faith in men; it is difficult for others to attain.
(172) He in whose body there is even a single rudrākṣa, possessing a disposition toward Śiva—his body is indeed a temple of Śiva; he is Śambhu, Śiva himself, manifest. || 333 ||
He on whose body there are no rudrākṣas and no wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)—
that body is indeed a cremation ground, and his mouth is a mountain cave.
He who has a garland of ornaments on his neck consisting of one hundred and eight beads interspersed with coral is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. (335)
He who daily fashions a rosary of one thousand and eight beads and wears it at the times of recitation is superior even to Rudra. (336)
The wise man who wears a mantle of rudrākṣas and bears a crown of rudrākṣas— indeed,
the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are merely the dust at his feet.
Having constructed a pavilion of rudrākṣa beads, the wise man should worship Śiva together with Ambā;
under his control remains Śambhu, along with his attendants, Soma, and Śaṅkara. (338)
The life of that person by whom the ear-ornament of rudrākṣa has been worn is truly fruitful, having realized the meaning of all the Upaniṣads. || 339 ||
He who beholds the Śaivas wearing rudrākṣa beads with a spirit of devotion to Śiva—
his eyes have become fruitful, and he indeed possesses true sight.
But he who regards those richly adorned with rudrākṣa rosaries as mere human beings—by him worship is rendered useless, and both recitation and fire-offerings are fruitless. (341)

Or whoever beholds those adorned with the ornaments of rudrākṣa beads with a spirit of devotion to Śiva, by him all austerity has been performed and by him the worship of Śiva has been accomplished. || 342 ||
He who is consecrated by water touched by Rudrākṣa beads has performed a bath in the Gaṅgā and has accomplished the highest pilgrimage to sacred fords.
He who devoutly gives a single rudrākṣa to a devotee of Śiva has given the earth filled with grain to those learned in the Vedas.
He who devoutly wears a garland consisting of one hundred and eight [flowers] rejoices on Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva together with his own kin. (345)
One should certainly not give rudrākṣas or a rosary to those who are not devotees;
if one should give them out of delusion, one becomes averse to Śiva. (346)
Having examined them, one should bestow upon the devotees the sacred ash and rosaries of rudrākṣa;
thus favored by Śiva, such a person attains union with Śiva.
Or, by means of obstacles against those who are not devotees, he should instill devotion to Śiva;
and as a devotee of Śiva, he should employ every effort to establish others as devotees of Śiva. (348)
With every effort and remaining ever vigilant, one should constantly make one's own home, one's own village, one's own kin, and one's own kingdom Śaiva.
Being pleased by that, the Supreme Śiva bestows His own state of union (sāyujya).
One who has become Śiva’s body, one who is devoted to Śiva, one who is a kinsman of Śiva, and one who worships Śiva—[these are the recipients]. || 350 ||
Surrounded by devotees of Śiva, he himself shall dwell in the kingdom of Śiva;
however, one who desires Śiva for himself must renounce a kingdom that is not devoted to Śiva. (351)
This person, the most excellent devotee of Śiva, has entered the kingdom of Śiva;
he is always engaged in conversation about Śiva and constantly contemplates the names of Śiva. || 352 ||
Possessing meditation on the Śiva-mantra and partaking of the nectar of Śiva, he who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva attains union with Śiva. || 353 ||
Even one who is himself a devotee of Śiva, by daily conversing with and associating with those who hate Śiva, partakes in the fruit of that sin. (354)
One should diligently avoid the proximity of such persons;
association with true devotees bestows the fruit of all desires upon devotees. (355)

Thus ends the eleventh instruction, titled "The Praise of Rudrākṣa," in the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the Vedas and Āgamas, composed by the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who was proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secrets of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita Siddhānta.
The commencement of the twelfth instruction:
In this twelfth instruction, I shall describe the method for the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra according to its proper application, following the path of the Purāṇas and Āgamas. (1)
The color, the deity, as well as the power, the support, and the meter;
the seer, the location, the Brahman, and likewise the weapons. (2)
Kalā, guṇa, vaktra, prakāśa, and likewise karaṇa—the vital airs and the organs of knowledge; thus these sixteen have been enumerated in order.
The letter *na* shall be yellow in color; its presiding deity is the Brahmāstra, its power (śakti) is said to be Sāvitrī, and its support is likewise the Earth.
It is indeed joined with the Anuṣṭubh meter and has Vasiṣṭha as its seer;
the western face is Sadyojāta, the first Brahma-mantra.
The weapon is said to be the thunderbolt alone, and the digit (kalā) is indeed cessation (nivṛtti);
the quality (guṇa) is said to be hardness alone, and the four [elements] follow in sequence.
The instrument is the mind itself, shining with the brilliance of a blazing fire;
joined with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), it is the perceiver of the sense-objects.
Thus, among these sixteen, the syllable *na* is said [to correspond to the first];
the syllable *ma* is of the nature of water, and its presiding deity is likewise Viṣṇu.
Lakṣmī is declared to be the Śakti, and water is indeed the support;
it is joined with the Triṣṭubh metre, and Viśvāmitra is likewise the seer (ṛṣi). || 9 ||
The northern face is Sthāna, Brahmā, and Vāmadeva;
its weapon is said to be the lotus, and it is endowed with the kalā named Pratiṣṭhā.
The wheel of the qualities (guṇas), joined with fluidity, is like a half-moon; it is the instrument endowed with intellect, manifesting through the light of the moon alone.
The sense organ of taste is conjoined with the apāna wind;
thus, this group of sixteen is called the syllable *makāra*.
The letter Śa is of the nature of fire, and Rudra is its presiding deity (adhidaivata).
It is conjoined with the power Gaurī; it is both the support and fire itself. (13)
It is joined with the Uṣṇik meter, and Jamadagni is likewise its seer;
its position is on the right, its face is Aghora, and it is indeed Brahman.
The weapon is said to be the svastika, and it is also called vidyā and kalā;
endowed with the quality of brilliance, the discus is indeed threefold.
But by means of the light of the lightning, my form is the instrument;
it is joined with the vyāna breath and endowed with the faculty of sight. || 16 ||
Thus, among these sixteen, the letter 'Śi' is said to be the seed-syllable;
the letter 'Va' is the form of Vāyu, whose presiding deity is Īśvara. (17)
Ambikā is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), and Vāyu is indeed Udāna;
it is joined with the Bṛhatī metre, and the sage is Kāśyapa.
The locus is said to face the east; it is Brahman by means of Tatpuruṣa.
The weapon is in the form of a bindu, and the kalā is likewise Śānti. (19)
Endowed with the light of the qualities, it becomes the tactile sense-organ;
thus, the letter *va* is said to consist of these sixteen.
The letter *ya* is indeed of the nature of space (*vyoma*), its presiding deity is Sadāśiva, and it is said to be the power Unmanī; for the support is indeed space itself.
One should know that it is joined with the Jagatī meter, has Bhāradvāja as its seer (ṛṣi), and its location is upward-facing; it is Brahman and Īśāna himself. || 22 ||
Among weapons, the trident (śūla) corresponds to the Śāntyatīta-kalā;
and among the qualities (guṇas), it is the Void (śūnya), which is the radiance of the moonstone.
The instrument (karaṇa) consists of the subtle element of form (rūpa), the air of equal breath (samāna-vāyu), and the sense organs of hearing; these sixteen [evolutes] follow in sequence. (24)
The syllable "Ma" is said to be neither past nor future;
it is the one and only primordial matter (pradhāna), remembered as the five-syllabled [mantra]. || 25 ||
Through the application for the accomplishment of desired aims, the direct manifestation becomes fivefold.
Thereafter, that which is called the "array" (prastāraka) shall consist of one hundred and twenty-one [units]. (26)
Thus the five-syllabled [mantra] has been declared; it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
The mantra is said to be of five kinds, and the ritual action (karma) shall be of eight kinds. || 27 ||
Others arise from the five syllables and dissolve back into that very same place;
the seventy million great mantras appear in manifold ways through various forms and faces. (28)
They dissolve back into the five-syllabled [mantra] and emerge from it once again;
that which is joined with the six paths and the bindu is known as the body (kalevara). || 29 ||
Endowed with sixteen digits, it abides in the form of Nāda;
subtle and situated within the Tapas region, it is established in the five syllables.

Therefore, the five-syllabled mantra, which is the designator, becomes fivefold: one should first utter "Oṃ," then "Namaḥ," and thereafter the three syllables "Śivāya. Thus, "Oṃ" is the single gross syllable, while from the letter "Na" onwards it is "Namaḥ Śivāya. This is "Śivāya Namaḥ."

"Maḥ śivāya na iti," "ya namaḥ śiva iti," and "namaḥ śivāya iti. The five digits (*kalā*) consisting of consciousness (*cit*) and the supreme will, knowledge, and action (*icchā-jñāna-kriyā*) transcend that; they are conjoined with the supreme digit (*parā kalā*), which is encapsulated by the pentad of the Sādākhya state, and thus transcends both the supreme and the Sādākhya.

The five-syllabled mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya* is the gross form of the *praṇava*, whose referent is the pentad of *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*; it is a body composed of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) in the form of the five syllables beginning with *na*; and it is the nature of the six syllables consisting of both the individual and the collective aspects, which are of one and the same nature, both gross and subtle.

The Great Liṅga is directly inseparable from the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), consisting of the *bindu* and *nāda*, expressible by *nāda*, and non-different from its designator. From the face of Īśāna come the syllables *a* and *na*;
from Tatpuruṣa come *u* and *ma*; and from Aghora come *ma* and *śi*.

The *bindu* is the letter *va*, from Vāmadeva; the *nāda* is the letter *ya*, from Sadyojāta. These letters, consisting of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), having attained the state of the collective, become "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," that is, "Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. He who studies this Upaniṣad becomes supreme over all.
It comes to pass. One attains union with Śiva. "Om, Truth"—thus ends the Upaniṣad.
This concludes the Pañcākṣara-Jābāla-Upaniṣad.
In the Pañcabrahma-Upaniṣad:

"Oṃ! O Blessed One, what was born at the beginning? "The Sadyojāta. "What, O Blessed One? "The Aghora. "What, O Blessed One? "The Vāmadeva. "And what, O Blessed One, are these? "The Tatpuruṣa. "And what, O Blessed One, are all these? "The bestower of all sciences."

"Īśāna"—[the Lord] who is the sovereign of the past and the future, of all gods and yogis. How many phonemes, how many divisions, and how many powers [are there]? To Him, that Great God, the Great Rudra, to whom all that is secret belongs, the Blessed Maheśa spoke.
O Śākala, listen: if there is anything in this world more secret than a secret, hear it from me.
Sadyojāta, Mahī, Pūṣan, Ramā, Brahmā, Trivṛtsvara, the Ṛgveda, the Gārhapatya fire, and likewise the seven pleasant musical notes (mandra-svaras).
The color is yellow; the action is power; it bestows all desired fruits.
Aghora is water, Candra is Gaurī, and [the mantra] is the second Veda.
The sound resembling a rain cloud, dense and resonant, is declared to be the Dakṣiṇāgni;
it is conjoined with the fifty letters and endowed with the powers of maintenance, will, and action.
(178) It is joined with the protection of one's power, it destroys the flood of all sins,
it pacifies all suffering, and it bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
Vāmadeva, the bestower of great awakening, whose nature is fire,
endowed with the light of knowledge, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The Sāmaveda is serene, endowed with eightfold melodies;
it possesses both steady and unsteady tones, and is the unsurpassed Āhavanīya fire.
Joined with the withdrawal of knowledge and endowed with two powers,
it is a white syllable mixed with darkness, a vowel that brings about full awakening.
The controller of the three abodes, endowed with the three abodes,
the bestower of all prosperity upon men, and the giver of the fruits of all actions.
That which is joined with eight syllables, situated within an eight-petaled [lotus],
and conjoined with the mandala of wind, is declared to be Tatpuruṣa.
Joined with the fire of the *upadhā*, it is governed by the power of mantras;
known as the fifty vowels and consonants, it takes the form of the Atharva Veda.
The presiding lord of millions upon millions of hosts, whose form is the indivisible cosmic egg,
red in color, the granter of desires, and the medicine for all mental anguish and physical disease.
The cause of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth, the sustainer of all powers,
transcending the three states, is that which is designated as the Fourth (Turiya) Brahman.
One should know the Supreme Lord as the one to be served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; the progenitor of all, the supreme, the impeller, and the witness of the intellect.
It is of the nature of space, unmanifest, adorned with the sound of the syllable Oṃ;
it consists of all the gods, is peaceful, transcends peace, and lies beyond the vowels.
The Great One, whose body consists of ether, who is the presiding witness over the vowels beginning with 'a',
the controller of the fivefold acts, and whose nature is the five Brahmas.
Having performed the withdrawal of the five Brahmās, he abides within his own self;
having withdrawn all things through the majesty of his own power, he remains established in his own self.
Transcending the nature of the five Brahmans, he shines by his own innate splendor;
from the beginning, through the end, and in the middle, he shines, not by any other cause.
Deluded by the Māyā of Śambhu, all the gods do not know Mahādeva, the teacher of the world and the cause of all causes.
His form does not stand within the range of vision;
he is the Puruṣa beyond the beyond, the abode of the universe,
by whom the universe is illumined and into whom it is dissolved.
That Brahman is the supreme peace; I am that Brahman, the highest state.
One should know the five Brahmans, beginning with Sadyojāta and the others;
for whatever is seen or heard is itself composed of the five Brahmans.
That which exists in fivefold form is known as the effect of Brahman;
having realized it as the effect of Brahman, one attains Īśāna.
Having dissolved everything consisting of the five Brahmans into one's own self,
the wise man should realize "I am He," and thus become the immortal Brahman.
He who knows this Brahman—Śambhu, who consists of five syllables and whose nature is the five Brahmans—is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood the five-syllabled mantra beginning with *na* and ending with *ya*, one should recite it;
one should know that everything consists of these five, because its nature is the five Brahmans.
He who, permeated by devotion, studies this knowledge consisting of the five Brahmans,
attains a fivefold nature and shines forth himself in five ways.
Having spoken thus to the high-souled Gālava, Mahādeva showed him compassion right there and vanished from his sight.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"For one who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge and whose soul is overwhelmed by devotion,
O Kṛṣṇa, there is never any duty whatsoever, neither internally nor externally."
Therefore, having gradually abandoned both the external and the internal,
and having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should also relinquish ignorance itself.
If the mind is not one-pointed toward Śiva, what is the use of performing ritual action?
(And if the mind is indeed one-pointed, what is the use of performing ritual action?
Therefore, whether having performed rituals or not having performed them, [one should practice] internally and externally in succession.
By whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Śiva;
for those virtuous ones whose minds are fixed on Śiva and whose intellects are firmly established [in Him].
In both the next world and this one, everywhere, there shall be supreme peace;
in this world, through this mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," all spiritual accomplishments are attained.
Therefore, he— Śrī Kṛṣṇa— should be realized for the sake of attaining both higher and lower perfections:
O best of great sages, O omniscient one, O great ocean of all knowledge!
You should now describe the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra.
Upamanyu said:
"The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years; therefore, hear it in brief."
In the Vedas and in the Śiva-āgamas, this six-syllabled mantra is present in both; however, in the world, the five-syllabled one is traditionally regarded as the primary one.
This six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Oṃ, is superior to all mantras;
it accomplishes every purpose for all devotees of Śiva without exception.

This statement consists of few syllables yet is rich in meaning; it is the essence of the Vedas, bestowing liberation; it is established by direct command, free from doubt, and has Śiva as its very soul.
That supreme speech of the Lord is endowed with various supernatural powers, divine, pleasing to the minds of the world, profound, and its meaning is perfectly certain.
The Omniscient One, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, proclaimed the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," which is to be uttered with ease and clarity by all embodied beings.
That seed-syllable, the first mantra of all vidyās, consisting of six syllables,
should be known as extremely subtle and of great significance, like the seed of a banyan tree.
The God Śiva is beyond the three qualities (guṇas), omniscient, the Lord who creates all,
omnipresent, and established in the single-syllable mantra "Om."
The subtle Brahman-mantras beginning with Īśāna, which consist of single syllables,
are situated in due order within the mantra *namaḥ śivāya*.
In the six-syllabled mantra, Śiva— whose body is the subtle five Brahmas—
abides directly by his very nature through the relationship of the signified and the signifier.
Śiva is the denoted object because he is an object of knowledge, and the mantra stands as its denoter;
this relationship of denoted and denoter between the two is established as beginningless.
Just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has proceeded from beginningless time,
so too Śiva, who is himself beginningless, stands as the liberator from saṃsāra.
Just as medicine is by its very nature the antidote to diseases,
so too is Śiva remembered as the antidote to the defects of saṃsāra.
If this Lord of the World did not exist, this world would become shrouded in darkness,
like this world deprived of light when bereft of the sun.
In the absence of a Lord, how could this creation of the world come to be,
given that primordial matter (prakṛti) is insentient and the spirit (puruṣa) is devoid of knowledge?
Whatever is insentient— beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna) and atoms (paramāṇu), and extending to all else—
is never observed to be an agent by itself without an intelligent cause.
The instruction on dharma and adharma, the investigation into bondage and liberation,
and the initial creation of beings— none of these are established for men without an omniscient being.
Just as patients suffer without joy in the absence of a physician,
so indeed does the world suffer when it is unassailed by Śiva.
Therefore, there exists the Lord Sadāśiva, who is beginningless, omniscient, and perfect;
he is the protector who rescues men from the ocean of worldly existence.
The Lord is to be known through the Śiva Āgamas as being free from beginning, middle, and end, pure by nature, omniscient, perfectly complete, and auspicious.
This [world] is merely its designation, and it is remembered as the designated object;
because of this relationship between designation and the designated, the supreme Śiva is established by the mantra.
For this much indeed is the knowledge of Śiva, and this much is the supreme state:
that which is the six-syllabled speech of Śiva, "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
This Śaiva scriptural injunction is not a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), for it is of the nature of Śiva:
"He who is omniscient is the perfect Śiva, whose very nature is stainless."
How could he who acts for the benefit of the world speak falsely?
For whatever a thing is established by its own nature through its qualities and defects, [he speaks of it exactly as it is].
And whatever the full fruit may be, just as the Omniscient One would declare it,
one might speak falsely because of being seized by defects such as passion and ignorance.
If those [defects] do not exist in Īśvara, how could he speak otherwise—
that which was spoken by Śiva, who is omniscient and free from every defect?
The most excellent and stainless word is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the words of the Lord should be trusted by the wise.
One who lacks faith in merit and demerit as they truly are falls downward;
for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation, that which has been spoken is most excellent.

That speech which follows after passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, desire, and craving should be known as ill-spoken; whereas that which is uttered by the peaceful, best of sages is to be understood as well-spoken.
Speech that is a cause for rebirth in hell is said to be "not spoken," even if it is in Sanskrit, soft, and elegant. What is the use of such speech?
By means of the discourse on ignorance and passion, which are the causes of the afflictions of cyclic existence, that which,
upon being heard, gives rise to the highest good and the complete destruction of passion and the other defilements.
Even that statement, though seemingly inconsistent, should be understood as most excellent,
for it was uttered by Śiva, the omniscient one, despite the multiplicity of mantras.
This mantra is sublime and stainless; there is nothing like it anywhere.
The Vedas and their auxiliary sciences are all established within the six syllables.
Therefore, there is no other mantra anywhere that is equal to it,
even when compared with the seven crores of great mantras and the various secondary mantras.
The six-syllabled mantra is differentiated just as a Sūtra is expanded by means of its commentary;
so too are all the various forms of Śiva-knowledge and whatever branches of learning there may be.
These are, in brief, the commentary on the six-syllable Sūtra;
what need has one for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent?
p. 183) He in whose heart this mantra, "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," is established—by him has everything been studied, by him has everything been heard, and by him has everything been practiced.
By whom the practice of the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" has been made firm—
those three syllables "Śivāya," joined with the prostration and so forth.
He upon whose tongue-tip this [teaching] resides has a life that is truly fruitful—
whether he be an outcaste, a low-born man, a fool, or even a scholar.
"One who is steadfast in the recitation of the five-syllable mantra is liberated from the cage of sins;
thus was it declared by the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the trident, when questioned by the Goddess."
For the welfare of all mortals, and especially for the twice-born,
the Goddess said:
"In the Kali age, a turbid time that is difficult to conquer and hard to transcend..."
In a world shrouded by the greatest demerit and turned away from the Dharma.
When the conduct of the castes and stages of life has declined, when a great crisis has arisen,
and when all authority is either rendered doubtful or has reached its inevitable end;
When that instruction has been destroyed and the lineage of teacher and disciple has vanished,
O Maheśvara, by what means are your devotees liberated?
The Lord said: By taking refuge in my supreme, heart-pleasing five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī),
men born in the Kali age whose souls are purified by devotion are liberated.
Of those who are corrupted by faults born of mind, speech, and body— beyond the reach of description or recollection—
those who are ungrateful, merciless, and evil-natured.
Even for those who are greedy and crooked-minded, if their hearts are inclined toward me,
my five-syllabled mantra is the savior from the fear of saṃsāra.
O Goddess, I have repeatedly made this vow upon the surface of the earth:
even one who has fallen may be liberated by this knowledge if he is my devotee.
(184) If a mortal has fallen in every respect, he becomes unfit for the rites of the Goddess;
indeed, whatever rite is performed by one who is unfit for the rite leads only to hell.
Then, how could one who has fallen [into this state] be liberated by this knowledge?
The Lord said: "What you have said is true; nevertheless, listen, O beautiful one."
Thinking this to be a secret, I previously concealed it;
yet, if one who is deluded should worship me while fallen [from his state], accompanied by the mantra.
Without my five-syllable mantra, there is no doubt that one will become a denizen of hell—
even those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others emaciated by vows.
For those who perform these vows, there is no meeting with me;
however, he who worships me even once with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra [attains it].
He too shall go to my abode by virtue of the majesty of this very mantra;
therefore, [compared to it], penances, sacrifices, vows, and likewise religious observances [are insignificant].
These are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the five-syllabled mantra;
whether bound or liberated, one who is freed from the fetter by means of the five-syllabled mantra [is so].

He who worships me—whether he be without Śiva or even hostile to Śiva—shall be liberated; there is no need for deliberation on this point. He who [worships] even once with the five-syllabled mantra...
Whether fallen or even deluded, a man who worships with either the six-syllabled or the five-syllabled mantra, O Goddess, is liberated.
If he should worship me with devotion through this limb of Brahman, he is liberated—whether he be fallen or not fallen; one should worship with this mantra.
My devotee— whether he has conquered anger or not, whether he is free from greed or indeed greedy,
and whether he has attained [spiritual wealth] or not— is here superior by millions upon millions of times more than others.
Therefore, O Goddess, having indeed obtained me, one should worship with this mantra;
for he who, endowed with qualities such as friendliness, obtains me and worships me, [attains success].
Devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) with devotion, one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with me.
What is the use of much speaking on this matter? All devotees are qualified [for this].
Therefore, he is indeed superior even to my five-syllable mantra;
by the power of the five-syllable mantra, the worlds, the Vedas, and the great sages [are sustained].
The eternal dharmas remain, as do the gods and this entire world; even when the dissolution has arrived and all that is stationary and moving has perished.
Everything has returned to its primordial nature and will merge therein;
I alone remain established, O Goddess, for there is no second anywhere.
At that time, the Vedas and all the Śāstras remained established in the five-syllabled mantra;
protected by my power, they did not undergo destruction at all.
Then, from me, creation arose through the differentiation of Prakṛti and the Self;
likewise, there was an intermediate dissolution of the qualities, the forms, and the selves.
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa lies upon the serpent-couch, having assumed a body composed of Māyā,
reclining in the midst of the waters.
From that lotus at his navel was born the five-faced Grandfather (Brahmā);
desiring to create the three worlds, he was indeed unable to do so as he lacked assistance.
In the beginning, the Grandfather created ten sages of immeasurable luster from his mind; for the sake of increasing their spiritual perfection, he spoke to me.
"O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant power to my sons.
Thus was I, the five-faced one, entreated by him.
He spoke the five syllables in succession to the Lotus-born;
the Grandfather of the World received them with his five faces.
Having known me, Maheśvara, through the relationship of the signified and the signifier,
and having understood the ritual application according to rule, Prajāpati became one whose mantra was perfected.
He bestowed the mantra and the true meaning of the mantra upon his sons;
they, for their part, received that jewel of a mantra directly from the Grandfather of the World himself.
Then, by the path commanded by me, for those desiring to propitiate me:
on the beautiful peak of Meru is a mountain named Muñjavat,
which is dear to me, ever glorious, and protected by my devotees.
In his vicinity, those eager for the creation of the world performed intense penance for a thousand divine years, subsisting only on air.
Seeing their devotion, I immediately became manifest before them;
[I appeared as] the seer, the meter, the ritual pin, the seed-syllable, the power, and the deity.

I have fully explained the ritual placement (nyāsa), the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga), the binding of the directions (digbandha), and their application for the sake of increasing the creation of the world for the noble ones.
Then, through the greatness of the mantra and strengthened by their ascetic penance,
those sages properly extended the creation, including gods, asuras, and humans.
The essential nature of this supreme vidyā is now stated:
first, the word "namaḥ" should be employed, and after that, "śivāya."
This very five-syllabled lore resides at the head of all the Vedas;
it is the eternal seed of the entire range of sound.
First, she who issued from my mouth is my own verbal command;
she resembles molten gold and possesses full, elevated breasts.
Four-armed and three-eyed, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
holding a lotus and a blue water-lily in her hands, she is serene, with her two hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
seated upon a white lotus throne, with dark, curly hair.
Its five-colored rays, forming shimmering circles of light,
are yellow, black, smoky, white-hued, and red.
If these are to be employed separately, they are adorned with the *bindu* and the *nāda*:
the *bindu* has the form of a half-moon, and the *nāda* has the form of a lamp-flame.
O fair-faced one, the second seed among these seeds of this mantra has a long vowel as its first part; one should designate the fourth as that [vowel] and the fifth as Śakti.
(187) The seer is named Vāmadeva, the metre is said to be Paṅkti,
and the deity of this mantra, O fair-faced one, is I myself as Śiva.
Gautama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Aṅgiras,
and Bhāradvāja are recorded as the sages of the social classes respectively.
The Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Virāj are the meters;
Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda are their respective deities.
O fair-faced one, they say I have five faces; their locations, from the east to the zenith, follow the sequence beginning with the letter *na*.
The first letter is acute (udātta), the fourth is secondarily acute (dvitīya), and the fifth is circumflex (svarita); the middle one is known as depressed (nihata).
One should know its names to be the Root-Vidyā, Śiva, the Śaiva Sūtra, and likewise the Five-Syllabled [Mantra]; this great Heart of mine is Śaiva.

The letter *na* is said to be the head, while the letter *ma* is called the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Similarly, the letter *śi* is the armor (*kavaca*), and the letter *vā* is declared to be the eye (*netra*).
Just as the syllable *ya* is a weapon (*astra*), so too are *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*,
and *phaṭ* constituent parts of mantras according to their respective phonemes.
There too, this is the root mantra due to its slight connection with variations;
therein, the fifth syllable is adorned with the twelfth vowel.
Therefore, with this mantra, one should perform the worship of us two through the divisions of mind, speech, and body, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.
According to one's wisdom, according to one's faith, according to the time, according to one's understanding,
according to one's power, according to what is available, according to what is appropriate, and according to one's inclination—
or at any time whatsoever, with devotion, wherever it may be performed.
O Goddess, by whatever means, worship will lead one to liberation.
O beautiful one, whatever has been done for me by you with a mind attached to me—
whether it be dear to me or even auspicious— whether performed in due order or out of sequence.
Nevertheless, for those of my devotees who are not entirely helpless,
I myself have established a restrictive rule regarding all the scriptures.
In this regard, I shall first explain the auspicious compendium of mantras,
without which recitation is fruitless, or by means of which it becomes fruitful.
Īśvara said: O fair-faced one, that which is devoid of the command (ājñā), devoid of ritual action (kriyā), devoid of faith (śraddhā),
and devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of the command— even if constantly recited, it is fruitless.
That which is accomplished through command, that which is accomplished through ritual action, that which is accomplished through faith, and that which belongs to my own self—
if these are likewise accomplished through sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), then the accomplishment of the mantra yields great fruit.
Having approached a preceptor who is a brahmin, noble, a knower of the true meaning of reality,
a practitioner of recitation endowed with virtuous qualities, and devoted to the yoga of meditation;
Endowed with purity of disposition, one should strive to please him through speech, mind, body, and material wealth.
A disciple should always honor the teacher with the utmost diligence,
offering elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, fields, and houses.
Ornaments, garments, grains, and wealth—
one should give these to the preceptor with devotion, provided one has the means.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires one's own success;
afterwards, one should offer oneself along with all one's possessions to the guru.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules and to the best of one's ability, without deceiving him,
one should receive the mantra and the knowledge from the guru in due order.
Thus satisfied, the Guru [should initiate] the disciple who has resided for a year as a worshiper,
who is desirous of service, free from egoism, bathed, pure, and having observed a fast.
Having bathed [the image] for the sake of purification with water held in a full jar,
which has been consecrated by mantras and endowed with auspicious substances.
Having adorned him with fine garments and decorated him with perfumes, garlands, clothes, and ornaments,
he should cause the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day and honor them with worship.
On the seashore, by a river, in a cow-pen, or even in a temple;
in a pure place, or at home, at a time when the lunar day (tithi) brings success.
When the lunar mansion is auspicious, joined with a favorable yoga, and free from all defects,
one should then bestow my knowledge according to the prescribed rite, having first shown favor.
With a very serene mind, one should correctly vocalize it with the voice in a solitary place;
having vocalized and repeated that supreme mantra of ours.
"May there be auspiciousness, may there be welfare, may there be prosperity, and may you be dear"—
thus the Guru should give the mantra and thereafter the command.
Having thus received the mantra and the command from the guru, one should remain composed in meditation.
Having made the formal resolve, one should recite [the mantra] daily preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
one should recite it daily for as long as one lives, eight hundred and more times.
Becoming single-minded and intent upon that alone, he attains the supreme goal;
indeed, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with devotion, multiplied fourfold.
He who eats only at night and observes self-restraint is known as one engaged in *puraścaraṇa*;
he who, having performed the *puraścaraṇa*, thereafter becomes a perpetual reciter [of mantras].
There is no one equal to him in the world; he is a perfected one (siddha) who bestows perfection.
Having bathed in a pure place and having assumed a beautiful posture, [he should practice].
Having meditated upon me in your heart, as well as your own gurus and all other teachers,
you should remain silent and one-pointed in mind, facing either the east or the north.
Having purified the five principles through burning, flooding, and other rites,
and having performed the placement of mantras and so forth, one whose body has been made manifest (sakalīkṛta).
One should meditate upon the conflict between us two, having restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
[and contemplate] the field of knowledge, the tone, the form, the seer, the meter, and the presiding deity.
Having recollected the seed-syllable, the power, and likewise the object of expression, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra.
They know that mental recitation is the best, while whispered recitation is middling.
Those learned in the meaning of the scriptures declare that the lowest [form] is vocal;
the highest has Rudra as its deity, and the middling has Viṣṇu as its deity.
(190) They say, in due order, that [recitation] with high, low, and circumflex tones, and with words and syllables that are clear or indistinct, is the lowest form, having Brahman as its deity.
One should recite the mantra with the voice; this is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa), or it may be uttered slightly even through the mere movement of the tongue alone.

That which is not heard by others, or is heard only slightly, is called whispered (upāṃśu). When one repeatedly contemplates the meaning of the words— syllable by syllable and word by word— through the mind along with a sequence of phonemes, that is described as mental recitation (mānasa-japa).
The verbal [japa] is said to be onefold, the whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold,
the mental (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold, and when accompanied by the internal visualization (sagarbha), it is more than a hundredfold.
Recitation accompanied by breath control is called "with seed" (sagarbha);
breath control at the beginning and end, even without recitation, is also praised as "without seed" (agarbha).
Having restrained the breaths for forty cycles, the wise one who knows the meaning of the mantra should recollect it; if he is unable, he should recite it according to his capacity.
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) five times, three times, or once;
it may be either "seedless" (agarbha) or "with seed" (sagarbha), but that which is with seed is highly praised.
Recitation performed with meditative concentration is said to be a thousand times more effective than even that which is done while pregnant [with worldly thoughts].
Among these five types, one should perform recitation according to one's capacity.
Counting with the fingers is declared to be a single unit;
one should know that counting with a line is eightfold, and with *putrajīva* seeds it is ten times more.
With conch gems there would be a hundred; with corals, a thousand;
with crystal, ten thousand; and with pearls, it is said, a hundred thousand.

With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are performed; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi); and with knots of kuśa grass or rudrākṣa beads, an infinite fruit is said to be obtained.
A rosary made with thirty beads bestows wealth during the practice of recitation;
one consisting of twenty-seven beads shall grant nourishment.
When performed with twenty-five [beads], it bestows liberation;
when with fifteen beads, it yields the fruit of malevolent magic (abhicāra).
One should know that the thumb bestows liberation, the index finger destroys enemies,
the middle finger bestows wealth, and this ring finger indeed effects peace.
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads therein is the most excellent of the excellent;
a rosary of one hundred beads is excellent, while one of fifty beads is middling;
a rosary of fifty-four beads is proclaimed as the best for the heart.
In this manner, one should perform the recitation with a rosary and not show it to anyone.
The little finger is said to be the "attractor" (ākarṣaṇī) and is auspicious for the rite of recitation;
one should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers.
Since a recitation performed without the thumb is fruitless,
one should know that recitation in the home is equal [in merit], while in a cow-pen it becomes a hundredfold.
In a sacred forest or a grove, it is said to be a thousandfold;
ten thousandfold on a mountain or at a flower-garden; and a hundred thousandfold by a river is declared.
They say that ten million [times] in a temple is infinite in my presence;
as is the case with the sun, fire, Jupiter, the moon, a lamp, and water.
The recitation of mantras (japa) is recommended in the presence of Brahmins and cows;
facing east therein brings subjugation, while facing south effects malevolent rites (abhicāra).
One should know that the western direction bestows wealth, while the northern direction brings peace;
this applies even in the presence of the Sun, fire, Brahmins, deities, and gurus.

Nor should one recite the mantra of other praiseworthy deities while facing away [from them]. One should not be wearing a turban, nor a tunic, nor be naked, nor have disheveled hair, nor have the neck wrapped.
One who has not purified his hands, who is impure, or who is lamenting, should never perform japa;
nor should one do so while experiencing anger, intoxication, sneezing, drowsiness, spitting, or yawning.
One should avoid the sight of those who are inferior to oneself during the practice of recitation;
if their presence occurs, one should sip water for purification or remember me along with you.
One may observe the luminaries or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) while not sitting,
while lying down, while walking, or even while standing.
One should not recite [the mantra] on a main road, in an inauspicious place, or in the midst of darkness;
nor should one recite with the feet outstretched or while sitting in the cock-posture.
Whether mounted on a vehicle or lying down, or even if distracted by anxious thoughts—if one is capable, one should perform all of this; if incapable, one should recite according to one's ability.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to this concise statement:
one who follows right conduct, recites prayers, performs oblations, and meditates attains auspiciousness.
Conduct is the supreme dharma; conduct is the supreme wealth;
conduct is the supreme knowledge; indeed, conduct is the supreme goal.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in this world and shall not be happy in the next; therefore, one should be possessed of good conduct.
Whatever action is prescribed for a person by the Vedas and the Vedic scriptures, his performance of that is right conduct; it is not otherwise.
Because it is practiced by the virtuous, it is called "right conduct" (sadācāra);
they say that the root cause of such right conduct is faith in the hereafter (āstikya).

If one is a believer (*āstika*) and does not fall away from right conduct due to negligence or other such causes, that person is not excessively tainted; therefore, one should embrace the state of being a believer.
Just as there is happiness and suffering here through good and evil deeds, so too it exists in the next world; this conviction is called faith (āstikya).
O beloved, I shall speak another secret that must be kept hidden;
it should not be told to just anyone, nor to an atheist or a beast.
For one who is devoid of virtuous conduct, for the fallen, or even for an outcaste,
there is no protection superior to the five-syllabled mantra in the Kali age.
Whether walking or standing, whether performing actions according to one's own will,
and whether impure or pure, this mantra is never fruitless.
For men who behave improperly and whose six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan) are impure,
this mantra is not fruitless even if it has not been specifically enjoined by a guru—
even for one who is an outcaste, a fool, an ignorant person, or fallen.
This mantra is not fruitless even for a base person who has transgressed all bounds; it is supremely effective for one who possesses devotion toward me, regardless of their condition.
(193) This succeeds, there is no doubt, but for no one else;
O Dear One, it does not depend on the conjunctions of the ascendant, lunar day, asterism, day of the week, and so forth.
One should never look upon this Great Man with excessive scrutiny, nor when he is asleep, nor when he is being struck;
for this Great Man is never the enemy of anyone.
Whether he is already perfected (susiddha), or one who has attained perfection (siddha), or even one who is yet to be accomplished (sādhya),
if he is instructed by a perfected guru, he is called "well-perfected" (susiddha).
Whether given by one who is unestablished, or established, or merely the object to be proven;
whether unproven or proven, it is indeed established—of this there is no doubt.
For one endowed with an excess of faith in me, in the mantra, and likewise in the guru,
therefore, having abandoned other mantras which are fraught with danger due to a lack of qualification;
A wise person should directly take refuge in the supreme knowledge, the five-syllabled mantra;
for even when other mantras have been mastered, this mantra may not be mastered.
When this great mantra is mastered, all others indeed become mastered as well;
just as I am not obtained among the gods even when they have been obtained, O Maheśvarī.
When I am attained, you have attained them; the procedure regarding these mantras is the same.
Whatever defects exist in all other mantras, they do not occur even in this one.
Because this mantra functions without depending on caste and other such factors,
nevertheless, it does not apply to inferior fruits that serve as its counterparts.
"One should employ it with haste, because this yields great fruit.
(Upamanyu continued):
"Thus [it was taught] directly by the trident-bearing Mahādeva to Mahādevī herself."
The method for the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra has been declared for the welfare of the worlds.
Thus [ends the work] by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one topics of the secret essence of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita Siddhānta.
In the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the *Nigama* and *Āgama* composed by the venerable Ācārya,
the twelfth instruction, titled "The Procedure for the Recitation of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," is completed.
Here begins the thirteenth instruction.
In this thirteenth instruction, the Supreme Lord, appearing in the form of a letter, proclaimed the supreme power of the five-syllable mantra.
In the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa], Śrī Kṛṣṇa says: "O Blessed One, the majesty of the mantra has been told by you and heard by me;
its application and ritual procedure as well have been heard by me directly, equal to the Vedas themselves."
Now I wish to hear about the supreme rite of purification for Śiva,
which was merely indicated and not explained in detail during the collection of mantras.
Upamanyu said:
"Indeed, I shall tell you of that supreme and meritorious consecration (saṃskāra), which purifies all sins and was proclaimed by Śiva."
Since a person who has properly performed their duty toward worship and other rites undergoes purification,
that is called *saṃskāra*, which is the cleansing of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*).
Since by means of this knowledge is given and the bondage of the fetters is destroyed,
it is for this reason that this very consecration (saṃskāra) is also called initiation (dīkṣā).
In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: the Śāmbhavī, the Śāktī, and the Māntrikī.
By the mere sight of the Guru, or even by his touch or conversation,
wisdom that brings about the destruction of the bonds is immediately produced.
That initiation is declared to be Śāmbhavī; it is further divided into two types:
the intense (tīvra) and the more intense (tīvratarā), according to the degree of destruction of the fetters (pāśa).
That [intense] state by which immediate liberation is attained is considered the most intense;
however, the [slightly less] intense [state] completely purifies the fetters of a living man.
The initiation of the Śakti, which possesses knowledge, enters the body of the disciple and is performed by the Guru through the path of yoga,
with the eye of yoga.
The initiation consisting of mantras and ritual action, preceded by the sacrificial pit and the mandala,
should be performed by the Guru outside [the temple] for those who are very dull or extremely dull-witted.
In accordance with the descent of power (śaktipāta), the disciple is worthy of grace;
for, in brief, that [descent] is the root of one's qualification for the Śaiva dharma.
Where power has not descended, there purity does not arise;
there is no knowledge, no Śiva-conduct, no liberation, and no supernatural attainments.
Therefore, having observed the signs of an abundant descent of power (śaktipāta),
the Guru should purify the disciple through either knowledge or ritual action.
The evil-minded one who, out of delusion, acts otherwise perishes;
therefore, the teacher should examine the disciple in every possible way.
The characteristic of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is the arising of awakening and bliss,
because that [power] is the supreme Śakti, whose nature is awakening and bliss.
The mark of bliss and awakening consists of modifications of the internal organ,
such as trembling, horripilation, changes in voice, eyes, and limbs.
The disciple, too, should examine the guru by means of these characteristics—
whether through his own observations during contact with him while performing the worship of Śiva and so forth, or through those observed in others associated with him.
But because the disciple is one who must be trained and because he is the cause of the teacher's dignity,
he should therefore practice respect toward the teacher with every effort.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
Or rather, the Guru is indeed Śiva himself, abiding in the form of knowledge.
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. The fruit resulting from the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Guru is identical.
This Guru is the essence of all gods and consists of all mantras;
therefore, with every effort, one should bear his command upon the head.
If one who seeks the highest good should not transgress the teacher’s command even in thought,
for by observing the teacher’s command, one attains the perfection of knowledge.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, he should not perform any other action;
if he must do so in the teacher's presence, he should do it all with the teacher’s permission.
One should not sit as one pleases in the presence of the guru or in his house;
for the guru is the manifest God himself, and his home is a temple of the deity.
Just as one becomes a partaker of the fruit of sin through association with sinners,
so too does one become a partaker of the fruit of that teacher's virtues through association with the teacher.
Just as gold here sheds its impurity through contact with fire, so too does the mind cast off its stains.
In the same way, a human being abandons evil through contact with a guru,
just as a pot of ghee melts when placed near a fire.
In the presence of the teacher, evil is indeed dissolved,
just as a blazing fire utterly consumes a piece of wood to its very end.
Likewise, this Guru, when satisfied, may burn away sin in an instant;
one should not provoke the anger of the Guru through thought, deed, or speech.
By his anger, indeed, longevity, prosperity, wisdom, and virtuous deeds are consumed;
and for those who provoke his anger, their religious merits become fruitless.
Regarding these restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), there should be no hesitation;
a person should never speak words that are contrary to the teacher.
If one speaks out of great delusion, one will certainly fall into the Raurava hell;
therefore, one should strive with mind, action, and speech toward the Guru.
If a wise person seeking the highest good should not practice false conduct,
then when his lack of virtue is made known, he shall become a partaker of a hundredfold lack of virtue.
When one's virtues have been proclaimed, all the fruit of merit arises in that same way;
therefore, one should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru, whether commanded or not.
Whether in his absence or in his presence, one should perform his service;
thus, being possessed of right conduct, one should always be devoted and have a mind ever-striving.
Therefore, a disciple who acts for the pleasure of the Guru deserves the Śaiva teachings,
provided that the Guru is virtuous, wise, and a radiance of supreme bliss.
One who is devoted to Śiva through the knowledge of reality attains liberation, and no other;
reality is that which generates consciousness and arises from supreme bliss.
He by whom that reality is known is indeed the one who reveals bliss;
not, however, he who is devoid of true consciousness and possesses it merely as a name.
A boat may carry one from another across; can a stone ever carry a stone?
For these [people], liberation exists merely by name; it is indeed a liberation consisting only of a name.
But those by whom reality has been known are liberated and liberate others as well;
for how can there be awakening in one devoid of reality, and how indeed can there be grasping at a self?
One who is devoid of [right] appropriation is called a "bound soul" (paśu); even if impelled by other bound souls, he does not transcend the state of being a bound soul.
Therefore, in this world, one who knows reality is considered both liberated and a liberator;
such a person, though endowed with all auspicious marks and learned in all the scriptures, is [the true teacher].
Even one who knows all methods and rituals is fruitless if devoid of reality;
however, he whose intellect is established in reality culminates in direct experience.
From beholding her and so forth, supreme bliss arises;
therefore, from contact with her alone, the birth of the bliss of awakening occurs.
A wise man should choose that very teacher and no other;
such a teacher is worthy of being served by disciples who are adept in disciplined conduct.
As long as [the truth] is being understood, it should be cultivated by those seeking liberation;
once it is known, their devotion should remain steadfast until they take refuge in the ultimate reality.
One should never abandon that place, nor ever neglect it,
where not even the slightest joy or awakening is found.
Even after a year, a disciple may resort to another teacher;
yet, even having approached another teacher, he must not disparage his former one.
Having first saluted the teacher’s brothers, as well as his sons, those who instruct him, and even those who urge him on,
he should then approach a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
The wise one should propitiate a guru who is fortunate, pleasing to behold,
the bestower of fearlessness in all things, and whose mind is overcome with compassion.
The disciple should strive to please him with effort through mind, action, and speech;
he should serve him until that teacher becomes truly well-pleased.
When he is pleased, the disciple’s bonds are instantly destroyed;
therefore, [one should offer] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses.
Ornaments, garments, vehicles, beds, and seats—
one should give these to the preceptor with devotion, according to one's means.
One should not practice stinginess with wealth if one desires the supreme goal;
he alone is father, mother, brother, kinsman, wealth, and happiness.
Since he is a friend and a companion, one should disclose everything to him;
having disclosed it, one should thereafter reveal oneself along with one's lineage and one's dependents.
Having offered himself along with water to him, he should remain perpetually under his control,
once he has surrendered his own self to Śiva, who is embodied as the Guru.
Then the embodied soul becomes a Śaiva; from that point on, there is no further rebirth.
Having assumed the form of a teacher, he completely severs the fetters of the bound soul.
"Having cut [the bonds], the Lord leads him to the supreme state"—so says the sacred tradition.
Furthermore, the teacher should examine the disciple within his own hermitage for one year.
Having treated a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya— who are two or three years senior—
as inferior through the withholding of life-sustaining goods, commands, or social intercourse, and having caused those of low status to perform the duties of the highest;
Those who do not fall into despondency even when reviled or beaten;
They are fit for the rite of Śiva’s consecration— self-controlled,
pure, non-violent, compassionate, always diligent in mind,
free from pride, wise, devoid of rivalry, and sweet-spoken.
They were upright, gentle, pure, disciplined, and firm-minded.
The twice-born who are devotees of Śiva, endowed with the conduct of Śaivas and likewise possessed of such behavior through their speech, mind, and physical actions;
"They are to be purified and awakened according to the rule"—this is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
A woman has no inherent entitlement to the ritual of Śiva-initiation.
If she is devoted to Maheśvara, she may indeed [perform it] by the command of her husband;
likewise, for one who is bereft of a husband, it may be done with the permission of her sons or others.
The authority indeed belongs to the father by his command in the case of a maiden,
especially for Śūdras, those of other castes, and the fallen.
Likewise, the purification of the path is not prescribed for those of mixed castes;
yet they too may possess unartificial devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause.
One should perform the purification of sins through such acts as offering water for washing the feet;
therefore, those born in the natural order (anuloma) are indeed properly included among the twice-born.
For them, one should perform the purification of the path and other rites as is appropriate for the mother's lineage;
however, a maiden who has been established in the Śiva-dharma by her father and others [is treated differently].
She should be given to one who is devoted, and not to another who is hostile;
if she is given to one who is adverse, she should, out of negligence, awaken her husband.
Being unable [to maintain her vows], she should abandon him and practice dharma with her mind alone,
just as in the past a devoted wife abandoned her husband and took another as her lord.
In former times, she had already accomplished her purpose by propitiating Śaṅkara through austerity,
just as Nālāyanī propitiated the god through austerity for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having obtained husbands in accordance with the Dharma, she was not constrained by her elders;
therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is no fault here arising from a lack of independence.
For one who is engaged in the dharma of Śiva out of reverence for the teaching of Śiva—what need is there for much speaking here? Even whoever else is a refuge of Śiva [is likewise honored].
If the one to be consecrated is dependent upon the guru, then the consecration is not differentiated [from the ordinary];
it occurs simply through the guru’s gaze, touch, or even conversation.
For one in whom wisdom has arisen, there is no further action;
for that which is cultivated by the mind is accomplished through the path of yoga.
That secret [initiation] is not described here, as it is accessible solely through the mouth of the Guru;
rather, that which is the ritual purification involving the sacrificial pit and the pavilion is for one who is engaged in ritual action (kriyāvān).
"He shall be described in brief; a detailed account of him is not possible"—by such words and other similar statements from the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*.
That very [mantra] is declared to be the five-syllabled one, which removes the fear of saṃsāra;
all action, however, agitated by fear, becomes the cause of bondage in saṃsāra.
This five-syllabled mantra is capable of severing bondage;
therefore, one who desires liberation from the fetters should meditate upon the five-syllabled mantra.
By the word "Śiva," this five-syllable mantra shines forth of its own accord;
by means of that mantra, the Rudra-hymn (rudrasūkta) is realized, and from the Rudra-hymn, the Yajurvedic revelation arises.
Through the Yajus-mantra with the central jewel, the Ṛk and Sāman shine forth very clearly;
therefore, there is nothing equal to the five-syllabled mantra even in the three worlds.
Some mantras may have results pertaining to this world, while others pertain to the next;
yet this five-syllabled mantra bestows fruits both in this world and the next.
From worldly speech, the primary [practice] is the recitation of the names of the deities;
from the non-recitation of the names of the deities, there arises reflection upon the cause of the world.
He who is the sustainer of all causes, the meditator, and the supreme cause—
the recitation of His name is most excellent, for His names are manifold.
The name "Śiva" is superior to that; the two syllables "namaḥ" are superior to that;
therefore, their recitation in that specific order is distinguished, and even more so when preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ).
This mantra, which constitutes both the collective whole and its individual parts, is the most supreme among all mantras;
by reciting this most supreme mantra, one attains that which is most supreme.
O wise one, for those who recite it, the fruit is indeed liberation;
therefore, the five-syllable mantra should be chanted by all who seek liberation.
By the power of the five syllables, all desires are perfectly accomplished.
This is the truth, the truth, and again the truth; it is the universal medicine that revives all beings.
Having drunk the nectar of the five syllables, one attains union with Śiva;
such a mortal does not return again, indeed, he certainly does not return again.

Thus ends [the section] on the essence of ritual action (*kriyāsāra*) within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṅgraha*, composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who was proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secrets of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
The thirteenth instruction, titled "Praise of the Nature of the Five Syllables," is completed. Here begins the fourteenth instruction:
in this fourteenth instruction, the sequence of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva [is set forth].
This work, a blending of the Nigamas and Āgamas, has been composed for the delight of the devoted. || 1 ||
These thirty-two instructions are considered to be within the worship of Śiva; when cultivated with devotion, they all lead to the attainment of union with Śiva. (2)
Now, another alternative is stated:
"The worship of Śiva for one's own sake must necessarily be performed by the Śaivas;
and between that which is Vedic and that which is mixed, the Śaiva [form] is the superior for them. (3)

Even that [practice] is praiseworthy when it is concise and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it may be performed by one who is devoid of power, or by one who is pure, or by one who is mixed, or even by one devoted to the Sun and other deities, provided it is accompanied by power (Śakti). || 4 ||
Therefore, having undertaken the worship of Śambhu together with Ambikā for my own sake, I shall demonstrate that which is proclaimed in all the divine Āgamas. (5)
The intermingling of the meanings of the divine scriptures (divyāgama) does not constitute a fault because they possess a single authority;
however, the intermingling of the meanings of the Pāśupatas and others within them is indeed a fault.
Even among those [liṅgas], one relies upon a single one and disregards the others;
this applies to the human liṅga, but not to those originating from the Self-born (Svayambhū) and so forth.

Even for one who relies upon a single tradition, the Lord has further instructed that what is taught therein should be set aside if it is rejected, and that which is praised by others should be accepted. (8)
Although the excellence [of the two] is equal, that which is required as a constituent of worship is what is needed;
he also taught that what is stated here and what is stated elsewhere are the same.
Therefore, this *Śrīśivārcanapaddhati* (The Manual for the Worship of Śiva) is composed using the necessary portions extracted from all the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*). (10)
Having sipped water for purification, with his body adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, he should consecrate the general arghya offering according to the prescribed rule.
Having meditated upon the abode of Śiva’s worship as consisting of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā),
one should perform the worship of the gatekeepers in sequence at its unsurpassed (anuttara) entrance.
Having expelled the three obstacles and entered, and having performed the worship of the weapons and so forth,
one should place all the materials for worship within reach.
On the southern side of the deity, facing north toward the fire,
and having taken his place upon the prepared seat, he should perform the five purifications.
When two muhūrtas remain before the rising of the sun, having risen, washed his feet and hands, and smeared himself with ashes; || 15 ||

One who has been initiated into the Nirvāṇa [consecration] should contemplate the Supreme Goddess as possessing the common commitment (samaya) within the heart, and as possessing the distinguished commitment within the Bindu at the crown of the head.
The practitioner should contemplate this teacher at the end of the twelve;
he should also recite his heart-pleasing names and deeds. (17)
Having gone to a suitable place, he should perform the voiding of feces and urine;
in the manner thus described, he himself becomes pure and purified in mind. (18)
This rule is prescribed for that Vīraśaiva who has performed his ablution with sacred ash alone and wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
and whose intellect is fixed solely upon the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
The smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) are thus proclaimed.
Having sipped water (*ācānta*), performed the ritual placement of mantras on the hands (*karanyāsa*), and restrained the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), while holding *darbha* grass, [one should say]:
"In this year, in this month, on this day, for the sake of pleasing Śiva, O Lord, I shall perform the ritual bath."

Having made this request, "Be gracious for the sake of your worship," one should dig the pure ground to a depth of four finger-breadths with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; then, having extracted the earth from there with that same mantra, one should [remove] the earth beneath it with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, using the heart mantra.

Having first filled the pit with earth extracted by the mantra ending in *namaḥ* recited from the heart, one should deposit it on a pure bank of a river, lake, or pond, ending the mantra with *namaḥ*. Having gone to the right bank of a river or similar body of water— which is highly recommended for bathing— one should [protect the site] with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having sprinkled the clay with water while reciting the *namas* mantra at the end of the *śiras* mantra, and having removed grass, roots, and other debris from the clay while reciting the *namas* mantra at the end of the *kavaca* mantra, one should divide it into three parts. With one part, one should wash [the body] from the navel down to the feet; the second part should be consecrated seven times with the *astra* mantra.
Having visualized the entire body as blazing through contact with the rays of the weapon-mantra (*astra-raśmi*), and having smeared it with the mantra, one enters the water; then,

having stirred the water with the weapon-mantra, one firmly closes the ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the nostrils with the two middle fingers, while reciting either the *praṇava* or the root-mantra (*mūla*).
Visualizing his own body as a blazing weapon in the heart of Japan, tawny with a mass of radiance, he should remain submerged in water for as long as he is able.

Alternatively, having divided the clay into two parts, one should smear all the limbs with one portion while reciting the *astra-mantra* and then bathe; this is the bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*). Or rather, the fetching of the clay is specifically for the purpose of the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) which will be described later; as for the bath for removing impurities, however—
The task should be performed using pastes of turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth. Here,
regarding the bodily impurities consisting of semen, feces, urine, and the filth of the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, nails, and feet:

Purification (*śuddhi*) consists of sprinkling with water following the rubbing with earth, tooth-sticks, turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth, which are included within the ritual acts ending with the bath for cleansing physical impurities. For verbal impurities, it is by the recitation of the *praṇava* and other mantras during the time of bathing; for mental impurities, it is by means of mantra-recitation, meditation, and so forth. Thereafter—
Having risen from the water, having gazed at the sun while reciting the Astra-mantra, and having sprinkled water upon his head,
he should emerge from the water, perform the ritual sipping (ācamana), and— if he is a non-detached twice-born—

perform the Vedic twilight worship (saṃdhyā) and also briefly perform the Śaiva twilight worship. This applies to one who is detached, a twice-born, or one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī).
One should worship only that which belongs to Śiva.
The method for the abbreviated Śiva-sandhyā:

Having sprinkled the head three times with drops of water from the tips of the fingers while reciting the Astra-mantra—“We know the weapon of Śiva; we meditate upon the fire of time; may that weapon impel us”—[one should proceed].

p. 204) Having offered *arghya* three times to the weapon (*astra*) residing in the solar orb with this *astragāyatrī*, one should recite the *gāyatrī* as much as possible. During the weapon-sandhyā bath, one should meditate on the blazing weapon-mantra. Then, for the sake of the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*), [one should draw water] from the place of the *bindu* into the midst of the holy bathing places (*tīrtha*), such as the Gaṅgā.

Having drawn one [of the waters] from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the *aṅkuśamudrā* while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having established it before oneself with the *udbhavamudrā* while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*,
one should visualize that lake, pond, or other body of water as being filled by it. Thereafter—
Having taken a portion of earth set aside for the purpose of the ritual bath, and having entered water reaching up to the navel,
one should stand knee-deep in rivers facing the current, or elsewhere facing east or north,
in order to avoid defects in the water caused by fish, frogs, and other creatures that may dwell therein.
One should fashion a square Śiva-tīrtha in front; the procedure for this is as follows:

having divided the portion of earth into three parts in the east, south, and north directions using the left hand, and having consecrated it all with the Śiva-mantra recited seven times, one should perform the "throwing of the weapon" (astrapāta) there with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

One should cast [the earth] in all directions, beginning with the east, using the *nārāca-mudrā*. Thus, by casting the portions of earth in the directions of Indra—who resides in the eastern quarter as the lord of obstacles in the heavens—all obstacles situated in the directions are pacified. Thereafter...
Having cast half of the portion of earth consecrated by Śiva into the water with the root mantra for the sake of accomplishing the Śiva-tīrtha,
one should cast the other half around the entire circumference as the Śiva-tīrtha by rotating the arms. Thus,
the portion of earth established in the direction of Soma becomes purely composed of nectar through the Śiva-mantra.
Since it flows by being stirred, it is a *tīrtha*; since it consists of nectar, it is conceived as the *śivatīrtha*.
Having thus prepared it for ritual bathing, one should first smear the entire body with half of that [water] using a portion of clay consecrated by the recitation (*japta*) of the Brahma-mantras.
Then, by touching the portion of earth situated in the direction of Dharmarāja,

all sins are destroyed. Likewise, having closed the doors of the senses, such as the ears, with the Ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa mudrā, one should immerse oneself in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Meditating, one should remain within the water for as long as one’s strength permits. Submerging all the limbs within the water is the best [form of bathing]; submerging half the body is middling;
submerging only the face is the least. Then, having emerged from the water, [one should wash] the left and right hands.

Having consecrated the head with water over which the *saṃhitā-mantras* ending in *vauṣaṭ* have been recited, using the *kumbhaka-mudrā* formed by Śakti and Śiva who are of the nature of Soma and Sūrya, and having scattered in all directions the water of the *tīrtha*— which destroys obstacles— with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [one should take] that *tīrtha*.

One should conclude with the *saṃhāramudrā*. Thus, if one is unable to go to a river or similar location, one should bathe right at home on a pure patch of ground smeared with cow dung, using nine, eight, or five jars filled with cold water from a cooking pot and consecrated by reciting the *Śiva-mantra*.
Kings, women, children, the sick,
and those living abroad should perform their bath with warm water if they are unable to bathe with cold water.
Kings, moreover, [should do so] for the sake of worshipping Śiva.

Having performed the ritual bathing according to the prescribed procedure for the bathing of Śiva, which includes all the ancillary services (*upacāra*), they should perform the bath while seated upon a golden throne, using water drawn from golden jars, preceded by the sounding of auspicious instruments such as conch shells. However, if one is unable to bathe the head, one should perform a neck-bath (*kaṇṭhasnāna*) or similar alternative. Thereafter—
Wiping the body with a clean, soft cloth; putting on two washed garments;

performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times while reciting: "Obeisance to the Ātma-tattva," "Obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva," and "Obeisance to the Śiva-tattva"; performing the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) of the Liṅga-tattva and the Aṅga-tattvas; and the bath of ashes (bhasmasnāna).
Having performed the application of the *tripuṇḍra* and other rites, one should perform the Śaiva twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsanā*).

The procedure for this is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Having restrained the breaths three times with the mantra *Hauṃ*, and having applied the divine mudrā to the two eyes with the thumbs using the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*—namely, *Hauṃ netrābhyāṃ namaḥ*—"
Having gazed at the water, having struck it with that same [mantra], and having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,

one should draw forth from the locus of the drop (*bindu*) any one of the holy fords (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā by means of the goad-mudrā and the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; then, having placed that holy ford into the water by means of the emergence-mudrā (*udbhavamudrā*) and the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Having consecrated [the water] with the root mantra, having protected it with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,

having enveloped it with the armor mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should render it nectar-like by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) and the power-mantra (*śaktimantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, one should meditate upon the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) as the form of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

The twilight (sandhyā) is threefold: Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī. Among them: She is red, wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with red ornaments, seated upon a swan-throne, and bearing matted hair and a digit of the moon.
Four-armed and four-faced, adorned with eight eyes,
she holds a rosary and a sacrificial ladle in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left.
Sustaining the Brahman as its deity, that morning twilight is threefold;
at the time of dawn, when the stars are few, it is the radiant Subālā, the bestower of liberation.
At dawn, when the stars have vanished, she bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
that Madhyamā, whose nature is the power of knowledge, has assumed the state of childhood.
