Bestowing enjoyment when the half-mandala of the sun is seen, she is the very nature of the power of action (kriyā-śakti); though mature, she has assumed childhood.
Seated upon a golden lotus, clothed in white garments,
adorned with a forest garland and a sacred thread, and possessing two eyes.
The Vaiṣṇavī Sandhyā of the middle [period] has one face and four hands; she holds a mace and a lotus in her right hands, and a conch and a discus in her left hands.
And that second watch is threefold in its fourth part;
in its first portion, she bestows liberation, being slightly blossomed in her youth.
In the middle portion, Vāgīśī, possessing middle youth, bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
in the third portion, Jvālābhidhā, in the full bloom of her youth, bestows liberation alone;
she stands amidst the bull and the lotus, three-eyed and moon-crested.
Bearing a trident and a rosary in her right hands, and granting fearlessness and power in her left, she is known as Raudrī, the evening twilight; she too, like the former [Dakṣiṇā], is threefold.
When the sun’s rays are slightly reddened, she is known as Jyeṣṭhā, her youth having moved on a little;
she bestows both enjoyment and liberation when the sun has fallen halfway through its youthful phase.
When the sun has set, she is called Raudrī, her youth having passed away, and she bestows worldly enjoyment.
Thus, the ninefold twilight rites (sandhyās) proclaimed by Śiva in the Śiva-śāstra are the witnesses of all; when worshipped, they grant one's desires.
One should contemplate Brāhmī as residing in the heart-lotus, Vaiṣṇavī as situated in the center of the bindu,
and Raudrī as located in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), each at their respective times.
The morning twilight is prescribed for the *samayin*, the midday for the *viśeṣin*;
for one who has been initiated into *nirvāṇa*, all three twilights are required.
Whether a Vīraśaiva performs [the rite] with a concentrated mind or does not perform it at all,
if it is performed there is indeed an increase in merit, and if it is not performed, he incurs no fault.
In this regard, the wise one should be inclined toward the temple of the seven times three;
she who abides in the triad of locations, namely Bindu, Śakti, and Sāmānya.
Slender like a lotus fiber, reddish-white and dark-blue,
the Twilight— known as Kriyā, Dṛk, and Icchā— should be visualized following the upward movement from the temple [of the heart].
But for one whose mind is fixed upon the temple of the twelve *kalās*, he should contemplate the supreme *sandhyā* which is manifested at midnight; from there,
[the path] extends from the navel to the end of the twelve, and then back down to the navel.
The fourth state (turyā) possesses coming and going, or it is formless and dark blue;
for the wise, however, it is the supreme twilight (parā saṃdhyā), whose very nature is the awakening of Śiva.
Residing in the *dvādaśānta* and resting upon Śambhu like moonlight upon the moon,
the single Sandhyā is in reality the very nature of Śiva and Śakti.
That very [practice] is described here as being differentiated according to the division of time and authority;
this contemplation of the twilight is what is called *sandhyāvandana*.
Whatever other acts there are, such as cleansing and so forth, are the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of this primary [rite].
Thus, having performed the duties of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so on, the worship of Śiva should be commenced.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows: then, with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, [one should take] the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*).

Having meditated, one should touch the eyes, nostrils, ears, shoulders, heart, navel, and head in sequence with the ring finger joined to the thumb, while contemplating: "May the Sun be satisfied; may Viṣṇu be satisfied. When this has been done:

The gods beginning with Sūrya and ending with Viṣṇu, who preside over the eyes and other senses, become augmenters of the performer's ritual practice; they are satisfied by the stream generated by the thumb when it is agitated through contact with the splendor of Śiva. Immediately after that—
For the purpose of purifying the thirty-five principles (*tattvas*) residing within the body, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

In this regard, the specific procedure is as follows: [one should visualize the deity] whose four hands are adorned with a golden lotus, a rosary of lotus seeds, a garland, and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*).

First, one should sip water (ācamana) with the mantra "Hāṃ, svāhā to the Ātmatattva," preceded by the meditation on the Ātmatattva as Brahmā, who has four faces and whose form is the principle of the Self. By this, [one purifies] one's own body.
One should contemplate the purification of the thirty-one principles (tattvas), beginning with earth and ending with Māyā.

Then one should meditate on Viṣṇu, who is blue in color, has eight hands adorned with the mudrās of the discus, arrow, lotus, sword, conch, bow, water-pot, and the gesture of fearlessness, has one face, and is the embodiment of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Preceded by meditation on the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva), one should sip water (ācamana) with the formula "svadhā" for the sake of the principle of Vidyā.

By this, one should contemplate the purification of the three principles known as Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. Then [one visualizes the deity] crystal-colored, with four hands holding a rosary of lotus seeds, a trident, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

"Having first performed meditation on the Śiva-principle with the thought, 'I meditate upon Rudra, who has five faces and is the very form of the Śiva-principle,' one should sip water (ācamana) with the mantra: *huṃ śivatattvāya svadhā*. By this, one should contemplate the purification of the Śakti-principle. Then, by means of the Astra-mantra..."

Having wiped the hands with the *hṛdayamantra*, one should touch the eyes and other [senses]. Furthermore, one should perform the meditation and so forth for the satisfaction of the respective deities as before. This is the sequence for the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Then, having consecrated the Lord of Gods and seated him upon the lotus-throne,
one should worship the seat, the form, and the body of wisdom (vidyādeha) therein.
Then, having invoked Mahādeva and worshipped him with ritual bathing and other rites,
and having mentally bathed him, one should offer garments and a sacred thread.
Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, and ornaments,
and having offered incense and a lamp, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana).
One should offer the food offering (naivedya), mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa), and betel leaf (tāmbūla).
Then, having presented the sacrificial oblation (bali), one should worship with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings, as well as with perfumes and flowers.
One who is authorized to perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) should perform it in the fire;
then, having gone into the presence of Śiva, one should offer the worship of Śiva.
Having offered incense and the ārārtika lamp, one should present the sacred thread (pavitra).
Having applied white ashes, one should worship with a mirror and other such items.
Preceded by recitation, praise, prostration, and circumambulation,
one should worship with the eightfold flower offering and then honor [the deity] with a special arghya offering.
Having performed the dismissal (udvāsana) of Śiva along with his retinue by means of the *parāṅmukha* arghya offering,
one should meditate on Śiva within the heart at the proper time and consume that which has been offered to him.
Thus has the sequence of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva been briefly described;
we shall now demonstrate it in detail, avoiding both excessive condensation and prolixity.
In that regard, the ritual rinsing (ācamana) is now described: having washed the feet up to the knees and the hands up to the wrists,
facing either east or north and seated in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture with both hands placed between the knees,
one should [place] *hāṃ* on the little finger and the other fingers of both hands.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ," "Hīṃ Śirase namaḥ," "Hūṃ Śikhāyai namaḥ," "Haiṃ Kavacāya namaḥ," and "Haḥ Astrāya phaṭ," one should form the right hand into the shape of a cow's ear and, with that—
Having taken water sufficient for immersing a black gram seed, and having contracted the thumb and little finger while releasing the index finger,

one should contemplate it as the form of Soma during the bright fortnight and the form of Sūrya during the dark fortnight by joining the thumb and index finger; then, through the consumption of that [water], [one worships] Bhāratī residing at the tip of the tongue.

Having meditated upon the seven purifications and the external purification of one's own body, one should thereafter rinse the mouth three times with the root mantra— preceded by the washing of the hands and ending with *svadhā*— using the *brahmatīrtha*. Then, [one should perform] the purification of one's own mouth, which resides within the cavity of the lips...
While contemplating the satisfaction of the deity of the Praṇava, one should wipe both lips twice with the base of the thumb.
Thus concludes the section on bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth. Now follows the application of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*).
There are four kinds of sacred ash: the primary ritual form (*kalpa*), the secondary form (*anukalpa*), the tertiary form (*upakalpa*), and the non-ritual form (*akalpa*). Among these:

Having worshipped a cow that is free from disease and accompanied by her calf, one should take her dung while it has not yet fallen to the ground but is still in the air; having formed it into a ball, purified it,
and burnt it in the Śiva-fire with the five Brahma-mantras, one should purify what has been prepared with the root mantra (mūla).

That which arises from the Agnihotra sacrifice is both [the primary] Kalpa; having taken dried cow-dung in the forest and burnt it in the Śiva-fire, purifying it with the root mantra, that which is thus prepared is the Anukalpa.
Having taken the ashes from forest fires, house fires, cow-pens, or brick kilns, and having purified them with a cloth, formed them into a ball with cow urine, burnt them again in the Śiva-fire,
and cleansed them with the root mantra, it is prepared; [otherwise] it is deficient in mantra and so forth.

If the cow dung has been collected by Brāhmaṇas, women, Śūdras, or others, or prepared from the hearth and so forth of the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), it is unfit. If it is unfit, having taken that [dung], one should perform the binding of the directions with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), [reciting]: *Hoṃ* to the head of Īśāna.

Namaḥ! Heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Huṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora. Hiṃ, obeisance to the secret place of Vāmadeva. Haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta. Hāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Hrīṃ, obeisance to the head. Hūṃ, obeisance to the crest-lock. Haiṃ, obeisance to the armor.
Hauṃ, salutation to the three eyes. Haḥ, salutation to the weapon (*astra*). Hrāṃ, salutation to Vivṛttikalā and the others.
(p. 210) Hrīṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhākalā. Hrūṃ, salutation to Vidyākalā. Hraiṃ.
"Oṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ; hrauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ.

Thus, one should purify [the ashes] with the mantras of the Kalās, along with the five Brahmans and the six limbs. The wearing of such ashes is of two kinds: smearing (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) is also of two kinds: that in the form of a bath for removing impurities and that in the form of a ritual bath.
One who has already bathed with water is qualified for the two kinds of ash baths.
If that is impossible, having washed [the feet] up to the throat,

the waist, or the knees, and having wiped them with a wet cloth, one should put on another garment, perform *ācamana*, and [purify] with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [visualized as] emerging from the big toe of the right foot.

Having contemplated that the mere external impurities within the body have been burnt by fire, one should flood the body with a stream of nectar flowing from the circle of Śaktis situated in the station of the Bindu, which has been agitated by contact with the fire. Then, while mentally uttering the root mantra up to the end of the Nāda:

One should contemplate one's body as being consecrated by a profuse stream of nectar flowing from the power (*śakti*) agitated by contact with that [object]. This mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) should always and everywhere be performed whenever there is a suspicion of impurity. Alternatively, having meditated upon that very power in the form of a cow—

One should bathe the body with the stream of nectar from the rays of its tail; this is the bath of bhāva (devotional immersion). Alternatively, one should sprinkle the body with the divine waters of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and other such rivers, or with the dust and soil from various sacred sites (kṣetra), while reciting the five Brahma-mantras and the root-mantras of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).

One should touch [the body]. Having performed one of these methods, one should mutter the five Brahma-mantras, the six auxiliary mantras (ṣaḍaṅga), and the root mantra either once or three times. Then, having performed the two rinsings of the mouth (ācamana) as before—

One should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), which wards off the entire collection of impurities, both external and internal, that have been accumulated. Its procedure is as follows: having avoided the presence of cows, Brahmins, gods, fire, gurus, and [one's] teachers and scriptures, one should go to a pure place on a path free from the sight of barbarians (*mleccha*), outcastes (*antyaja*), ungrateful persons (*kṛtaghna*), and the like.

Facing either east or north, having placed the ashes— measuring a mere handful, or one *niṣka*, or two and a half *niṣkas*— in the form of the *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, and so forth, according to the order starting with the Brahmins,
he should discard that portion belonging to the *Rākṣasas* in the southwest corner (*nairṛtyakoṇa*), [and then take] the *akalpa*.

Having first performed the ritual binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), one should purify the four kinds of ash with the five Brahma-mantras and the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantras; then, having consecrated the ash seven times with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
one should apply it starting from the feet up to the head if one is detached (*virakta*), or starting from the head [downward] if one is not detached.

With a small amount of ash held between the right thumb and forefinger, one should perform the *uddhūlana*— the act of touching the limbs, with the exception of the hands and soles of the feet that are to be traversed— up to the ends of the feet.
This is the bathing for the removal of bodily impurities.
Then, with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*),
one should apply them to the head, face, heart, private parts, feet, and limbs using the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Īśāna;
and to the shoulders and the remaining limbs using the Sadyojāta mantra alone, with the right hand.
One should apply the ash to the parts of the body that are not to be touched with the left hand.
The remaining ash should be sprinkled on the head with the root mantra using the *kumbha-mudrā*.
In this manner, the Vīraśaiva should perform the smearing of all limbs. Others, however, [apply it] in sequence on the forehead...
Having made four squares and three lines, they should smear themselves with ashes from the neck down to the navel.

A Śūdra, however, should avoid the smearing and perform the ash-bath consisting only of the tripuṇḍra to be described hereafter. This [practice] pertains to Śūdras other than those who are ascetics (tapasvin). For this very reason:

In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "If an ascetic, having duly taken up sacred ash, should perform a bath with it," and so forth; this constitutes a qualification for the specific eligibility regarding the two forms of *uddhūlana*—namely, the ritual bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*) and the ritual bath [performed with ash].
The state of being an ascetic has been described. Likewise, even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are not ascetics should perform the ash-bath consisting solely of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Furthermore, all four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, when unable to perform the smearing (uddhūlana), should likewise perform that which consists of the triple mark.

They should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*). With the specific intention of the ash-bath consisting solely of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), certain Āgamas have prescribed the quantity of ash as one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, or half of that [half], following the sequence of the Vīraśaiva and other traditions. In that regard, by initiated householders...
It should be performed with water during all three junctions of the day (sandhyās). However, it should be performed without water by women,
ascetics (yatis), those under a vow (vratins), forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), maidens, and others who have not received initiation.

Before midday, it should be performed with water; after that, it should be done without water. Likewise, when performing the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), one should sip water (*ācamana*) after putting on another garment, or sip water alone even without putting on another garment.
Now, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

And regarding that [measurement], among the various positions taught in the scriptures—such as seven, five, four, three, or two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for the castes in sequence; or four finger-breadths on the forehead, heart, and arms for all; or one finger-breadth on other limbs, and so forth—[one should choose].

Adopting the position stated by the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*), some maintain that it should be applied to the forehead and other parts with the three fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers; or alternatively, it may be applied to the forehead with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers. This *tripuṇḍra* consists of three thick, continuous lines.
And it must be done in such a way that it becomes manifest.
The wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) should be performed after meditating upon the God of Ashes (*bhasmadeva*), who has three faces,
three hands, three feet, and three eyes, who is smeared with ash, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance, fierce, and adorned with red flowers— at the place where the triple mark is worn.
One should wear the square or semi-circular lamp-mark (dīpa) obtained through family custom, or the triple-line mark (tripuṇḍra), within [the forehead].
And every mark should be made with pure ashes, or with ashes mixed with sandalwood paste, moistened with water. Whatever kind of mark is on the forehead...
In the heart, navel, arms, belly, and chest, [the mantras] have Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha as their presiding deities;
and in the eight locations— the head, forehead, throat, shoulders, heart, navel, and back— [the mantras] have [their respective deities].
Having Brahmā, Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Agni, and Candra as their deities,
[these mantras are to be placed] upon the sixteen locations: the head, forehead, neck, chest, shoulders, upper arms, elbows, wrists, sides of the abdomen, navel, and the pair of flanks and back.
The nine [deities] beginning with Śiva and Maheśvara, along with the nine beginning with Vāmā, have the two aspects of Consciousness as their presiding deities;
[they are located] in the places of the head, forehead, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, neck, shoulders,
and elbows— [namely] Śiva, Śakti, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, and Puruṣa.
[It consists of] the non-inherent ego, intellect, mind, ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose,

speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, as well as sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and so forth; and furthermore, the elements such as earth, water, and the rest, along with their constituent principles and presiding deities.
This should be performed as appropriate, taking into account the place, time, science, and art.
In the system of thirty-six locations, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with space (ākāśa) are circular in shape,
[and are made of] crystal, moonstone, sunstone, cow’s milk, coral, green vitriol, antimony, a rainbow, Indra’s bow, and Indra’s elephant.
[The colors] are like those of a cloud, ruby, coral, sapphire, saffron, hibiscus flower, rainbow, sun-gem, gold, dūrvā grass, turmeric, oleander,
black cloud, blue gem, pearl, ruby, gold, and crystal; [one should meditate on] the wind as black and quadrangular, and fire as red and triangular.
Having visualized white water in the shape of a half-moon and yellow earth as the *pṛthivītattva* (p.
213), one should apply sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*) at their respective locations with mantras such as: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, whose nature is the *śivatattva*," and so forth. Thus...

This should also be inferred in other cases. One should wear the *tripuṇḍra* of ashes obtained through the traditional practices of one's respective lineage, or *puṇḍras* associated with various internal deities, in the locations prescribed for the forehead and so forth. Thus is the method for wearing the ashes.
The Procedure for Wearing Rudrākṣas:

Now, regarding the wearing of rudrākṣas—it is as constant as the wearing of ashes during the worship of Śiva. Beginning with [the passage]: "For the sake of the worship of Śiva, which arose from the eye of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva)... and so on, it mentions the rudrākṣa.

The white, red, yellow, and black colors should be specifically adopted by Brāhmaṇas and other Vīraśaivas. In the absence of the aforementioned colors, all four types may be worn by Vīraśaivas. The three beginning with red are for Kṣatriyas; the two beginning with yellow are for Vaiśyas; and as for Śūdras—

One should wear [the beads] of black color alone; or all [colors] may be worn by everyone according to what is available. Alternatively, they may be worn on the head, neck, ears, arms, wrists, and chest, in specific quantities appropriate to the respective measurements of those parts. On the head...
Forty [hair-pores] on the neck; thirty-two on the ears, six on each; sixteen on each arm; twelve on each wrist;
and one hundred and eight on the chest.

Thus, the total number is two hundred and forty-eight; or, including one for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), it is two hundred and forty-nine. One at the crest-lock, thirty-six on the head, fifty on the chest, and a sacred thread (*upavīta*) consisting of one hundred and eight [strings]. [The remaining strings are placed] on the neck, the ears, the arms, and the wrists.

"As before" means either numbering two hundred and ninety-five, or, in the absence of obtaining one hundred and eight on the head, three [should be placed there]. "As before" regarding the throat, ears, arms, chest, and wrists means that either numbering five hundred and two should be worn.

The wearing of rudrākṣa beads together with the five jewels— diamond, ruby, lapis lazuli, coral, and pearl— is a remover of fever, planetary afflictions, piśācas, urinary disorders, leprosy, fistula-in-ano, childhood seizures, epilepsy, and possession by spirits.

Wearing it on the crown, earrings, ear-ornaments, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, waist-bands, and so forth, destroys untimely death; elsewhere, the wearing of rudrākṣas increases longevity, prosperity, and fame.
Wearing it on the crest-lock (*śikhā*) yields ten million-fold fruit. On the ears and arms, the fruit increases tenfold for each subsequent location. On the hands, the fruit is immeasurable.
A single-faced *rudrākṣa* should be worn hidden within the crest-lock.
It removes the fear of great calamities such as the sin of killing a Brahmin, weapons, fire, lightning, thieves, and excessive rain;

it bestows longevity, prosperity, and fame; and it grants enjoyment, liberation, and all spiritual perfections (*siddhis*). The two-faced [form] removes the sin of killing a cow and other such faults; the three-faced [form] removes the sin of killing a woman and other such faults; and the four-faced [form]...

The five-faced [Liṅga] removes the fault of approaching those who should not be approached and eating what should not be eaten; it removes all sins. The six-faced [Liṅga], when held in the right hand, removes the sin of killing an embryo.
The seven-faced [Liṅga] removes the faults of stealing gold and killing a cow, and it is also a remover of poison. The eight-faced [Liṅga]...
The nine-faced [form] removes the sin of violating the Guru’s bed and removes the fault of all cruel conduct;

it removes the fault of great sins numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions. The ten-faced [form] removes the fear of planets, piśācas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, serpents, lions, tigers, and so forth.
The eleven-faced [Liṅga], when worn on the crest,
bestows the fruit of one hundred thousand horse-sacrifices, one hundred thousand Vājapeya sacrifices, and the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
The twelve-faced [Liṅga], when worn on the region of the throat, [bestows the same].
It bestows the fruit of the Gomedha and Aśvamedha sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; it causes the increase of sovereignty,
removes the fear of fanged beasts, horned animals, thieves, and fire, destroys all sins,
and grants incomparable enjoyments to those with thirteen faces.
It brings about the accomplishment of alchemy, elixirs, metallurgy, and the preparation of medicinal pills;
it removes the sin of killing one's father, mother, brother, or wife; it possesses fourteen faces;
it accomplishes all undertakings; it dispels all diseases and calamities; and it grants the perfection of the yoga of knowledge.

Except for the head, arms, and ears, the wearing of rudrākṣas is to be avoided on other parts of the body during times of physical decline or growth, childbirth, sexual intercourse with women, the voiding of excrement or urine, and while consuming liquor, meat, garlic, onions, and the like.
The gift of Rudrākṣas, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Rudrākṣadānakalpa*,
bestows the fruit of studying all the Vedas and Purāṇas, performing all sacrifices, and visiting all sacred fords,
and it removes all diseases.

It yields the fruit of giving a hundred lingas, establishing a hundred lingas, feeding a thousand devotees of Śiva, and giving away a thousand maidens; it bestows sons, friends, all desired enjoyments, and liberation in union with Śiva (śivasāyujya);
and it grants these same fruits even to the recipient who is a devotee of Śiva.

Wearing rudrākṣas on auspicious days— such as the full moon, the new moon, the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (saṅkrānti), eclipses, birth asterisms, and so forth— causes the destruction of all sins. At the time of worship, the wearing of rudrākṣas should be performed on the head with the Īśāna mantra, and on the ears with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
In the throat and other locations with the Aghora mantra, and on the chest with the Vyomavyāpin mantra;
for those who have transcended the castes and stages of life, who are solely devoted to that [mantra], who are initiated for as long as they live,
the illustrious Vīraśaivas who are ever perfectly pure— for all of them, indeed— [the purification is performed].

Because time is of supreme importance, the Rudrākṣas held by means of the Īśāna and other mantras as well as the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra) should be worn at all times; for every physical, verbal,
or mental suffering or happiness must be offered solely to Śiva.
Because there is no specific time for prohibition; however, at the time of worship, they should be worn especially because it is a distinguished time.
(215) Now, since the wearing of ashes and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads are to be determined within their respective specific contexts,
they must follow the formal propositions of those respective contexts.

If it is argued that the two topics of wearing ashes and wearing rudrākṣas are not to be described here because they have already been described, and because this would contradict the formal promise (*pratijñā*) consisting of the title "Worship of Śiva," we say no;
for just as one who intends to perform the Soma sacrifice makes the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādhāsye*) for each individual rite, so too [is the present case].

Just as in the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by the Soma sacrifice), the act of establishing the fires is both a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice and an independent rite (*karma*),

so too the wearing of *bhūti* (sacred ash) and *rudrākṣa* beads is both an independent rite and a constituent part of the worship of Śiva. If it is asked, "What is gained by such a circuitous argument?"— to this it is replied:

Just like the initial installation of the sacred fires (*apūrvādhāna*), the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads and the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra mark are each distinct rites; having established as a settled doctrine that even a child who has not yet begun the worship of Śiva must necessarily wear the insignia of Śiva according to the specific initiation, [the author] treats each individually.

Although this was already established in the [preceding] section, it is treated again in the section on the worship of Śiva because it is also an ancillary part of that worship; thus, there is not even a trace of room for doubt here.

Now, it might be argued that those auxiliary elements, such as the six sacrifices and so forth, attain syntactic unity with the principal element (the *śeṣin*) and thus constitute an action enjoined in conjunction with that principal; likewise, there is no engagement of the principal without its auxiliaries. However, in the present case, this is not so for one who has not commenced the worship of Śiva.
When the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads is being performed, it is not logical to conceive of them as being ancillary parts (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śiva;
for since the performance of an ancillary is observed even in the absence of its primary (*śeṣin*), it is difficult to establish the relationship of ancillary and principal in the present case.

If you say this is not so, [we reply] no; for he who has made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall wear the sacred ash and wear rudrākṣa beads for the sake of perfecting my qualification before performing the worship of Śiva," is distinct from one who has resolved, "I shall establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya) while intending to sacrifice with Soma. Just as...

Just as one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) is not entitled to perform the Soma sacrifice, so too one who bears the marks of Rudra is not entitled to worship Rudra. The established conclusion is that the wearing [of the marks] as an ancillary to the worship of Śiva is indeed something entirely different, based on the principle: "Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva."
Now, the procedure for *sakalīkaraṇa*:
for Vīraśaivas, there is the daily recollection of the *sakalīkaraṇa* performed by their Guru;
for others, the distinction is that the *sakalīkaraṇa* is performed only at that specific time.
Now follows the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, which consists of the placement of the *kara* (hand) and the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). That is threefold:

for householders, it takes the form of *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation); for celibate students (*brahmacārins*), it takes the form of *sthitinyāsa* (the rite of maintenance); and for ascetics and forest-dwellers...

[This is] in the form of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and placement (*nyāsa*). For the Vīraśaivas, all three [types of nyāsa] may be performed according to their preference. Among these, first the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* is described: having smeared both hands with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should begin from the wrist of the left hand and proceed over its palm and back up to the base of the fingers with the right hand, [reciting] "haḥ."
Saying "Astrāya phaṭ," he should wipe [the hand] twice with the mantra repeated;

then, with that same mantra, he should wipe the palm of the right hand and its back once with the left hand, and contemplate both hands as pervaded by the splendor of the weapon-mantra up to the wrists.

Having joined the two hands in the *sampuṭa* gesture and meditated upon the circle of power (*śakti-maṇḍala*) in the form of nectar between the two thumbs, and having bathed both eyes with that nectar,
one should [perform the gesture] with the two thumbs joined as the pericarp in the lotus of the hollowed palms, reciting: *Hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ*.
Having laid down the Śivāsana with "Hāṃ Haḥ, obeisance to the form of Śiva," one should lay down the subtle form of Śiva—
the youthful, stable Vidyā consisting of radiant energy— and then, with the thumbs and forefingers, lay it down on the two thumbs with "Hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna."

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the four mantras beginning with "Hreṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa" using both thumbs starting from the index finger to the little finger, one should place the thumb— consisting of thirty-eight kalās and having Sadāśiva as its essence— into the palms with the mantra "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of Vidyā."
Having projected the gross body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), and having projected the eyes with "Oṃ *netrebhyo* namaḥ" upon the palms of the hands,
one should invoke Śiva, who pervades the body of Sadāśiva, using the thumbs and ring fingers with "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva. This is the invocation (*āvāhana*).

The continuous contemplation of the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) established by the Guru through the mantra is the distinction; for others, however, it is merely temporary. Then, having sequentially deposited the five mantras—excluding the *netra* mantra—beginning with "HĀṂ, obeisance to the Heart" on the little finger and so forth, [one proceeds] on the left and right...

(For the arms: Having covered the two hands with the other two hands while reciting "Kavacāya namaḥ," and having joined the two hands together, one should perform the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. This applies to the [mantras] placed on the heart, head, crest, and so forth, as well as to the digits (*kalā*).

Paramīkaraṇa (the act of making supreme) consists of the contemplation of attaining that same color by means of the exceedingly white [light] of the supreme Śiva-tejas invoked within those [substances] of various distinct colors.
Then, one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* (placement on the limbs). With the right thumb and ring finger, [one recites] *hāṃ*.

Having offered salutation with "Oṃ *śivāsanāya* namaḥ" and having placed the white lotus-seat of Śiva, which has arisen from the *mūlādhāra* in the center of the body or in the heart, one should [place] the form of Śiva consisting of light, starting from the *nābhikanda* or the heart up to the space between the eyebrows, with "Haṃ hāṃ *śivamūrtaye* namaḥ.
(The mind...)
Having placed the subtle form of Śiva [therein] (p. 217), having formed a fist, and having placed the Īśāna mantra on the head with the thumb,
one should place it on the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet using the index finger and the others joined with the thumb.

Having sequentially deposited the *tatpuruṣa* mantras and so forth, one should deposit the *vidyādeha* with the mantra "HĀṂ HAUṂ, salutation to the *vidyādeha*" from the space between the eyebrows up to the *brahmarandhra* using the *indra-mantra*; then,
with the *netra-mantra*, [one deposits it] in the three [eyes].

Having placed [the mantra] with the three middle fingers, one should invoke Paramaśiva upon that [seat] with the thumb and ring finger, reciting: *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ*. Then, [one should place] those residing in the heart and head into the locations of Śiva.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart, head, and crest with the thumbs, little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers respectively,
and having placed the armor (*kavaca*) with the two index fingers as a covering for the ears extending to the center of the breasts,
one should place the weapon (*astra*) on the palms of the hands with the two ring fingers. All these mantras end with *namaḥ*.

The weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), however, ends with *phaṭ*. Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) preceded by three claps (*tāla*) using the weapon-mantra ending in *namaḥ* *huṃ* *phaṭ*, and having enveloped [the area] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*),
one should display the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, from the head down to the feet.

Touching with both hands is the Mahāmudrā. Thereafter, one should contemplate oneself as having a form identical to Śiva. Having thus performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), and being terrifying with a bound turban, a head-encircling cloth, a helmet, bracelets, and weapons grasped in hand—
Since one becomes as invincible to the base as a soldier, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa must indeed be performed by the learned Vīraśaivas.

Then, having washed the general *arghya* vessel with the *astra* mantra, and having filled it with pure water— conceived as nectar flowing from the station of the *bindu*— with the mantra "HĀṂ, obeisance to the Heart,
Vauṣaṭ," and having consecrated it seven times with "HĀṂ, obeisance to the Heart," [one should proceed].
Having enveloped [the vessel] with the Kavaca mantra and worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should display the Dhenu-mudrā.
This is the water for the general arghya; setting aside Śiva, it is common to all others, including the gatekeepers and the rest.
Now follows the worship of the door-keepers;

this is its sequence: while meditating on oneself as situated within the fivefold armor of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should mentally transcend the group of thirty-one principles beginning with earth and ending with *māyā*.

Meditating upon the temple of Śiva-pūjā as circular, red in color, and consisting of the principle of Śuddhavidyā, one who desires worldly enjoyment and liberation should worship the door-keeper at the eastern gate;
one who desires fame, victory, and good fortune should worship him at the southern gate.

One who desires only liberation alone [should worship] at the western gate. Worship should not be performed at the northern gate. Having sprinkled the door with the water of the general *arghya* while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should first worship the guardians of the outer gates. These are Gaṇapati and the others. In that regard:

At the top of the door, within the opening of the *udumbara* beam, Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī are seated in the right, left, and middle sections respectively. The arrangement of left and right should be understood either with reference to the deity or with reference to the worshipper entering the door. Of the door—

Outside, on the right side, is Nandin; on the very same right side, in the northern part of Nandin's position, is Gaṅgā; on the left side is Mahākāla; and on the very same left side, in the southern part of his position, Yamunā is situated. Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.
I worship Gaṇapati, who is dark-complexioned and holds a rosary of teeth, a noose, a goad, a lotus, and a citron in his hands. Hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī;
she is white-complexioned and holds a rosary and a book.

I worship Sarasvatī, whose two lower hands are occupied with playing the lute; Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī, who holds a bilva fruit, a lotus, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons,
while streams of nectar flow from the golden jars held in the trunks of the pair of elephants stationed at her two sides.
I worship Mahālakṣmī as she is being sprinkled with water. Hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin;
I worship Nandin, who wears a crown of reddish-brown matted hair, holds a trident, a rosary, and a threatening mudgara-staff, and has a large face. Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā.

I worship Gaṅgā, who is white in color, whose vehicle is a makara, and who holds a jar of nectar and a chowrie. Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla! [I worship him] who is black in color, with a massive body terrifying due to his fangs and knitted brows.

I worship Mahākāla, who holds a trident, a skull-cup, a mallet, and the tarjanī mudrā. Hāṃ, obeisance to Yamunā! I worship Yamunā, who is dark-complexioned, whose vehicle is a tortoise, and who holds a chowrie and a nectar-filled jar—at their respective places.
One should worship them. All these door-keepers, with the exception of Gaṅgā and Yamunā, have three eyes; and all of them have faces equal in size to the doors.
O All-pervading One, whose form is the entire universe known through the Vedanta;
O Virupaksha, devoid of poison and lordship;
O Ishvara of the universe, the root of all distinctions without exception.
Open the door, O Death of Death!
With this verse, one should contemplate the request for the opening of the door within the *sajjikā* [preparatory rite].
The worshipper, having opened the door with the *astra-mantra*, should apply the mantra "Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva" to his two eyes.
Having caused the celestial obstacles (*vighna*) situated in the sky to tremble with divine meditation and vision,
having caused the obstacles in the atmosphere to tremble by tossing flowers with the union of the index finger and thumb,
and having caused the terrestrial obstacles to tremble by striking the ground three times with the heel of the right foot, [one should act] with the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*.

One should dispel the three kinds of obstacles. Then, standing by the left door-jamb of the entrance while not touching the right jamb with the right foot, one should enter the temple of Śiva, saying: "Hāṃ, salutation to the Weapon; [I salute] the fire-colored one with four faces."

"I worship the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), who stands in the middle of the threshold facing the form of Śiva, possessing four hands—two of which hold a spear and [the gestures of] granting fearlessness and boons; who is adorned with a crown of matted hair and the crescent moon on his head; and who is the dispeller of all obstacles. Thus, one worships the King of Weapons situated there.
Having turned back toward that [deity], one should perform worship. Then, inside the door on the right side,
[one should worship] with "Hrāṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Śrī Nandikeśvara," who is red in color, has three eyes,
and wears a crown of matted hair adorned with a crescent moon.

I worship Nandikeśvara, who has four hands bearing the mudrās of the deer and the axe, who carries a staff at his armpit and a small knife at his waist, who wears ashes and rudrākṣa beads, and who has the face of a monkey.

One should worship on the right side inside the door: "Hāṃ Suṃ, obeisance to the goddess Suyaśā; I worship the goddess Suyaśā, who is dark-complexioned and whose right hand is adorned with a blue lotus. Thus one should worship the goddess Suyaśā inside the door. Then, Śiva.

Having circumambulated [the site], one should worship Brahmā in the southwest corner (Nirṛti-kona). The worship of these [deities] consists of the offering of a seat, invocation, installation, making present, binding, and the presentation of water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, incense, and lamps.

Or, each [of the door-keepers] should be worshipped individually up to the offering of food (naivedya) and betel (tāmbūla). If one is unable [to do so], one should worship all the door-keepers together in the middle with scents, flowers, and so forth, saying:
"O divine door-keepers, protect the door of the Lord with diligence, warding off obstacles."

One should cause [the disciple] to hear the command of Śiva: "This is the command of the Supreme Lord: 'Saṅghāta'. In the worship performed for one's own sake, because it is both prescribed and prohibited according to different Āgamas, it is optional; thus, there is no deficiency if it is not performed, while its performance results in an accumulation of merit. This is indeed an option, according to the principle of the *ṣoḍaśi-graha* (the cupping of the sixteenth vessel).

Then, having placed all the articles of worship before Śiva, standing on the right side or the southeast (āgneya) side of the deity and facing north, he should assume a beautiful posture such as the Svastika or the Abhyasta, and sit upon a seat covered with either red silk, linen, or a variegated cloth.
Having assumed the threefold posture according to the measurement of twenty-four cubits (p.
220), [one should perform] first among the five purifications— of the self, the locus, the substance, the mantra, and the liṅga.

One should perform self-purification (*ātmaśuddhi*). This method of worshiping Gaṇapati and others beneath the *udumbara* tree and so forth—characterized by the aforementioned features—is to be performed prior to self-purification when a temple of Śiva exists.
And that [temple] is prescribed as follows: situated in the northeast quarter of the house, consisting of stone, brick, or clay...
It should be made of pure wood or clay, either square, oblong, or circular, and measured by the middle joint of the sacrificer’s middle finger, or by the third joint, or [measuring] three,
five, seven, nine, thirteen, seventeen, twenty, or twenty-one [finger-breadths].

It should be constructed with a measurement of twenty-four *hasta*s— known as the "twenty-four" (*caturviṃśati*)— according to the standard of a *hasta* consisting of thirty-two fingers divided into the categories of superior, middling, and inferior lengths;
it may have one story or two stories according to that same twenty-four *hasta* measurement, or three stories.

Having constructed a shrine room and divided it into five parts, one should fashion an altar in its central portion— avoiding stone or plaster— either made of clay or built of bricks, marked with four corners and two cubits [in length],
and sixteen finger-breadths in height, or eight finger-breadths in height.

Above that, on the western side, one should construct a space corresponding to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), measuring one tāla in width and length and five aṅgulas in height; and on its eastern side, a space corresponding to the area for the offering altar (arghapīṭha), with the same dimensions in length, width, and height.

To its eastern side, one should prepare a space corresponding to the sanctum (beramaṇḍapa), measuring five tālas in length, four tālas in width, and eight aṅgulas in height. Within that, in the area corresponding to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
there should be a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, which may be square, oblong, or circular.

One should prepare a casket for the *sajjikā*. In a place suitable for the temple pavilion (*beramaṇḍapa*), having placed a casket adorned with lotuses— measuring two cubits in length, one cubit in width, and twelve finger-breadths in height— one should install upon it a lid of the same dimensions.
Having spread out [the ground] and placed in its center a pedestal made of ivory and the like,

one should install upon it a lotus-pedestal fashioned from gold or other materials, facing east and accompanied by a halo fashioned at its western side. In this case, having encircled it with three strands of woolen thread—

"Your purifier is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as the Lord, you encompass all limbs from every side. He whose body has not been heated by austerity does not partake of that which is raw; only those who have been cooked [by austerity] and are bearers [of the rite] attain it. Thus he mutters. This is the position stated in the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*). However, according to the primary position known as *karapīṭha*, this is indeed purely mental.

The word "all" is the qualification. And one should decorate the worship pavilion with scattered flowers, the fragrance of sandalwood paste, canopies, strings of pearls, banners, flags, mirrors, lamps, and so forth. In the absence of such a worship pavilion:
Having mentally conceived the very place of Śiva’s worship as such a pavilion for worship (*pūjā-maṇḍapa*), one seated near the Śiva-pīṭha— being Śiva himself—
should perform the worship of the door-keepers (*dvārapāla*) either before or after the purification of oneself.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the gatekeepers.

Now, one might object that all of this is inconsistent: the individual soul (*paśu*) is the *jīva*, the Lord (*pati*) is the Supreme God (*parameśvara*), and the net of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), both insentient and sentient, which is distinct from both of them, is the bond (*pāśa*). Among these, it is the one denoted by the word *pati* [who is meant].
"The Supreme Lord alone is to be worshipped, sought for refuge, meditated upon, and heard. In this regard,

through a thorough reflection on the scriptural statement "one only, without a second," the determination that every other deity apart from Śiva is denoted by the term *paśu* (bound soul) constitutes the state of being a Vīraśaiva.
If it is argued that the worship of door-keepers distinct from Śiva is not appropriate, we say no;

for Nandikeśvara and the other door-keepers are specific manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Śiva, in accordance with the Vedic scripture which states, "The One alone exists in many ways. Furthermore, this constitutes the state of being a Vīraśaiva, characterized by single-minded devotion to Him.

This refers to the transcendence of other deities and the worship of their devotees. In the present context, since the gatekeepers are solely the executors of Śiva’s command, one must cultivate the very same cognition of non-difference from Śiva toward them as well;
this is clearly evident in the consistency with other scriptures regarding the mobile forms [of the deity].

The realization of non-difference from the form of Śiva and the superiority of the *jaṅgama* (human devotee) over one's own chosen *liṅga* have been described. Furthermore, since the worship of the attendants (*gaṇas*) of Śiva, such as Nandikeśa and others, is frequently established in other scriptures,
all that has been prescribed regarding the worship of the gatekeepers must be performed.
The established conclusion.

If it is objected: "Since mudrās that are auxiliary to worship, such as the *dhenumudrā* and others, must be accomplished through the operation of both hands, their placement on a separate seat must be asserted; and if that were accepted, there would be a severance of the vital channel (*prāṇaliṅga*). Therefore, how can this be justified?"—then [the response follows].
In the Vātulottara, having fashioned chariots and other vehicles out of gold alone,

one performs the worship of Śiva preceded by the installation of the chosen liṅga therein; there is also the grasping [of the vehicle] with a woolen thread, and in that context, the Vedic mantra "tatra ca pavitraṃ ta" is used along with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
Because it has been demonstrated many times that [the mantra] is accompanied by the word "namas" at its end.
Alternatively, since the mental factor alone possesses preeminence in worship, everything is purely mental; thus, all is entirely consistent.
Now, the procedure for the worship of Śiva, clearly demonstrated through the correct examination of the scriptures, is explained in the fourteenth chapter of the Upadeśa.
At the beginning, Śaivism is said to be threefold: the first is remembered as the General (sāmānya), the second is the Particular (viśeṣa), and the third is the Supportless (nirābhāra).
Thus, the Vīraśaiva is of three kinds:
the purely Vedic, the one who follows both the Vedas and the Āgamas, and the one who is an expert in the Tantric Āgamas.
Whether one is a non-devotee or a devotee, let them perform the worship of Śiva;
if they are a non-devotee, they attain devotion, and if they are a devotee, they attain union (sāyujya).
The devotee is also said to be of two kinds: the one-pointed and the indolent. The indolent devotee should worship Śiva with the root mantra and with devotion to Śiva.
Content with that alone, he gradually bestows liberation through union (sāyujya);
then, the devotee who is single-mindedly focused is the most excellent among the supreme devotees of Śiva.
Relying on the path of the *nigamas* and *āgamas*, a worshiper of Śiva should perform whatever form of worship in which his devotion remains unimpeded.
Such worship as is possible should indeed be performed by him according to his own means;
worshippers should never harbor thoughts of poverty in their minds while performing worship.
One should worship the three-eyed Lord accompanied by Ambā solely through the manifestation of one's own mind;
if the worshipper is wealthy, he should perform the worship without greed for riches.
That man is considered poor whose mind, though accompanied by his own wealth and kinsmen, is not directed toward the worship of Śiva; such a person does not obtain the fruit of worship.
He himself should become a perfected devotee, one who has offered all his wealth to Śiva;
those mortals who are favorable toward Śiva, they called his own kinsmen.
Those people who are not favorable are not one's own;
thus, according to the method taught in the two Agamas, I have described the means for achieving purity of mind.
Speaking of the purification of the body and the self immediately thereafter, I shall describe the worship of Śiva.

Now, regarding the purification of the self: it is twofold. One is the purification of the individual soul (*jīva-śuddhi*), consisting of the attainment of the state of Śiva by the worshipping soul; [the other is] the purification of the worshipping soul...

It consists of the purification of the body, which has the nature of bringing about the attainment of the body of Śiva. In this regard, the method for purifying the individual soul (*jīva*) is as follows: having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times, one should expel the impure air within the body by means of the exhalation (*recaka*) of breath control while reciting the Weapon Mantra (*astramantra*), and then fill the abdomen with external air.
Having filled [the body], starting from the two big toes up to the *mūlādhāra*,

she becomes twofold; then, rising upward until the end of the *brahmarandhra*, she becomes one, joined with downward-facing lotus buds, extremely subtle within the interior of the body like a streak of lightning.
Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā channel as radiant and possessing an internal cavity, and having meditated upon the blazing seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā-bīja*), *hrūṃ*, in its center,
[one should contemplate] those [channels] situated with their openings facing downward at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Having visualized the lotus buds as opened, uplifted, and turned upward by means of *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka* breath-retentions, one should meditate on the syllable *hrūṃ* blazing like the flame of a lamp in the region of the *mūlādhāra*,
rising upward through the continuous utterance of *hrūṃ phaṭ*, and by that—

Having visualized that all five knots, beginning with the knot of Brahmā within the lotus of Brahmā’s heart— the knots of the lotus stalk— have been pierced, one should draw back the syllable *hrūṃ* and exhale the breath. Again, one should [place] the *hrūṃ* mantra at the *mūlādhāra*.

Meditating with the *pūraka* breath, one should take up the individual soul (*jīva*)— which has withdrawn the consciousness pervading the entire body and is seated in the heart-lotus, accompanied by the subtle body in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*—
from that *puryaṣṭaka*, [visualizing it] as the form of a shimmering star, extremely subtle and solitary, while uttering "Hāṃ."

Having encapsulated the heart-seed syllable and placed the syllable *hrūṃ* at the crown of the head, one should perform the *kumbhaka* breath-retention and cause the vital air to move upward; then, taking it up with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should lead it as far as the *dvādaśānta* and join it with the Supreme Śiva situated above that.
And thus, the individual soul (jīva), when liberated from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies,
becomes pure through union with Śiva, endowed with stainless powers of knowledge and action.

Alternatively, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by leading the individual soul (*jīva*) as far as the *dvādaśānta* and then enclosing it within the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*) right there in the heart-lotus. The procedure for this is as follows:
upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, [one says] "Hāṃ, obeisance to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*). Hāṃ...
"Hāṃ, salutation to the Moon-maṇḍala; hāṃ, salutation to the Fire-maṇḍala;

hāṃ, salutation to the Śakti-maṇḍala. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should take up the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as pervading the body with the mantra "hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self," and [thereby] withdraw its pervasive form.
Having visualized that [seed-syllable] in the form of a shimmering star and placed it above the circle of Śakti, and having sequentially placed the circles of Śakti, Fire, Moon, and Sun above that,
[one should contemplate it] as being flooded by a flood of nectar flowing from the two circles of Śakti situated above and below.

One should meditate thus: only the protection of the individual soul (jīva) needs to be performed. Since it is already pure at the very time of initiation, purity need not be sought for it on a daily basis during the time of worship.
Purification of the Body (Dehaśuddhi):

Now follows the purification of the body. It is of two kinds: purification of the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) and purification of the gross body (sthūladeha). Among these, [the purification of the subtle body consists of] the cognitions of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell...
For the sake of purifying the subtle body consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*)— namely, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and form (*rūpa*)—

I dissolve sound and touch into Brahmā, and taste into Viṣṇu, among the causal persons (the *kāraṇapuruṣas*) residing respectively in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

"I dissolve form and smell into Rudra; I dissolve intellect and ego into Īśvara; I dissolve the mind into Sadāśiva"—thus one should dissolve the components of the subtle body, beginning with sound. Then:

For the purpose of purifying the gross body, one should meditate upon the five great elements— situated within one's own body at the locations from the feet up to the dvādaśānta (the twelve-finger space above the head), possessing the forms, shapes, and characteristics of the locations to be described hereafter— and then dissolve earth into water, and water into fire.

One should contemplate thus: "I dissolve [the earth] into water; I dissolve fire into air; I dissolve air into space; I dissolve space into the Supreme Power (parāśakti); I dissolve the Supreme Power into the Supreme Śiva. This [process occurs] within their respective causes.

The purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) consists in the dissolution of the earth and the other elements. Another form of *bhūtaśuddhi* consists in the exhaustion of their respective qualities (*guṇa*). This exhaustion of qualities is twofold:
that which takes the form of individual purification and that which takes the form of mutual purification. Of these, the first is as follows:
From the feet up to the knees, it is square, yellow in color, solid in nature, marked with a vajra, joined with the heart-seed syllable *hāṃ* together with the seed-syllable of earth,
presided over by Brahmā as the Lord of Causes, and is the form of the *nivṛtti-kalā*.

Having reflected, "I shall meditate upon the circle of the earth," one should expel the qualities of earth—smell, form, taste, touch, and sound—by means of five *udghātas* with the mantra: *hrāṃ nivṛttikalāyai huṃ phaṭ*. Then...

The watery mandala, which has the form of the half-moon extending from the knees to the navel, is white in color, liquid by nature, marked with a lotus, joined with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* of Śakti together with the syllable *āpya*, presided over by Viṣṇu as the Lord of Causes, and is the embodiment of the *kalā* of Pratiṣṭhā.

Thinking "I shall meditate," one should expel the qualities of taste, touch, form, and sound from the waters by means of four upward thrusts (*udghāta*) with the mantra *hrīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai huṃ phaṭ*. Then,
[one should visualize] a red-colored triangle extending from the navel to the throat.

(p. 225) Having reflected, "I meditate upon the fire-maṇḍala, which has the nature of cooking, is marked with the svastika, is joined with the *śikhā*-mantra 'hrūṃ' together with the seed-syllable of fire, is presided over by Rudra, the Lord of Causes, and consists of the form of the *vidyā*-kalā," one recites: *hruṃ vidyākalāyai*.

With the mantra *huṃ phaṭ*, one should expel the forms, touches, and sounds residing in the fire by means of three upward thrusts (*udghāta*). Then, from the throat up to the space between the eyebrows,
one should visualize a black hexagon, mobile by nature, marked with six dots, and [associated with] *hraḥ*.

Having contemplated, "I meditate upon the wind-maṇḍala, which is conjoined with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra) together with the seed-syllable of air, presided over by Maheśvara as the causal Puruṣa, and whose form is the Śāntikalā," one should [recite] the mantra: *hrauṃ śāntikalāyai huṃ phaṭ*.
By means of two expulsions (*udghāta*), one should drive away the qualities of touch and sound from the wind. Then,

[one should visualize] from the space between the eyebrows up to the *dvādaśānta*, a circular form, smoke-colored, having the nature of space (*ākāśa*), and marked with the *bindu-śakti* syllable *hraḥ*.
Having contemplated, "I meditate upon the sphere of space (ākāśamaṇḍala) conjoined with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and presided over by Sadāśiva,
the Lord of Causes," one should [purify] the space with a single expulsion (ekodghāta) using the mantra: *hrauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai huṃ phaṭ*.

One should cast out the quality of sound (*śabda*). Having visualized these spheres of earth and the other elements as being located in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should purify them.
This is the method for individual purification. However, in the case of mutual purification, this is the distinction: all [the spheres]...

At the time of purifying each respective element, one should visualize the spheres of earth and the other elements as pervading from the feet up to the crown of the head. During the purification of earth, immediately after the five qualities of that element have been expelled, one should contemplate the earth as being overcome by its opposite, wind, and thus transformed into the form of wind. This is likewise during the time of purifying wind.

One should meditate upon the wind as being overcome by its own opposite, earth, and as having assumed the form of earth. In the same way, one should meditate upon water and fire as well, after the respective qualities have been removed, as being overcome by their own opposites, fire and water, and as having assumed the forms of fire and water.

Immediately after the removal of the quality of space, one should meditate upon the sky as being pure like a clear crystal, having assumed the form of that supreme space (parākāśa), which consists of the supreme power (parāśakti) endowed with qualities such as eternity, omnipresence, and purity— the very opposites of those [qualities] previously associated with it— and thus being overwhelmed by that supreme space.

Thus, having visualized the purification of the body— which consists of a collection of elements whose power is exhausted due to the depletion of qualities through the individual purification or mutual purification of the great elements— one [should contemplate] that which is situated on the big toe and presided over by the power of Śiva.

Having meditated upon the body as being completely consumed by the fire of time (kālāgni) through the mantra "HAḤ ASTRĀYA HUṂPHAṬ," leaving behind only the residual kalās such as nivṛtti and so forth, and reducing it to the mere form of the defects residing within the body that remain to be spoken of.
One should flood [the body] with a rain of nectar flowing from the circle of power (*śakti-maṇḍala*) situated at the *dvādaśānta*. Thus,
having performed the expulsion of the qualities of the elements that constitute the body according to the stated method for the purpose of drying up the body,
one [visualizes] the gross body as the seed of the five elements, earth and so forth.

The banyan tree, cast down upon the field of illusion, having dharma and adharma as its root, the sense organs as its branches and sub-branches, the perception of objects such as sound as its sprouts, conceptual proliferation as its flowers, pleasure and pain as its fruit, to be enjoyed by the bird-like Puruṣa, with roots above and branches below.

Having meditated thus and performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should contemplate [the tree] as being motionless and devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit by means of the first half of the inhalation (pūraka) consisting of six mātrās, joined with the fivefold utterance of "hrām"; then,
by means of the second half of the inhalation joined with the fourfold utterance of "hrīm".

Having visualized [the tree] as endowed with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruits, one should, with a single exhalation (*udghāta*) and twelve measures of retention (*kumbhaka*), accompanied by the threefold utterance of "hrūṃ," visualize it as dried up and burnt by the fire of time (*kālāgni*) from the big toe of the left foot.

Having visualized [the body] being reduced to ashes and scattered in all directions by the first half of the exhalation (*recaka*) joined with the two utterances of *hraim*, one should then contemplate it as pure, clear like crystal, having the nature of the pure void, by means of the second half of the exhalation joined with the single utterance of *hraum*, and flood it with nectar (*amṛta*). Thus...
Having performed the burning of the body through the aforementioned number of *udghātas*, or until the respective qualities (*guṇas*) have been expelled,
the earth and other elements cease to act as bondages even without the specific contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of expelling those qualities.

Thus, preceded by such contemplation, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) up to the point of fixing the breath and the mind in their respective locations. By the word *udghāta*, according to the etymology "that by which [impurities] are driven out" (*uddhanyate 'nena*), that which is the means for expelling the qualities of the elements or their impurity is expressed.

Having performed inhalation preceded by the utterance of the respective *kalā*-mantras, one performs the action of driving the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) upward through the *suṣumnā* as far as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).
Having performed that inhalation, during the time of retention (*kumbhaka*), one effects the upward impulsion of the vital air and [then] that...
Having turned back [the breath] through the right channel until its exhalation is complete; and thus, in each single *udghāta*,
there are three *prāṇāyāmas* beginning with inhalation (*pūraka*), so that for the five *udghātas* on earth, fifteen *prāṇāyāmas* are accomplished.

In the [elements] beginning with water, there are twelve, nine, six, and three [respirations]. And in each individual breath-control (prāṇāyāma) consisting of exhalation (recaka) and so forth, there are three sets of twelve mātrās each. Consequently, each single udghāta consists of thirty-six mātrās. Alternatively, for the purpose of retention (dhāraṇā), it is for the purpose of filling.
The *kumbhaka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) itself consists of a regulation of twelve *mātrās*.
For *pūraka* (inhalation) and *recaka* (exhalation), the duration should be taken according to what is possible.
[This is measured by] rotating the knee-circle once, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
The time for snapping the fingers while performing a circumambulation is the measure of time (*mātrākāla*).
However, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other texts that the time for snapping the fingers while performing three circumambulations is the measure of time.
This is the shortest measure of time; double that is the middling, and triple that is the superior.
Thus,
without depending on the *udghāta*, which consists of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) delimited by specific durations of time,
[one proceeds] by means of the utterance of mantras consisting of as many *kalās* as there are respective qualities.
Or [it may be] in the form of reflecting upon the removal of those respective qualities;

or, by reciting the mantra of each respective *kalā* once, [one effects the removal] of the earthly mandalas and so forth—along with their respective *kalās*, *tattvas*, worlds (*bhuvanas*), phonemes (*varṇas*), words (*padas*), and mantras—with respect to one's own self. (p. 227)
Or one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), which consists merely in severing the fetters through the contemplation of the cessation of obstructiveness.

Furthermore, the spheres beginning with the earthly (pārthiva) consist of the kalās of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatīta; these are situated within the body at the feet and so forth, the knees and so forth, the navel and so forth, the throat and so forth, and the space between the eyebrows and so forth.
Alternatively, they are situated in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
their dimensions begin at one hundred yojanas and increase tenfold for each subsequent location,
and their shapes are square, semi-circular, triangular, hexagonal, and circular respectively.
Marked with the double-vajra, lotus, svastika, six dots, and a single dot, they are yellow, red, white, black, and smoke-colored respectively,
and have the natures of solidity, liquidity, heat, mobility, and space.
The five elements— earth and the others— possessing five, four, three, two, and one quality respectively, are presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
they are joined with the seed-syllables of earth and the other elements, which take the forms of the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* accompanied by the *bindu*.

These are to be cultivated. Therein, in the *nivṛtti-kalā*, there is one earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*), one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*s), the letter *ka* as the single phoneme, twenty-eight words, and two mantras known as Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya. In the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, there are twenty-three principles beginning with water and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
There are fifty-six worlds; twenty-four phonemes beginning with *kha* and ending with *ma*; thirty-two words; and two mantras known as Vāmadeva and Śiras.
In the Vidya-kalā, there are seven principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā, and twenty-seven worlds.
Such are the seven phonemes, the twenty-one words, and the two mantras named Aghora and Śikhā.
In the Śāntikalā, there are two principles (tattvas)—Śuddhavidyā and Maheśvara—and eighteen worlds; the two phonemes are Ha and Kṣa, and the twelve words are those named Puruṣa and Kavaca.
There are two mantras. In the Kalā beyond Peace (Śāntyatīta), there are two principles (tattva): Sadāśiva and Śakti; fifteen worlds; sixteen vowels as phonemes (varṇa); one word (pada);
and three mantras known as Mūla, Īśāna, and Astra. Thus, it consists of eleven mantras.
The path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*); the path of words (*padādhvan*), consisting of the ninety-four words contained within the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra;
the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), consisting of two hundred and twenty-two worlds beginning with Anāśrita;
the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), consisting of the fifty letters; and [the path of kalās], consisting of the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti.

The path of the *kalās*. In this way, the spheres (*maṇḍalas*) beginning with Earth, which contain the entire path, are to be meditated upon. Alternatively, their state of containing all paths may be meditated upon in brief.
For example: the path of mantra consists of the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
The path of words (*padādhvan*) consists of the five states characterized by waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (*turīya*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turīyātīta*).

The path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) consists of the fivefold installation (*sthāpana-pañcaka*), beginning with the word or the heart, and extending from the earthly sphere (*pārthivamaṇḍala*) onwards.

The path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of the three phonemes beginning with *a*, together with the *bindu* and *nāda*, or alternatively, it consists of the five phonemes of the root mantra. The path of kalās (*kalādhvan*) consists of the five kalās. Having thus visualized all these as containing the entire cosmic paths (*sarvādhva*), they are to be purified by means of any one of the previously mentioned methods.

Without [the realization of] being the womb of all time-periods, one should purify [the objects] by visualizing them as endowed with their previously mentioned forms of configuration, color, intrinsic nature, marks, and seed-syllables.

Thus, it takes the form of the dissolution of earth and the other elements; or the form of burning the body by casting off their respective qualities; or the form of burning only the external and internal defects residing in the body;
or the form of burning the body alone without the destruction of the qualities; or [the form] without burning.

Bhūtaśuddhi consists of the complete eradication of each respective quality, as well as the mere severing of the fetters consisting of the contemplation on the cessation of the state of being a bound soul.
This entire [system] is twofold: with removal (*sodghātā*) and without removal (*nirudghātā*).

Furthermore, it is twofold: the destruction of specific qualities (*tattadguṇakṣapaṇa*), which consists of individual purification, and mere mutual purification (*parasparaśodhanamātra*). Finally, its structural arrangement (*saṃsthāna*) is twofold by virtue of containing the entirety of the paths (*sarvādhvagarbhatvena*).

The contemplation of the elements (*bhūtacintana*) is also twofold: as being the womb of all time-periods (*sarvādhvagarbha*) and as mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Furthermore, the contemplation of being the womb of all time-periods is twofold: in detail (*prapañca*) and in brief (*saṃkṣepa*).
Thus, among the aforementioned methods of purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), whichever [is appropriate] according to former tradition, place, time, and so forth—
A certain purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is to be performed. Thus, the purification of the body consisting of the purification of the elements has been described.
Or, one should perform the purification of the body consisting of the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*),

as follows: [the sequence] of nature (*prakṛti*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hand, foot, anus, genitals, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, water, and earth— these being the forms of the principles.
The pure principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is the gross body;
the pure-and-impure principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), consisting of the principles of māyā, kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati, and puruṣa, is the subtle body.

Having meditated upon the pure Śivatattva— which consists of the principles (tattvas) of Śiva, Śakti, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śuddhavidyā— and likewise upon the supreme body (paradeha), one should dissolve the gross body into the subtle body and that [subtle body] into the supreme body. Following the performance of any one of the aforementioned methods of purification, [one recites] *hrauṃ*.

With the mantras beginning with "Obeisance to the Śāntyatīta-kalā," one effects the creation of the subtle body consisting of the five subtle kalās; and in the case of their respective dissolution, one effects the creation of the gross body consisting of the five gross kalās by means of those very same Śāntyatīta-kalā mantras.
Having meditated thus, one should bathe [the deity] with a stream of nectar flowing from the circle of Śakti, reciting: *HĀṂ ŚAKTAYE VAUṢAṬ*. Then, upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus:
*HĀṂ ĀDHĀRAŚAKTAYE NAMAḤ*, *HĀṂ DHARMĀYA NAMAḤ*, *HĀṂ*... (p. 229) ...*HĀṂ*.

Having installed the sixfold seat in the center and in the four corners starting from the southeast— namely: *jñānāya namaḥ*, *hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*, *hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*, and *hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*— therein...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Self," which consists of the gross and subtle bodies and has an undivided form of hands, feet, and so forth; and having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva composed of the thirty-eight *kalās* with "Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*), [one should recite] "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva."

Thus, having invoked the individual soul (*jīvātman*)— which is of the nature of the sacrificer’s form, stainless, endowed with the powers of knowledge and action, and in union (*sāyujya*) with Supreme Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*— and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and other mantras in the locations of the heart and so forth, and having consecrated it as supreme by means of the root-mantra, [one should worship] with the power-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

One should consecrate [the disciple] with a thick stream of nectar flowing from the maṇḍala of Śakti situated at the dvādaśānta. Then, one should perform the nyāsas of Daṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Kalā, Śrīkaṇṭha, and the others.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: one should place the Śivāsana and the unmanifest form of Śiva within the heart. With the words "Hrūṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna," one should touch the head with the tip of the thumb while forming a fist;
with "Heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa," one should touch the face with the thumb and forefinger.

*Huṃ*, "Salutation to the heart of Aghora"—with the thumb and middle finger, on the heart; *Hiṃ*, "Salutation to the secret part of Vāmadeva"—with the thumb and ring finger, on the secret part; *Haṃ*, "Salutation to the form of Sadyojāta"—with the thumb and little finger, on the foot; *Hoṃ*.
*Īśānāyordhvavaktrāya namaḥ*, *Heṃ tatpuruṣāya pūrvavaktrāya namaḥ*,
