*Huṃ aghorāya dakṣiṇavaktrāya namaḥ*, *Hiṃ vāmadevāyottaravaktrāya namaḥ*, *Haṃ sadyojātāya paścimavaktrāya namaḥ*— thus [the worship] of the upper [faces].
In the positions of the east, south, north, and west faces, they should perform the placement with the respective fingers in the manner previously described.

Thus, immediately after the placement (*nyāsa*) of Daṇḍavaktra and Bhaṅginī, the members of the three castes (*traivarṇika*) should perform the placement of the *kalās*—either accompanied by their respective *śaktis* or devoid of them—in the locations to be described hereafter. Others, however, should perform the placement using only the *śaktis*. For example: *hoṃ śaśinyai namaḥ*, *hoṃ aṅgadāyai namaḥ*.

Hrūṃ, obeisance to Iṣṭadā; hrūṃ, obeisance to Marīcī; hrūṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī—with these [mantras], one should perform the placement on the top, the east, the south, the north, the west, and the crown, using the mudrā of the clenched fist with the tip of the thumb. Heṃ, obeisance to Śānti; heṃ, obeisance to Vidyā.
*Namaḥ*, *heṃ* to Pratiṣṭhā, *namaḥ*; *heṃ* to Nivṛtti, *namaḥ*.
Thus one should place [these] on the eastern, southern, northern, and western faces with the thumb and forefinger.
*Huṃ* to Tamā, *namaḥ*; *huṃ* to Mohā, *namaḥ*; *huṃ* to Kṣudhā, *namaḥ*; *huṃ* to Nidrā.
*Namaḥ*, *huṃ* to Death, *namaḥ*; *huṃ* to Māyā, *namaḥ*; *huṃ* to Bhayā, *namaḥ*;
*huṃ* to Tārā, *namaḥ*. With these, one should place [the mantras] on the heart, throat, two arms, navel, belly, back, and chest using the thumb and middle finger. *Hiṃ* to Rajā.
*Namaḥ*, *hiṃ* to Protection, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Delight, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Preservation, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Desire, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Restraint, *namaḥ*;
*hiṃ* to Action, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Intellect, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Purpose, *namaḥ*.
*Hiṃ* to Dhātrī, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Brāhmaṇī, *namaḥ*; *hiṃ* to Mohinī, *namaḥ*;

*hiṃ* to Manonmanī, *namaḥ*. Thus, with the thumb and ring finger, [one should worship] the mūlādhāra, the private parts, the two testicles, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, the two buttocks, the waist, and the right [side].
One should place [the mantras] on the right side and the left side: *Haṃ Siddhyai namaḥ* (or *Haṃ Ṛddhyai namaḥ*),
*Haṃ Dūtyai namaḥ*, *Haṃ Lakṣmyai namaḥ*, *Haṃ Medhāyai namaḥ*,
*Haṃ Svadhāyai namaḥ*, *Haṃ Svahāyai namaḥ*, *Haṃ Dhṛtyai namaḥ*.

Thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the two feet, the two hands, the nose, the head, and the two arms using the thumbs and little fingers. One should perform the limb-placement (*aṅganyāsa*) conjoined with the six ritual utterances (*jāti*) beginning with *namaḥ* and *svāhā*. This should be done by one who has the opportunity and whose mind is not agitated.
He should also perform the *nyāsa* of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, as well as the *nyāsa* of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and so forth.

Thus, having first purified the individual soul (*jīva*) and the body, and having attained the nature of Śiva through a form whose body consists of the deposited mantras, he becomes fit for the worship of Śiva; one who is not Śiva [is not so fit].

For they declare, "One should worship Śiva. Thus, if one is unable to perform the purification of the living body, one should perform the mere ritual placement (*nyāsa*). If one is unable to perform even the entire *nyāsa*, one should perform at least the *daṇḍanyāsa* or the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*.
By that alone, through the purification of the body and the self and the attainment of the nature of Śiva, one becomes fit for the worship of Śiva.
The sequence of the internal sacrifice:
having thus performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should perform the internal sacrifice. The sequence therein is as follows:
within the space of the inner heart, one should mentally [visualize] a pavilion for the worship of Śiva made of divine jewels.
Having formed the mental resolve, one should mentally bring forth all the substances required for the worship of Śiva,
purify them, and fill the arghya-vessel and other vessels with a stream of nectar flowing from the lunar orb situated at the *dvādaśānta*.
Having performed that consecration and having carried out the worship of the gatekeepers, one should—

preceded by the request for permission from Gaṇeśa and the lineage of gurus in the manner to be described [worship] that which is adorned with a blue-colored stalk arisen from a ruby-colored navel-kanda.

Having meditated upon the *liṅga*— which is of the nature of *nāda*, perceivable through the union of the ears and the thumb, and shaped like the flame of a lamp— within the *pīṭha* consisting of the *bindu* and having the form of the *kuṇḍalinī-śakti* situated in the pericarp of the white-colored eight-petalled heart-lotus, according to the method to be described for the *pīṭha*:

Having worshipped the seat of Śiva (śivāsana), beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, and having worshipped the form of Śiva (śivamūrti) and the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) within the liṅga, one should meditate upon Paramaśiva there through the sequence of invocation and so forth, and worship Him with internal purificatory rites (antassaṃskāra).
Having bathed [the deity] with a profuse stream of nectar flowing from the *dvādaśānta*,

and having adorned [him] with garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as with the sandalwood of dispassion (*vairāgya*), one should offer the flower of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth in this manner.

One should worship with eight flowers in the form of non-violence, restraint of the senses, forbearance, self-control, knowledge, austerity, truth, and sincerity. Then, having conceived the fire of the vital breath (*prāṇāgni*) and the crest of smoke that is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) within the vessel of the mind, one should offer incense. One should conceive and offer the lamp which is the very knowledge of Śiva.
Having contemplated that the mind withdrawn from sense objects is the *naivedya* (food offering), one should offer it.
One should contemplate the very coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the path of the *suṣumnā* as the act of recitation (*japa*).

By means of those [offerings] fashioned through meditation on the collection of limbs of Sadāśiva, which have been stabilized by the fivefold concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) beginning with the earth element...
One should adorn [the deity] with various ornaments. One should also perform self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*) in the form of the contemplation of identity with Śiva, thinking, "I am Śiva.
Alternatively, after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*),...

One should offer the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of smell, sound, touch, form, and taste, consisting of sandalwood, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*). The sequence therein is as follows: preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, [one offers] sandalwood, which consists of the subtle element of smell, to Śiva as Sadyojāta with the syllable *hvāṃ* (or *hlāṃ*).

I offer. Hrauṃ (Hoṃ), to Īśāna Śiva, I offer a flower consisting of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Hraiṃ, to Tatpuruṣa Śiva, I offer incense (*dhūpa*) consisting of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*). Hrūṃ, to Aghora Śiva, [I offer] that which consists of the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*).

"I offer the lamp. Hrim! To Vāmadeva Śiva, I offer the food-oblation consisting of the subtle element of taste. Then, after washing the hands and offering mouth-perfume, [one offers] that which consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
One should contemplate: "I offer betel. Then, having mentally prepared the *nīrājana* (lustration):
"The mirror and the auspicious objects are fashioned by the wind residing in the intellect;
your manifold mental fluctuations are conceived in the form of the dance."

The sounds, through their various divisions of vocal music, instrumental music, and speech, take the form of the *dhvaja* (banner); and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), beginning with *prāṇa*, take the form of the *cāmara* (fly-whisk).
The ego is fashioned as the elephant, the body as the chariot;
the mind takes the form of the reins, and the intellect the form of the charioteer.
"Everything else has been fashioned by me as an instrument for you.

Thus, one should offer all that belongs to oneself—the intellect, mind, vital breath, and so forth—as instruments for the worship of Śiva. At that time, one should also perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*) in the manner that will be described.
Then, having rendered Śiva favorable by means of circumambulations and prostrations,
one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) according to his command.
The procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*):

therein, this is the sequence—one should visualize a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with three ridges at the navel, and within it, the fire as self-established; having kindled that fire with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), [one proceeds] there in that fire.
Having visualized some of the coals as being a portion of the flesh-eating spirits (kravyāda), one should discard them in the southwest corner (nirṛtikoṇa). Then,
having purified the fire situated in the sacrificial pit through the rites of inspection and so forth, one should,
for the sake of establishing its status as the Śiva-fire, [draw] that [fire] into the heart by means of the out-breath (recaka) along with the vital air in the form of consciousness.

Having led [the soul] there and united it with the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*), then having led it through the *suṣumnā* to the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) and united it there with the Supreme Śiva, one should contemplate it as being reddened by a mass of light, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns; then, having brought back that [light] which is of the nature of the fire of knowledge—

One should place [the fire] in the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*). When this is done, it becomes the Śiva-fire without requiring any further consecration. There, having meditated upon the Śiva-fire as being red in color, four-faced, ten-armed, and possessing weapons identical to those of Sadāśiva, [one should meditate] within his heart-lotus.

Having first performed the placement of the seat, the form, the vidyā, and the body, one should invoke Śiva; then, using the *suṣumnā* as a ladle, having reached the *dvādaśānta*, one should offer the clarified butter of the stream of nectar with the root mantra one hundred and eight times, twenty-eight times, or eight times.

Having visualized the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) as having its base in the navel-center filled with the ghee of the nectar of Power (*śāktāmṛta*), and its shaft as the Suṣumṇā-stalk consisting of the heart-lotus, one should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with it, saying "Hāṃ Śaktaye Vauṣaṭ," and [thus] satisfy Śivāgni (or Śiva).
Having joined [the consciousness] with Śiva, who is worshipped in the heart-lotus via the path of the navel, and having honored Him with the eightfold offering of flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā),

one should present the worship. Thereafter, one should meditate upon Śiva in the space between the eyebrows as possessing both manifest and unmanifest forms— complete in all His limbs and resembling a pure lamp.
One should concentrate the mind on the thought: "I am indeed Śiva himself, existing in two forms through the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper.
This is the purification of the self (ātma-śuddhi).
Now, the purification of the place (*sthāna-śuddhi*);

its procedure is as follows: having placed the two hands with palms facing upward at the heart, and having performed three claps (*tāla*) while reciting *hraḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should drive away the obstacles in the ten directions with the *astra-mantra* by means of the *coṭikā* (the snapping gesture).

Having formed a rampart outside [the mandala] with the color of blazing fire, one should form three moats by rotating the right index finger while reciting "HAIṂ KAVACĀYA NAMAḤ. Then, reciting "HĀṂ ŚAKTAYE VAUṢAṬ," one should visualize the Śākta light-form falling upwards and downwards, and [form] the Mahāmudrā.
One should display [this]. Thus is the purification of the site for the purpose of warding off obstacles.

(p. 233) Now, regarding the purification of substances: having placed all the substances required for the sacrifice to be described hereafter on the left side of the deity, one should place a water-vessel filled with pure water strained through a cloth on the right side.

Having set aside perfumes, flowers, and other materials for the purpose of self-worship and the worship of the *āvaraṇas* separately from the substances intended for Śiva, one should worship the waters for the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya*.
There are four types of *arghya*: the general *arghya*, the special *arghya*, and the *nirodha-arghya*.
Regarding "the *arghya* for the one turned away" (*parāṅmukhārghya*): it is the general *arghya* for the gatekeepers, the deities of the enclosures, and so forth;

it is the special *arghya* at the times of offering *arghya* to Śiva; it is the *arghya* of restraint (*nirodhārghya*) at the time of the consecration of restraint (*nirodhana-saṃskāra*) for Śiva alone; and it is the *arghya* for the one turned away (*parāṅmukhārghya*) at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*).

For these four worthy recipients, there should be four vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or any other suitable material, measuring ten palas, five palas, or two and a half palas, and rising five finger-joints in height.
They are five finger-breadths wide, circular or square in shape,
marked on the outside with eight-petaled lotuses,
measuring one finger-breadth in height, and having a thickness equal to a fourth of eight finger-breadths; they are made of the aforementioned material.

Alternatively, pleasing objects of half that size may be taken. In the absence of gold and other precious materials, they may be fashioned from mother-of-pearl, sword-blades, horns, stone, wood, coconut shells, and so forth;
or they may take the form of vessels made of fresh clay, or leaf-cups made from *palāśa*, lotus, or plantain leaves.
The vessels for the *arghya* offering should be taken up.

The vessels for the *pādya*, *ācamana*, *pañcagavya*, *pañcāmṛta*, as well as those for the fragrance, incense, lamp, bell, and so forth, should also be made according to the same previously mentioned measure of ten palas and so on. Among these, the *pādya* vessel—

The *ācamana* vessel should be made with a width of six *aṅgulas* and a height of four *aṅgulas*, with a base (*pāda*) having a width and height of four *aṅgulas*, a spout (*nāsikā*) of four *aṅgulas*, and a lip (*oṣṭha*) of one *aṅgula*; or it may be made with half those measurements, or even half of that again. This applies to the *ācamana* vessel as well as the vessel for offering water for the feet (*pādya*).
It should have a height of two or three finger-breadths and a width of sixteen finger-breadths;
it should be provided with feet that are four finger-breadths high and eight finger-breadths wide,
and its lip should be one finger-breadth thick, measuring either half the size of the aforementioned style or half of that again.

The two sides should be fashioned with rounded bracelets (*vṛttakaṅkaṇa*); the water-vessel (*ācamanapātra*) should have a belly twelve finger-breadths in height and width, and be provided with a base (*pāda*) six finger-breadths wide,
or six finger-breadths high, or two finger-breadths high.

The neck should be two or three finger-breadths in height, the lip one finger-breadth thick, and the mouth three finger-breadths wide; its dimensions may be according to one's preference, it should be provided with a bud-shaped lid,
and it should have three sections each measuring two finger-breadths, with a hole of three barley-corns in size starting from the base.

It should be provided with a nose whose dimensions gradually decrease, or it may be half that size. Alternatively, the vessels for water for the feet (*pādya*) and for sipping (*ācamana*) should be made circular, just like the vessel for the respectful offering (*arghya*). The vessel for throwing away the water used for sipping (*ācamana-kṣepa-pātra*) should also [be made in this manner].
It should be made like a vessel for casting out the water for the feet (pādyakṣepapātra). As for the stands for the arghya, pādya, and ācamana vessels,
they should be in the form of tripods, joined with three faces and three legs, eight finger-breadths in height,
and marked with lion faces on the upper part above the legs, below the rim.

In the absence of gold and other such materials, vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth should also be accepted— just like the vessel for the *arghya*— in the form of stone, wood, leaves, or folded leaf-cups. In that regard, the general substances for the *arghya* are sesame seeds and rice.
For the special *arghya*, there may be cardamom, cloves, camphor, rose-apple, nutmeg, and *uśīra* (or *mura*); or water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice, flowers, sesame seeds, and barley;
or *darbha* grass and the like, rice, sesame seeds, milk, water, and white mustard seeds.

The materials for the *arghya* are either six—consisting of barley (*yava*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), and items other than these such as *darbha* grass; or four—consisting of barley, white mustard, water, and sesame seeds (*tila*);

or three—consisting of sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and camphor (*karpūra*). For the *nirodha-arghya*, there are five materials: *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, barley, rice grains (*taṇḍula*), and white mustard; or those same materials together with sesame seeds.
There are six substances for the *arghya* intended for those who have turned their faces away (*parāṅmukha*). For the *pādya*, there are six:

*dūrvā*, sandalwood (*candana*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), vetiver (*uśīra*), *hrībera*, and saffron (*kuṅkuma*); or those same five excluding saffron; or four: *dūrvā*, white mustard, sandalwood, and vetiver.

There are three substances for the *hrībera* [ointment]: sandalwood and *uśīra*. For the rinsing (*ācamana*), there are either eleven substances—cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, *jātīkoṣṭha*, rose-apple, the three myrobalans, sandalwood, and *uśīra*—or six: cardamom, cloves, camphor, rose-apple, *uśīra*, and nutmeg.

There are five substances— cardamom, cloves, camphor, vetiver, and nutmeg— or three substances— cardamom, cloves, and camphor. Each of these substances used for the *arghya* and other offerings is categorized as superior,
middling, and so forth, with quantities of eighty, forty, twenty, ten, or five grains of rice respectively.
These are to be given.
The Worship of Water for the Feet and Other Offerings: Now, the procedure for the worship of water for the feet and other offerings is described—
namely, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the general oblation (*sāmānyārghya*), and the special oblation (*viśeṣārghya*).

Having placed the tripod (tripadī) for the water of cessation (nirodhārghya), the water of honor (arghyārghya), and the water for those turned away (parāṅmukhārghya) before the deity in the sequence starting from the left,

one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra at their feet, and the six supporting powers (ṣaḍādhāraśakti) on their rings; then, the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth [should be purified] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) or the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having filled [the vessels] with pure water, one should place the substances for the foot-washing and other offerings into their respective containers using the *kavaca* mantra. (p.
235) In the absence of the specific substances, one should perform the mere filling with pure water. Then—

Having lifted the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the others up to the crown of the head (the *bindu*), and having visualized the vessels as filled with the waters of all sacred bathing places such as the Gaṅgā— consisting of streams of nectar flowing from the *bindu*— one should place them upon the *yantrikās*. Alternatively:
Having drawn in the divine nectar consisting of the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords from the station of the Bindu by means of the Aṅkuśa-mudrā,
and having taken it up with the Saṃhāra-mudrā, one should deposit it— by means of the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and using the Udbhava-mudrā—
into the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, which are already situated within the Yantrikā. Then, [one should do the same] into the water of the special *arghya*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*), the forms, the five Brahmans, the body, the eyes, and the root-limbs, one should worship with the root mantra using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and then consecrate [the vessel] with the Brahma-mantras, the limb-mantras, and the root-mantra. Or, one may consecrate it solely with the Brahma-mantras, the limb-mantras, and the root-mantra. The *nirodhārghya* [offering] is performed with the mantras beginning with Brahmā.
One should consecrate the *parāṅmukha* water-offering with the *aṅga-mantras*, and the common water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) with the *astra-mantra*.

One should consecrate the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the *brahma-aṅgas* or with the *astra-mantra*. Then, having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra-mantra* and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the *kavaca-mantra*.
One should consecrate [the offerings] with nectar by displaying the *dhenumudrā* while reciting the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

For each item, from the *pādya* (water for the feet) up to the *arghya* (offering water) for those facing away, one should perform the rites beginning with the placement of the three-lamp stand (*tripadī*) and ending with the consecration with nectar, according to the method of sequential performance (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).
Then, near the *arghya* for the one facing away, the worship of the conch (*śaṅkha-pūjā*) should be performed.

The conchs—superior, middling, and inferior—are to be filled with water in measures of one *prastha*, one *āḍhaka*, or one *kuḍuba*. Likewise, they should be thick at the base, the tip, and the middle respectively.

It takes the forms of male, female, and neuter. At the base of the conch resides the Earth (Vasundharā), in the rim the Sun, in the belly Viṣṇu, on the side the Moon, in the edge Aghora, and in the mouth the seven sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell. Nevertheless, the conch is impure like a bone at its exterior base and tip.

One should fashion ornaments of gold, gems, and so forth for those two. Having thus prepared the conch, cleansed it with half [the usual amount] and washed it with the Astra-mantra, one should place it upon the three-legged stand (tripādikā) previously worshipped,
worship it with the special arghya offering, and [place] oneself upon the head.

One should sprinkle [the deity] three times with that water. Thus, when one is unable to prepare many vessels or perform the worship, the *nirodhārghya* and *parāṅmukhārghya* should be performed using only the water from the *nirodhārghya*.
Even the three *arghya* vessels should be prepared using only the water from the *viśeṣārghya*. In this manner...
Both the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) should be performed using the special *arghya* water itself.

In the absence of another vessel even for the special *arghya*, both the water for the feet and the water for sipping, as well as the threefold *arghya*, should be performed using the water from the conch (*śaṅkha*) alone.

The general *arghya* for the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) and so forth should be consecrated in another vessel. Thus, according to the method of reducing the number of vessels (p. 236), the subsequent ritual service (*upacāra*) is performed with its water; indeed, it is that very [water] which is used.

Taking up the vessel, its consecrations (saṃskāras) should be performed; or alternatively, even the consecrations belonging to another [vessel] may be performed on the enclosing-stick (paridhi), provided they are not contradictory, just as the sacrificial post-rites (yūpadharma) are applied to it.
Now, the procedure for the *pañcagavya* (the five products of the cow) to be performed during solstices, equinoxes, eclipses, and so forth, is described:

having smeared with cow dung a square area measuring either three cubits or two cubits on the eastern side of the deity or in the northeastern direction, [one should draw] four lines directed toward the east.
Having drawn out nine squares, each measuring one *tāla* in size, by means of four northward-pointing lines, one should spread in each square either *āḍhaka*-measurements of rice,
or half that measure of husked grain, or half that again of *kuśa* grass, and then face north toward the west.

Having strewn around the directions with darbha grass numbering five, with tips pointing north and tips pointing east, and having adorned it all around with flowers, [one should offer salutations thus]: "Obeisance to the Śiva-tattva; obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva;
obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva; obeisance to the Puruṣa-tattva; obeisance to the Kāla-tattva."
"Salutation to the earth element (pṛthivītattva), salutation to the water element (jalatattva), salutation to the air element (vāyutattva),

salutation to the primordial nature element (prakṛtitattva). Having thus worshipped the central square and the squares to the east, south, north, west, southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, [one should place] vessels made of gold or bell-metal that are unbroken.
Having washed nine black earthen vessels and placed them in nine compartments,
[one should offer] salutations to the well-established vessel (supratiṣṭhāpātra), salutations to the well-purified vessel (suśāntapātra),
salutations to the vessel consisting of splendor (tejomayapātra), salutations to the vessel of jewel-water (ratnodakapātra), and salutations to the vessel of nectar (amṛtapātra).

Having worshipped the vessels according to the sequence of the previously mentioned grid— namely, "Salutation to the Manifest Vessel," "Salutation to the Solar Vessel," "Salutation to the Combined Vessel," and "Salutation to the Unmanifest Vessel"—
one should place three *kuḍuba* measures of milk from a cow of copper-colored hue into the central vessel, and curd from a cow of white hue [into the other].
Two *kuḍuba*s of [milk] from a white cow go into the eastern vessel; one *kuḍuba* of ghee from a tawny-colored cow goes into the southern vessel;

one *prastha* of urine from a dark-colored cow goes into the northern vessel; and cow dung from a black-colored cow, measuring one *kuḍuba*, combined with five *kuḍuba*s of water, is filtered through a cloth.

In the western vessel: rice, *āmalaka*, and turmeric ground together in quantities equal to a wood-apple (*kapittha*) fruit, or half that size, or half again; [these are placed] in the vessels of the southeastern, southwestern, and northwestern corners.

p. 237) Kuśa-water, prepared thirty-six, twenty-five, twelve, or six times, should be circumambulated; it is joined with a bundle (*kūrca*) of *darbha* grass wound around the northwest direction, measuring one cubit or one palm, with knots two finger-breadths apart and tips four finger-breadths long.
Having poured an *āḍhaka* measure of fragrant *dūrvā* grass into the vessel in the northeast corner while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
one should then place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)— milk and so forth, ending with cow dung—
in sequence using the mantras beginning with Īśāna, repeated five, four, three, two, and one time respectively, along with rice flour.
One should consecrate the *āmalaka* fruit with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the turmeric with the *śiras-mantra*, and the water of *kuśa* grass with the *kavaca-mantra*;

furthermore, one should consecrate them six times with the *brahma-pañcaka* repeated. Thereafter, one should place the cow dung in cow urine, both of these in clarified butter, those three in curd, and all four of these in milk.
Having poured water with *kuśa* grass into that very place with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), one should pour it with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having consecrated it with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), and shielded it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should display the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), worship it with scents and flowers, and [offer] incense and lamps with the weapon-mantra.
Having displayed it, one should consecrate it with the root mantra.
The Ritual of the Five Nectars (Pañcāmṛta-vidhi):

Now the procedure for the five nectars is described—the worship of these must be performed even before the worship of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). In that regard, [the sequence] extends up to the worship of the vessel.

In the east, middle, and so forth, up to the end of the west, there should be milk, curd, honey, clarified butter, and sugar, each measuring one *prastha*, or three-quarters of a *prastha*, or half a *prastha*.
In the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*), fruits such as plantain, jackfruit, and mango should be placed as available, and in the northeast corner (*īśāna*).

The consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the scented water for those residing in their respective places is as before, like [the consecration of] water with *kuśa* grass. [The scented water] is mixed with sugar and cow dung along with water; however, there is no [further] mixing. Alternatively, one may perform the procedure for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) accompanied by mixing. Its sequence is as follows:
As previously prepared, having drawn five squares on a mound made of rice in the directions starting from the east and in the center, as well as an eight-petaled lotus in the northeast direction,
one should [worship] with the six names— Śiva, Niyati, Kāla, Vyakta, Avyakta, and Sumaṅgala— in the sequence beginning from the center.
Having worshipped those [vessels],

one should worship six vessels within them with the names of Amṛta, Soma, Vidyā, Ratna, Uda, Sudhā, Prītā, Asura, and Prītā; then, according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should place the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in the central and other vessels.

Having poured coconut water into the vessel in the northeast corner and consecrated it just as one would the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *kuśa* water, one should gradually mix sugar and other ingredients with the milk as one did with the cow dung and so forth,
and then add the coconut water just as one did with the *kuśa* water. Then, [the mixture becomes] abundant.

Having thrown a plantain fruit consecrated with the root mantra, one should rub it with the root mantra. One should perform the services of incense, flowers, and so forth, just as in the case of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
In the event that the aforementioned substances for the *pañcagavya* and other purposes are unavailable, [one may use] curd, milk, cow urine, and cow dung.

There is mutual substitution among these. Ghee is the substitute for all four [substances]. For sugar, there is sugarcane juice. If the prescribed quantity of the vessel-substances for the *pañcagavya* and so forth cannot be obtained, cow-dung measuring half the size of a thumb [should be used].
Cow urine, ghee, curd, milk, and kuśa-water should be taken in the proportions of one, two, three, five, and one part respectively.

In the case of the *pañcāmṛta*, the milk and other substances suitable for sprinkling upon the deity's *liṅga* should be taken. In the absence of cows of the aforementioned colors, [milk] from a healthy cow that has a calf and is free from disease or pregnancy may be used.

Milk and the other substances are to be taken. Milk that has not been touched by the saliva of a calf, curd that has not been churned, cow dung situated in the open air, ghee, and cow urine filtered through cloth are to be taken.
Now, regarding the procedure for the bathing water:

having obtained permission from Śiva, one should take a pure water-pot and go to a riverbank possessing excellent color, fragrance, and taste, or to a pure sacred ford such as a natural lake or a pool dug by the gods.

Having consecrated that water with the mantras of the limbs of Brahmā, and having filled the pitcher— which has been cleansed with the *astra* mantra— with that water filtered through a cloth while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should bring it and place it on the right side of the deity;
[the water] should be scented with cardamom, *uśīra*, cloves, sandalwood, camphor, *pāṭala*, blue lotus, red lotus, *karavīra*, and other such fragrances.

One should perform this. This preparation of the water for the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) must be done prior to the purification of oneself and the worship of the gatekeepers. The bathing water should not be fetched at a time when the sun is absent. The fetching of flowers should also be performed by the worshipper.

One should fetch [the materials] oneself. However, if one is unable or if the proper time is not available, the fetching of flowers and water, as well as the grinding of scents, the preparation of food offerings (*naivedya*), cooking, and so forth, must be performed by attendants who have bathed, are wearing clean garments, and hold purificatory grass (*pavitra*) in their hands; this is because of the same underlying principle applied to cases such as "when [an ingredient] is cut, [use] flour" and so on. Thus...
Having brought together the entire collection of substances to be used as required, one should perform their purification.
Regarding the purification of substances,

the procedure is as follows: while gazing at the substance with the eyes formed by the touch of the thumb and ring finger and reciting the root mantra, it is sequentially dried by the eyes of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, which consist of the powers of vision, action, and will.
One should contemplate [the object] as being burnt and then drenched with nectar. Then, for the sake of purification, having sprinkled it with the flag while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
one should strike it with the middle finger using that same *astra-mantra* in order to manifest the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Then, sprinkling all that with the water of the special *arghya* or the water from the conch while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should meditate on the emergence of sparks of the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*) from the mass of substances— just as sparks of fire fly forth from a struck stone.

Thus, the group of four substances— the four purificatory rites beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa*— having been abandoned in their impure, illusory form, become of the nature of pure conscious power (*śuddhacicchakti*) and fit for the fitness of Śiva. Thereafter, [the purification is performed] with *sadyojāta* for the scent and *vāmadeva* for the cloth.
One should consecrate the ornaments with the Aghora mantra, the food offering (naivedya) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, the flower with the Īśāna mantra,

and all other substances intended for Śiva as well as the materials for the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā) with the Heart mantra. Then, one should protect the entire collection of materials with the Astra mantra.
Having enveloped [the offering] with the *kavaca* mantra, having rendered it nectarine by means of the *śakti* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the *dhenu-mudrā*,

and contemplating that "all this prepared for the sake of Śiva is indeed of the nature of Śiva," one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps using the *hṛdaya* and *astra* mantras. Then:

Having sprinkled a drop of *arghya* water on one's own head with the *astra-mantra*, and having offered a flower upon one's seat saying "Salutation to the Seat of Śiva" (*śivāsanāya namaḥ*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form of Śiva upon one's own body, apply a tilaka of sandalwood paste on the forehead,
place a flower on one's own head with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and likewise offer the *arghya* water upon one's own head.

Thus, having abandoned the notion of being a bound soul (*paśu*) regarding oneself, one should worship the Self while contemplating, "I am pure, possessing stainless knowledge and action like Śiva. Although the purity of the Self has already been explained, nevertheless, because it is the agent of worship, it serves as an instrument of worship just like any other material substance.
Once he has entered, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings just as one would with other ritual substances; this concludes the purification of the substances.
Purification of Mantras:
Now, for the purpose of removing the impure nature of illusion produced by the activity of the teeth, palate, and lips of the mantras.

Furthermore, purification must be performed in order to awaken the capacity of those [seeds] which, being obscured by the impurities of the office of sovereignty (*aiśvaryādhikāra*), are unable to bestow their fruit; that method is now stated:
having formed the *añjali* at the heart, [one should project it] to the end of the *bindu*, to the end of the *brahmarandhra*, and to the end of the *śikhā*.

One should slowly recite the root mantra three times in sequence, ending with *namaḥ* preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) in its short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) forms. Then, one should likewise perform the recitation of the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantras*) in the same manner.

(p. 240) Having thus performed the purification of the mantra, one should thereafter perform the worship of the retinue deities (parivāradevatā) when they are present. How is there the presence of the retinue deities in the worship of [the deity] with or without his Śakti? It is thus that the subtle [aspects] have been explained.

The forms of Śiva-worship known as *śuddha* (pure), *kevala* (isolated), and *miśra* (mixed)—beginning with those performed by the powerless (*aśaktika*) and the powerful (*saśaktika*), and extending from the solar (*saura*) up to the fierce (*caṇḍa*)—are each threefold according to the divisions of *kevala*, *sahaja*, and *miśra* as stated in the *Aṃśumat*:
"The *kevala* [form] is the worship of the *liṅga* devoid of attendant deities (*parivāradevatā*); the *sahaja*..."
The worship of the *liṅga* accompanied by the fourfold retinue in the forms of Nandin, Vṛṣabha, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Pārvatī is called *nāma*.
That which is accompanied even by Maheśvara in his dancing form (*nṛttamūrti*), Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and others, is called *miśra*.

The worship of the *liṅga*. Thus, there are nine kinds of worship: the purely pure (*kevala-śuddha*), the innate pure (*sahaja-śuddha*), the mixed pure (*miśra-śuddha*), the purely absolute (*kevala-kevala*), the innately absolute (*sahaja-kevala*), the mixed absolute (*miśra-kevala*), the absolutely mixed (*kevala-miśra*), the innately mixed (*sahaja-miśra*), and the mixed-mixed (*miśra-miśra*). Among these:

Prior to the commencement of the Śiva-pūjā, having performed the Sūrya-pūjā and, following that, the Caṇḍa-pūjā, one invokes Śiva alone—without the Śakti—into the Liṅga; the worship of Him, devoid of the attendant deities (parivāradevatās), is "purely simple" (kevalaśuddha). By contrast, [the worship] accompanied by the fourfold retinue...

The previously mentioned worship is *sahaja-śuddha* (naturally pure). The previously mentioned worship performed together with Maheśvara and others is *miśra-śuddha* (mixedly pure). Having omitted the worship of Sūrya and Caṇḍa at the beginning and end, one invokes Śiva along with his Śakti in the *liṅga* and performs that worship without the ritual of the retinue (*parivāra*).
*Kevalakevalam* (the purely solitary) is the aforementioned worship alone, accompanied by the adoration of the fourfold retinue (*parivāra*).

*Sahajakevalam* (the innate solitary) is that which is also accompanied by the worship of Maheśvara and the others. *Miśrakevalam* (the mixed solitary) is that which is accompanied by the worship of Sūrya and Caṇḍa at the beginning and end, whether for one who possesses the power [of the consort] or one who does not.

The worship of a *liṅga* devoid of an entourage of deities is "purely mixed" (*kevalamiśra*). That same [worship], when accompanied by the adoration of the fourfold entourage, is "naturally mixed" (*sahajamiśra*). When it is accompanied by the adoration of Maheśvara and the others, it is "mixed-mixed" (*miśramiśra*). And thus, although there is an absence of an entourage in both the "purely pure" (*kevalakevala*) and the "naturally pure" (*sahajakevala*), [the distinction remains].

Since the retinue is present in both the *Miśra* and *Kevala* [forms], it is indeed appropriate to describe the worship of the retinue even in the *Kevalakevala* form immediately after the purification of the mantras. In that case, one should worship Vṛṣabha in the eastern part of the deity’s [mandala], facing westward; and Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Pārvatī facing eastward.

One should worship [the deities] in the southern, western, and northern directions. When worshipping Pārvatī in the form of Durgā, one should worship her facing south. The followers of the Purāṇas, however, state that there is a quartet of attendant deities consisting of the forms of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, and Durgā.
In all four [images] beginning with the Bull, when there is a desire for results such as health and so forth,
the worship of the Sun and others must also be performed among the attendant deities. The Sun is on the left side of the Bull, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti is on the right side of the Deity.

In the western part is Skanda, on the left is Viṣṇu, in the northern part is the Goddess, and in the eastern part is the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti). In this manner, the locations for other deities to be worshipped according to specific desires, as taught in the Āgamas, should be observed.
(p. 241) Now, regarding the purification of the *liṅga*:

having opened the casket of the deity situated within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), and having worshipped Bhīmarudra—who stands before it, possessing four faces and three eyes, and holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a parasol (*cchatra*) and a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in his hands—[one should proceed].
"O God, destroyer of night-stalkers, for the purpose of worshipping the Lord, please go to the right side of the Śuddhadvāra;
be gracious to me. Having thus entreated, [he addresses] the Lord situated within the casket: "Oṃ, salutations, O Lord of the gods of gods, sole leader of all worlds! Arise!"

Having thus prayed, "For the purpose of the ritual bath and for the sake of self-protection," one should grasp the *liṅga* with both hands, discard the garment, and [place it] upon the bathing altar (*snānavedi*), which has already been worshipped on the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*).

Having placed [the image] upon a circular base that is elevated in the center and covered with a spread cloth— constructed from any one of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, tin, lead, or milky trees, and adorned with rows of blooming lotuses, *karavīra* flowers, *karṇikāra* flowers, and circles of lotuses and horses;

Having worshipped the worship performed on the previous day at the *liṅga* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having offered the *arghya* with the water of the general *arghya* using the root mantra ending in *svāhā* over the head in the sequence beginning with Īśāna,
and having presented incense and lamps, [one should worship] the five [faces] beginning with Īśāna with the thumbs and ending with the little fingers.

Having performed the placement [of the mantras], and having grasped the flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger, one should lower the worship from the top of the *liṅga* by means of the thumb and forefinger while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, having placed that flower upon the crown of the *liṅga*, one should discard the *nirmālya* (the used offering) in the northeast direction while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having placed [the linga] in a pure vessel, one should wash the linga with the Astra-mantra and the pedestal (pīṭha) with the Pāśupata-astra;

then, one should consecrate it with the water of the general arghya while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra. When this has been done, at the conclusion of the previous worship, after the withdrawal of the mantras deposited upon the linga and the pedestal, those [mantras] attached to the linga and the pedestal—

The obstacles that hinder the enjoyment and liberation of the worshipper are dispelled. Furthermore, by bathing the *liṅga* with water from the heart-vessel, it becomes pure and fit for the subsequent application of mantras. Thus concludes the purification of the *liṅga*.

Then follows the consecration with food; having displayed the *liṅgamudrā* while reciting "Obeisance to Śiva and Śakti," one should worship the form on the seat with the root mantra or with eight flowers, and present incense and lamps.
Having consecrated [the image] with a stream of water from a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, conch, mother-of-pearl, cow-horn, or any one of these—

measuring four finger-breadths in length or the size of the tip of a cow's horn— and having anointed it with oil produced from a hand-press or with cow-ghee, or having sprinkled it with flour-powder and the like;
Having sprinkled [the head] with lukewarm water and placed a flower upon the head,
one should [apply] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
interspersed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consisting of the juices of the fruits of each of the five nectars.
Having completed the offering of flowers, incense, and lamps with the mantras of the Head and the Crest, one should sprinkle [the disciple] while ringing the bell with the Astra-mantra.
[One should offer] various fragrant substances, including cinnamon, cardamom, coconut pieces, pomegranate with its rind, and citron.
Water provided with *iku*, mangoes, and plantains;

water accompanied by *yava*, *nīvāra*, rice, mung beans, molasses, white mustard, fragrant substances, and seeds of golden *śāli* rice—this is "seed-water" (*bījodaka*). Having consecrated [the disciple] with that, one should worship him with the root-mantra using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Water combined with crystal, pearl, ruby, coral, hessonite, topaz, emerald, and sapphire is "jewel-water" (*ratnodaka*). Having consecrated [the disciple] with that using the *varṇamantra*,
one should further consecrate him with perfumes and other offerings.

Water mixed with the powder of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, camphor, realgar, cardamom, costus, black pepper, lāmañca, uśīra, and campaka buds is "fragrant water" (gandhodaka). Having consecrated [the deity] with that,
one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings while reciting the name-mantra.

Water joined with *campaka*, *mallikā*, *ketakī*, *pāṭala*, *kunda*, *puṇnāga*, *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *jātī*, *manda-araka*, *karavīra*, *padma*, *nīlotpala*, and *giripuṣpa*, mixed with *hrībera*, *damanaka*, and so forth, is "flower-water" (*puṣpodaka*). Having consecrated [the disciple] with that—

One should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth with the Śiva-mantra. Then, reciting the name-mantra, one should slowly sprinkle pure food around it; having fashioned that food into the shape of a liṅga situated around the [actual] liṅga, one offers perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, milk-rice (pāyasa), and betel.

Having offered that food and rinsed [the vessel], one should place the root-syllable (mūlabīja) upon the head of the liṅga, offer scents, flowers, incense, and lamps, touch it with the Brahma-mantras, and form the dhenu-mudrā.
This food-consecration wards off untimely death, bestows the increase of longevity, health, and sovereignty,
effects total subjugation, and brings about all forms of peace.

Then one should perform the water-worship (*jalārcana*). Having filled a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or any one of the sacrificial trees with pure water sanctified by the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and having placed that vessel upon the palm of the hand, one should establish the *prāṇaliṅga* within it.
Having offered *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. This is the water-worship (*jalārcana*).

Then, having lifted [the vessel] and wiped it clean, one should place it upon the altar (*vedi*) situated in the form of the hand-pedestal as before. By this consecration with water, the sin accumulated over thousands of millions of aeons is destroyed. [This should be done] for a month...

By the consecration with ghee, one attains the state of Śiva together with twenty-one generations of one's lineage. By the consecration with sesame oil produced from a hand-press, one attains the state of Śiva.
By the consecration with milk, one obtains the fruit of giving away ten thousand cows adorned with ornaments.
Through an ablution with curd, preceded by the destruction of all sins, one attains the world of Śiva.

Through an ablution with honey, one attains the world of Vahni (Fire). Through an ablution with sugarcane juice, one attains the world of the Vidyādharas. Through water infused with camphor and agallochum, one attains the state of Śiva.

It should be understood that through fragrant water one attains the world of the Gandharvas, through water with flowers the world of the Sun, through water with gold the world of Kubera, through water with pearls the world of Indra, and through water with *kuśa* grass the world of Brahmā, and so forth. In the absence of those specific substances, [the rite should be performed] with water filtered through a cloth.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with pure water. By that, it is said, one attains the world of Varuṇa, which is enriched with all desires;
therefore, one should perform the consecration by pouring streams [of water].

And that [image], according to the principle of worship for one's own sake, is best when twelve finger-breadths in width, one finger-breadth in height, and three barley-corns in thickness; it is middling when seven finger-breadths in width, half a finger-breadth in height, and two barley-corns in thickness;
and it is [inferior] when five finger-breadths in width and a quarter-finger-breadth in height.
The lowest [quality] is one with a thickness of a barley grain (*yava*). It should be made square or circular out of gold, silver, or copper. If it is square, one should draw nine compartments;
there is a single hole in the center of the middle compartment, and eight [holes] around that very middle compartment.

On the nine lines, one should make four holes in the cardinal directions and twelve holes in each of the compartments starting from the east; thus, one should make one hundred and eight holes in the excellent vessel, with one additional hole in the center of the middle compartment.
One should make forty-nine holes for the central vessel: one in the center of the central square, and five each in the eight squares starting from the east.
For the middle [vessel], there is one in the center of the central square, and three holes each in the squares starting from the east.
One should make twenty-five holes in the middle vessel. Having drawn a circle with an eight-petaled lotus, one should make nine holes in the center and around the pericarp (karṇikā),
twelve holes on each petal, and [twelve holes] outside the petals in the circle at the cardinal directions.
And one should fashion four [projections] for the superior bowl; for the other two bowls, the apertures should be seen as being like squares upon eight-petaled lotuses.

Having held such a vessel above the deity with his hand and filled it with pure water, while supporting the vessel with his hand, he should consecrate [the deity] with streams [of water] using the root mantra.
These are for the purpose of consecration.

p. 244) Having sprinkled with the *astra* mantra oils and other substances that are distinct from the previously prepared *pañcagavya* and so forth, having enveloped them with the *kavaca* mantra, and having protected them with the *astra* mantra, one should employ the heart-seed (*hṛdayabīja*) for the consecration (*abhiṣecana*). Thus, for one who is unable to perform the consecration through such an elaborate procedure:

One should sprinkle [the image] with pure water. Then, having offered a flower with the root mantra and presented the mantra-food (*mantrānna*), one should gently wipe it with a clean, soft cloth and place it upon the lotus-seat (*padmapīṭha*) in the hand-lotus.
Then, rising up (as if arisen), one should mentally circumambulate Śiva and depart.

Having gone from the station of Brahmā— the lord of the Vāstu situated in the northeast corner— to the northwest corner of the temple of Śiva, which constitutes the northern portion [of that corner], one should visualize [the deity] there as dark-complexioned, holding in his hands a staff, a rosary, a noose, and a goad, and in his trunk a citron fruit.

Having seated Gaṇapati facing south and worshipped him with all the ritual services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should pray: "O Lord Gaṇeśa, always ensure that my worship of Śiva is free from obstacles.
Then, in the eastern part of the Śiva-pīṭha, which corresponds to the northern direction—

Having likewise worshipped Mahālakṣmī—who holds a *śrīphala*, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), is three-eyed, is the embodiment of Śiva and Śakti, and is seated facing south—one should pray: "O Mother, always grant me abundance of materials for the worship of Śiva. Then, in the eastern direction:
In the northeast corner of the temple of Śiva,

[one should visualize] Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Ambikā, Guha, Viṣṇu, and Dhātṛ— of fair complexion, with serene countenances, wearing yogic cloths, and their two hands adorned with the gesture of exposition and a rosary.

Having seated seven gurus facing south, or all the gurus from Śiva down to one's own immediate guru, and having worshipped them with all the ritual offerings (upacāras) in that same manner, [one should say]: "O Śiva and the other gurus, you should grant me permission; I shall perform the worship of Śiva."

"By means of the path shown by you"— thus one should pray. Having worshipped either the sandals of the Śrī Guru with the mantra "Obeisance to the Sandals of the Śrī Guru" in the place of the Guru, or having performed the worship of Gaṇapati, Mahālakṣmī, and the Guru’s sandals,
and having prostrated before all, one should remain with knees steady upon the ground and palms joined in *añjali*.

"O Mother Gaṇanātha, O sandals of my Lord, O Teacher of the World! Grant permission to me, who am performing this sacrifice, so that I may act according to what has been prepared. Thus one should pray simultaneously.

Then, having contemplated the receipt of permission from them in the form of the words "O son, perform the worship of Śiva," and being seated on a beautiful seat in the south-eastern corner or the southern part of the temple, he should resolve: "I shall perform the worship of Śiva according to my ability, preceded by the intention for the attainment of my desired fruit."
Having made this resolve, one should begin the worship.
p. 245) Therein, first is the worship of Śiva.
Therein [the seat] has the form of a lotus divided into the bulb (kanda), stalk (nāla), knots (granthi), petals (dala), filaments (kesara), and pericarp (karṇikā);
it rises to a height reaching from the earth element up to the thirty-two principles ending with the Śuddhavidyā-tattva, and is situated above—

Along with Mūrti, there is the expansion beginning from Nivṛtti and ending with Śāntikalā. Above that is the Vidyā-deha, which has the dimension of Śāntyatītakalā. For the sake of thoroughly understanding its essential nature, the dimensions of the kalās starting from Nivṛtti and the nature of the tattvas contained within them are now analyzed:
The Nivṛtti-kalā takes the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), measuring one hundred crore yojanas;

within it lies the single element of earth (pṛthivī-tattva). Above that is the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, measuring one thousand crore yojanas, wherein reside the four elements beginning with water, as well as the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with smell.

The twenty-three principles (*tattvas*) consist of the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, mind, ego, intellect, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Above that is the *vidyā-kalā*, measuring ten million times ten thousand (*ayuta-koṭi-yojana*) in extent.

Therein are the seven principles consisting of the individual soul (*puruṣa*), attachment (*rāga*), necessity (*niyati*), limited knowledge (*vidyā*), time (*kāla*), and illusion (*māyā*). Above that—

The Śāntikalā extends for a measure of one hundred thousand crores of yojanas; therein lie two principles (tattvas): Śuddhavidyā and Maheśvara. Above that is the Śāntyatītakalā, extending for a measure of one million crores of yojanas; therein lie two principles: Sadāśiva and Śakti. Above that is the immeasurable Śivatattva.
The earth-tattva, consisting of the kalā of nivṛtti, extends as far as the kanda;
the twenty-nine tattvas included within the kalās of pratiṣṭhā and vidyā extend as far as the nāla;
and the seventy-five worlds situated within the tattvas from water up to time constitute the thorns.

The fifty states (*bhāvas*), which are the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) of the living beings residing within those various worlds, are like the threads within a lotus stalk. The *māyā*-principle, situated above *kāla* within *vidyā* itself, is the knot at the base of the lotus stalk. [That which] resides in the *śāntikalā*...

The lotus consists of the petals, filaments, and pericarp of the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva). Above Pure Knowledge is the principle of Maheśvara, extending as far as the subtle form of Śiva.
Within the Kalā of Beyond Peace (śāntyatīta-kalā) is the pair of principles of Sadāśiva and Śakti, extending as far as the body of knowledge (vidyā-deha).
The worlds are situated within the stalk;
there are eight worlds each in the kalās, manas, vāyu, gagana, ahaṅkāra, buddhi, and prakṛti, making fifty-six in total. There are six in the puruṣa, five in rāga, two in niyati, and [two] in kalā.

Two in knowledge, two in time, and two [in power]—thus there are nineteen worlds from Puruṣa down to Time; these constitute the seventy-five worlds which are the "thorns. Ignorance consists of the five forms of error: tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra. Reasoning (ūha)...
Sound, study,
the destruction of the three types of suffering, the acquisition of friends, and charity— these are the eight perfections (*siddhis*).
The four internal ones are named Nature (*prakṛti*), Means (*upādāna*), Time (*kāla*), and Fortune (*bhāgya*).
There are nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*), consisting of the five external ones produced by the cessation of objects and so forth;

eleven defects of the organs (*indriyavadha*), such as blindness and dumbness; and seventeen defects of the intellect (*buddhivadha*), including the previously mentioned failures of the perfections (*siddhi*) and others like lack of inquiry (*anūha*). Thus, there are twenty-eight types of pain (*rakta*). So it is said.
The fifty meditations are the threads of the net.
Here, an alternative view regarding the measurements of the *kanda*, the *nāḍī*s, and so forth, is presented.
The earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*), which consists of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, is exactly one hundred crore *yojana*s in extent, as previously stated.
Air is ten times the size of the earth-principle, and space (*vyoma*) is ten times the size of air; from that...

Ego (ahaṅkāra) is ten times [the size of] that; intellect (buddhi) is ten times [the size of] ego; the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) is ten times [the size of] intellect. Thus, up to the principle of the qualities, there is an increase by a factor of ten.
Nature (prakṛti) is one hundred times [the size of] the principle of the qualities; attachment (rāga) is one hundred times [the size of] nature.
Niyati is a hundredfold greater than rāga; vidyā is a hundredfold greater than niyati; kalā is a hundredfold greater than that;
kāla is a hundredfold greater than that; and māyā is a hundredfold greater than that. For Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, there is an increase by a factor of one thousand from māyā.

Śuddhavidyā is a thousandfold [greater] than that; Īśvara is a thousandfold greater than Śuddhavidyā; Sadāśiva is a thousandfold greater than Īśvara. From there, the increase is by the number of a hundred thousand (lakṣa): Śakti is a hundred-thousandfold greater than Sadāśiva. Beyond that, the Śivatattva is immeasurable. And this—

It proceeds by accepting the principle of Mahat as the primordial constituent (*prakṛti*) and the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), and by accepting Puruṣa as distinct from Prakṛti. Thus they say:
"The earth-principle (*kṣmātattva*), beginning from water, consists of the secondary [elements] and extends for a hundred crores of *yojanas*."
In a row, he pervades those [levels] up to Prakṛti by his own qualities; up to Māyā, by a hundred;
and up to Sadāśiva, by a thousand. Beyond that, up to the end of Śakti, he pervades by a hundred thousand.
And Sadāśiva, whose power is immeasurable, is the presiding lord of the Bindu, pervading even above it.
Thus it is said.
If it is asked, "In that case, how many *yojanas* in number has the stalk (*nāla*) become?", the answer is: it is indeed an incalculable number of *yojanas*.
Nevertheless, by attributing some particular mode [of calculation], the number of *yojanas* is demonstrated.
When the count increases tenfold for each successive position starting from one, the twentieth place is the number *parārdha*. That is the final number of all.
And these are the names of the twenty places: one (*eka*), ten (*daśa*), hundred (*śata*), thousand (*sahasra*).
Ayuta, lakṣa, prayuta, koṭi, arbuda, padma, kharva, nikharva, bṛnda, mahāpadma, śaṅkha, mahāśaṅkha, mahāsamudra, and antima. (p. 247)
The middle and the highest limit.
And so they have said:
One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a lakh, a prayuta, a koṭi, an arbuda, a padma, then a kharva, a nikharva; likewise—

"A *bṛnda*, a great lotus (*mahāsaroja*), another *śaṅkha*, the ocean (*samudra*), the end (*anta*), and the middle (*madhya*)— the wise know this number as being designated by the term *parārdha*. Thus, having placed the number one hundred million (*śatakoṭi*) in a single position, [one calculates] the water-principle (*jalatattva*) and the others.

The calculation is performed as follows: one hundred koṭis is the number called a *padma*. From that, the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*) is one *padma* yojanas; the water element (*jalatattva*) is one yojana; the fire element (*tejastattva*) is ten yojanas;
the air element (*vāyutattva*) is one hundred yojanas; and the space element (*gaganatattva*) is one thousand yojanas.

The principle of ego (ahaṅkāra) is ten thousand *yojanas* in extent; the intellect (*buddhi*) is one hundred thousand *yojanas*; the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) is one million *yojanas*.
Beyond that, since it is to be increased by a factor of a hundred, the number one hundred is to be understood as "one hundred and more" (ekāntanirata). For example, primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Padmayojanā is a *nikharva* of *yojanas*, Mahāvidyā is a *mahāśaṅkha* of *yojanas*,

Kalā is a *mahāsamudra* of *yojanas*, and Kāla is a *parārdha* of *yojanas*. Thus, the stalk (*nāla*), which consists of the collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with Water and ending with Kalā, is ten hundred thousand times ten thousand [yojanas].
It is measured in *yojanas* by a total number consisting of thirteen designations: *lakṣa*, *prayuta*, *koṭi*, *padma*, *nikharva*, *mahāpadma*, *mahāśaṅkha*, *mahāsamudra*, and *parārdha*.
This is stated without superimposing the nature of unity upon the number *padma*.
But when it comes to calculation, one is not capable of conceiving the existence of numbers exceeding a *parārdha*, such as the *kharva*, *nikharva*, *bṛnda*,
*mahāpadma*, *śaṅkha*, *mahāśaṅkha*, *samudra*, *madhya*,
a *parārdha* multiplied tenfold, a *parārdha* multiplied a thousandfold, and a *parārdha* multiplied ten millionfold.
The height, measured in *yojanas*, is equal to the numerical total of thirteen forms multiplied by a *parārdha* increased a hundred-thousandfold;
this applies both to those situated within the stalk and to the worlds contained therein.

Since it is accepted that there is no separate measurement in *yojanas* for the five elements— the support of the world— along with the five objects beginning with smell, the five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, and the mind, there is no measurement in *yojanas* among them.
Multiplied.
Now, another opinion is presented, based on a separate calculation of yojanas for those [elements] as well, by virtue of their being the support of the worlds:
from the element-earth (bhūtattva), which measures one *padma* yojana, [arise] the elements beginning with water and ending with the mind (*manas*).
p. 248) There is a tenfold increase for each successive stage among the twenty principles:

a hundredfold for *ahaṅkāra* and *buddhi*, a thousandfold for *prakṛti*, ten thousandfold for *puruṣa*, a hundred thousandfold for *niyati* and *kāla*, and one millionfold for *rāga*, *vidyā*, and *kalā*.

From that [limit], Māyā is ten million times greater; Śuddhavidyā is one hundred million times greater; Īśvara is one billion times greater; Sadāśiva is ten billion times greater; Śakti is one hundred billion times greater;
and for the Śiva-tattva, there is no numerical measure in *yojanas*. This refers to the principles (*tattvas*) situated between Puruṣa and Māyā.

This doctrine proceeds by relying on a sequential distinction among the five [elements] based on their upper and lower positions. In this system, the twenty-one principles beginning with earth and ending with the mind increase tenfold at each successive stage.

In sequence, there are ten, eleven, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, ten-million, hundred-million, billion, ten-billion, hundred-billion, trillion, ten-trillion, hundred-trillion, quadrillion, ten-quadrillion, hundred-quadrillion, quintillion, ten-quintillion, hundred-quintillion, sextillion, ten-sextillion, hundred-sextillion, septillion, ten-septillion, and finally a hundred-septillion *yojanas*. The *ahaṃkāra* and *buddhi* increase by a factor of one hundred in each successive stage.
At a distance of a hundred thousand times a thousand, multiplied by a *parārdha* of *yojanas*, is Prakṛti;

at a distance of a hundred billion (*arbuda*) times a hundred thousand, multiplied by a thousand, is Puruṣa; and from there, at a distance increased by a factor of ten million (*yuta*), are Niyati and Kāla, at a distance of a hundred trillion (*vṛnda*) times a hundred thousand *yojanas*.
By increasing ten-fold at each step (*lakṣaguṇavṛddhyā kramāt*), [the measurements become] a *mahāśaṅkha* multiplied by a *padmaparārdha*,
a *parārdha* multiplied by a *śataparārdha*, and a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha*-multiplied *parārdha* [in *yojanas*].
And thus, in this view, the stalk (*nāla*) consists of the collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with Water and ending with *Kalā*.
It measures a number of *yojanas* equal to the sum of twenty-nine numerical units, beginning with ten and ending with a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha*.
In this regard, even according to both positions set forth by resorting to the increase of the principles (*tattva-vṛddhi*), there is no contradiction with the *Nāla-grantha*.

And the lotus would be exceedingly long. For instance: here, in the first position, among the principles (tattvas) contained within the stalk, time (kāla) alone measures one *parārdha-yojana*; the *kalā* principle is measured by a hundredth part of that; and the same applies to the principles beginning with *vidyā*, *niyati*, and so forth.
The stalk measures one hundredth part of that, being slightly more than one *parārdha* yojanas;
the knot, which is of the nature of *māyā*, is a hundred times a *parārdha* yojanas, because *māyā* is a hundredfold of *kāla*; the lotus is a hundred thousand times a *parārdha* yojanas.

Because *śuddhavidyā*, which has the form of a lotus, is a thousandfold greater than *māyā*. Thus, even according to the other view, it results in the knots (*granthi*) and the lotuses being situated in a state of vertical extension. In this way, from the *kanda* onwards, the length of the knots and the lotuses is not [determined] in relation to the stalk (*nāla*).
It resembles the shadow of a worldly lotus;
it resembles the shadow of the heart-lotus located within the region of the heart, starting from the nine-navelled *kanda*. (p.
249) It is simply the resorting to the waxing phase during other times.

This is conducive to the meditation on the lotus-seat of Śiva. Furthermore, this lotus contains within it the five seats in the form of the seat of Ananta, the lion-throne, the yoga-seat, the lotus-seat, and the stainless seat (*vimalāsana*). Among these, the *kanda* is commensurate with the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*).

Thus, the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is the stalk itself, measured by the principles (tattvas) beginning with water and ending with limited agency (kalā); together with the lotus bud situated above it,
it is the serpent accompanied by the circle of jewel-crests on its hoods, which has emerged from the Ocean of Milk in the form of the foundational power.
The Anantarudra, who is among the eight Vidyeśvaras beginning with Mākṛtiśāli— these two together are called the Anantāsana.
The stalk (nāla) situated all around, beginning from the water-tattva up to the limit of the guṇa-tattva, is [the support].

The lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). Above that, extending to the knot (*granthi*), is the yoga-seat (*yogāsana*). Above that is the lotus-seat (*padmāsana*), consisting of petals and filaments. The pericarp (*karṇikā*) itself is the pure seat;
or it consists of the three qualities, the three mandalas, and the three principles situated upon the pericarp.

Although Ananta is described as a serpent adorned with a thousand hoods, his "stalk" (nāla) is actually his coiled body standing in an upward position, and the "bud" (padmamukula) here is simply that contracted circle of hoods; there is no lotus existing apart from these.

Nevertheless, that very [lotus] is to be meditated upon in the form of an eight-petaled lotus during the state of *vikāsa-dhyāna* (expansive meditation); thus it is called *padmāsana*. Alternatively, it is circular in shape, possessing the luster of ten million suns, and situated below the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
It is established in the form of the infinite serpent, or as the infinite lotus-seat distinct from the stalk of the infinite lotus;
it is circular in shape, or else it has the form of the eight great nāgas— Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kārkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and Gulika— standing one above the other.
Alternatively, the infinite seat (anantāsana) should be meditated upon in this way:

upon a couch consisting of four planks representing non-virtue (*adharma*) and so forth, which rests on a lion-throne supported by four legs in the form of a bull, a lion, a spirit (*bhūta*), and an elephant, [the deity sits] with five hoods.

Together with his tail, the King of Nagas has the form of a man at the center of his hoods; he is clothed in linen garments, adorned with all ornaments, and has two hands displaying the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness. Surrounding him in the directions starting from the east are [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Gulika, each having a single hood and joined palms in reverence.

Beholding the Nāga king, the great serpents [perceive] upon the head of the Nāga king a blossoming eight-petaled Ananta-lotus. Here, following the first alternative, the sequence for the worship of Śiva is also demonstrated.
Hāṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti;
she who is white in color, whose form is the hollow of the lotus-throne of Śiva, which has the dimensions of the Earth-tattva— the cosmic egg measuring one hundred million yojanas.
I worship the lower Śakti, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness. Homage to Anantāsana.
[She is] in the form of a stalk whose dimensions consist of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Water and ending with Kalā, together with the knot of Māyā.

Or [a height] of eleven thousand koṭis of yojanas; or [measures expressed by] kharva, nikharva, vṛnda, mahāpadma, śaṅkha, mahāśaṅkha, samudra, madhya, parārdha multiplied tenfold, nikharva multiplied, sahasraparārdha, lakṣaguṇitaparārdha, and koṭiguṇitaparārdha.

Or [a height] of one hundred thousand yojanas, which is a number to be counted as a collection of fourteen numerical units—namely, parārdha multiplied by padma, and parārdha multiplied by kharva; or [the sequence of numbers]:
śata, sahasra, ayuta, lakṣa, prayuta, koṭi, arbuda, padma, kharva, and nikharva.
Bṛndamahāpadma, Śaṅkhamahāśaṅkha, Samudramahāsamudra, Madhyaparārdha, ten times Parārdha, thousand times Parārdha,
hundred-thousand times Parārdha, Mahāparārdha, and Arbuda times Parārdha.
A great ocean multiplied by a *bṛnda* of *parārdhas*,
multiplied by a thousand *parārdhas* of *parārdhas*, multiplied by a *parārdha* of *padma-parārdhas*,
and multiplied by a *parārdha* of *mahāśaṅkha-parārdhas*.

Its height is measured in *yojanas* equal to the sum of the number of *padma* units multiplied by thirty, where a *padma* unit is defined as a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* struck by a *parārdha*, which is itself multiplied by a *parārdha* struck by a *parārdha* multiplied by a hundred *parārdhas*.

Or else, above that, I worship the seat of Ananta (Anantāsana), which has the form of Ananta Rudra, is adorned with a single face and four arms, bears a lotus bud upon a circle of a thousand hoods, and performs the gesture of salutation (namaskāramudrā) at the heart: *Hāṃ, obeisance to the thorns of the stalk of the lotus-seat of Śiva*.
O Lord of the Immortals, from the parts of the lotus-stalks of the auspicious throne risen from the bulbous root of the earth— resting upon the principles beginning with water and ending with water—
[arose] Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Āṣāḍhi, Ḍiṇḍi, Muṇḍibhāra, Bhūtalaguḍīśvara, Hariścandra, and so forth.
Andra, Śrīśaila, Japyeśvara, Āmrātakeśvara, Madhyameśvara, Mahākāla, Kedāra, Bhairava, Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhalaka, Nakhala, Vimalēśvara,
Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, Bhīmeśvara, Avimukta, Vastrāpada, and Rudrakoṭi.
Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, Sthāṇu, Chagalaṇḍa, Duraṇḍa, Mākoṭi,
Maṇḍaleśvara, Mahākāla, Añjana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, Sthaleśvara, Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yakṣa, Gandharva, Aindra, Saumya, and Prājāpatya.
Brahmākṛtakṛta-bhairava, Brahma-vaiṣṇava-kaumāra,
Śrīkaṇṭha-vāmadeva, Bhīma-ugra-bhaveśāna-ekavīra-pracaṇḍa, Umāpati-jānanta-ekaśiva-krodha-caṇḍa.

I worship the seventy-five thorny deities (*kaṇṭaka*) who embody the forms of the worlds, namely: Dyuti, Saṃvarta, Śūra, Jyotipiṅga, Sūraga, Mantrarūpin, Subāhu, Bhāsura, Kāladaṃṣṭra, Piṅgalākṣa, Viśāla, Kālarūpin, Hutāśana, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and the one named Śikhī. Hāṃ.

Homage to the Sūtras! I worship the lotus-stalk threads of the seat of Śiva, which consist of fifty meditations: the five errors, the eight perfections, the nine contentments, and the twenty-eight forms of attachment.
Thus, immediately after the worship of the stalk consisting of infinite seats, one should worship the lion-throne and the yoga-seat situated around the stalk. Hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma.
This is the lion-shaped form of the foot located in the southeast corner of Śiva’s lion-throne.

I worship Dharma, who rises as high as the elements beginning with water and ending with the principles (*tattva*), facing the southeast, with mouth wide open, neck turned back, looking like a lion toward the northwest corner, surrounded by ten million lions, and having the color of camphor. Hāṃ, homage to Knowledge!
In the southwest corner of Śiva’s throne is a lion-shaped form, which serves as the leg [of the throne];
it is elevated from the elements such as water up to the principle of *guṇatattva*, faces the southwest, has its mouth wide open,
its neck turned back to gaze at the lion in the northeast corner, and is surrounded by ten million lions.
I worship the saffron-colored Jñāna. Hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya.

This is the form of the leg of the Śiva-siṃhāsana located in the northwestern corner, lion-shaped, elevated from the qualities and principles beginning with water up to the principle of air, facing northwest, with its mouth wide open.
I worship Vairāgya, who has turned his neck to gaze like a lion toward the southeast (āgneya) corner, who is surrounded by ten million lions, and who is golden-hued. Hāṃ, homage to Aiśvarya!
[He is] in the form of a foot at the northeast (īśāna) corner of the Śiva-siṃhāsana, having the shape of a lion and facing the northeast (īśāna).

I worship Aiśvarya, who is elevated from the element of water up to the principle of *guṇatattva*, with mouth wide open and neck turned back, gazing like a lion toward the southwest corner, surrounded by ten million lions, and cloud-colored. Hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma. [This is] of the Śiva-siṃhāsana.

I worship Adharma, who has the form of the eastern palm-leaf, whose color is white and black, who is in human form, with his head to the south, his feet to the north, and facing downward. Hāṃ, obeisance to Ignorance (Ajñāna). [He is] in the form of the southern palm-leaf of the Śiva-siṃhāsana.

I worship Ignorance (Avidyā), who has a white and red complexion, the form of a man, with his head toward the east and feet toward the west, and facing downward. Hāṃ, obeisance to Non-detachment (Avairāgya). [He] has the form of the western plank of Śiva’s lion-throne and is red-yellow in color.
I worship the one in human form with his head facing north and his right foot pointing downward, who is devoid of dispassion (*avairāgya*). *Hāṃ*, salutation to Anaiśvarya.
He has the form of the northern seat of the Śiva-lion-throne, is yellowish-black in color, and is in human form.
I worship [the deity] with his head facing west, his feet facing east, face down, and devoid of sovereignty.
Immediately thereafter, having worshipped the entire lion-throne with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-lion throne," one should worship the yoga-seat (yogāsana).
His elemental forms— white, red, yellow, and black—
