are the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas, which, as the feet beginning with the southeast (Āgneya), represent the Unmanifest, Niyati, Kalā, and Kāla,
possessing the colors of crystal, a dark cloud, a pomegranate flower, and powdered collyrium respectively.

Having worshipped [the seat] by way of its eastern and other planks, one should worship Viṣṇu in the center—blue in color, three-eyed, and holding a conch, a discus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—with the mantra: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, whose form is the central plank of the Śivayogāsana. Then, [one worships] the one who is ruddy with the quality of *rajas*.

Having worshipped the lower covering, which has the form of a bed spread out beneath the upper girdle of the yoga-seat, with the mantra: "Obeisance to the lower covering, whose form is *māyā* and which is filled with the cotton-like *tamas* quality," [one worships] with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to that which is whitened by the *sattva* quality."

Having worshipped the upper covering— the form of the bedsheet and the upper cover— on top of the girdle with the mantra "Obeisance to the pure illusory form of the upper covering," and having worshipped it in the southwest corner (nairṛtakoṇa),
one should worship the entire yogic seat with the mantra "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-yogic seat."
In the view that the Śivāsana consists of three seats— namely the Yogāsana, the Vimalāsana, and [the third]—
one should meditate upon the Siṃhāsana itself as being elevated up to the knot of Māyā; then, after worshipping its foot-rests, [one proceeds] to the corners beginning with the southeast.
Having worshipped the four ages, beginning with Kṛtayuga, as the two pegs that join the two side-panels (phalaka) for stability,
and having worshipped Śrī Mahāviṣṇu as the central panel itself,
one should worship the lower covering and the upper covering.

Then, having meditated upon a lotus bud in the form of a circle of the jewels on the hoods of Ananta [Śeṣa] as being in full bloom, one should worship its petals and filaments: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the petals of the lotus of Śiva’s throne;
I worship the petals of the lotus of Śiva’s throne, which are white in color and have the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras."

Hāṃ, salutation to the filaments (kesara). At the base they are golden-colored, in the middle they are coral-colored, and their tips are adorned with pearl-like forms; I worship these filaments, which are the embodiments of the sixty-four arts, or the forms of the eight Rudras accompanied by the powers beginning with Vāmā.

In the view that the filaments (kesara) possess the form of the eight Rudras, each of the eight filaments should be meditated upon as being one individual Rudra. Alternatively, since the lotus of Ananta possesses a thousand petals in the form of hoods, it likewise has a thousand filaments; thus, all of them [should be so meditated upon].

Having divided the number one hundred and twenty-five into eight parts, they should be worshipped in the form of the eight Rudras beginning with Vāma; or alternatively, only the eight filaments together with the pericarp should be worshipped in that manner. Or again, only the eight filaments together with the pericarp should be worshipped in that manner.

These are to be worshipped. Furthermore, this same principle should be applied to the petals, which are to be worshipped as the forms of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvara). Hāṃ, obeisance to the pericarp. I worship the pericarp of the lotus-seat of Śiva, which is golden-hued and embodies the power Vimalā. Hāṃ, obeisance to the seeds.

I worship the seed-syllables of the lotus at the seat of Śiva, which take the form of the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, or the form of the fifty letters. Then, having visualized the lotus complete with all its parts, [one recites] *hāṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ *namaḥ* to the lotus seat," one should display the lotus mudrā with "Hāṃ, oṃ *namaḥ* to the lotus mudrā. Then, proceeding clockwise from the east, one should worship the eight powers, beginning with Vāmā, one by one upon the eight filaments: "Oṃ *namaḥ* to Vāmā."
Salutation to Jyeṣṭhā; salutation to Raudrī; salutation to Kālī; salutation to Kalavikaraṇī;

salutation to Balavikaraṇī; salutation to Balapramathinī; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī—[these goddesses], reddish in color, holding chowries, with one hand placed upon Śiva’s seat, facing toward Śiva.
I worship the powers beginning with Vāmā who reside upon the filaments. Homage to Manonmanī;

I worship Manonmanī, crystal-colored, holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, situated either in the northeast direction or in the center upon the pericarp of the lotus seat of Kṣīrā.
I worship. Then, one should worship the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, Fire, and Śakti, together with their presiding deities, one above the other:
*Hāṃ, obeisance to the solar maṇḍala*. I worship the solar maṇḍala, which resembles ten million suns and pervades the tips of the petals of Śiva’s lotus seat. *Hāṃ*.
Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disk.
Having five faces, four arms, and three eyes on each face,
with the luster of molten gold, and endowed with the *namas* mudrā.
I worship Brahmā, the cause of creation, whose nature is the essence of the Self, the sovereign of the solar orb.
Hāṃ, salutation to the lunar orb. [I worship him] who pervades the tips of the filaments of the lotus seat of Śiva.
I worship the lunar mandala, as cool as ten million moons. Hāṃ!

Homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar mandala, dark as a rain cloud, possessing four hands endowed with the gestures of salutation and holding the conch and discus, the cause of the cause of preservation.

I worship Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala, whose form is the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire maṇḍala. I worship the fire maṇḍala pervading the pericarp of the lotus of Śiva’s throne.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire maṇḍala, who is the color of ruby.

I worship Rudra, the lord of the fire-mandala, who possesses four hands bearing the trident, the fire, the *namaḥ* [gesture], and the *mudrā*, who is the cause of the cause of dissolution, and whose form is the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
According to the view that the pure seat (*vimalāsana*) is distinct from the pericarp, [one worships] from the southeast to the northeast.

Having worshipped the three qualities from the south to the north, the three mandalas from the southwest (nairṛta) to the northwest (vāyavya), and the three principles (tattvas), one should worship this entire pure seat with the mantra: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the pure seat (vimalāsana)."

Immediately after that, in the center: *hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. I worship the Śakti-maṇḍala, which is white in color, pervading the three maṇḍalas, and is the embodiment of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). *hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalādhipataye maheśvarāya namaḥ*.

I worship Maheśvara, the lord of the circle of powers (śakti-maṇḍala), who is crystal-colored, has eight arms, and holds a sword, trident, arrow, rosary, water-pot, the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting boons, and a lotus; thereafter, the entire [rite].
Having visualized the Śivāsana, one should worship the Śivāsana—which consists of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti)—upon it with the mantra: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śivāsana.
In this sequence of seats, the Ādhāraśakti [is worshipped] in the self-oriented worship (ātmārthapūjā).
Having performed worship upon the lotus-seat situated in the Brahma-world,

one should worship [the deities] from Ananta onwards up to the end of the Śakti-maṇḍala, arranged one above the other on the pedestal of the liṅga, extending as far as the neck (nāla) of the liṅga. In this manner, for each [deity] individually...

If one is unable to perform the worship of the individual components of Śiva’s throne, one should meditate upon the throne of Śiva together with its limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas), and worship it simply by saying: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the throne of Śiva.
This is the method of worshipping the throne of Śiva which contains many thrones within it. Alternatively, [one may use] a lotus during the invocation (āvāhana).
One should meditate upon Ananta during the bath, Vimala during the worship, Yoga during the food offering,

and Siṃhāsana during the other services such as clothing; or alternatively, one may meditate upon Siṃhāsana during the bath, Ananta during the clothing, Padma during the ornaments, scents, and flowers, and Vimala during the food offering.

One should arrange the yoga and other services. Having thus worshipped the Śivāsana, one should worship the form of Śiva—consisting of the Maheśvara-tattva, resembling steady lightning, staff-shaped, and with undivided limbs—within the neck of the liṅga, reciting: *Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva*.

At the length of the *liṅga*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Īśāna and the other [deities] from the head down to the feet in the manner of a staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*) using mantras such as "Hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna," and then place the thirty-eight *kalās*— either with their respective *Śaktis* or without them— in those various locations.

If one is devoid of initiation according to the *Śaivakriyottara* and other such texts, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vaśinī; thereafter, one should also perform the placement of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others. Having thus performed the placement for the sake of attaining the body of Sadāśiva, one should [perform] the placement of the limbs in their divisions, saying: "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the Body of Knowledge (*vidyādeha*)."
Having worshipped Sadāśiva, whose body is knowledge, one should meditate upon His true nature through the phenomenal expansion.
From Earth up to Śuddhavidyā, it is endowed with the bulb, stalk, and petals,
joined with the pericarp and filaments, and adorned with the orb of the sun.
With a form resting on the lap of the Lord, possessing the brilliance of a steady lightning flash,
with undivided limbs, she shone upon the upper surface.
From the element earth up to the principle of Īśvara, together with the form already described,
it possesses a height of many millions of yojanas consisting of various palatial pavilions.
I ever worship Sadāśiva, who is seated upon a lotus, situated on a great lotus measuring ten million *yojanas*, and who sits in the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*).

Or rather, [he is worshipped] by means of the multitude of *yojanas* rising up in hundreds of millions— peaks, limbs, tips, bracelets, dancers, dancing girls, performances, food, drink, meditation, knowledge, and the *anīkīnaka*—
which are divided tenfold and sevenfold among the forms of fire, earth, the moon, Kāma, and so forth.
Seated upon an excellent lotus throne at the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), which is immeasurable in its calculated proportions.
I take refuge in him who has attained a height of a *parārdha* of *yojanas* increased by ten times a *prayuta*, and whose domain extends for a *parārdha* of *yojanas*.
Sadasiva, seated upon a lotus throne.
In the bulb (*kanda*) and the stalk (*nāla*), there is an increase tenfold from the *kramuka* fruit; in the twenty [sections], there is a doubling;
in each of the one, two, and three [subsequent parts], there is an increase by a factor of a hundred, up to a final number of ten million mouths (*mukha*).
Then, at the knot (*granthi*), there is ten million, and starting from the lotus (*padma*) onwards, there is an increase by these numbers up to ten times ten million.
Or he may be situated on a great seat of yoga (mahāyogapīṭha), which possesses vast majesty extending for thousands of yojanas.
Above that, the form of Maheśvara, whose measurement is celebrated as a mass of one hundred koṭis of yojanas, shines forth;
it increases by ten thousand koṭis above that and by another ten million koṭis in every direction.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with three eyes in each face;
in his right hands, he holds a trident, a vajra, a sword, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness.
And in the left hands, he holds a snake-noose, a bell, fire, a goad, or else the five: the excellent khaṭvāṅga, a trident, and the [remaining] three weapons.
The upper face of this god, charming in its childhood state, holds a necklace, a hand-drum, a serpent, a blue lotus, and a rosary.
The eastern face of Maheśa is serene, turned upwards, with the luster of stainless crystal,
and possesses the brilliance of refined gold.
The southern face of Śambhu, rendered steady by pride, gentle, having attained fresh youth,
and possessing the luster of a mass of black collyrium.
His three eyes, red and round, were terrible with brows knitted in a frown;
he was formidable with fangs bared, difficult to withstand, and his sprout-like lower lip was quivering.
Candrāpīḍa, with his flaming hair and radiant mature youth,
was like the northern face of Śiva, possessing the luster of fresh coral.
Adorned with a tilaka on his forehead, embellished by dark locks of hair,
he was a source of enchantment, possessing three eyes and radiant with the ornament of the moon.
It was curved like the playful creeper-like brow on the face of Pārvatī,
resembling the western moon, and marked with the characteristics of a king.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord Sadāśiva, who is beautiful with the moon as his crest-ornament and whose eyes are tranquil through meditation, one should meditate upon him once again.
The three eyes of which the play consists of will, knowledge, and action;
whose crest is the digit of the moon of wisdom; and whose circle of arms extends through the ten directions.
It possesses faces that are the five Brahmās, faces that are the five Sādākhya-sounds,
and it is beautified by shoulders shaped like the venerable five-syllabled mantra.
It is the form of the entire Tantra and consists of all the kalās of Brahmā;
it extends to the knees by means of Nivṛtti, and to the navel by means of Pratiṣṭhā.
It is perfected by the Vidyā-kalā up to the neck, while the region up to the forehead is formed by the Śāntā-kalā;
above that, it is fashioned by the kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
Thus, this body of Sādāśiva consists of the five Kalās;
Nivṛtti, four-faced and the color of lightning, holds a vajra.
Single-faced and moon-like in luster, she holds the *pratiṣṭhā* mudrā and a lotus;
fire-colored and three-faced, she is Vidyā, her hands radiant with power.
Śānti is black in color and four-faced, holding a banner;
Śāntyatītā is five-faced, holds a noose, and has the luster of the moon.
All of them are adorned with two lotus-garlands and the gesture of granting fearlessness;
they have four arms and three eyes, and their breasts are full and elevated.
p. 257) Because these [five] contain the five paths within them, Sadāśiva consists of the six paths:
the path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme, and the path of world-sphere.
The path of reality (tattvādhvan) and the path of limited powers (kalādhvan)—these are considered the six paths. As for the two hundred and twenty-four worlds (bhuvanas), they are as follows:
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) of the All-pervasive Lord is to be contemplated as being of the nature of the multitude of his body hairs;
meanwhile, the conceptualization of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is effected by means of the fifty phonemes, which take the form of the fifty Rudras.
This [body] of the trident-bearing God of gods is to be contemplated as being composed of the skin,
by means of the seven crores of great mantras arising from the root-vidyā.
This path of mantra (mantrādhvan) of the Lord of Pārvatī should be contemplated as being of the nature of blood;
it is a collection of words consisting of mantras divided into many varieties.
O Lord, the path of the feet should be contemplated as consisting of veins and flesh;
likewise, the thirty-six principles beginning with earth are [contemplated] by those who know the Āgamas.
By these [elements], the path of reality (tattvādhvan) has been described as consisting of the forms of semen, marrow, and bone;
yet in his body there is no bone, no blood, and not even the slightest amount of flesh.
Like a reflection in a mirror, like a rainbow in the sky,
this body of Sadāśiva is established as consisting of pure light.
Nevertheless, this [manifestation] of the sounds pervaded by the *kalās* is mere conceptualization:
[the face] at the head is [consecrated] by Brahmā, and the four-faced one by Īśa and Tatpuruṣa.

One should meditate on the heart and other [limbs] with the Aghora mantra, the secret parts and so forth with the Vāma mantra, and the feet and other [limbs] of the Lord of the World with the Sadyojāta mantra.
All are remembered as having five faces and being adorned with ten powerful arms;
they carry a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a water-pot, and a rosary.
Their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they hold tridents and lotuses;
among these, Aghora and Ghora have such forms, while the others possess gentle appearances.
Having thus meditated upon the omnipresent Lord as the essence of the five Brahmans together with his retinue, one should proceed.
One should fashion the limbs by distinguishing them through the various divisions of the digits of that Brahman.
The five digits (kalās) of Īśāna have attained the nature of the five heads;
those four [digits] of Puruṣa are to be meditated upon as having the form of the four faces.
The eight digits (kalās) of Aghora, the Lord of the entire world,
are said to be the heart, the throat, the shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest.
The thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva, proclaimed by Śiva,
are considered to be located in the secret parts, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, the hips, and the flanks.
The digits (kalās) of Sadyojāta are proclaimed to be eight in number;
they are considered to be the two feet, the two hands, the two nostrils, the head, and the two arms.
The thirty-eight deities of the Kalās have three eyes and four faces; their lotus-like hands shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as the axe and the spear.
Alternatively, they may bear the forms, colors, and weapons of their respective Brahmās;
and on their left side are the Śaktis, beginning with Vaśinī.

One should meditate upon the Rudras, headed by Śrīkaṇṭha, together with their Śaktis, possessing the colors and forms [of their respective directions], with smiling faces, and holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
One should meditate upon the limbs of the Lord according to the method of ritual placement (nyāsa-vinyāsa),
and one should remember the Rudras together with their Śaktis, in the form of Ardhanārīśvara.
Their left and right sides resemble vermilion and gold,
and they are resplendent with the gestures of the noose, the goad, the rosary, and the boon-granting mudrā.
With lotus-like faces serene, bestowing all desired objects,
[he beheld] the wish-fulfilling lotus-feet and the pair of ankles born of yoga.
The form of the toes of the feet is Cintya; the two hands are the cause; Ajita is the pair of knees; and the two thighs of the Lord are Dīpta.
The subtle essence of the secret seed-syllable consists of a thousand [petals] at the brow;
its posterior part is the radiant sun, and its navel is the Śrīsuprabhedaka.
They say Vijaya is the belly, Niśvāsa is the heart,
Svāyambhuva is the pair of breasts, and Anala is the three eyes.
The Vīrāgama is the region of the throat; Raurava is the two ears;
Makuṭa is the crown; and the Vimalāgama is the two arms.
The moon is the knowledge of Śambhu’s chest, his orb is his lotus-face;
the upward-sounding chant is the Lord’s tongue, and the pair of cheeks is his graceful play.
The forehead-plate is perfected, as are the lineage and the two earrings;
the sacred thread is declared by Śarva, and the necklace and garland belong to the Supreme Lord.
One should contemplate the form of the Lord as consisting of rays, his jewel-ornaments, his wind-like nature, and his essence of latent impressions; such is the nature of the Lord as the Tantra.
It bestows the knowledge of Śiva upon men, promotes the dharma of Śiva,
is utterly pure, and is known as the seat of Śiva, like a mass of lightning in the sky.
One should know that the light which has burst forth everywhere is the upward-facing mouth of the All-pervasive Lord;
it is formless, known as Sādākhya, and is heard of as the "Root Pillar."
One should meditate upon his northern face as a liṅga consisting of a pillar of light,
arising from a single portion of that Jyotirliṅga, having one face and three eyes.
One should meditate on the western seat called Mūrtisādākhyam,
[holding] a trident, a thunderbolt, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness with the right hands.
Holding a noose, fire, a bell, and a boon-granting gesture with his left hands, he wields a ritual knife; he is known as Sādākhya and is radiant with four lotus-like faces.
One should meditate upon the southern face arisen in the middle of the *liṅga*—
five-faced and ten-armed— emerged from the pedestal of the *liṅga*.
The well-known *sādana* rite belongs to the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), whose faces are first [the east], then the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western ones; these are the five Brahmans.
One should meditate upon the lotus-faces of the Lord, beginning with Īśāna and proceeding in order;
the heart is white in the heart, and the head is tawny in the head.
One should visualize the red crest-syllable at the location of the crest, the white armor on the two sides,
the dark blue eye in the eyes, and the black weapon in the hand.
They have four arms and three eyes, are adorned with crowns of matted hair,
and hold in their hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a skull-cup and a trident.
The gentle Aṅgadevas are known as his eyes;
yet, when he assumes a fierce form, they say his trident is the three *guṇas* and his axe is his devotion to truth.
For Śambhu, majesty is his sword and indestructibility is his thunderbolt;
fire is his power of destruction, and invincibility among serpents is his power.
The noose consists of impurity, māyā, and karma; the bell and the sound are its essential nature.
They know the power that protects from fear to be the goad, which represents self-restraint.

The powers (śaktis) are considered to be the trident (triśūla), consisting of will, knowledge, and action; those very same powers, which set the pure principles (tattvas) in motion, are said to be the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
She is called Bījapūrā because she sets in motion the seeds of the world;
endowed with the agitation of the *ḍamaru* drum, she is the activator of the principle of *māyā*.

The power that impels the mind, which brings about the performance of all duties headed by the primary arts, is considered to be Indīvarā. She is the "Kākodara" (the one with a black belly) and the initiator of the collection of activities beginning with the "Kalā-mukhya."
She should be known as Akṣamālā, the activator of the senses;
she is Śakti, whose nature is the weapon Śakti, the destroyer of the wicked.
The *vara* [mudrā] bestows enjoyments, the *śakti* [mudrā] grants fearlessness, and the *abhaya* [mudrā] bestows liberation;
thus she holds ten weapons and is as cool as ten million moons.
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, adorned with all ornaments,
and graced by a crown of matted hair divided into rows of finger-widths.
On its right extremity is placed the crescent moon with its tip measuring three and a half finger-breadths;
on its left extremity rests the celestial river in the form of a drop.
He was captivating, wearing the triple-tilaka, the half-moon, the yantra, the lamp, and the crescent moon in sequence,
with these marks applied to his faces beginning with the Īśāna face.
One should meditate on Manonmanī of divine form upon her left side—
resembling a hibiscus flower and adorned with white garments.
Fully adorned with all ornaments, with full thighs, hips, and breasts,
she holds a thousand lotuses, blue lotuses, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus, visualizing before him the Liṅga as the Lord Sadāśiva himself, united with Manonmanī, one should abandon the notion that it is a mere physical Liṅga.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) upon the three eyes with the mantra "hāṃ to the eyes" in due order,
one should invoke Paraśiva, together with the Goddess, into the lotus of the heart.
Now follows the sequence of invocation:
immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, free from disease,
subtle, all-pervading, eternal, stable, imperishable, and undecaying.
"I shall consecrate you with the mantra prescribed by your lordship," having thus informed him, he straightened his body, restrained his mind and gaze,
filled his breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril], performed *kumbhaka*, and placed his cupped hands, filled with flowers, at his heart.

Having firmly formed the *āvāhana-mudrā*, one should draw up the three mantras situated at the *mūlādhāra* within one's own body as the light of Paramaśiva; then, bypassing the *ahaṅkāra* located from the *mūlādhāra* upward, one should lead them to the heart.

While sequentially transcending, through prior contemplation of each respective stage, the net of bonds consisting of earth and the other elements situated in the locations of the heart, throat, palate, and so forth, along with the twelve kalās beginning with *ā* that are accompanied by the causal lords such as Brahmā, he proceeds all the way to the *dvādaśānta*.
Having led even the handful of flowers as far as the *dvādaśānta*, and having united the light consisting of mantra with the Supreme Śiva stationed at the *dvādaśānta*,
one should bring [the offering] back from there in the form of drops dripping incessantly with the supreme nectar.
Having contemplated [the deity] resting in the pavilion of Śiva located between the eyebrows,
and having visualized him as shining like a thousand autumn moons, one should place the hands in *añjali* at the region of the heart,
exhale the breath through the *piṅgalā* channel, and [bring] the light of Paramaśiva along with that breath [back].

Having visualized [the deity] as having reached the center of the handful of flowers, one should join him to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) of Sadāśiva with the mantra: "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva."
In order to clarify the meaning already stated, the locations of the root mantra, its *hakāra* (the letter *ha*), and its twelve digits (*kalā*) are demonstrated.
Beginning from that location in the center of the body which is the *mūlādhāra*:

Extending as far as the *brahmarandhra*, the interior of the body measures four *tāla*s; above that, the location of the crest (*śikhā*) measures one *tāla*. Therein, within the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus situated at the *mūlādhāra*, arises the *prāsāda* mantra.
From that point upward to the navel, there is the letter *ha*, as fine as a lotus fiber and possessing the luster of lightning.
From the navel upward to a distance of twelve finger-breadths, there is the letter *ha* joined with the letter *ra*, having the brilliance of lightning. Beyond that—

The heart-lotus measures four finger-breadths. Beginning from there up to the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), there are the locations for the twelve *kalās*. Among them, the letter *A*, which has three morae (*trimātra*) and possesses the luster of a mass of glowing embers, pervades the four petals of the heart-lotus; and it [is associated] with the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
It is presided over by Brahmā together with the twenty-four principles beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti). Above that,
it imitates the pervasion of a sixteen-petaled lotus measuring eight finger-breadths, situated in the region of the throat.

The two-mātrā [vowel] possesses the luster of the moon and sun arising simultaneously; it is presided over by Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by the six principles beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Kalā, along with the principle of Pratiṣṭhā.
Above that—
The letter *M* is four finger-breadths in measure, located at the root of the palate; it consists of a four-petalled lotus and possesses one *mātrā*.
It is lightning-colored and is presided over by Rudra, together with the *vidyā-kalā* and the *māyā-tattva*. Above that—

Situated two finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows, it has the extent of a double-petaled lotus; it is circular in shape, possesses half a mora, is the color of lightning, and is presided over by Maheśvara together with Śāntikalā and the two principles of Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara.

Above that, in the middle of the forehead, is the *ardhamātrā*, shaped like an upward-pointing half-moon, one-quarter of a measure (*pādamātrā*) and moon-colored. Above that, on the forehead, is the *nirodhī*. It is shaped like an upward-pointing triangle, eight parts of a measure (*aṣṭāṃśamātra*) and smoke-colored. Above that—

In the head is the *nāda*. It has the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*), is joined by two *bindus* at both ends, measures sixteen units, and is the color of rubies (*māṇikya*). Beyond that, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), is the end of the *nāda* (*nādānta*).
It has the form of a plowshare facing south and is joined by a *bindu* on its right side.
It is thirty-two parts in measure and the color of lightning.

Thus, for all four— namely the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructing one (*nirodhinī*), the sound (*nāda*), and the end of sound (*nādānta*)— which reside in the locations starting from the place of the *bindu* up to the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhra*) situated eleven finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows:
Accompanied by the principles (tattvas) of Śāntyatīta-kalā and Sadāśiva, Sadāśiva himself is the presiding deity.

Above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), situated at a distance of one finger-breadth, is the Power (Śakti), shaped like a plough with faces on all sides and accompanied by a bindu on its left side; she measures exactly sixty-four parts.
Then, situated at a distance of three finger-breadths, there is the pervasive power (vyāpinī) in the form of a trident,
accompanied by a bindu on its right side, measuring one hundred and twenty-eight parts.
Above that—
Above that straight line situated between the pair of curved lines within the space between two dots measuring four finger-breadths,
there is a syllable-mora numbering two hundred and fifty-six; above that, it remains for four finger-breadths.

The *manomātrā* consists of a line in the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*) that extends upward from the locus of the *bindu* of *manonmanī*. Here, situated one above the other at the location of the crest (*śikhā*), reaching up to twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in a sequence of one, three, and four finger-breadths respectively.

Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā possess the radiance of seven hundred million suns and are presided over by Anāhata Śiva. When these four are united, they are called the Supreme Space (Paramākāśa).
Thus, the letter A is four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), U is eight finger-breadths, and M is four finger-breadths.
The *bindu* extends for two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); the half-moon, the *nirodhin*, *nāda*, and *nādānta* extend for eleven finger-breadths;
the *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, *samana*, and *unmanā* extend for twelve finger-breadths; thus, these twelve *kalās* together span forty-one finger-breadths.

The locus of pervasion. And thus, within the aforementioned locations extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *dvādaśānta*, one should contemplate the syllable *ha* conjoined with the syllable *ma*, or the syllable *ha* [conjoined] with the vowels *o* and *ū*, in the form of a circle.
The *bindu* has the form of a semi-circle with its apex pointing upward; the *ardhacandra* has the form of a triangle with its apex pointing upward;
the *nirodhinī* has the form of a staff situated between two *bindus*;
and the *nāda* has the form of a plowshare (*halā*) with its apex pointing upward and facing right, situated on the right side of the *nāda* and accompanied by a *bindu*.
The Nāda is shaped like a plow with its tip pointing upward and its left end facing outward, accompanied by a Bindu situated on its left side;
the Śakti is shaped like a trident with its tip pointing upward, accompanied by a Bindu situated on its right side;
and the Vyāpinī is likewise [shaped].
One should contemplate *samanā* in the form of a straight line situated between the two curved lines within the space between the two *bindus*,
and *unmanā* in the form of a straight line with its tip pointing upward, established upon the substratum of the *bindu*,
together with the *kalās* and their presiding lords located in the stations beginning with the heart, in due order.

Having quickly contemplated with the mind by means of discarding each preceding element, one should visualize upon that [the lotus] which possesses five [petals], its filaments consisting of the thirty-six principles, cool as ten million moons, and radiant with the syllable *praṇava* (OṂ), which has a luster equal to ten million suns arisen from the river of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*).
[He is] the form of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), frequented by intoxicated bees filled with the honey of supreme bliss enriched by the seeds of the syllables;
situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus,
His radiance resembles the simultaneous rising of many tens of millions of autumnal moons.
One should mentally plunge into the partless Supreme Śiva, who is an ocean of supreme bliss.
In order to clarify the *kalās* beginning with *bindu*, the nature of the twelve *kalās* is written here:
having thus brought Paraśiva [to the heart] preceded by such contemplation (*bhāvanā*) by means of the root mantra,
and having caused him to reach the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva by means of the heart-mantra and the invocation mudrā (*āvāhanamudrā*), [one should proceed].

Having established [the deity] therein with the *sthāpana-mudrā*, having caused [them] to face oneself with the *sannidhāna-mudrā*, having announced, "Welcome to you, O Great God," and having mentally contemplated the deity's reply, "Child, welcome," one should offer the *svāgatārghya* (welcome-offering) with the *sannirodha-mudrā*.

"Having restrained [the deity], O Lord, Sovereign of all the worlds, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship. Having thus prayed with the heart and the gesture of joined palms (*añjali-bandha*), and having contemplated Śiva’s consent, one should offer the *nirodhārghya* (the water of restraint).

Having dispelled the obstacles with the weapon-mantra *kālakaṇṭhyā huṃ phaṭ*, having enveloped Śiva with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart, head, crest, and armor upon the respective locations of the deity’s body— namely the heart and other parts— with their corresponding mantras;

After performing the sakalīkaraṇa, which consists of the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the limbs such as the heart and so forth, one should offer a flower, consecrate it with the root mantra (mūla), and transform it into nectar using the dhenumudrā.

Herein, *āvāhana* (invocation) is the bringing forth of Śiva into the body of Sadāśiva; *sthāpana* (installation) is the establishing of Sadāśiva within the lotus of the heart; *sannidhāpana* (consecration) is the act of making him face [the worshipper]; *sannirodhana* (confinement) is the prayer for his presence until the completion of the worship; and *avakuṇṭhana* (veiling)...
The covering with the *kavaca* (armor) is for the purpose of manifesting [the deity] among the devotees and for the purpose of ensuring that obstacles do not arise.
*Sakalīkaraṇa* is the application of the five limbs, beginning with the heart. *Paramīkaraṇa* is the [application of] the white, yellow, red, and black colors to the heart and the other [limbs].
The contemplation on the single color of Śiva; the immortalization of the body and the realization of its non-difference from Śiva.
Now, one might ask: how can there be an invocation (*āvāhana*), which consists in bringing [the deity] to a desired location, for Śiva who is all-pervading? It is said in reply:
for Śiva, whose powers are inconceivable, marvelous, and infinite, there exists both pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness.
Its reaching another location is thus logically established. Alternatively, even for the all-pervading *jīva*, reaching another desired location is not contradictory—

just as it occurs through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body— nor is it contradictory for Śiva, who possesses the splendor of the mantra, to reach another location through the limiting adjunct of that mantra-splendor.

Alternatively, just as fire pervading wood is manifested in a particular place by the act of friction, so too the invocation (*āvāhana*) is simply the manifestation of Śiva in a desired location, such as a Śivaliṅga, by means of an act consisting of the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*) of bringing him to that intended place.

Now, one might ask: what is this "manifestation" of Paramaśiva, whose nature is the eternally risen light of the bliss of Śiva, which is present everywhere? It is said: it is like a mass of glowing coals that, though self-luminous, is covered by ashes.
Just as manifestation occurs through an action preceded by the removal of ashes, so too,
although Paramaśiva is self-luminous, [the mind] is directed toward Him through the operation of the worshiper’s mind upon other objects.

The very commencement of the continuous stream of mental attention— intended for the offering of various services throughout one’s entire life— at a chosen location such as a *liṅga*, preceded by the act of invocation performed with undistracted mind, is indeed [the first stage].

The *vyañjana* (manifestation). Alternatively, according to the method described in the *Śiva Purāṇa*, the *āva-hana* is simply the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the manifestation of the divine form of Paramaśiva—consisting of consciousness and bliss and accompanied by Umā—within the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva.
And that [contemplation] is precisely the meditation upon the divine form as instructed by the Guru at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
There is no room for the suspicion that it is a new invention.
That method is now demonstrated:
having meditated upon Sadāśiva in the *liṅga* with an unwavering inner self,
one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās* upon one's own body, just as [one does for the deity].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having abandoned the notion that the linga is the self,
[one should contemplate] Śiva, the supreme cause, as possessing form within that image.
One should contemplate the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa) together with Ambā as the location of the seat;
there reside Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise other gods and asuras.
Even today, those who long for a vision of him perform fierce austerities;
from him proceeds all this world, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra.
Together with the collection of elements and sense organs, he is first brought forth;
he is the creator of the causes, the meditator, and the supreme cause.
He is never produced from anything else at any time;
he is himself the Lord of All (Sarveśvara), complete with all sovereignty, by his very name.
Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space, whose abode is above all, and who is the eternal refuge of all, is to be meditated upon by all those seeking liberation.
Consisting directly of the sixfold path, he is the Lord of the entire universe;
he is the highest among all beings in ascending order, yet he is himself unsurpassed.
An ocean of infinite majesty, his splendor is unfathomable;
he is the manifestation of pure, unerring intelligence regarding all objects of knowledge.
Eagerly longing for the abundance of joy from tasting the nectar of his own power,
he is a bee at the honey of the nectar-juice of infinite bliss.
He is the master in condensing all the unbroken cosmic eggs;
he is the ocean of magnanimity, heroism, profundity, and sweetness.
Incomparable among all beings, the king of kings, the Great Lord—
him whose body is non-material and whose form surpasses the god of love.
His form is composed of being, consciousness, and bliss, solidified by the flow of clarified butter;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and beautified by every limb.
With red face, hands, and feet, his countenance bears a gentle smile like a kunda flower;
he resembles pure crystal and possesses three eyes like full-blown lotuses.
The Lord has four arms and noble limbs, wears the beautiful crescent moon,
holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and carries a deer and an axe.
One should contemplate her as far removed from all categories of comparison;
then, one should meditate upon Maheśvarī at her left side.
Her wide and long eyes had the luster of the petals of a full-blown blue lotus;
her face possessed the radiance of the full moon, and her hair was dark and curled.
Resembling the petals of a blue lotus, with a crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
she possesses breasts that are exceedingly round, firm, lofty, smooth, and full.
She had a slender waist and broad hips, was dressed in very fine yellow garments,
was adorned with all ornaments, and was radiant with a ruby tilaka.
Adorned with a mass of hair strewn with various flowers, her form was pleasing in every respect, and her face was slightly downcast with modesty.
Holding a blooming golden lotus in her right hand,
she sits upon her throne with her other hand resting like a staff.
To the Goddess who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
and who is the mother of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Hara, Śrīśa, and Druhiṇa.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord and the Goddess— both appearing sixteen years of age— as the leaders of the entire circle of powers (śakticakra) such as Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and the rest;
One should worship in due order with devotion and the collection of ritual services.
Thus, in the view that maintains the manifestation of the form of Śiva-with-consort (Sāmbaśiva) within the heart-lotus of Sadāśiva, [one should worship] Him.

The placement [of the deity] within the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva, the act of making him face toward oneself, and so forth—all of this is perfectly logical. However, the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of immortalization), which takes the form of the non-differentiation between the body and the embodied soul, is only possible on the view that the physical form of Sāmbaśiva is being manifested. This is in accordance with one's own intended position.

When the form of Sadāśiva has been invoked into the *liṅga* or other substrates, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worshipper— who, through the face of Īśāna, requests the manifestation [of the deity] for the purpose of worship—

it is indeed Śiva’s own Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), distinct from [the material substrate], that [manifests] by virtue of the power and majesty of His inconceivable and wondrous energy.

Just as a drop of water manifests in the form of a pearl or the like, so too does [the Self] manifest in the form of the complete physical body of Śiva accompanied by Ambā (Sāmbaśiva), possessing all its limbs; such is the established doctrine of the Śiva Purāṇa and other scriptures. In this same way, it manifests in the form of consciousness and bliss (cidānanda).
Precisely because the form of Sadāśiva is whitened by the radiance of the body of Paramaśiva,
it is appropriate to contemplate the body of Sadāśiva— which, although composed of thirty-eight kalās of various colors—
as being crystal-colored. This applies to the faces of Sadāśiva, such as Tatpuruṣa and the others.
The yellow, blue, white, and red colors, however,

belong to the lords of the directions starting from the east— Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera— and are employed to imitate those respective colors for the purpose of stabilizing the yellow, blue, white, and red hues as required for their specific functions.

When such an invocation of Paramaśiva is being performed, one should contemplate that although the face of Sadāśiva facing upward— the Īśāna face— is like the Tatpuruṣa face, its orientation toward the east [for the purpose of dismissal] should be visualized. Thus, the consecrations beginning with the invocation and ending with the nectarification (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) [are to be understood].
In the view that [the deity] is manifested as the form of Sāmbaśiva, the [offerings] should be performed within the very body of Sadāśiva.

Therein, the services such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth should be performed for both Paramaśiva and Ambikā individually, according to the sequence of the successive presentation of each object. Within the form of Sadāśiva—
In the case of the ritual of invoking the pure consciousness of Paramaśiva alone, one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) and other services after that invocation;
in the case of the form of Manonmanī, having consecrated Ambikā through invocations and so forth,
one should worship her with the offerings of water for the feet and other services.

Regarding the manner of offering water for the feet and so forth: having placed the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) together with their three-fold supports in the left hand,
[one offers] the water for the feet up to the Īśvara-tattva, the water for sipping up to the Sadāśiva-tattva, and the respectful offering...

Having meditated upon [the deities] up to the Śiva-tattva, and having visualized that the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings lead the worshipper to the principles of Īśvara and Sadāśiva, one should offer the Prāsāda-mantra and others, rising from the Mūlādhāra, in the sequence of the water for the feet and so forth.

Visualizing the Lord from the center of the eyebrows up to the *brahmarandhra* and the *dvādaśānta*, one should recite the mantra sequence "Hāṃ Hauṃ Śivāya," ending with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *svadhā*,
while using a flower held in an upward-facing hand according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta.

With the tips of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger of the right hand, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the two feet in the order of left and right; water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) to the faces in the order of Tatpuruṣa and the others;
and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to the heads in the order of Īśāna and the others. Then, [one offers] fragrant flowers.

Having bestowed the mantra— which consists of knowledge and is the cause for union with Śiva— and having visualized it being uttered as far as Śiva situated above the Dvādaśānta, one should offer it at the head in the sequence beginning with Īśāna and so forth, using the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

One should also offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and other articles to Ambikā at those very same times, according to the method of offering each item individually (*padārthānusamaya*). The same should be understood to apply to the perfumes (*gandha*) and other offerings as well. In that regard, the specific difference is that the mantras are "Obeisance to Śivā" (*śivāyai namaḥ*) and "Svadhā to Śivā" (*śivāyai svadhā*), and so forth. Then, one offers incense and a lamp with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) and the arghya offering to Śiva and Śivā according to the previously mentioned method,
while touching the lower part of the pedestal with the left hand, one should take a flower with the right hand;
having removed the previously worshipped flower with that [new] flower and having discarded that flower, [one should proceed].
Having mentally visualized everything, beginning with the *aghamarṣaṇa*, according to the manner previously described, one should perform it all.
It should be understood that wherever an action is prescribed as being accomplished by both hands, it is to be performed mentally alone;
thus, there is no contradiction with the worship of the hand-pedestal (*karapīṭhapūjā*). And so it is stated in the *Pūrvatantre*:
The established conclusion is that in the case of the *sānnāyya* offering made of clay and so forth, it is purely mental (*mānasa*).

This should be understood in the same way for what follows. Having bathed [the deity] with a drop of water from the *arghya* vessel while reciting "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle," and having offered the *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya* as before, [one should worship] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having offered two garments, two sacred threads (*upavīta*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*), [one should perform] three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the following:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the *ātmatattva*; Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the *vidyātattva*; Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the *śivatattva*. Thus, three handfuls of flowers.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Goddess with the mantra "Obeisance to Śivā," one should [worship] with ornaments such as golden garments, bracelets, crowns, earrings, necklaces, and armlets— prepared mentally and visualized— which end with the word "namaḥ" [to the root mantra].
Having adorned it with the two mantras, one should offer perfumes and flowers.
Regarding the fragrant substance: therein,

the fragrance consists of either camphor, black agallochum, dārū, kuṣṭha, and musk powder, or else a paste of equal parts of sandalwood, rocanā, saffron, elā, and camphor ground with clarified butter from the Malaya mountains.

Or a powder of sandalwood, agallochum, costus, camphor, saffron, patra, jala, and ushira in equal parts; or a powder of sandalwood, agallochum, costus, and saffron mixed with an equal amount— or half as much— of camphor.
Either a powder of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor,
and saffron in equal parts, or a powder of sandalwood, camphor, musk, and saffron in equal parts, with an amount of nutmeg measuring one *niṣka* according to its availability.

Either powdered sandalwood mixed with camphor and other substances, or pure powdered sandalwood, or pure powdered pieces of *bilva*, or pure powdered pieces of *kṛtamāla*— all these are fragrant substances.

These are exceedingly pleasing to Śiva. Even the mere scent of *dhṛṣṭaka* and *devadāru* wood leads to the attainment of the world of Śiva for as long as a kalpa. Furthermore, the mere scent of *bilva* bestows great sovereignty in this life and brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva in the hereafter.

Even the scent of *kṛtamāla* alone bestows long life and brings about the attainment of the status of a general (*gāṇāpatya*) in the next world. Such being the case, the fragrance of worshipping with sandalwood scent is twice as effective; furthermore, white *agaru* is eight times more potent than sandalwood. Beyond that—
Black agallochum is double [the amount], and saffron is four times that;

therein, according to the previously mentioned method, there is a special mode of worship through the addition of camphor and other substances. Having placed the resulting fragrance produced from such ingredients into a vessel possessing the characteristics described for the *arghya* bowl—

Visualizing the parts of the god’s body, such as the forehead and so forth, as being worthy of unguents, one should offer perfume— whether sufficient for the pedestal of the *liṅga*, sufficient for the *liṅga* itself, or whatever is available— using the heart-mantra.
Then there is the flower-base (*puṣpapīṭhikā*), which is twenty finger-breadths in width, eight finger-breadths in height,
with legs eight finger-breadths high and wide, and possessing stalks eight finger-breadths long on both sides.

[The water] should be placed in a vessel made of gold or other materials, or fashioned from leaves and the like, which is provided with a lid that has no handle or foot, or is half that size; [the water] contained therein should be free from buds, fallen [leaves], decayed [matter], smelled [impurities], insects, and contact with limbs, and [the vessel] should be wrapped with creepers or threads.

One should worship with excellent flowers— free from defects such as being worn out, crushed, or gathered improperly, and which have been thoroughly cleansed and stripped of their stalks— using the root mantra and the deer-mudrā. And the excellent flowers are the *droṇa*, *baka*, *puṃnāga*, *mandāra*, *nandyāvarta*, *karavīra*, *arka*, *bakula*, *kuravaka*, and *lodhra*.
The *śatapatra*, *dhuttūra*, *palāśa*, *pāṭala*, *campaka*, *kṛtamāla*, *karṇikāra*, *munimātuluṅga*,

*arjuna*, *priyaṅgu*, *devadāru*, *tamāla*, *agnigandha*, *maruvaka*, *aśoka*, *kuśa*, *apāmārga*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *pūga*, *sarala*, *kovidāra*, *kadamba*, *āmra*, *madhūka*, *jambu*, *maru*, and *hemākulī*.
Guljā, musalī, vejjī, ajājī, mallikā, paṭṭikā, mālatī, lakṣmī, nirguṇḍī, viṣṇukrānti,
kadalī, śāribā, devatālī, vikarṇī, bahuparṇī, granthiparṇī,
bhadrā, arvājitā, kamala, kahlāra, atasī, raktotpala, nīlotpala, kusumbha, kuṅkuma, and giripu.
[Flowers] beginning with *ṣpa* [are mentioned]. Among them, white-colored flowers are *sāttvika*, bestowing liberation;

red-colored flowers are *rājasa*, bestowing enjoyment; yellow-colored flowers are mixed (*miśra*), bestowing both, accomplishing all undertakings, and bringing about the prosperity of sons and grandsons; black-colored flowers...

Flowers other than the blue lotus (nīlotpala)—which are characterized by the quality of darkness (tāmasa)—are to be avoided. Nevertheless, those specifically prescribed such as flax (atasī), kuraṇḍa, and viṣṇukrānti grant nourishment. Among these, flowers of all colors [may be used].
The worship performed with flowers of a single color is the most excellent; that performed with black-colored flowers is middling;
and worship with flowers of two colors, such as white and red, or with flowers of a single color, is progressively inferior.
As for garlands, those fashioned from flowers each of a single color are the best.
Those fashioned from flowers of many colors are middling; those fashioned from leaves and flowers are inferior.
[The flowers and leaves include: arka, karavīra, bilva, gandhapatrikā, puṇḍarīka, śatapatra, sahasrapatra, bakula, dhuttūra, droṇa, apāmārga, kuśa, śamī, kṛtamāla, śaṅkhinī, vyāghrī, and sadābhadra.

The *rṣṇā*, *nirguṇḍī*, *bṛhatī*, white *arka*, *brahmadroṇa*, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) yield fruits that increase tenfold at each successive stage. Among them, an *arka* flower is equal to the gift of ten gold pieces (*daśasuvarṇa*), while a blue lotus is equal to the worship of a thousand gold pieces.
Viṣṇukrānti, śyāmā, priyaṅgu, nṛpapuṇḍra, puṣpa, and others are equal to the arka flower.
Nandyāvarta, vijaya, śatapatra, mandāra, cūta, madhūka, śvetagirikarṇikā,
mālatī, kadali, śāribā, and other flowers are equal to the karavīra.
Lakṣmī, sahadevī, nāgadantī, campaka, and others are equal to bilva leaves; pāṭala, bakula, and others are equal to lotuses;
and flowers such as jasmine (jāti), mallikā, madhūka, śaṅkha, nāga, sūryāvarta, siṃhakesara, mahābhadra, and so forth—
Pāṇi and apāmārga flowers are equal [in measure]; japā, kadamba, punnāga, and other such flowers are equal to a droṇa;
as well as aśoka, white mandāra flowers, barley, wheat, nīvāra, śāli rice, bamboo shoots, sesame, mung beans, niṣpāva, uśīra, and sprouts of māṣa beans.

And those blossoms that have grown for seven days are equal to *kṛtamāla* flowers. [Blossoms of] diamond, ruby, emerald, pearl, sapphire, great sapphire, sun-gem, and moon-gem are like *karavīra* and blue lotus flowers. The blue lotus—

"Supreme among all" is established by all the Āgamas. In one Āgama it is said that *karavīra* is supreme; in another, *bakapuṣpa*; elsewhere, *giripuṣpa*. Some say the lotus (*padma*) is supreme among all. The excellence of specific flowers depends on specific times. For example:

In the spring season, flowers of the kadamba, campaka, kahlāra, punnāga, kuśa, and bṛhatī, when offered in the worship of Śiva, bestow the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. In summer, flowers of the pāṭalī, mallikā, and śatapatra are equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. In the rainy season...

Lotuses and jasmine flowers are equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice. In autumn, dhattūra, kahlāra, sujāta, and blue lotuses yield the fruit of a sacrificial session (satrayāga). In winter, karavīra and beautiful blue lotuses are equal to a hundred sacrifices (śatakratu). In the cool season (śiśira), the karṇikāra flower [is likewise meritorious].
It bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. Likewise, during the twelve months beginning with Jyeṣṭha [p.
271], one should offer arka, bilva, apāmārga, droṇa, nīlotpala, paṅkaja, kṛtamāla, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, śamī, and camu...
Ripe pāṭalī flowers are most highly recommended. Likewise [are] nandyāvarta, śriyāvarta, white arka, white lotus petals, punnāga, mālatī, paṭṭikā,
red agasti, bakula, lakṣmīdvikaṇṭī, vejikā, pāṭala, palāśa, aśoka, kadalī, and śaṅkhinī.
Īpu flowers are recommended for worship during the morning time.
Droṇa, karavīra, kṛtamāla, dhuttūra, vyāghrī, bṛhatī, pāṭala, lotus, utpala, campaka,
and kuraṇṭa flowers are recommended for worship during the midday time.
Campaka, dhuttūra, mālatī, mallikā, vejikā (also known as balakarṇi and sabhadrā), bhadrā, mausali, atasī, śamī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and fragrant leaves are recommended for the evening worship.

The leaves of the *jātī*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), golden *kadamba*, wild lotus (*sthalakamala*), *ketaka*, betel nut (*pūga*), *punnāga*, *dantī*, *hrīvera*, and *bilva* are for worship at midnight. Flowers such as the golden *kadamba* and *jātī* are to be offered only at night. [Regarding] *mādhavī*—

The flowers of these— ānanda, yūthikā, madayantī, śirīṣa, sarja, bandhūka, vibhītaka, kumuda, dāḍima, lañjālikā, śrīparṇī, kārpāsa, nimba, kūṣmāṇḍa, śālmalī, śindita, voṭa, girivaṭa, matsyākṣika, kapittha, and tintriṇī— are to be avoided.

The prohibition regarding the *ketakī* flower pertains to times other than midnight; likewise, the prohibition regarding the *kadamba* and *śirīṣa* flowers pertains to daytime. The prohibition regarding the *girikarṇikā* pertains to the blue *girikarṇikā*;
the prohibition regarding the *kiṃśuka* pertains to the thorny *kiṃśuka*. The same applies to the *japā*, *vakula*, and others.

In some cases, where there is a prohibition regarding things prescribed in another scripture, the resolution should be understood as follows: it may be based on a difference in the fruit [of the action], or on a difference in the mode of worship, or on a difference in the form of the deity to be worshipped according to the specific modes of worship established by the respective traditions of former teachers following their respective scriptures. This applies even to flowers that are prohibited.

These [flowers] are to be taken from the ornaments of the pavilion and so forth. However, one who is intensely devoted, in the absence of prescribed flowers, with a mind dedicated to Śiva, perceiving all flowers as being of the very nature of Śiva, should mentally contemplate the "flower of all fruits" together with its accessories, associated with mental activity.
One should determine that [the worship] has been performed as prescribed by the scriptures, with the necessary materials, and according to the mantras.
That it is precisely this determination (*niścaya*) that bestows the fruit is clearly stated in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures. In the *Caryāpāda*:
"In the ritual of worshipping Śiva, the devotee [should perform] the worship according to his own capacity."
One should contemplate the flower, the fruit, and the complete collection of conditions as being perfectly fulfilled.
O Goddess, when worship is performed with complete devotion, I am the bestower of its fruit;
I am the increaser of the devotion of all devotees.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, hear these signs of my devotion:
single-minded dedication to the mantra of Śiva and inquiry into the Śiva Āgamas.
The possession of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, the avoidance of other sectarian marks,
and constant residence with fellow Śaivas who understand the meaning of the Śaiva Āgamas— these belong to the true self.
One who is constantly eloquent with the word "Śiva" in all matters—
whether knowing the true meaning or ignorant of it— is liberated from the affliction of worldly existence.
Whether he be a devotee of Śiva by word alone or through hypocrisy—whosoever he may be, he is not a true one;
one should recognize him as a mere ritualist (tāntrika), base, and should not meditate upon him.
O Maheśvarī, I am of that very form for the devotee who meditates thus;
even one who is himself endowed with devotion [should not treat] a person devoted to Śiva with mere words.
In that case, O Maheśvarī, devotion is considered futile;
therefore, a mortal endowed with devotion [should regard] another as equal to himself or even inferior.
Or even one who is lowly, through the mere ornamentation of Rudrākṣas and ashes,
that devoted person shall behold everything as being of the most excellent form.
He who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) nor a rosary of rudrākṣa beads is an enemy of Me,
even if he is possessed of devotion, and is excluded from all sacred rites.
He who is hostile toward the people marked by the [Viṣṇu] emblem is my enemy;
he is cast out and shall experience all forms of torment as a Caṇḍāla for ten million births.
Having entered the womb of a dog, one becomes an eater of pus and excrement;
therefore, one who desires their own welfare must never even look upon my deer.
If a devotee of Śiva has performed the worship of all the gods according to the prescribed rites,
yet fails to observe the non-Śaiva perspective at the time of worship, there is no atonement for that.
One who desires my grace, whether at the time of worship or at any other time, [should avoid] a Caṇḍāla who has experienced all forms of torment throughout ten million births.
One must never engage in conversation or even look upon one who is hostile toward me;
however, if conversation occurs by force or through the power of destiny, [one should remain indifferent].
At that time, having placed some Śaiva person in front, one should speak to him;
desiring my grace, one should not look directly at his face.
(273) Avoiding non-Śaivas is the first mark of my devotee;
the second is the sense of ownership toward those adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Whether of one's own caste or another caste, whoever possesses such power—that one should contemplate as Śiva; a trivial perception regarding him brings fear.
To remove the sin of non-Śaiva doctrines, one should worship Śiva with one hundred and eight or even a thousand bilva leaves.
In reciting [the mantra], there would be three thousand [merits]; in touching [it], exactly one hundred thousand;
and if doing so ten times, it is as stated, with double the merit for each act of worship.
The body of the devotee who worships is indeed my own body;
by merely avoiding what is forbidden, one obtains the fruit born of performing prescribed worship.
The performance of prohibited acts alone leads to the destruction of prescribed worship;
therefore, a devotee should with great effort avoid the sight of those who harbor malice toward Me.

To remove the defects arising from speaking with, touching, or conversing with those who hold non-Śaiva views, one should take up on leaves bilva, āragvadha, campaka, darbha, dūrvā, apāmārga, karavīra,
nandyāvarta, śamī, and viṣṇukrāntā.

The leaves of bhadra, mahābhadra, jātī, jambuka, kadamba, cūta, palāśa, the two types of munidvaya, aṅkola, kuraṇṭaka, the two types of girikarṇikā, rudraparṇī, bhūta, padma, hrīvera, damana, maruvaka, droṇa, sindhuvāra, śaṅkhinī, gokṣura, bakula, kṛtamāla, and so forth.

These are recommended. Among flowers, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is recommended; among leaves, the *bilva* leaf is most highly recommended, while the two types of *āragvadha* and *droṇa* are even more highly recommended. For those whose flowers are recommended, their leaves are likewise recommended. [This applies to] the *padma*, *nīlotpala*, and *kuṭaja*.

[The vessel] should be made of gold, shaped like the flowers and leaves of the *campaka*, *jātī*, *karavīra*, *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *bilva*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *pāṭalī*, the five kinds of *bilva* flowers, *dūrvā*, *agastya*, or *gandhapattrā*,
or else in the form of any flower or leaf of one’s own preference among those auspicious flowers and leaves.
A leaf and a flower are highly recommended. The invocation of the *vidyā-deha* and Śiva into the seats and forms is performed with handfuls of golden leaves,
using one hundred and eight, eighty-one, fifty, or twenty-five [leaves].
Worship performed daily with golden flowers yields immeasurable fruit.
If one is unable to procure golden flowers, one should worship with fragments of gold or silver flowers.
There is no fault of being "worn-out" (nirmālya) regarding a golden flower; it becomes "worn-out" only after a year has passed.
Even after a year has passed, it should be purified with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and worshipped again.

Likewise, there is no fault of being "worn-out" (*nirmālya*) regarding blue lotuses, *palāśa* leaves, *bakula*, oleander (*karavīra*), mountain flowers, or *bilva* leaves. [This applies to] the leaves.

Flowers produced in one's own garden are the most excellent. Those purchased from another's garden, or flowers requested at the time of worship, are progressively inferior. However, flowers originating from a temple garden (devārāma) are to be avoided. In the absence of flowers...

One should worship with the leaves themselves of those flowers that are worthy of Śiva. In the absence of even those leaves, one should worship with their fruits. Among fruits, the citron (*bījapūra*), lime (*jambīra*), plantain (*kadalī*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), and others are recommended for worship. In the absence of even fruits—

One should worship with sesame seeds, rice, and white mustard. Worship of Śiva with black sesame seeds destroys all sins. Thus, having worshipped with flowers and other offerings using the root mantra, [one recites]:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva; Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva; Hāṃ Hauṃ."

Salutation to Śiva. Hoṃ, salutation to the one whose head is knowledge (jñānamūrdhan). Heṃ, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Huṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora. Hiṃ, salutation to the secret place of Vāmadeva. Haṃ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta. Thus, [one worships] the form of the seat with the root mantras.

Having worshipped with the five Brahmans and the eight flowers, one should worship with the limbs [of the mantra], beginning with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth. Then, one should worship with either the thousand names or a hundred names.
In the absence of that opportunity, [one should worship] with: "Obeisance to Śarva, the earth-form; obeisance to Bhava, the water-form."
Salutation! Salutation to Rudra, whose form is fire; salutation to Ugra, whose form is wind;
salutation to Bhīma, whose form is space; salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer;
salutation to Īśāna, whose form is the sun; salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is the moon; salutation to Śiva.

Salutation! Salutation to Maheśvara; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Pitāmaha; salutation to the Physician of Saṃsāra; salutation to the Omniscient One; salutation to the Supreme Self.
Or, one may worship with these eight names. Salutation to Prabhu, salutation to Śambhu, salutation to Umāpati.

One should worship with the three names beginning with "Namaḥ. Or, having worshipped with the single name "Namo nīlakaṇṭhāya namaḥ," one should also adorn [the deity] with garlands of flowers as available. These garlands should be composed of gold flowers numbering a hundred or more, or composed of blue lotuses numbering a thousand or more.

Garlands fashioned from *karavīra*, white lotus, *vijayā*, black *pāṭala*, *puṇnāga*, white *mandāra*, *nāgakesara*, and *campaka* flowers are recommended. These, as well as garlands woven with various other flowers, should be richly bound on both sides of the staff. However, in the case of a linga-shaped staff:
A circular garland called *muṇḍa*, fashioned from jewels and gold or made of flowers, consisting of one, two, three, or four tiers, should be offered.
p. 275) The Procedure for the Offering of Incense:
Thus, following the offering of flowers, comes the offering of incense. Its method is as follows:
[the incense burner] should be made from any one of gold, silver, copper, or brass, and measure four finger-breadths in length.

Its height should be half of that [measurement], with a lip eight *aṅgulas* wide; on its rear side, it should have a neck marked with lotus petals measuring two *aṅgulas*, and feet shaped like well-rounded hoofs rising two *aṅgulas* high;
it should be provided with a cloth nozzle having a circumference of two *aṅgulas* and endowed with the previously described characteristics of the feet.
Having filled an incense burner— equipped with a cover shaped like a lotus bud, whether having many perforations or a single one— with pure (charcoal) fruit-fire,
and having placed the incense substance therein and closed the incense burner, one should consecrate it by means of inspection and other rites.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and displayed the incense mudrā, one should take the incense vessel with the right hand; with the left hand, [one holds] a vessel made of pure bell-metal,
having a height of four, five, or six finger-breadths, and a width of the same measure.
It should have a tongue measuring one unit, a nose three times that, lips half a finger-width, and be provided with a fillet; its crest should be one, two,
or two-and-a-half units, and its neck half a finger-width.

Holding a bell— whose handle is three *aṅgulas* in thickness and three, four, five, or six *aṅgulas* in length, and which is marked above with a trident, a lotus, or a bull, or with symbols other than the conch and the discus—
one should announce it while offering incense near the nose of the Lord, reciting: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya dhūpaṃ*.

Having presented incense with the mantra "svāhā," and having lifted the incense vessel over it, while rotating it, one should contemplate the *nāda* in the form of a staff with two dots on its sides upon the crown;
the letter *ha* in the orb of the face and the body of the *bindu*; the letter *o* in the two arms; and the letter *u* in the two feet.
One should perform the visualization by rotating the incense burner.
The incense substances consist of camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, *takkola*, nutmeg, cloves, *siṃhaka*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*,
and *mustā* powder; these ten ingredients combined with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and musk.

The powder of *takkola*, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon leaves, and *nāgapuṣpa* is known as *yakṣakardama*. The powder of sandalwood, *agaru*, camphor, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon bark, leaves, *siṃhaka*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *prajāpati* is named *prājāpatya*. [Sandalwood and *agaru*...]
The powder known as *vijayā* consists of camphor, musk, cloves, *tilaka*, *hasita*, and *mustā*.

The powder named *śītāri* consists of camphor, black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāgaru*), *hrīvera*, saffron, *kuṣṭha*, resin (*niryāsa*), and sandalwood, taken in successive proportions of one, two, three, four, five, and six parts, mixed with honey.

The powder of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, silhaka, sarjarasa, kuṣṭha, and mustā is called Vijaya-karpūra; that which is named Kalyāṇa consists of the powder of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, mustā, and silhaka; and that which is named Amṛta consists of the powder of sandalwood, agallochum, kastūrī, mustā, and silhaka.

The powder of *takkola*, *pūga*, camphor, *jātīphala*, and cloves is called "fragrant" (*sugandha*). Such substances for incense are well known by their individual names. Likewise, there is the powder of sandalwood, *agaru*, camphor, *kuṣṭha*, and *guggulu*.
Powdered sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and kuṣṭha mixed with ghee and honey;
powdered resin of agallochum, sandalwood, and camphor mixed with sugar, honey, and ghee; and powdered agallochum-resin and sandalwood in successive proportions of one, four, six, and seven parts.
In successive order: powdered agallochum, sandalwood, and ushira mixed with a little camphor and honey;
powdered kuṣṭha and sandalwood mixed with honey;
and powdered guggulu and bilva fruit mixed with clarified butter, as well as powdered guggulu mixed with clarified butter.
Alternatively, the incense substance may consist solely of *guggulu* resin, or the powder of any one of the following: sandalwood, agarwood, *saugandhika*, and so forth.
Among these, incense made of pure *guggulu* removes the sins committed during seven lifetimes; sandalwood incense [removes the sins of five lifetimes].
The *saugandhika* incense removes all sins and accomplishes all desires and aims.
The *kṛṣṇāguru* incense removes all sins. The *śvetāguru* incense bestows liberation.
The incense of lac and musk bestows the birth of a Brāhmaṇa who studies the four Vedas.

Incense made of guggulu mixed with clarified butter, offered for half a month, brings about the enjoyment of the city of Śiva and birth as a sovereign for a period extending to a thousand crores of kalpas.
Incense made of mahiṣākṣa-guggulu, two thousand times [the potency], combined with the powder of the tamāla tree, [yields the same result].

He is the bestower of union with Śiva. Among the five faces beginning with Īśāna, incense made respectively from sandalwood, white agallochum, black agallochum, saugandhika, and guggulu is recommended.
The sequence for the offering of light:

thus, following the offering of incense, comes the offering of light. Its vessel is three finger-breadths in measure, shaped like an elephant’s trunk, and provided with a stand as described for the incense vessel.

The wick should be made of camphor, or of pieces of cloth, or of strands of thread, or of cotton; it should be four finger-breadths in length, and its circumference should correspond to the flame, being four, three, two, or one finger-breadth respectively.
If it is made of pieces of cloth and so forth, it should be of the superior grade and so on, provided that such materials are available.
It should be prepared containing the powder of camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, and so forth. Among these, the ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā) is the best;

the ghee of other cows is middling; the ghee of a goat and sesame oil are inferior. Ghee from camels, buffaloes, and the like, as well as oils derived from tree seeds and such, are to be avoided. Or else:
Cow’s ghee is the best; goat’s ghee and buffalo’s ghee are middling.
Oil with a foul odor, such as that from *nimba*, *karañja*, *eraṇḍa*, and so forth, is to be avoided. Any oil at all is inferior.
Thus, one should examine with inspection and other means the lamp placed upon a wick prepared in a vessel according to the aforementioned characteristics.
Having consecrated [the offering] with perfumes and flowers, worshipped it, displayed the lamp-gesture (*dīpamudrā*),
lifted up the lamp-vessel, and while ringing the bell,
one should display it before the eyes [of the deity], reciting: *HĀṂ HAUṂ ŚIVĀYA NAMO DĪPAṂ SVĀHĀ*.

Like the incense vessel, one should rotate the lamp-vessel from the crown of the head down to the feet through the meditation on the placement of their respective colors. Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the respectful offering (arghya) to Śiva as before, and having meditated upon the God as satisfied, [one should pray: "O Blessed One, grant permission for the limbs of enjoyment."
Having made the request, "I worship," one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
The worship of the enclosures:
the first enclosure is with the five Brahmans and the six limbs; the second is with the Vidyeśvaras.

The third [enclosure] with the lords of the Gaṇas, the fourth with the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fifth with all the weapons— having worshipped Śiva in the pericarp of this fivefold enclosure lotus-seat of Śiva, [one worships] at the bases of its petals, in the middle of the petals, between the base and tip of the petals, and at the tips of the petals.

And one should worship in its lower parts; or rather, one should worship in the forms of the roots of the petals of the *śivāsana* lotus at the base of the *liṅga*, in the forms of the tips of those petals at the front part above the pedestal (*pīṭha*), at the neck of the pedestal, at the feet of the pedestal, at the location of the *brahmaśilā*, and in the lotus-pedestal. *Hoṃ*.

Homage to the head of Īśāna. I worship Īśāna, who is crystal-colored, holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, and is accompanied by Umā. Heṃ, homage to the face of Tatpuruṣa. [I worship him] who is golden-colored and wears yellow garments and a sacred thread.

I worship Tatpuruṣa, who holds a citron and a rosary, accompanied by Gaurī. Hūṃ, homage to the heart of Aghora! [I worship him who is] cloud-colored, with tawny beard and hair, a face formidable with fangs, and adorned with garlands of snakes, scorpions, and skulls.

I worship Aghora together with Gaṅgā, whose four left hands hold a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose, and whose four right hands hold a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff. Hiṃ! Homage to the secret of Vāmadeva.

I worship Vāmadeva, who is of a deep red hue, wearing a deep red garland, clothing, and sacred thread, holding a sword and a shield, accompanied by Gaṇa and Ambikā. Haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta! [I worship him] who is white in color, wearing a white garland, white perfumes, white garments, and a turban, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, accompanied by Ambikā.
"I worship Sadyojāta. Thus, in due order, at the time of worshipping each respective deity— Īśāna, Indra, Yama, Kubera, and Varuṇa— in their respective directions,
one should draw [the deities] from their respective locations— the upper face, heart, secret place, and feet— by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.

Having meditated upon those [deities] as non-different from the lamp by means of the procedure of the lamp which has been set in motion, one should worship them. Alternatively, all five [faces], beginning with Īśāna, should be visualized as having four beautiful hands holding a trident, a pickaxe, a boon-granting gesture (varada), and a gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). In this manner, their meditations as established in other Āgamas should also be observed.
Hāṃ, salutation to the heart; Hīṃ, salutation to the head; Hūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock;

Haiṃ, salutation to the armor; Hauṃ, salutation to the three eyes; Haḥ, salutation to the weapon—thus [one should contemplate] those [syllables] having the colors of the moon, refined gold, vermilion, a bumblebee, lightning, and fire.
