"I worship the deities of the heart, head, crest, and armor— seated in the lotus posture, wearing crescent-moon crowns, four-faced, with three eyes in each face, holding a skull-cup, a trident, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness, accompanied by Vāminī, Nīlinī, Cakriṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Gaṅginī, and Śakti."
Having drawn [the deities] from their respective locations— the heart, head, crest-lock, and so forth— by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*,

one should worship the four petals starting from the east on the petals situated in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners, as well as the *astra* (weapon) at the tips, and [the deities] on the petals starting from the northeast.
One should worship Brahmā, Sva (Vāyu), and Īśāna on the limbs, and the Eye on the head, in sequence, according to their respective directions from north to east.
Alternatively, one may worship Īśāna and the Eye in front of the deity situated in the pericarp.
Or, because the Eye is associated with the weapon-mantra, one may worship it in the [southeastern] direction.
Now, the second enclosure: salutation to Ananta together with Bhūmi; salutation to Sūkṣma together with Svāhā;
salutation to Śivottama together with Svadhā; salutation to Ekanetra together with Kṣānti.
"Obeisance to Ekarudra accompanied by Puṣṭi; obeisance to Trimūrti accompanied by Śrī;

obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha accompanied by Kīrti; obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin accompanied by Medhā"—thus [one should worship] those who have the colors of gold, coral, and crystal in the golden, fire, and conch vessels respectively.
"I worship the Vidyeśvaras, who hold the gestures of granting boons (*vara*), fearlessness (*abhaya*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), as well as rosaries of rudrākṣa beads; who possess three eyes;

who are the revealers of the knowledge of Śiva; and who are accompanied by their respective Śaktis"—thus one worships them in the cardinal and intermediate directions, starting from the east and proceeding to the northeast, or within the corners beginning from the east and ending with the northeast.

One should worship: "Obeisance to Nandikeśvara, together with Kuṇḍalinī. I worship Nandin, who is reddish-brown in color, holding a trident, a thread, and making the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, accompanied by Kuṇḍalinī. "Obeisance to Mahākāla, together with Padminī. [He is] yellow and black in color.
I worship Mahākāla, who has tawny beard and hair, who holds a trident, a skull-cup, a sword, and a shield, and who is accompanied by Padminī.
Homage to Bhṛṅgin, who is accompanied by Hlādinī and whose body is adorned with flower-garlands from previous offerings. He is white in color.

I worship Bhṛṅgin, who holds a staff and a rosary, whose topknot is radiant, who is intent on beholding Śiva, and who is accompanied by Hlādinī. Homage to Gaṇapati together with Bhṛṅgiṇī. [I worship] Gaṇapati, who has a red body, who holds a noose, a goad, a tusk, and a ripe mango fruit, and who is accompanied by Bhṛṅgiṇī.
I worship. Homage to Vṛṣabha accompanied by Bhadrā. I worship the bull, crystal-colored, whose nature is Dharma, intent on meditation upon Śiva, and accompanied by Bhadrā.
Homage to Skanda accompanied by Devayānī. [I worship him] golden-colored, in the guise of a child.
I worship Skanda, who holds a spear, a cock, an elephant goad, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, accompanied by Devayānī.
Homage to Ambikā! I worship Umā, who is dark-complexioned, mounted upon a lion, and holds a trident and a mirror in her two hands, together with Rūpiṇī.

Salutation to Caṇḍeśvara. I worship Caṇḍeśvara, who is cloud-colored, four-faced, bearing a water-pot, a rosary, a trident, and an axe, adorned with a serpent-bracelet and a sacred thread, and accompanied by Rūpiṇī.
One should worship [the deities] starting from the east and extending to the northeast corner.
Or else, [one may worship] Vṛṣa, Nandikeśvara, Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla, Skanda, Bhṛṅgi, Gaurī, Caṇḍa; or alternatively, Nandi, Gaṇapati, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgi, Vṛṣa, Skanda, Gaurī, and Caṇḍa.
One should worship them in the sequence starting from the east.

Alternatively, Gaurī, Caṇḍeśvara, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha, Bhṛṅgin, Skanda, or else Gaurī, Caṇḍeśa, Mahākāla, Vṛṣa, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Bhṛṅgin should be worshipped in the order starting from the north.

Umā, Vṛṣabha, Gaṇapati, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Caṇḍa, Skanda, Kubera, Śakra, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśāna, and Agni should be worshipped respectively in the directions of the north, east, south, west, southwest, northwest, northeast, southeast, and fire.
The specific variations in their meditative visualizations (dhyāna) should be understood as they are well-known from their respective Āgamas.

Having thus worshipped the third enclosure with the lords of the Gaṇas, one should worship the fourth enclosure with the world-protectors (lokapālas). *Oṃ namo indrāya śacīsahitāya*: Salutation to Indra together with Śacī;
he is golden-hued, mounted upon Airāvata, and holds a thunderbolt, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness in his hands.

I worship Indra together with Śacī. Homage to Agni together with Svāhā. I worship Agni, who is red in color, mounted upon a ram, and endowed with the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), the spear (*śakti*), and the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*), together with Svāhā. Homage to Yama together with Kālakaṇṭhī.

I worship Yama, who is black in color, holding a staff, a noose, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, mounted upon a buffalo, and accompanied by Kālakaṇṭhī. Homage to Nirṛti, who is accompanied by Ḍākinī, red in color, holding a sword, a shield, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and mounted upon a spirit (bhūta).

I worship Nirṛti together with the ḍākinīs. Homage to Varuṇa together with Bhoginī. I worship Varuṇa, moon-colored, holding a noose, a lotus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, mounted upon a makara, together with Bhoginī. To Vāyu...

Homage to him accompanied by Ghorā. I worship Vāyu, smoke-colored, holding a banner, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, mounted upon a deer, and accompanied by Ghorā. Homage to Kubera accompanied by Gambhīrī. [I worship him] tawny-colored, holding a mace and other weapons, mounted upon a horse.
I worship Kubera together with Gambhīrī. Homage to Īśāna together with Harṣiṇī.

I worship Īśāna, who is moon-colored, who holds a trident, a noose, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who has three eyes, who is mounted upon a bull, and who is accompanied by Harṣiṇī. Thus one should worship in the sequence starting from the east. To Brahmā...

Salutations to him accompanied by Sāvitrī. I worship Brahmā, who is golden in color, four-faced, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), a garland, and a staff, mounted upon a swan, and accompanied by Sāvitrī. Salutations to Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī. [He is] lightning-colored.

"I worship Viṣṇu, who is adorned with a thousand hoods, possesses infinite forms, holds the conch, discus, mace, spear, and lotus, is mounted upon a tortoise, and is accompanied by Lakṣmī"— thus [one worships him] between Indra and Īśāna, and between Nirṛti and Varuṇa.
One should worship Vidhātṛ and Vaikuṇṭha; or alternatively, one should worship them on the northern side of Yama and the southern side of Kubera.
The fifth enclosure:

Now, the fifth enclosure consists of the weapons of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Homage to Vajra, who is accompanied by the power of the gracious self (*prasannātmaśakti*), who bears various colors and possesses a firm and harsh form.

I worship the blazing Vajra with a diamond-peak, together with its serene self; homage to Śakti! I worship Śakti, who is of a reddish hue, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who bears a spear upon her head, and who has the form of a woman; homage to Daṇḍa, who is accompanied by the Śakti of the nature of wrath!

I worship Daṇḍa, who is black in color, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose eyes are red, whose head is a staff, and who is accompanied by the Power of Wrathful Nature. Homage to Khaḍga, who is accompanied by the Power of Qualities, who is dark-complexioned, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose eyes are like those of a bull.
I worship the sword, whose head is adorned with a scorpion and which is endowed with the power of the self-nature of the qualities (guṇātmaśakti).

Homage to the noose, which is endowed with the power of a tender nature; it has the color of a *kiṃśuka* flower, is shaped like a serpent from the navel downwards, and has the form of a man above that.
I worship the noose (pāśa), which has a head endowed with seven hoods and is accompanied by its own gentle power (ātma-śakti).

Homage to the banner (dhvaja) accompanied by its own poisonous power (viṣātma-śakti). I worship the banner, which is yellow in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with an open mouth, adorned with a banner upon its head, and accompanied by its own poisonous power.

I worship. *Namaḥ* to the mace (*gadā*). I worship the mace, which is yellow in color, in the form of a woman, with a radiant head. *Namaḥ* to the trident (*śūla*) accompanied by the power of the deformed self (*vikṛtātmaśakti*), which is dark in color, has its top marked with a trident, and is joined in *añjali*.

I worship the trident accompanied by the power of the transformed self (vikṛtātmaśakti). Homage to the lotus accompanied by the power of the great self (mahātmaśakti). I worship the lotus, which is conch-colored, whose top has the shape of a lotus bud, and which is accompanied by the power of the great self. [Homage] to the one accompanied by the power of the auspicious self (maṅgalātmaśakti).

Salutation to Cakra. I worship the Discus (Cakra), which is dark-hued, whose head is marked with a hundred-spoked wheel, and who is accompanied by Maṅgalātmā. And these deities of the enclosure, facing Śiva and gazing upon Śiva and Ambikā with devotion.

They should be visualized as seated upon their respective seats. These [deities] may be visualized as having two arms or four arms, or with their hands joined in the *añjali* gesture. Thus, if one is unable to perform the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), one should worship a single enclosure consisting of the forms of the Five Brahmās and the Six Limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). And of these:

One should perform the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the six limbs of Brahman, known as invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), bringing near (*sannidhāpana*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), and the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), and flowers (*puṣpa*); or else,
one may simply recollect the eight purificatory rites beginning with invocation as a collective whole.

Having offered a mere *arghya* to each [deity], and at the conclusion of the *arghya* for the Brahmās, one should sequentially display the mudrās known as the Surabhī, Padma, Triśūla, Makara, and Srag, and then display the *namaskāra*-mudrā for the limbs (*aṅga*). [This applies] when there is an inability to perform the worship of the five Brahmās and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
One should worship either the enclosure of Brahmā alone or the enclosure of the limbs alone.

Alternatively, having worshipped the powers such as Vāmā and others in their respective places in the directions starting from the east, one should worship Manonmanī, who is situated on the left side in the lap of Sadāśiva. Thus, after the worship of the enclosures:

Having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should present a flower with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). This is for the sake of accomplishing the splendor produced by the true presence of Śiva’s attendants (*āvaraṇasadbhāva*);
for one who is inclined toward worshipping the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and so forth as distinct from Śiva.
For the sake of removing the fault of the impurity of being insentient,

all the deities of the coverings are of one color with Paramaśiva, by virtue of being immersed in the mass of rays consisting of Paramaśiva, which flow with the supreme nectar and possess a brilliance like that of ten million autumnal moons.

One should meditate upon [the deities] as non-different from Paramaśiva. Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* to Śiva, and having worshipped the bell with perfumes and flowers using the *astra-mantra*, one should present incense and lamps to the deity together with his retinue. Such is the worship of the retinue (*āvaraṇārcana*).
It has been deliberated whether [certain acts] should be performed or should not be performed,
because in some scriptures the worship of the limbs of enjoyment is prohibited within the worship of Śiva for one's own sake.
p. 282) The Ritual of the Food Offering (Naivedya-vidhi):

Now follows the ritual for the food offering. Regarding the Vīraśaivas, there are two traditions: that which holds that anything whatsoever may be offered, and that which holds that only as much as has been offered [to the Guru] may be offered. In the latter tradition (*yāvannivedana*), that which has been offered to the *jaṅgama* [Guru]...

They consider [the former view] to be inconsistent because it is not possible for it to be an act of grace (*prasāda*). Whatever is offered, one should give whatever has been presented by the *jaṅgama* to those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*).
Even when offering [to the stationary image], since there is no difference between the *jaṅgama* and the *liṅga*, that which is offered to the *jaṅgama* is indeed offered to the cherished *liṅga*.
Those [cases] stated in the scriptures as "it might be" should not be recorded here.
Now, following another school of thought, the manner of offering is as follows:
among them, *vrīhi*, *śāli*, *priyaṅgu*, *nīvāra*, *godhūma*, *vaiṇava*, and barley (*yava*) are recommended.
Among these, *vrīhi* is the lowest; *śāli* is middling; the others are superior. Among those—

Priyaṅgu, nīvāra, wheat, and bamboo-seeds yield fruits that increase a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, and infinitely, respectively, in successive order. Alternatively, śāli rice is the best;
barley, bamboo-seeds, and so forth are middling; and vrīhi rice is the lowest. [These refer to] white-grained rice.
*Śāli* rice and other *vrīhi* varieties constitute the distinction. For worship performed for one's own sake, quantities from one *kuḍava* up to four *droṇas* are increasingly recommended.
Two hundred and twenty-five *vrīhi* grains are said to constitute one *śukti*.

Two *śukti*s are a *tala*. Two *tala*s are a *prakuñca*. Two *prakuñca*s are a *prasṛti*. Two *prasṛti*s are a *kuḍava*. Two *kuḍava*s are an *añjali*. Two *añjali*s are a *prastha*. Two *prastha*s are a *pātra*. Two *pātra*s are an *āḍhaka*. Two *āḍhaka*s are a *śiva*.
Two *śiva*s make one *droṇa*. Alternatively, two *guñjās* make one *māṣa*; twenty *māṣas* make one *niṣka*; eight *niṣkas* make one *phala*; four *palas* make one *pāda*;
four *pādas* make one *prastha*; four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*; and four of those [make one *droṇa*].

Regarding the *droṇa*: for the purpose of the sacrificial offering (*naivedya*), one should select four *droṇas* of rice grains that are free from hair, insects, and the like; devoid of husks, broken kernels, and chaff; whole and unbroken; and possessing an extreme whiteness.

Having repeatedly rinsed [the grains] six times with water that has been strained through cloth and possesses excellent color, fragrance, and taste— preceded by squeezing [the water out]— and having thoroughly purified the sand and other materials with the six-limbed mantras,
one should pour more than half as much water into those [grains] placed in a cooking vessel smeared with cow dung.

In the kitchen— which has been sprinkled with water, is free from the sight of birds and the like, and is situated outside the range of the gaze— having placed the cooking vessel, which was lifted out with the Vāmadeva mantra, upon the hearth honored with the Hṛdaya mantra, and having established the fire with the Aghora mantra, [one should proceed] with the Mukha mantra.
Having ignited the fire, one should cook with care so that the food is neither undercooked nor overcooked;

such is the cooking of pure food. [This may be done] with twice the amount of milk relative to the rice, or with half as much mung bean pulse along with the rice, or with three times the amount of milk relative to the rice.
The cooking of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is performed with rice combined with a fourth part of mung beans, or with that same amount of rice combined with jaggery and plantains;
or [it may be prepared] with sesame powder measuring a fourth part of the rice,
or with sesame powder measuring a fourth part [of the rice], or with half the measure of sesame.

The cooking of *kṛsarā* may be done with ghee measured at one-fourth the quantity of sesame seeds; or alternatively, the cooking of *kṛsarā* may be done with half as much rice as there is of mung beans, mixed with sesame powder and a small amount of salt powder. [This applies] to each [ingredient] measuring half the quantity of rice.

The preparation of *guḍānna* (jaggery-rice) is made with milk and jaggery, along with ghee measuring half that amount. Alternatively, it is prepared with twice the amount of milk relative to the rice, together with half as much jaggery and half as much ghee. Or else, it may be prepared with three times the amount of milk relative to the rice.
The preparation of jaggery-rice (*guḍānna*) is made with one-third part mung beans combined with rice, mixed with one-fourth part jaggery, and accompanied by plantain fruit;
or it may be prepared with one-fourth, one-third, or an equal amount [of jaggery] relative to the rice.

The cooking of mung beans may be prepared either with pieces of coconut or without them. Pure rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), kṛsara-rice, jaggery-rice, and mung-bean rice yield fruits that are each a thousand times more meritorious than the preceding one. Likewise, food mixed with curd and food mixed with honey [yield similar results].
This is commendable. Among these, one, several, or all should be prepared according to one's means.

The offering (naivedya) should be made with any one of the following—mung beans, pigeon peas, black gram, kidney beans, flat beans, or horse gram—using an eighth or a sixteenth part of the quantity of the main offering.

Likewise, if available, mung beans and other such items should be taken in their peeled form. Regarding the vegetables, they should measure either two *prasthas* for the two offerings (*naivedya*), or one *pala* each;
these include plantain, jackfruit, pumpkin, eggplant, snake-gourd, *kāravallī*, the two types of *vyāghrī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and the two types of *kośātakī*.

Mangoes, coconuts, and other fruits; young tubers, creepers, tubers, sūraṇa roots, and other items with excellent taste and fragrance— whether fresh or dried— prepared as appropriate with all the seasonings such as salt, black pepper, cumin, cardamom powder, sugar, and so forth.

The preparations should be fried in clarified butter (*ghṛta*). A cooling draught (*coṣya*) should be made with sour thickened buttermilk (*ghanatakra*), combined with the powders of salt, black pepper (*marīca*), cumin (*jīraka*), horse-gram (*kulattha*), and white mustard (*siddhārtha*), along with sugar.
Various preparations of the flours of black gram (*māṣa*), green gram (*mudga*), wheat (*godhūma*), and rice (*śāli*), mixed with abundant sugar, should also be consumed.
Many cakes and drinks such as *pānaka* should be prepared, scented with powders of camphor, cardamom, and other ingredients.
For the food offering (*naivedya*), the clarified butter should be one-sixteenth, one-thirty-second, or one-sixty-fourth part [of the total];
thick curd should be one-eighth part. In all cases, the milk, curd, and clarified butter must be derived from cows.
These items are to be accepted. The vessels (sthālikā) should be made of gold, silver, copper, or pure bell-metal.

Those that are forty-eight finger-breadths in length, one finger-breadth in height, and possess lips two finger-breadths thick are the very best. According to the sequence beginning with the "best," however:
Those with a length ranging from thirty-six finger-breadths down to twelve finger-breadths,
having lips measuring from nine barley-corns down to one barley-corn,
or having reed-stalks equal in measure to the lips, or lacking those stalks, and having a length of nine finger-breadths;
Those measuring half of that are the smallest. All of them should be made without feet, perfectly circular in shape, and provided with three-legged stands for supporting the cooking pots. (p. 284)

They should be made as high as the height of the pedestal of the worshipable *liṅga*. And all the food offerings (*naivedya*) should be presented by attendants who have been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva, who are bathed, dressed in clean garments, adorned with ashes and *rudrākṣa* beads, and whose hands are purified.

One should have [the rite] performed; or, having had it performed by women of such a nature, at the time of purifying the substances, the worshipper should mutter the mantras for washing rice and so forth. If the food offering (naivedya) has been prepared uncooked, overcooked, too cold due to the lapse of time, or stepped over by people;
In that case, other cooked offerings should be presented.
Then, for the offering of the food oblation (naivedya):

having offered water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful offering (arghya) to the deity, one should prepare a square mandala with cow dung in front of the deity and decorate it with powders made of flour and other materials.

Filled with pure rice, milk-rice, and other foods, as well as desired fruits such as plantains, coconuts, mangoes, jackfruit, grapes, and dates, and with cakes, flour-balls, sweetmeats, and other pastries;
With vegetables such as plantains and breadfruit, with preparations of elixirs like fresh *urvāruka* and the like, with various kinds of drinks, foods to be sucked,
licked, and chewed, with milk, curd, butter, and ghee, and with cardamom, *campaka* buds, camphor, musk, and *lāmañca-pāṭalā*...

The offering plates for Śiva and Śivā, as well as for Sadāśiva and Manonmanī, were adorned all around with small cups filled with quantities of water measuring one *āḍhaka* or half an *āḍhaka*, drawn from pitchers used for bathing that were scented with *alipuṣpa* flowers and other fragrances and rendered pleasantly cool.

Having placed the food-offering plates for the attendant deities and the protective deities, and having set a vessel upon the plates, he should sprinkle them with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
perform the three *tāla*-claps, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the concealment (*avakuṇṭhana*), and form the *dhenu-mudrā* and the *anna-mudrā*.

Having displayed the mountain mudrā and lifted the vessel previously placed there, having sprinkled it with water while reciting the weapon mantra (astra-mantra), and having offered āpośana to each guest while reciting the heart mantra (hṛdaya-mantra), one should first offer [the food] to Gaṇapati with the deer-mudrā accompanied by flowers; then, having discarded that flower and performed the ritual washing of the hands.
Saying "Hāṃ Haṃ, svāhā to Śiva," one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) to Śiva five times,

three times, or once; having offered the food with the deer-mudrā accompanied by flowers while making the gesture of offering the food, and having also presented water for drinking, one should discard that flower.
Having washed his hands and likewise offered the food offering (*naivedya*) to Śivā,
he should offer the food offering to all [the deities] individually, following the sequence beginning with Sadāśiva.
If separate vessels are unavailable, [he may offer] to all the attendant deities in a single vessel.

One should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) individually. Then, having presented fragrant water to Śiva and offered a flower upon his head with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should contemplate that the entire collection of ritual substances, though incomplete, is now complete.

Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having offered sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and other ingredients for the purpose of rubbing the left and right hands of the deity, one should contemplate the washing of the hands, gargling, the washing of the feet, and so forth. And all [these acts]...

Having removed the floral offerings (*nirmālya*), one should place the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva in the northeast direction and present the fragrant flowers and *nirmālya* to Caṇḍeśa, who is seated nearby.
Now, by which face does Sadāśiva consume [the offering]? He consumes it with his upward-facing mouth (*ūrdhvavaktra*).
Food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, meals, drinks, and so forth, as well as various kinds of foods to be licked and sucked—
whatever has been prescribed here should be offered with the face turned upward.

Thus, from the *Sarvajñānottara*: "O Six-faced One, the fivefold offerings— what is to be chewed, what is to be eaten, what is to be drunk, what is to be licked, and what is to be sucked— should be presented with the Heart-mantra into the upward-facing mouth."
This is also because of the statement in the *Dviśatī*:

"Alternatively, he enjoys [the offering] with all five faces—for it is observed that there is also an injunction for the offering of the *naivedya* to each of the five faces individually, as stated: 'The *naivedya* is in the five faces, or else again in the upper face.'"
The offering of the food-oblation (*naivedya*) should be made to the upward-facing [deity],
and that upward-facing [offering] must be performed while visualizing it as facing south at the time of worship; for the worshipper stands to the south of the deity, facing north.
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and in a mobile liṅga, Śiva faces the practitioner;
however, in the case of a water-pot and so forth, he faces westward, while in a fixed image, he faces toward the door.
Thus, because it is heard in the *Caraliṅgārcana* that the Lord faces the worshipper,

so too, in the worship for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*), even the heart, the secret parts, and the feet are situated in the southern direction, in order to ensure that Śiva faces the practitioner. As for those [parts] which belong to the worshipper...
Statements regarding the avoidance of standing facing Śiva:
"One should not stand in the east before Śambhu, nor in the north where there is a woman, nor in the west because [Śiva's] back is turned; therefore, one should take recourse to the south."
(286) Passages such as these refer to a fixed *liṅga* facing the east;

for in the case of worship of a mobile *liṅga*, there is the specific scriptural statement: "In the case of worship on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or a mobile *liṅga*, Śiva faces the practitioner. Furthermore, it is said: "One should worship the God whether situated in the southeast (*agni*) or the southwest (*nirṛti*)."

If it is argued that, according to the scriptural injunction, the worshipper’s stationing in the southeast (āgneyī) direction would not result in Śiva facing the worshipper, this is true; however, even that statement refers specifically to a fixed linga (sthiraliṅga). A fixed linga is common to all.

And because it bestows grace upon the worlds, its face is turned toward its own desired direction in each of the four quarters; thus, in whichever direction the door is located, the [deity] faces that direction. Therein, together with the heart, the secret place, and the feet, it faces upward and is oriented toward that door—facing the door.

Based on the statement "one should fashion [the faces] facing upwards" and the statement "whichever direction the door is in, one should designate that as the east," starting from that very point and proceeding clockwise, the faces of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva are to be fashioned.
The door that faces the *liṅga* is considered to be the east;
there, the face of Tatpuruṣa should be directed upward and facing [the *liṅga*].

Thus it is stated. Alternatively, the single upward-facing face alone faces the door together with the faces of the heart, the secret place, and the feet; however, the faces of Tatpuruṣa and the others are situated precisely in the directions starting from the east, and are not differentiated by the distinction of doors.
Let the door of the palace be as desired by means of wood;
yet the faces of the [deities] such as Tatpuruṣa do not abandon their positions in the eastern and other directions.

Because of this statement, both of these two positions regarding the faces of the Tatpuruṣa and other [deities] are approved by the Kāmika [Tantra]. For this very reason, it says there regarding the worship of the western door:
"One should visualize the body facing the door and with its face turned upward."
Having begun thus:
"One should contemplate the Puruṣa in the eastern direction or in the western;
or one should contemplate him in the south or in the north, as possessing many forms."
The Guru should visualize Vāmadeva in the north or the south;
visualizing Sadyojātamukha in the west or the east, he should perform the placement.
Thus it has been said. In that very same [text], regarding the worship at the southern door, it is also stated:
"One should properly worship Aghora or Puruṣa in the south;
or else, one should worship Aghora or Sadyojāta in the west."
One should worship Sadyojātamukha in the north, or Puruṣa or Vāmadeva in the east. Thus it is said.
Even a stationary linga must be worshipped facing north;
whether it be a linga, an image, or anything else that is fashioned, it should face whichever direction [is appropriate].
"Upon each [occasion], the sacrificer, facing north, should worship Śiva"— according to this statement, in the case of the primary worship of a liṅga facing east,
it is only logical that the worshipper, standing in the primary southeast direction, faces directly north.

However, in the case of worshipping a *liṅga* that faces east— which is secondary (*gauṇa*)— because it is situated in the west, which is also secondary— it is logical that the deity faces north, which is secondary because it is the south. And this is not on the left side of the deity.

Since the Goddess is seated in the southwestern direction (nairṛtadeśa), if the worshipper were situated there, it would follow that a woman could not be positioned to the north, resulting in the contingency of violating the prohibition against such a placement. As stated in the *Kāmika*, in the chapter on worship with a western entrance: "Manonmanī should be installed either to the left or to the right."
Like a deity, she is joined with faces, endowed with two arms and a single face.

Thus, since the placement of the Goddess on the right side has been accepted even in the worship of the Linga facing west, it is logical for the worshipper situated in the south-western direction (Nairṛti) to conceive of the Goddess as being seated on the right side of the Deity. In this way...

In the worship of a *liṅga* that faces east as a secondary orientation relative to the southern direction, one who stands in the southeast (the fire-quarter) as a secondary orientation relative to the southwest (the nairṛta-quarter) has an orientation facing north as a secondary orientation relative to the east;

and in the worship of a *liṅga* that faces east as a secondary orientation relative to the northern direction, [one stands] in the northeast (the īśāna-quarter) as a secondary orientation relative to the southeast (the agni-quarter).
For one situated in such a direction, it is also consistent that the northern face is secondary in form as the eastern face.
Thus, in the worship for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*), the rule that the deity faces the worshipper is not violated;
for in every section concerning worship for one's own sake, it is stated: "having become facing north."
This is according to the injunction beginning with "seated upon a beautiful throne" and so forth. In this regard, there is this specific detail:
those who desire the destruction of their sins should, relying on the fixed orientation of the faces toward the directions, visualize the Aghora face as being directly in front.
One should not stand before the Lord, nor behind him, nor even near a woman;
for the sake of destroying sins and attaining liberation, one who is skillful should worship while standing to the right of the skillful one.
Just as the wind carries away snow and the lotus carries away cold,
so too does the non-terrible [Aghora] mantra, though peaceful, effect the removal of sin.
Just as even a great elephant follows its driver,
so too should one perform sacrifice facing the north by means of the words of a trustworthy person.
Thus, because the Aghora face is seen to be praised for its quality of removing all sins:
"Fearing birth, people seek refuge in this very southern face of Rudra for protection, considering it alone to be unborn."

This is because the *Vāyusaṃhitā* likewise shows praise for the southern face as being the bestower of liberation; however, for those who seek liberation preceded by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), [the northern face] is [approached] according to the logic of facing the door or the logic of facing the practitioner, with respect to the *tatpuruṣa* face.
Relying on the perspective of being oriented toward the practitioner, the face of Tatpuruṣa should be meditated upon as being turned toward him.
The graciousness that belongs to Īśa is the same as the gentleness of Puruṣa.
The ferocity of the multiformed one is the cause of liberation, maintenance, and destruction.

Thus, because it is heard that the face of the Tatpuruṣa is the cause of stability, the southward orientation of the upward-facing [face] is established in every respect. And in this way, the deity’s facing toward [the worshipper], which is effected through invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, attains its natural consistency even in worship performed for one's own sake. Otherwise—

In the case of worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), since that which follows it is solely intent upon the abandonment of facing upward, some way of accounting for it might be possible. In worship for the sake of others, whose purpose is to benefit the world,
it is appropriate that specific orientation toward the worshipper is not required.
In the previous case, the orientation toward the door was somehow justified as a figurative orientation; however, here,

in the context of self-centered worship performed for the purpose of favoring the practitioner, the orientation toward the practitioner occurs directly by the force of the statement "and on the sacrificial ground."
The view of some is that it should be disregarded. Others, however, say:

in worship for one's own sake, the upward-facing face, along with the faces of the Heart, the Secret, and the Feet, as well as the Tatpuruṣa face, should indeed be oriented toward the worshipper; this is stated in the Aṃśumat-tantra and other scriptures.
In the very section on worship for one's own sake:
"One should not stand before the All-pervasive Lord, nor behind him, nor even close by; one should not be near a woman, nor in front of the Master, nor at his back."

Because such statements have been recited, and because they cannot be interpreted as referring to worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), and because the statement regarding the practitioner facing [the deity] is recited within the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*), the practitioner’s facing [the deity] is not obtained for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) from that source. Nor, in the case of initiation...

Since there is no possibility of being occupied with the worship of a mobile liṅga (caraliṅga), it must be stated that the statement regarding the [liṅga] facing the practitioner in the case of a mobile liṅga (p. 289) refers exclusively to the subject of daily worship (nityapūjā).
This is because there is no fault even in the worship of a mobile liṅga during initiation (dīkṣā). Therefore, as this is free from exception...

Because of the statement "in the east, in front," Śiva is always the presiding authority in all matters— whether obligatory, occasional, or optional— and occupies the eastern seat; Lakṣmī, whose body consists of the western and rear digits, occupies the [western] seat.
Thus, in the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Keśava: "In initiations and other rites, one should contemplate the Guru as Ghaṭeśa in the western direction—
the Lord, Tatpuruṣa, Śānta, the all-pervading, eternal, and ancient one."
Thus, regarding the face-mirror:

"One should always meditate upon Śiva, eternally facing east, with his face and chest [aligned]; at the beginning of initiation and other rites, one should meditate upon Him as the support of the water-pot, facing west. Thus it is said.

And in the case of Bṛhadbhārgava and others, by means of the terms "always" (sadā) and "eternal" (nitya), [the rule applies] to all rites— whether obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), or optional (kāmya)— excluding those for which specific initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth have been prescribed, for both Īśāna and Puruṣa.
Because of the scriptural injunction regarding the requirement of facing east,

and because these statements necessarily refer to movable liṅgas, non-liṅgas, and so forth— by setting aside the fixed liṅgas that are invariably oriented toward the door— it follows that [this applies] to worship for one's own sake.
In the rites of Śiva consisting of the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) types, facing the east is the general rule (*autsargika*).
In the case of occasional rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), specific scriptural injunctions constitute exceptions (*apavāda*) to that rule, such as facing the south and so forth.
Furthermore, they say this other thing: even between the faces of Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa...

Sadāśiva consumes [the offering] through the face of Tatpuruṣa alone; for it is stated in the Sūkṣmāgama: "The western face is the gateway, while the food offering (naivedya) belongs to the eastern face. Furthermore, because the form of Īśāna constitutes the head-face, offering food there would be contrary to worldly custom. Let this be so.
There is also the view that one may eat through the mouth of another, for there is no rule that one must eat only with one's own mouth;

this is supported by the previously cited scriptural statements of the *Āśumad-āgama*, such as "one should cause the oblation to be offered into the upward-facing [mouth] of Mahāsena," regarding food, edibles, grains, drinks, and so forth.
Since it is understood from the statements of the *Catuḥśatī*, the *Kālottara*, and other scriptures that one may eat with the face turned upwards,
there should be an offering of sacrificial food (*havis*) from that [offering] into the five faces, according to the statement: "The food offering is for the five faces."
To Īśāna, however, pure rice; then to Puruṣa, rice with jaggery.
One who is composed should offer *kṛsara* into the southern face and likewise *mudgānna* into the northern;
and into the western [face], *pāyasa*, each by its own name.

"One should cause [the offerings] to be given in one's own respective direction; they should be in front of Īśāna," and so forth—since from this collection of statements explaining the various types of food offerings (*naivedya*) for each of the five faces, eating is understood to be performed by the five faces. For the authority of the scriptures (*āgama*) is indeed not undifferentiated.
It is logical that a particular meaning should be practiced by one person and not by another;
therefore, it is indeed appropriate that there be an option even among the three positions established by the statements of those respective scriptures.

Now, when one who worships offers the food offering (*naivedya*) to Śiva using the *naivedyadāna-mudrā*, should it be placed into the hand of Śiva, or rather directly into His various mouths? Here too, there is indeed an option.
As stated later:
Having rendered it immortal with *gostanī* [milk], one should offer a flower;
one should place the food offering in the right hand and give excellent water for drinking.
Thus, because it is heard that the food offering (naivedya) is to be presented with the right hand:
"Whatever has been prescribed here should be given into the upward-facing [mouth];
O Mahāsena, one should cause the oblation (āhuti) to be offered into the upward-facing [mouth]."

This is because it is heard [in scripture] that [the offering] is to be presented in the mouth (*vaktra*). Thus, in this case, the option is determined according to suitability: whatever is to be offered in the human mouth—which is equal in measure to the heart and so forth—namely all foodstuffs such as *bhakṣya* and *bhojya*, with the exception of liquid substances, having abandoned [all else], [one should place them] in the left hand with the *abhaya-mudrā*.
It should be offered. Whatever is to be presented at the other mouths, and whatever collection of substances such as water and so forth—

all of that, like the oblation of the *agnihotra*, one should imagine as emerging from the vessels in the form of a subtle essence and arriving together with the *naivedya* mudrā up to each respective mouth.

It must be offered directly into that very mouth. Thus, since offering into the hand is possible, the wiping of the hands is not in vain; for the worshipper’s hand does not perform the act of casting the food offering (*naivedya*) into the respective mouths. Therefore, the worshipper’s hand [is not rendered useless].
There would be the consequence of [the offering] becoming like discarded floral remains.
Thus ends the procedure for the food offering (*naivedya*).
Now follows the offering of mouth-freshening betel (*mukhavāsa-tāmbūla*):
Next, one should offer the mouth-freshener, betel, and so forth, into the mouth immediately after the meal.
That which is given for the purpose of fragrance is called *mukhavāsa* (mouth-perfume) based on the etymological derivation "that which perfumes the mouth.
It is described as a powder made from cardamom, cloves, *takola*, nutmeg, and camphor, ground with cold water and formed into pills.

The powder of cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, jātiphala, and camphor, combined with a small amount of honey and sugar—or even just these five alone—is known as the "Five Aromatics" (*pañcasaugandhika*) and is considered superior. The powder of camphor, *jātī*, cloves, and nutmeg alone is middling. (That which consists solely of cloves is [inferior]).

Having gathered all of this— namely, two types of soft pieces cut from the *prastha* offering, four, six, or two leaves relative to the size of the betel nuts, which are four, three, or twice as many [as the nuts], white, with their bases and tips trimmed, and stone powder— [one should proceed].
One should offer betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) prepared with camphor and other ingredients, well-ripened and refined, together with *ātulaṅga* and coconut fruits. Then,
having offered the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*) with the root mantra, [one should present] a lamp provided with one, three, five, seven, or nine wicks.

Having displayed lamps, and having displayed lamps placed within vessels shaped like the three-fold and five-fold *tāla* measures, as well as the *nāga*, *cakra*, *padma*, human, deer, elephant, and the forms of Indra and other gods, according to one's means, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony.
The ritual procedure for the *ārātrika* lamp, its method:
[it should be] made from any one of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths.

It is adorned with a pericarp (karṇikā) made of a fillet (paṭṭikā) measuring half of that [width], or half of that again, or thirty times [the thickness of] the stalk, or with a height equal to one-fifth of its own width, and a length and height of two barley-corns; outside of that, it is joined with eight petals and surrounded by a lip (oṣṭha) of the same measurement as the pericarp.

In a vessel of circular shape, having prepared thousands of lamp-stands made of rice-flour (śālipiṣṭha) around the pericarp (karṇikā) and in its center, and having placed wicks made of camphor and other substances upon them,
one should arrange either nine, five, or even a single lamp in the very middle.

Having placed [the vessel] on a tripod and consecrated it through visualization and other rites: if there are nine [sections], one should place the Sun in the center, Guru, Śukra, Budha, and Candra in the cardinal directions, and Bhauma, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu in the intermediate directions; if there are five, one should place Vahni (Fire) in the center, and Ākāśa, Vāyu, Jala, and Pṛthivī in the cardinal directions; if there is one, [one should place] Vahni.
And one should worship [it].

Alternatively, one should worship the powers beginning with Vāmā, the five Brahmans, and Śiva within nine, five, or one lamps. Having thus worshipped with perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra-mantra*,
one should display the *surabhi-mudrā*, extract [the substance] with the two *prāṇi*-fingers, and place it upon the head of the deity.

Having circled [the vessel] three times around the heart and the feet with [offerings] made of gold or other materials, shaped either circularly or quadrangularly, and provided with bases adorned with bud-like tips;

(292) There should also be lustrations performed with vessels containing lamps lit by wicks made of camphor and other substances placed upon lamp-stands, which stands are provided with various lamps made from flour of *sahaja* rice; these lustrations are likewise consecrated by the rites of inspection and so forth.
Having whirled it like an *ārātrika* lamp and placed it upon the ground, one should extinguish it with the *astra-mantra*.

There are three types of *nīrājana* vessels: the best is one with a width of one *prādeśa*, a thickness of two barleycorns (*yava*), and a stem eight finger-breadths long, with a bud-shaped top corresponding to that [stem]. Of that...

In the center, there is one lamp-seat; in the five enclosures, there are respectively nine, fifteen, twenty-one, twenty-seven, and thirty-three lamps, totaling one hundred and six lamps. Alternatively, there are eight, fourteen, and twenty [lamps] respectively in the enclosures.
There are twenty-six and thirty-two lamp-seats, making one hundred and one lamps in total.

A vessel measuring half the size of the supreme vessel is considered medium. In its center there is one [lamp-seat], and in the four enclosures there are eight, thirteen, eighteen, and twenty-three lamp-seats respectively.

There are sixty-three lamps. The smallest is half the measure of the middle one. In the center of this [mandala] is one lamp, and in the three enclosures are six, ten, and fourteen lamp-seats respectively; thus, there are thirty-one lamps.
Then, having offered the mirror, umbrella, chowrie-fans, and palm-leaf fans in sequence with the mantras beginning with Īśāna,
for the sake of removing the defects of speech, mind, and body acquired on that particular day, and for the attainment of union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
[Offer] a handful of flowers together with *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and bilva leaves, [reciting]: "Hāṃ Hauṃ!
Salutation to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva; Hāṃ Hauṃ! Salutation to Śiva, the Lord of the Vidyā-tattva; Hāṃ Hauṃ! Salutation to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātman-tattva. Thus.

One should offer [the oblation] three times; if one desires liberation, then in the sequence beginning with the *ātmatattva*. Alternatively, one may offer it only once, saying: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of all *tattvas*. Then, [one visualizes the deity] satisfied by the worship, facing toward oneself, and being served by all the limbs of enjoyment while his hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture.

Having meditated upon Śiva— the ocean of the nectar of boundless compassion, who is praised by Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, Candra, Sūrya, and others standing outside the door of the sacrificial hall, and who grants all desired objects to his devotees— one should perform the recitation of the venerable five-syllabled mantra (Pañcākṣara) according to one's capacity for the sake of ensuring the perfection of the worship.
One should perform [it].
Now, the procedure for the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra—
the method of reciting the venerable *pañcākṣara*— is set forth.
It should be kept secret with great effort according to the path instructed by the Guru.
On the southern petal of the lotus-throne of Śiva, on the right side of the form of Aghora:
[one should meditate on her] who resembles molten gold, with full and elevated breasts,
four arms, three eyes, and a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Holding a lotus and a water-lily, gentle, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
endowed with all the auspicious marks, and adorned with all ornaments.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, with dark, curly hair,
she is the glorious Pañcākṣarī Vidyā, [to be worshipped] with rites such as the offering of a seat and invocation.
Seated on a comfortable seat, with his senses guarded, facing north, he should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
The knower of reality, fixing his gaze upon the tip of the nose, should perform self-protection,
[visualizing] all the quarters of space drenched by a mass of flowing nectar.
One should visualize above and below a pair of moon-discs forming a casket,
situated within which is the central image, completely drenched by streams of nectar.
One should contemplate one's own body as consisting of nectar through showers of nectar from the Śaktis;
this becomes self-protection that cannot be pierced even by the gods.
Having thus performed the protection of oneself, one should then practice the protection of the mantra:
one should expel the air from the abdomen through the right channel (nāḍī) with the Astra-mantra.
One should fill the interior with external air through the *iḍā* channel by means of the breath of Śambhu;
having drawn the *apāna* upward and having restrained both *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
With the mind in the form of a jar, one should join the vital air within the *suṣumnā*,
which is situated in the middle of the *suṣumnā* at the region of the heart, united with Śiva.
The practitioner of mantra should apply the mantra to the power of consciousness, the Mother of Mantras;
he should contemplate the letters of the mantra as the deity of the mantra, radiant like a jewel.
The wise practitioner, through the practice of going and returning, should recite the mantra while remembering it;
with his mind absorbed therein, he should recite the mantra while contemplating the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
This Saṃhitā, protected by the gods, shall be a guardian of the mantra;
having understood this, one should diligently perform the ritual actions.
Now, the sequence of the practice of recitation (japa) is clearly explained:
[one should contemplate] the form of the Moon, Sun, and Fire extending from the navel to the dvādaśānta.
Having awakened that supreme power, whose form is bliss and which resides within the *suṣumnā*,
by means of the vital breath (*anila*), starting from the *ādhāra-cakra*;
One should [visualize] Brahmā, Keśava, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva in their respective locations: the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having repeatedly abandoned the portions of the weapon-mantras which resemble streaks of lightning, the wise one,
having uttered the mantra ending in *nāda*, [places it] again in the *mūlādhāra*.
One should likewise recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times through the practice of going and returning,
or twenty-eight times, or eight times, or as instructed by the Guru.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) in this manner, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) shall attain union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*). Recitation should be performed either internally, by means of the garland of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, or externally, by means of a rosary made of rudrākṣa beads and the like. Among these, the method of internal recitation is now described.

At the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should meditate upon a white eight-petaled lotus situated atop a square yantra. In its pericarp is the void (vyoma), which is the seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of the collection of the first letter, the fourteen vowels, and the visarga. On the filaments are the eight [vowels].
The pairs of vowels and so forth; on the petals are the five groups of five letters beginning with *ka*;

in the directions of the square diagram is the seed-syllable of nectar (*sudhābīja*), and in the intermediate directions is the seventh letter. A *mātṛkā*-lotus of this form removes specific diseases and death through mere meditation. Then—
Having entered the aperture of the *suṣumnā* together with the power of *kuṇḍalinī*— whose root-flame is fanned by the wind arising from the contraction of the gates—
and having reached as far as the *brahmarandhra*, [one perceives] that which flows forth from that *mātṛkā*-lotus, touched by the rising *iḍā*.

One should contemplate the stream of nectar-drops in the form of a row of letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, which remains pervading from the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) down to the root-support (*mūlādhāra*).
This is the power Kuṇḍalinī, who, through her state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the flame of the fire at the root-support, [remains there].
One should contemplate that very Mātṛkā-śakti, which has ascended as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the radiant Suṣumṇā path;

having become nectar-like through its state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya) with the continuous flow of trickling drops of nectar issuing from the lotus of Mātṛkā, she is of the nature of supreme bliss. As they say:
Manifest at the first departure,
yet becoming like nectar upon the return,
moving along within the path—
"Let us behold the Seal of Bliss. Thus [it is said].

In that regard, within the Śakti whose form is the Mātṛkā, which is situated at the *brahmarandhra* and extends down to the *mūlādhāra* by pervading [the body] in the sequence beginning with the letter *a* from the *mātṛkā*-lotus onwards,
there is one [syllable] formed by the eight letters beginning with *a*.

There is one group [of letters] beginning with *ka*; another group consisting of eight [letters] beginning with *ḷ*; and seven groups consisting of five letters each beginning with *ka*. These nine groups correspond, in order, to the forms of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu.

One should meditate upon [the nine gems] in the forms of ruby, lapis lazuli, topaz, diamond, coral, sapphire, pearl, hessonite, and emerald. This very [meditation] consists of the nine gems representing the nine planets, extending from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the root-support (*mūlādhāra*).
A rosary composed of all suitable letters is an internal rosary;
a rosary fashioned from beads of ruby, pearl, lapis lazuli, topaz, diamond, coral, powerful gems, emeralds, and gomedaka stones is praiseworthy.
One should contemplate this rosary, filled with all the letters consisting of the nine planets,

as being either the form of the light of the Supreme Lord situated within the lotus of the heart like a lamp, or as consisting of sound emitted from the power called Parā; and in front of it, one should [contemplate] the Mālā-mantra.

Having visualized the letter *kṣa* as if emerging from a flower at the tip of a wish-fulfilling creeper made of the nine gems, one should take Mount Meru as the basis and visualize the movement of the root mantra back and forth upon the rosary according to the sequence beginning with the letter *la*. During that visualization of the mantra’s ascent upon it, [one should focus] on the head of the mantra.

Having placed the letters beginning with *la* together with the *visarjanīya*, and having performed the visualization of descent (*avarohaṇa*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) after placing the letters beginning with *a* and ending with the *bindu* at the beginning of the mantra. When this is done, there are one hundred repetitions of the mantra. Following that—

Having sequentially deposited the mantra within the eight groups consisting of the sixteen vowels, the five groups of *sparśa* consonants, the group ending with the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), the group of sibilants (*ūṣman*), and the group of nasals (*varga*), one should repeat the mantra eight times.
In this way, the recitation (*japa*) reaches the count of one hundred and eight. Furthermore, at the time of beginning the recitation:

With the root mantra, one should visualize his supreme deity as being in a state of flavor-union (*samarasībhūta*) with the jewel, like its radiance; and together with the root mantra, one should visualize his syllables, beginning with the letter *na*, in yellow, black, smoke-colored, yellow, and red hues, having become that deity's very form through flavor-union with it.
Having visualized Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva,

one should gradually abandon Brahmā and the others— along with the letters beginning with *na*— in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) respectively. This entire meaning has already been set forth in the verses written previously.
It has been indicated in brief. Thus, for one who is unable to perform the recitation (*japa*) with the internal rosary of the senses,

at the time of beginning the recitation according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should visualize the mantra as mounted upon the power of the *mātṛkā*, and then visualize the letters of the *mātṛkā* encapsulated by the mantra— or indeed, [the mantra] alone.
One should recite the mantra while counting it with an external rosary made of rudrākṣa beads or similar materials.
Its varieties are as follows:

according to the sequence of superior and so forth, they have the size of an *āmalaka*, a jujube (*badara*), or a chickpea (*caṇaka*); they may have one face, three faces, or four, five, six, seven, eight, ten, or eleven faces.

By joining faces to one another on a thread made of gold, silver, or similar materials, or made of silk cloth and the like— measuring one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-seven units, and consisting of faces of various numbers mixed with those of a single number.
And having joined them back-to-back and sewn them together with *rudrākṣa* beads that match the colors [of the respective faces], one should fashion [the rosary] from those joined with Mount Meru,
sequentially reciting the *sadyojāta* and other mantras one hundred times for each.

At the time of beginning the recitation, one should worship the *erukā*— which has undergone the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) consisting of washing, rubbing, smearing with unguents, consecration with mantras, and adorning with form— having consecrated it either with the Īśāna-mantra or the Aghora-mantra, and having worshipped it according to the sequence of Śiva-pūjā through the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth.
For the vocal recitation (*vācikajapa*), one should take into the right hand a rosary that has been sprinkled with water using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
worshipped with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth, accompanied by the display of the garland-mudrā,
and covered with a cloth.

One should count by placing [the beads] on the middle finger using the index finger and thumb for whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa), on the ring finger using the middle finger and thumb for low-voiced recitation (mānasa-japa),
and on the little finger using the ring finger and thumb for mental recitation (mānasa-japa).
One who desires worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should move the rosary downward; one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) should move it upward.
If the fault of crossing the Meru occurs, the expiation is the recitation of the Aghora mantra one thousand times. To avoid being touched by that fault, a rosary lacking a Meru bead should be used.
Thus regarding the two ends of the rosary.

If [the flower] falls on the ground, there should be a thousand recitations (*japa*) of the *aghora* mantra; if it falls on her [the deity’s] body, three hundred recitations; if it falls on the garment, one hundred recitations of that same mantra. At the time of beginning the recitation, one should place a single flower between the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger of the right hand, and then perform the recitation. One may also perform the recitation using a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads.

For ease of grasping it, one should place the flower held in the right hand into the left hand and then perform the recitation. Having completed the recitation—neither too fast nor too slow, and with full concentration—one should place the Astra, Kavaca, and Hṛdaya mantras one above the other upon the palm of the left hand; thereafter, during the time of recitation...

Having placed the held flower, having encapsulated it with the heart, armor, and weapon mantras, having protected it with the weapon mantra and veiled it with the armor mantra, having taken it again in the right hand and placed it at the region of the heart, one should meditate upon the recitation as being centered therein, resembling the full moon.

Placing the right knee upon the ground, one should say: "Hāṃ! O protector of the secret, more secret than the secret, accept this recitation performed by us. O Lord, may success be mine through your grace, for you abide within me.
Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, svāhā! O venerable Paramaśiva, [I offer] this recitation unto you."

Thinking, "I offer," one should present the recitation to the hand of Śiva, which is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada-hasta*), using a handful of water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) containing unbroken rice grains, *kuśa* grass, and flowers. This is done out of fear that the recitation performed by the seeker of enjoyment and liberation might be destroyed by the proclamation of its wonders or by contact with water used for the destruction of karma.
For the sake of its protection, it is placed in the hand of Śiva. This is the meaning of the mantra-verse:

You alone are the protector of the secrets of the most secret [teachings], such as the reality of the mantras. Therefore, because you are the protector of all, accept even our recitation (*japa*). By which, while you remain present during this recitation—

"By your grace, the attainment of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) will surely come to us. Therefore, out of compassion for me, please accept that. Then [he says]: *Hāṃ*—O God, whatever action there may be, whether well-done or ill-done.
O Śaṅkara, eat that and destroy it for me, who am established in the state of Śiva.

p. 297) *Hāṃ Hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva; I offer my good and evil deeds to Paramaśiva.* Thus, one should offer all one’s own actions consisting of good and evil deeds with water from the hollowed palms (*culakodaka*) according to the previously mentioned sequence. Among those, regarding that which has arisen from good deeds for the sake of enjoyment...

This is an announcement for the purpose of avoiding obstacles to liberation and for the sake of its preservation; it is for the purpose of exhausting the collection of misdeeds. Therefore, the construction is as follows: "Enjoy [the fruits of] good deeds, protect them; exhaust [and destroy] evil deeds. However, for one who is free from desire for enjoyment and seeks only liberation—

The request for protection is: "Enjoy only that which is well-performed [merit] for the sake of avoiding obstacles to liberation. However, regarding merit performed for the sake of enjoyment, it is incidental as a byproduct of the worship of Śiva.

For one who seeks liberation alone— whose mind is disgusted with sense objects that bring about enjoyments ranging from human bliss up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha, and who, according to the manner stated in the Purāṇas, "O dear one, these are indeed hells compared to the state of the Supreme Self"— [the aforementioned acts] constitute a form of evil deed (duṣkṛta) that leads to hell.

This is merely a request for protection. Although, according to the rule that the root *bhuj* takes the *parasmaipada* when meaning "to protect," the form should have been *bhuṅkṣi*, nevertheless, in this verse which has the nature of a mantra—
just like the usage of *rakṣasva* in Vedic mantras— this is an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) permitted by the rule "there is much variation in the Vedic language" (*chāndaso 'yaṃ vyatyayo bahulam*).
Therefore, the middle-voice (ātmanepada) ending is used. Alternatively, "enjoy" (*bhuṅkṣva*) refers specifically to experience (*bhoga*), and not to protection (*pālana*).

By the word "well-performed deeds" (*sukṛta*), only that merit of the worshiper seeking mere liberation which is intended for the sake of enjoyment—and not that which is required for liberation—is meant. That is its enjoyment.

For King Śiva, there is the enjoyment of sovereignty and independent administration, but not eating himself. And this independent administration consists of the installation [of the deity] among the beloved kinsmen or friends of the worshipper; for one desiring liberation, such merit is not required.
It is well known from the Śruti that Śiva bestows [the fruits of merit] upon his kinsmen and friends;
although there is also a scriptural tradition that he bestows one's evil deeds upon one's enemies, nevertheless,
the worshiper of Śiva, regarding all as the form of the eightfold Śiva, does not [view them as distinct].

Thinking "he hates me," it is appropriate for him to pray only for the destruction of his own evil deed—that is, its failure to produce a fruit within himself; thus, that prayer is incorporated into the mantra. Thereafter:
"Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is this entire world."
Śiva is victorious everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one.

"Hāṃ Hauṃ! Svāhā to Śiva! I offer myself as the Supreme Śiva unto you"—thus one should offer with water from the hollowed palms (*culaka*) according to the method previously described. In this verse of the mantra, by the portion "so 'ham" (I am He), the relationship of body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) between oneself and Śiva is established.
Because Śiva is the body by virtue of being the controller (niyāmaka), and because the worshiper is the body by virtue of being the controlled (niyamya);
the knower of dharma [realizes] the relationship of body and embodied through the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of "I am He" (so'ham), just as one might say "I am handsome."

It is like the word *rājā* (king). The particle *eva* serves to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). As for the one who is "Śiva"—the word *śiva*, which denotes the supreme auspiciousness—by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), he is untouched even by the threefold impurity (*mala*) consisting of the *āṇava*, *māyika*, and *kārma* types.
Because it is by its very nature free from the prior non-existence of the attachment to beginningless impurity,
it is called "Śiva" by the wise who know the true meaning of the Śiva-principle.
The meaning is that [this] is well-known in such passages as these.
Alternatively, by the derivation from the root *śī* with the addition of the *uṇādi* suffix *van*, and through the irregularity (*nipātana*) of shortening [the vowel],
it is etymologically explained as "that in which the collection of auspicious qualities exists in a state of equilibrium" (*sāmarasya*).

Thus, [it refers to] the mutual non-opposition of specific qualities such as magnanimity (*audārya*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), knowledge (*jñatva*), unsurpassability (*niratiśayatva*), and forbearance (*sahiṣṇutva*).
"He is a mine of all the jewels of auspicious qualities necessary for being worthy of refuge.
Whatever is inauspicious does not exist in him at any time;
rather, every single auspicious quality exists in him, because he is Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that [the word] is well-known in such instances as these. Alternatively:
"The word *siṃha* is derived from the root *hiṃs* (to injure); *śiva* is traditionally remembered [as derived] from *vaś* (to desire);
[the word *kaśyapa*] is established through the transposition of phonemes, just like *paśyaka*."

Or [the name Śiva is derived] by means of this indeclinable; or through the etymological derivation "one who desires auspiciousness," meaning "one who aspires for the welfare of all beings. Because he constantly promotes the commencement of all undertakings, desiring the well-being of human beings, he is therefore remembered as the God Śiva.

The meaning is that [the word] is well-known in such contexts as these. Alternatively, from the word *śiva*, which denotes "auspiciousness," by applying the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "one who performs that" (*tat karoti*), then the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class), and finally the elision of *ṇi* according to the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, one arrives at the etymological derivation: "one who makes everything auspicious.
Thus, he is the benefactor of all living beings.
All the Dānavas and the immortals are equal to me;
I am Śiva to all beings, and for that reason, O gods, I possess the nature of Śiva.

The meaning is that [the word] is well-known in such passages as these. Alternatively, from the verbal root *śyaiñ* (to go), by means of the *auṇādika* suffix *van* and the elision of the letters *a* and *ya*, through the etymological derivation "that which is approached (*śyāyate*) or attained," it means that which is to be worshipped by those seeking enjoyment and liberation.
At whose gate there are rutting elephants and horses with the speed of the wind, and women with faces like the full moon— this is the fruit of the performance of Śiva’s worship.
Having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone, the bringer of auspiciousness, the supreme Lord of Gods, is to be meditated upon; thus concludes the Atharvaṇa Śruti.
The meaning is that [the name] is well-known in such passages as these. Alternatively:
"That two-syllabled name of a mountain, when uttered even once by men through incidental contact, swiftly destroys their sin."
Alas, you, being other than auspicious, hate that Śiva, whose fame is pure and whose command is inviolable!

The meaning is that which is well-known as the denotation (*vācya*) of the word *Śiva*, who is taught [in passages] such as these to be the remover of all evils. "Śiva is victorious everywhere" means that in all worlds, Śiva alone prevails, abiding as the one qualified for dharma. He alone consists of all living beings who are subject to karma.
The meaning is "the controller. Śiva is this entire universe;
the meaning is that he is the controller of the whole world consisting of all insentient and sentient beings, as well as the elements and their derivatives.
He is the enjoyer and the protector of those who have sought refuge. He is the giver to those who have sought refuge in the event of calamity.

When obstacles such as sins (pātaka) arise, He is the purifier thereof. These qualifiers are applicable to Śiva in relation to the surrender of one’s self and its constituent parts. For instance, this applies to both the worshipper who is subject to discipline and to Śiva, who is the discipliner.

The offering of oneself (*ātmanivedana*) consists precisely in the contemplation, "I am yours," by you, the worshiper, directed toward Śiva, who exists in the relationship of body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*), characterized by the nature of the controller, the controlled, and the instrument of control. Thus,

in the phrase "I am indeed He" (*so 'ham eva*), the term "He" (*tat-pada*) refers to Śiva, while the term "I" (*ahaṃ-pada*) expresses the state of having Him as one's own body, and the particle "indeed" (*eva*) [emphasizes this].
By means of that [particle] which excludes non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), its necessary concomitance (*niyatatva*)—
which consists in being the object of recollection— is stated as the ground for its justification.
They say that this self-surrender has five constituent parts:
the resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition,
the conviction that [the Lord] will protect, and likewise the choice of Him as protector.
Regarding the term "kārpaṇya" (helplessness): in that context,

the entire multitude of living beings constitutes the means for accomplishing the two constituent parts of worship toward Śiva— the refuge— who consists of acting in accordance with all beings and avoiding what is contrary to them.

This has been designated as "the body. Therefore, it is understood that every living being who worships Śiva should behave with favorability toward the king's body, like a servant, and avoid any hostility toward it. For this very reason, it is stated regarding Śiva in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
In the section defining the eight forms:
"The Self is the eighth form of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
because it pervades all other forms, the universe is therefore of the nature of Śiva."
They know that performing every act of assistance, likewise bestowing favor upon all,
and granting fearlessness to all, constitutes the worship of Śiva.
"If restraint is imposed upon any embodied being whatsoever, that is undoubtedly an offense committed against the Eightfold Formed One (Aṣṭamūrti). Thus it is said.
Regarding the assurance that "He will protect," it has been established by all the qualifying attributes as well.

First, the statement "I alone" expresses the state of being His very body (*svaśarīrakatva*), which serves to justify the confidence in His protection; for who indeed would not protect their own body?

The term "Śiva" denotes: freedom from the impurities that cause attachment, aversion, and other such factors which oppose the confidence expressed in liberation; the possession of all auspicious qualities necessary for being worthy of refuge;
the state of desiring the welfare of all beings; and the state of acting for the welfare of all beings.

The fact that He is denoted by the word "Śiva," which removes all evils contrary to one's welfare—all of this also serves as a proof for that [nature]. The two qualifiers stated in the verse, "Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; Śiva is this entire world," consist in His being the controller of the entire phenomenal universe, comprising both the sentient and the insentient.

The state of being the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratva*) is also a means of establishing that [divinity]. For it is possible to have confidence that the Lord of All is capable of granting the desires of His devotees;
this is because the root *bhuji* (to enjoy/protect) and the root *dai-p* (to purify) carry the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

It is quite clear that the two attributes expressed by the terms "the enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*) and "the giver" (*dātṛ*) serve as the basis for his nature of protecting devotees and his nature of removing all the misfortunes of those devotees, such as great sins committed through negligence. Even in the prayer for protection (*goptṛtva-varaṇa*), it is precisely the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) that serves as the supporting reason.
How could He, whose very nature is that of a protector, not protect when entreated as "be a protector"?
(By the word *tu*) [it is meant] that which establishes His lack of dependence on other deities— a state of non-supplication—
and the absence of the relationship of the governed and the governor between Himself and other deities.
The distinction is that this has been stated by the word "tu" (but).
Thus, after performing the recitation and self-surrender with three handfuls of water,
one should also recite the mantras of the five Brahmans and the six limbs in conjunction with a tenth part of the root mantra;
then, having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold flower offering and three handfuls of flowers, [one stands] before Him.

Standing with palms joined in *añjali*, one should also offer a hymn of praise (*stotra*), either through the hymns of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-stotra*) or through other hymns composed by former masters that are seen in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, *Āgamas*, and so forth. (p. 301)
One should offer praise according to what is appropriate; the authors of the Purāṇas say that a hymn composed by oneself is equal to the revealed scripture (śruti).
The procedure for circumambulation:
having thus offered praise and presented a handful of flowers, one should prostrate with the eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga),
perform three circumambulations, and prostrate five times again.
One should perform circumambulation. For the sake of ensuring the success of the worship, circumambulation is essential.
One should move from footstep to footstep with hands free from movement;
praise with speech and meditation in the heart—this is the four-limbed circumambulation.
Just as a woman near childbirth, carrying a jar filled with oil,
proceeds slowly, so should one perform the circumambulation.

That circumambulation is threefold: clockwise (savya), counter-clockwise (apasavya), and both clockwise and counter-clockwise (savyāpasavya). That which is performed by keeping the deity to one's right is clockwise; the opposite is counter-clockwise; and the combination of both is clockwise-and-counter-clockwise. This applies to all three types.

It should be performed starting from the direction of Indra and ending with the direction of Indra; or it may be performed moving clockwise (savya) and counter-clockwise (apasavya), beginning from the location of the *somasūtra* and ending at the location of the *somasūtra*.

In this regard, the clockwise path is for celibate students (*brahmacārins*), the counter-clockwise path is for ascetics (*yatis*), and both clockwise and counter-clockwise paths are for householders and forest-dwellers (*gṛhins* and *vānaprasthas*).
One view is that the left [hand] is common [to all], while the right is for ascetics alone, and both left and right are for those who have been initiated; this is another view.

The procedure for prostration consists of four types: the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*), the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*), the three-limbed (*tryaṅga*), and the single-limbed (*ekāṅga*).
