The eight-limbed prostration is of two kinds: the full-length prostration (*daṇḍapraṇāma*) and the simple prostration (*kevalapraṇāma*).

A prostration like a staff (*daṇḍapraṇāma*) is performed with the two feet, the two hands, the chest, the head, and the speech. An alternative view holds that a prostration like a staff is performed with the two feet, the two arm-pits, the chest, the head, the speech, the mind, the intellect, and the vision. In this regard:

By the word *manas* (mind), the state of single-minded concentration is expressed; by the word *dhī* (intellect), the hymn consisting of the contemplation of Śiva’s majesty is discerned—this is the distinction.
Furthermore, [the worship] is performed with both knees, both hands, the chest, the head, the mind, the speech, and the gaze. (p. 302)

Another alternative: it is performed with the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, the chest, the head, the mind, and the gaze—this too is another alternative. It is performed with the two feet, the two arms, the chest, the head, the speech, and the gaze—this is yet another position. [With the head...]

A prostration performed by touching the ground with both hands, both ears, the chin, and both arms is the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) salutation. A prostration performed by touching the ground with the head, both hands, and both knees is the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) salutation. [The components are] the head and the two hands...

Another alternative is that it is called "five-limbed" (*pañcāṅga*) when performed by placing both knees upon the ground. Joining the palms in *añjali* with both hands at the head is the "three-limbed salutation" (*tryaṅga-namaskāra*).
A mere bowing of the head alone is the "one-limbed salutation" (*ekāṅga-namaskāra*). These are the prostrations.
They should be employed as appropriate, taking into account the place, time, strength, and other such factors.
The procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is as follows:
having gratified the Supreme Lord with hymns of praise, circumambulations, and prostrations,
and having requested permission by saying, "O Master, I shall perform the fire-ritual," one should receive the command from Śiva.

Having performed the general *arghya* offering and gone to the fire-sanctuary (*agnyagāra*), one kindles the fire— produced from the fire-drill (*araṇi*) or a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), or brought from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)— upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit, made of either clay or sand, which has been purified by the four rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).

Having performed the sprinkling and striking with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having sprinkled [it] again with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should [unify] the consciousness of the fire by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the *pūraka* breath, reciting: *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*.
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus,

it is distinguished by names such as Ananta, Avyaya, and Eka-prabhu; it extends to the edge of the ocean, bestows unsurpassed bliss upon the phenomenal world, and resembles the great radiance within the calyx of a non-material lotus.
Having known the heart to be downward-facing, situated above the navel, extending to the root-aperture (mūla-randhra) along with the suṣumnā channel, pervading the entire body,
the great abode of the whole universe, continuous, and surrounded by seventy-two thousand channels, [one knows] the iḍā.

Having known that the heart— surrounded by the channels (nāḍīs) called Suṣumnā and Piṅgalā which have become one in essence, resembling the calyx of a great lotus, and hanging right there— to be exceedingly subtle in the middle region of the shoreless ocean;

Having visualized the delightful, hollow space— which serves as the cause for the diversion of all worldly existence and is the foundational support for the entire universe— in its center, one should contemplate the fire Vaiśvānara, which is matted with great flames, possessing rays of every color, and facing in all directions.
There, [the practitioner perceives] the Supreme Lord, who exists as the presiding deity over all things such as the various *rasas*, who is undecaying, the ancient poet, immortal,
and of the nature of the *liṅga*, heating the practitioner from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
Having meditated upon Vaiśvānara— the Supreme Lord renowned as the presiding deity— blazing in the midst of the flame of fire and smaller than the awn of wild rice, right in the center of that flame,
as that very Full Supreme Self;
Through the grace of the Guru’s glance, the *prāṇaliṅga*— which has become an object of direct perception by virtue of the firmness of *sāmarasya* (perfect identity)—

is established as the denotation of the jewel of mantras in the form of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), and serves as the cause of all the principles (*tattvas*) such as the vowels *A*, *U*, *M*, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and so forth.
The form of Īśvara as the collective whole (samaṣṭi), the form of Sadāśiva as both the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective,
and the nature of the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga) consisting of the state of equilibrium between the relationship of both the individual and the collective—
[all these] are distinguished by infinite auspicious qualities such as omniscience and universal sovereignty.
To the Lord of Pārvatī, who is supremely compassionate and solely initiated in the grace of his devotees;
whose lotus feet are worshipped by the entire host of gods, including Brahmā, Upendra, and Mahendra;
and who is Paraśiva, abiding within the non-material world known as Somaloka, which transcends all worlds beginning with Unmanā.
Having meditated upon Śrī Sāmbaśiva, whose manifestation is established within the heart,

one should unite him with the fire situated there by means of the previously mentioned sequence of exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), reciting "Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala. Then, accompanied by that fire, one should lead him through the path of the Suṣumṇā to the Dvādaśānta.

Having united [the fire] with Paramaśiva and expelled it through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] by means of exhalation (*recaka*), one should cast it into the blazing fire with the *udbhava-mudrā*, reciting: "Hāṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire (*vahnicaitanya*). Thereafter, one should worship the fire with the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, ending with "obeisance" (*namaḥ*).

Having rendered [the offering] nectarine by means of the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the *dhenumudrā*, having concealed it with the *kavaca* mantra, protected it with the *astra* mantra, and worshipped it with the *hṛdaya* mantra; having contemplated it as the virility of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-vīrya*),
one should meditate upon Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī, who have entered into a state of non-dual union and are situated in the directions of Īśa (the northeast).

One should visualize that seed-syllable being cast by Vāgīśvara from the aperture within the womb of Vāgīśvarī toward the inner self (adhyātman). Then, having offered five oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should assign it the name:
"Hāṃ, you are the Śiva-fire, the consumer of oblations."

Having visualized the fire as consecrated by the five purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, and having worshipped and dismissed the two parents with the heart-mantra, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and its girdle (*mekhalā*) with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*; then, in the directions of the girdle, [one should place] blades pointing toward the northeast.

Having spread ten darbha blades each as armor in the east, west, south, and north directions of the girdle, and having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Ananta, he should inform them: "Protect the sacrificial fire."
He is endowed with five faces, red in color, and adorned with seven tongues;
he has ten arms, three eyes, and is decorated with all ornaments.
"Clad in red garments, seated upon a lotus, sitting in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), and endowed with ten weapons. Thus [it is said].

Having meditated upon the Śivāgni, one should meditate on the three tongues—Kanaka, Bahurūpā, and Atiriktā—in its upper face; and on the four tongues—Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, and Hiraṇmayī—in the faces starting from the east. Then, having worshipped with "Hāṃ Agnaye Namaḥ," [one recites] "Hāṃ Hrūṃ."
Having offered five oblations of sesame seeds with the mantra "To Agni, Svāhā," [he says]:
"O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, for you are the supreme purifier;
therefore, having established you within the lotus of my heart, I satisfy you."

Having thus informed the fire, and having performed the invocation of the seat, the form, and Sadāśiva within the heart-lotus of the fire, one should worship with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*). Then, visualizing the presence of the mouth of Śiva within the mouth of the fire, [one should offer oblations] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having offered a hundred or half that number of oblations according to one's capacity with fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), sesame seeds (*tila*), and so forth, and having offered an oblation consisting of a tenth part of the limbs of Brahmā, one should offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the upward-facing [mouth] with the mantra "Hauṃ Śivāya Vauṣaṭ," and then [offer] the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the root mantra ending in "Svāhā."

Having offered three mouthfuls as oblations, having offered one oblation each for the limbs of Brahmā, having provided water for sipping (ācamana), and having given sandalwood paste and betel leaves, he should wash his hands and worship with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā). In the absence of clarified butter and other such substances, he may offer leaves, flowers, and so forth. Then—

Having gratified [the deity] with hymns of praise, circumambulations, and prostrations, and having offered the *arghya* for the turning away (*parāṅmukha*), one should then raise Śiva and unite him with the Śiva residing in the *liṅga*. Then, taking up the *darbha* grass used for the surrounding strewn layer (*paristaraṇa*),
and having sprinkled their tips, middles, and roots with clarified butter (*ājya*), one should take hold of a single *darbha* blade.

One should burn the remainder, starting from the tip. Then, having cast a single blade of *darbha* grass into the fire, one should make a *tilaka* on the forehead with its ashes. Wearing those ashes increases longevity, prosperity, and fame, and brings about victory and health. Then, having drawn a square mandala on its southern side...
On the periphery of the mandala, in the great directions from east to north, one should place the Rudras, the hosts of Mothers, and the Yakṣas;

in the corners starting from the northeast, the planets, Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas; and in the center of the mandala, in the northeast, southeast, and southwest corners, the lunar mansions, the zodiac signs, and the Viśvedevas.
Having worshipped Kṣetrapāla in the intermediate direction between the quarters of Vāyu and Varuṇa and having offered arghya,
one should present the bali offering to Rudra and the others with food mixed with water and then give water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana).
For the worship of Rudra and the others, their respective mantras end with "namaḥ," while for the offering of the bali, they end with "svāhā."

The distinction is that for the Kṣetrapāla there is the singular number, while for the others there is the plural. Then, on the square mandala in the eastern part, one should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu. After that, on the cow-dung mandala in the courtyard outside the pavilion, [one offers] to the crows and so forth.

Having offered separate oblations (*bali*) with the words: "Svāhā to those who break the covenant (*samaya*); svāhā to Agni and the others; svāhā to all the planetary (*graha*), household (*vāstu*), and divine beings," one should also cast one oblation for dogs, spirits (*bhūta*), outcasts (*patita*), ghosts (*preta*), and so forth. Alternatively, one may do so in brief.
With reference to all [beings]:
"Those Rudras whose actions are fierce and who dwell in fierce abodes,
and whoever are gentle and dwell in gentle abodes."
The Mothers who have the form of Rudras, those who are lords of the Gaṇas,
as well as others who are obstacles residing in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
May all of you, with joyful minds, accept this offering;
may you swiftly grant us success and always protect me from fears.

With this mantra, one should cast a single *bali* offering. All of this *bali*-ritual must be performed only by one who is authorized for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), not by everyone. Even when there is authorization for the fire-ritual, if there is a deficiency of the implements for the *homa* or an inability [to perform it], [one may perform] the *homa*-mantras...
One should recite the mantra ten times the number of oblations offered in the fire sacrifice; thereafter, one should perform the worship of the knowledge of Śiva.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the knowledge of Śiva:

the "knowledges of Śiva" (śivajñānāni) are the great divine scriptures beginning with the Kāmika. Among them, the Kāmika has three divisions and consists of one hundred million verses (parārdha). The Yogaja has five divisions and consists of one hundred thousand verses (lakṣa). The Ajita...
The *Caturbheda* consists of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣagrantha*). The *Dīpta* consists of nine divisions and one hundred thousand verses.

The *Sūkṣma*, which is the single *Ekatantra*, consists of the *Padmagrantha*. The *Sahasra* consists of ten divisions and the *Śaṅkhagrantha*. The *Aṃśumat* consists of twelve divisions and five hundred thousand verses.

The *Suprabheda* is a single-tantra consisting of three million verses. The *Vijaya* consists of eight divisions and three million verses. The *Anala* is a single-tantra consisting of thirty thousand verses. The *Vīratantra* consists of twelve divisions and one hundred thousand verses.
The *Cintyaja* is of six kinds and consists of one hundred thousand verses. The *Kāraṇa* consists of seven divisions.

The Niśvāsa, with its eight divisions, consists of ten million verses (*koṭigrantha*). The Svāyambhuva, with its three divisions, consists of fifty million verses (*sārdhakoṭigrantha*). The Raurava, with its six divisions, consists of eighty million verses (*aṣṭārbudagrantha*).
The Makuṭa, with its two divisions, consists of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣagrantha*). The Vimala has sixteen divisions.

The *Candrajñāna* consists of three hundred thousand verses and has fourteen divisions; the *Bimba* consists of one hundred thousand verses and has fifteen divisions; the *Prodgīta* consists of three hundred thousand verses and has sixteen divisions; the *Lalita* is distinguished by ten divisions and consists of eight thousand verses; [and] the *Siddha*.
The *Caturbheda* consists of one and a half million verses; the *Santāna* consists of seven divisions and six thousand verses;
the *Śarvokta* consists of five divisions and two hundred thousand verses;
the *Pārameśvara* consists of seven divisions and twelve hundred thousand verses; and the *Kiraṇa*.
The *Navabhedam* consists of five crore verses; the *Vātulam* consists of twelve divisions and one hundred thousand verses.

Thus, there are twenty-eight divisions of the divine scriptures (*divyāgamas*). [The total] is less than a *parārdha*, a *śaṅkha*, and a *padma*, by sixty-six lakhs and fifty-six thousand [verses]. A *padma* is...

Thus, there are this many texts; their subdivisions number two hundred and eight. Among all such divine scriptures (divyāgama), one should obtain as many as possible—whether several, or even just one, or at least only that *saṃhitā* which is useful for one's own worship—provided they possess the defining characteristics.
One should look [for it] in books.
The characteristics of the book:

the *pustaka* is twenty-two finger-breadths long and three finger-breadths wide, containing the venerable syllables (*śrīmadakṣara*). The *śrīrakṣa* is twenty-one finger-breadths long and three finger-breadths wide.

Twenty finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width minus one barley-corn is the *candrakānta*; these three constitute the superior [category]. Eighteen finger-breadths in length and two and a half finger-breadths in width is the *nalina*. Seventeen finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths plus three barley-corns in width is the [next category].

Śrīnivāsa is sixteen aṅgulas long and two aṅgulas plus two barley-corns wide; Śrībhadra is this third of the three medium types. Lakṣmīnivāsa is fifteen aṅgulas long and two aṅgulas plus one barley-corn wide.
The Umābhadra is fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length and two finger-breadths in width;
the Vīrabhadra is thirteen finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths minus one barley-corn (yava) in width;
these three constitute the smallest [size]. Among such manuscripts, those which are favorable to the patron (yajamāna) [should be used].
Having caused [the leaves] to be made with a central perforation situated between the third parts of the four leaf-quarters,
one should bind them with cotton threads the thickness of a barley grain.
For the worship of these books of Śiva-knowledge, [they should be placed] to the south-west of Śiva.
Or, in the northwestern quarter, having constructed a library for the Vidyās of any one of the dimensions starting from thirty-three cubits down to three cubits,
in the center of that building— whose walls are smeared with fragrant sandalwood and other substances— one should install [the image] fashioned from ivory or similar materials.
Having placed there a throne of knowledge (*vidyāsiṃhāsana*) adorned with gold lines and other ornaments,

and having spread silk cloth (*dukūla*) or similar materials upon it, [one should place] in its center [an image] made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), brass (*ārakūṭa*), iron, wood, bamboo, split bamboo, or other such materials.

Having placed a casket in the form of a jewel-box for knowledge (vidyāratnakaraṇḍa), one should deposit the books within it. Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, saying "Salutation to all the auspicious knowledges" (sarvebhyaḥ śivajñānebhyaḥ namaḥ)—
I worship Śambhu, the bestower of all knowledge and the destroyer of all ignorance,
who resides in the seat of Vidyā, with my body, mind, and speech.
Having praised [the deity] thus, one should pay homage. In the absence of a book,
having drawn an eight-petalled lotus within a square maṇḍala,
and an eighteen-petalled lotus surrounding it, one should place "hauṃ śivāya" in the pericarp (karṇikā).

Having worshipped Śiva together with Vāgīśvarī with the mantra *namaḥ*, one should worship the divine Āgamas known as Śaiva— beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Suprabheda— which were directly created by Śiva without dependence on any other source, upon the ten petals starting from the east; and [then] upon the eighteen [petals].
On the petals, one should worship those known as Raudra— beginning with Vijaya and ending with Vātula— because they were created by Śiva as the locus for the beginningless Rudras and others.
Now, the worship of the Guru:
Having approached the Guru seated upon his own seat, having washed his feet,
and having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while perceiving him as Śiva, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
Having prostrated three times with the eight limbs, rising and placing both knees upon the ground,
he should speak with palms joined in reverence, saying, "Forgive me. If—
just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower within the forest—
Likewise, a disciple who is greedy for knowledge may go to another teacher from his own guru.

If, following the scriptures, one approaches another guru for the sake of further knowledge, one should nevertheless continue to honor the previous guru as well. Then, having approached Śiva and worshipped him with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and having presented the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*), one should make a request for one's desired goal preceded by prostration.
Whatever I have done out of delusion, whether deficient or excessive,
may all that become complete for me through your grace, O Lord.
Having thus prayed:
"O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night; considering me as Your servant, they should be forgiven."
O Master, though I, a lowly servant of defiled intellect, have caused you distress, please forgive that, for you are pleased by the power of my devotion.
Thus he should inform [the deity]. Then, having worshipped Śiva on the five heads according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta,
and having worshipped the limbs (aṅgas) from the weapon (astra) up to the heart (hṛdaya) in reverse order,
he should pray as before, "Be facing upwards as you desire," and [offer] *hāṃ hauṃ* to Śiva.

Having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with the mantra "Svāhā to the one with limbs" (*sāṅgāya parāṅmukhārghyaṃ svāhā*), one should join the Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta and the limb-mantras (*aṅga*) beginning with Astra—
which constitute the form of the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*)— to the limbs of the Deity. This also applies to others.

One should offer the *parāṅmukha-arghya* to the deities of the respective veils. Reciting the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, while casting flowers upward with the tips of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands in the *nārāca-mudrā*, one should awaken the mantras with: *hāṃ hauṃ haṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ*.
Having joined them with the divine mudrā at the heart-center of Śiva, one should contemplate their dissolution there. Thereafter,
[one should likewise offer] to the Guru, Vidyāpīṭha, the seven Gurus, Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the Door-keepers.
Having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with their respective mantras, one should dismiss them. Then,

having also offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* to the deities of the retinue, and having covered each of them individually with garments and flowers, one should place them at the sides of the chest (*peṭaka*) using the *astra-mantra*.
Then, having recited the Śiva-mantra, one should take the liṅga from the lotus-seat, wrap it in fine silk (*dukūla*) and other cloths,

place it within a casket, and while meditating on Bhīmarudra, request the command of Śiva, saying "Protect [it]," and then perform the covering. Thereafter, performing the mixed worship (*miśrapūjā*), one should proceed.

One who has not previously performed the fivefold worship (pañcapūjā) should perform the Caṇḍa-pūjā, complete with all the ritual services beginning with invocation (āvāhana), immediately after the dismissal (udvāsana) of Śiva. In this manner, one may perform it at the times of morning, midday, evening, and midnight, or during two periods such as morning and so forth.
Or worship should be performed at the mere time of dawn, or within a three-hour period [of the day].

Except for times such as the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and so forth, one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) must avoid performing worship at night. Even by him, if the three-times-a-day worship (*trikālapūjā*) is performed, [it should end before] sunset.
Having begun [the rite], the evening worship must be completed within three *ghaṭikās*.

However, for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is no restriction regarding time; or rather, even for one seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), there is no restriction regarding time. Rather, it should be performed at whatever time is possible, for as many *nāḍikās* as are possible.
One should perform sacrifices for one's own sake according to one's capacity.
This is also because of the observation of scriptural tradition (*āgama*). Thus, being unable to perform the sixteen elaborations (*prapañca-upacāra*), one may perform ten or five elaborations.
The varieties of ritual service consist of invocation, the seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, perfumes, flowers,
incense, lamps, food offerings, and mouth-fresheners.
The sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) consist of praise, prostration, circumambulation, and dismissal. Alternatively, they are:

the seat, invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the bath, clothing, fragrance, flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, incense, lamps, the waving of lights (*ārārtika*), and a handful of ashes and water.

The sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacārāḥ*): the ten services consist of seat (*āsana*), invocation (*āvāhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), bathing (*snāna*), clothing (*vastra*), fragrance (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and food offerings (*naivedya*).
The five services consist of fragrance, flowers, incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and food offerings. Although—
Earthly [substances] consist of fragrances, flowers, and so forth, as well as bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like;
aqueous [substances] consist of water, milk, clothing, curd, cow urine, and so forth.
The southeast (Āgneya) direction includes gold, jewels, lamps, ornaments, and the like;
the northwest (Vāyavya) direction includes the fly-whisk, incense, the fan, and the palm-leaf fan.
Celestial songs, instrumental music, and the like, such as the sounds of the lute and the flute—
these are declared by those who know the scriptures to be the five types of offerings.
Thus, the fivefold offerings have been shown in detail; nevertheless, for those who are incapable,
there are only five offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering, which correspond respectively to the earth, ether, air, fire, and water elements.
All ritual services (upacāra) for Śiva must be performed like the invocation (āvāhana), by means of the cessation of the movement of the moon and sun in the form of inhalation and exhalation;
this is well-known from the scriptures (āgama). In some ritual services, this is done by counting the mātrās.
The rule regarding the duration of time is also shown in the Āgamas: there are twelve *mātrās* for the invocation (*āvāhana*);

five for the water for the feet (*pādya*); three for the water for sipping (*ācamana*); one for the respectful offering (*arghya*); six for the scents (*gandha*); twelve for the incense (*dhūpa*); six for the lamp (*dīpa*);
twenty-four for the food offering (*naivedya*); seven for the waving of lights (*ārārtika*); and sixteen for the circumambulation with lamps (*nīrājana*).

Seven [recitations] for the offering of ashes; five for the umbrella; ten for the fly-whisks; and three for the fan. Thus, while the services are being performed by means of arresting the movement of the moon and the sun, their respective mantras should be recited mentally. And the mantras are the Prāsāda, the Śiva-mantra, and the Pañcabrahma.
The six-limbed forms are to be employed according to the rules in their respective services.
Among these— namely, invocation, water for the feet, clothing, unguents, ornaments, mirror, umbrella,
chowries, fan, recitation, hymns, and prostration— and in other services not specifically mentioned, [the mantra is used] ending with the mantra itself.

The word "namaḥ" is used for the offering of water (arghya), the seat, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), drinking water, mouth-freshening water, the waving of lights (nīrājana), the sacred thread (pavitra), recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), self-surrender (ātmasamarpaṇa), and the fire-oblation (homa). The word "svāhā" is used for sprinkling (mārjana), pouring (secanam), flowers, and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). [The word "vaṣaṭ" is used] for cleansing from impurities and bathing.
The sounds *huṃ* and *phaṭ* are used for covering with the noose (*pāśacchadana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), piercing (*bhedana*), and warding off obstacles (*vighnanivāraṇa*).

The sound *phaṭ* is used for protection (*rakṣā*). The word *svadhā* is used for sipping water (*ācamana*). One who is unable to perform even the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) according to these stated rules should worship with the "eight-flower offering" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) alone.
First, a flower should be offered upon the seat with a pure mind;
then, one should perform meditation on the form with the heart, while another flower is used for the [deity].
By the offering of five flowers, one should arrange the five limbs;
likewise, with the eighth, Śiva is worshipped—this is declared to be the "Eightfold Flower Offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā).

The five limbs are the head and so forth; or the five Brahmans are the heart and so forth, excluding the eyes. These eight flowers are common to all, bestowing all accomplishments here as well as in all stages of life.
And one should worship [these], which are common to all castes,
once, twice, or thrice a day.
At dawn, at midday, and likewise when the sun has set,
one should worship with supreme devotion according to the rite of the eight flowers.
[It is] for the poor, the protectorless, children, women, and the simple-minded;
for those addicted to enjoyments, those afflicted by disease, and likewise for those whose souls are absorbed in meditation.

"Regarding those devoted to the Śiva scriptures, whose nature is beneficial through various supernatural powers (siddhis), and who are both attached and detached, the 'Eight-Flower Offering' (aṣṭapuṣpikā) has been taught"—according to this statement from the *Kālottara*. "Bhoga" refers to the protection of a kingdom; those who possess this are "bhogins" (enjoyers). For them...

The meaning is: for those who are engaged in the protection of the kingdom. By protecting the kingdom, great merit is obtained through the promotion of worship in many Śiva sanctuaries and in the homes of Śiva-devotees. [This applies to] those who are devoted to the Śiva scriptures...
The meaning is: "for those intent upon its exposition and its study. For indeed, by expounding the Śiva-śāstra and by correctly promoting the worship of Śiva in the world, one obtains great merit.
The Ritual for Worshipping the Kapila Cow:
Having completed the worship of Śiva, one should perform the worship of the Kapila cow. As follows:
[The five types of cows are] Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting: "Obeisance to Kapilā, who has the form of the five mother-cows," [one should pray:
"O daughter of Surabhi, Mother of the World, bestower of nectar upon the gods;
accept this morsel, O granter of boons, and grant me my desired object."
Having thus offered a morsel [of food], he says:
"You were saluted by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Janhu;
O Kāpili, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me."
Having thus prayed:
"May cows always be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows also be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows."
Thus one should recite.
By reciting the mantra in this manner at the three junctions of the day, being self-controlled and pure,
a person is liberated from all sins and attains the world of Śiva.

Then follows the vision of the temple for the sake of others. Thereafter, staying near the *ālaya*, one should go to the temple of Śiva at the conclusion of the worship and perform service (*sevā*) there as well. The procedure therein is as follows:
Having gone near the temple, one should perform a salutation outside the gateway (gopura), or outside the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha), or to the vimāna in the form of a gross liṅga. Then,
one should also perform salutations to the auspicious liṅga (bhadraliṅga), the sacrificial altar, the flagstaff (dhvajastambha), and the bull (vṛṣabha).

Having performed [these] within the inner precinct for the vision of Śiva and the worship of Śiva, and for the attainment of the perfection of their fruit— O Blessed One, being gracious, grant permission to me who am prostrate at your lotus feet.

Having thus prayed to the Bull (Vṛṣabha), one should prostrate with the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma) to Śiva in the area below the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). One should not prostrate while covering the body with a garment.
One should bow toward the front, back, left side, and the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) of Śiva. [This applies] when [the deity] faces west.

One should also bow to the *liṅga* facing the northern direction and to that on the left side. Having bowed, one should scatter a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) before the God of gods. Then, one should perform a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). The circumambulation within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is for the worshipper alone; the circumambulation within the inner circle (*antarmaṇḍala*) is for those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*) alone.
For all [mantras] within the *antarhāra* and other regions: therein, in the *antarhāra*, it is single-fold (*ekaguṇa*) in a clockwise direction;

in the *madhyahāra*, threefold; in the *maryādā*, fourfold; in the *mahāmaryādā*, fivefold; and at the boundary of the field (*kṣetrāvadhau*), hundredfold. Thus, in a location corresponding to the strength and time [of the mantra].
One should perform twenty-one, fifteen, seven, five, or three circumambulations; even when there is absolutely no opportunity, one should perform at least one circumambulation.
While performing circumambulation in this manner, one should [visualize] what is conceived within the inner sanctum and the maṇḍala.

One must not cross the *somasūtra*. To avoid crossing it, one should proceed only by the left (*savya*) and right (*apasavya*) paths within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), starting from the *somasūtra*. Beyond that, only the outer and inner mandalas are to be traversed by the left and right paths. It has been stated previously that this may be performed either starting from the direction of Indra (*aindra*) or from the *somasūtra*.
At dusk,
however— one should worship [the deities] beginning with Vṛṣa and ending with Caṇḍanātha, starting with the bull and the Soma-thread,
then again the bull and Caṇḍanātha on the side of the region of the stalk (nāla).

How does this [argument] from "because of going" cohere? For it is described that the fruit arises from circumambulating the Śivaliṅga, and that the abundance of fruit results from an abundance of repetitions. In that very same work, in another section, the fault of transgressing the *somasūtra* is also heard.

If it is argued that— since the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) obtained immediately after hearing the injunctive sentence has its fruit heard of, and since there is also a hearing of a prohibition— there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to a conflict between two equally primary and equal forces,

and that this is like the option in the sentences "He offers when the sun has risen" and "He offers when the sun has not yet risen" based on the investigation of the Smṛti— [the answer is: no, [it is] not so.

By describing the superiority of the prohibitive rule over the injunctive statement— namely, that while one might prepare a meal of salted food with curd for a peaceful guest who has arrived at home, saying "one should eat curd and honey at night," one should instead satisfy him by giving a meal of honey and rice— the prohibition itself is shown to prevail over the injunction.
Because of the description of its superior strength, it is more appropriate that the prohibition against crossing the *somasūtra* takes precedence over the injunction for circumambulation.
Now, if this were the case, [what would happen to] the prohibition "one must not kill" in relation to the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice]?

If it is argued that, because the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" possesses greater force in view of its specific mandate, there would be a contradiction with the scripture [prohibiting killing], we say no.

Since that [injunction] is a general rule and thus pertains to violence outside of ritual contexts, it lacks equal force compared to the prohibitory rule— just as the rules "he offers when the sun has risen" and "he offers before the sun has risen" do not have equal force— and therefore it is set aside by the specific timing of the ritual.
Because the injunction would have fulfilled its purpose, it would follow that the prohibition would apply at a specific time and place;
furthermore, one should again proceed fiercely and likewise upon the back of a bull.
Thus, moving from left to right is here called *pradakṣiṇa*.

The starting and ending points of the god Vṛṣabha are declared to be the locus of the principles (*tattva*). It is joined with the station of the three-fold *caṇḍa*, consisting of two stations and the *somasūtra*.

It should be performed in the manner thus described. Furthermore, the *somasūtra* outside the temple at the location of the stalk (*nāla*) should have a width equal to that [of the temple] as before, or half that measure;
there is a fault in overstepping it. However, there is no fault in overstepping it on the outside of the *sūtra*, nor even within it.
In a narrow space, one should cover [the path] with grass and so forth before crossing over.
Having again covered the Soma-thread (the boundary) with grass, wood, leaves, stones, clods of earth, and the like, one may then cross over it.
Because of this statement, there is also a prohibition against the *apasavya* (leftward) direction in certain cases:

"Wherever there are two *soma*-threads or wherever there is a temple of Viṣṇu, one should not perform the *apasavya*; one should indeed perform the circumambulation in the *pradakṣiṇa* (rightward) manner."

Thus, having paid homage to the two gatekeepers and Nandikeśvara, and having entered within with their respective permission, one should pay homage to Vighnarāja by scattering handfuls of flowers and striking the head [with them], and then,
having entered the pavilion and paid homage to the Deity, [one should touch] the head and the heart.

Having joined his palms in *añjali*, he should offer praise with Vedic, Āgamic, worldly, Puranic, Dravidian, and other hymns according to his qualification. Among them, the service of the Preceptor alone consists of entering the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*); for the other Brahmins, it is the middle pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*).
Having entered, he stands at the entrance of the half-pavilion for the Kṣatriyas; at the head of the bull for the Vaiśyas;
and on the back of the bull for the Śūdras. For the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, having drawn a square mandala with cow dung at both the head and the back of the bull, right there—

A handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) should be offered. In this manner, salutations preceded by an offering of flowers should also be performed for the forms of the dance (nṛttamūrti) and the others. After the salutation to Śiva, one should salute Caṇḍeśvara. Thus, after the salutations beginning with the pedestal (pīṭha) and ending with Caṇḍa—

In order to expiate various offenses committed within the temple, one should recite the root mantra as much as possible in the presence of the Deity and then depart without turning one's back on the Deity. Such offenses include mounting a vehicle or walking about wearing shoes within the precincts of the Śiva temple.
Stepping over the shadows of the images on the gate-towers, touching discarded offerings (*nirmālya*), stepping over them, walking through the middle of the sacrificial altar (*balipīṭha*) of Śiva,
touching women with lustful intent, looking at them with passion, laughing or singing in vain, and [wearing] ornaments along with one's upper garment...
These include saluting without circumambulation, saluting with only one hand,
saluting from the left side, and saluting at improper times. Having asked for forgiveness for such possible faults that ought to be avoided while serving Śiva in this manner, one should depart.

One should serve [the Lord] only after performing service— whether by means of materials ranging from village ornaments to leaves and flowers, or by bodily activities such as sweeping, or even by mere verbal acts culminating in the benefit of the temple—
on a daily basis.

If one is unable to perform the service daily, one should perform it on the eighth day and other such occasions. By performing it on the eighth day, sins committed over eight days are destroyed; on a festival (parvan), sins of a fortnight; at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), sins of a month. However, at the time of Pradoṣa, even the most grievous sins acquired through the three types of action are destroyed.
Through service during the great festivals of the equinoxes, solstices, eclipses, and so forth, one attains the state of Śiva.
All of this must necessarily be practiced by those other than the Vīraśaivas; for them, however,
there is merely the full knowledge of it all, but not its practical execution, because they have meditated upon their own body as the very abode of Śiva.

Then, having returned home, one should— avoiding the presence of those who have not been initiated— listen to even a small portion of the Siddhānta scriptures or practice them at the appropriate time together with those who have been initiated.
O fair-faced one, this knowledge must not be disclosed to those who lack devotion;
it should be protected with great effort, just as wealth is guarded against thieves.
Thus it is stated. Now, at the time of midday, one should perform worship either elaborately or in a condensed manner with the Aṣṭapuṣpikā mantra.
This applies even when, due to some deficiency, the worship of the liṅga personally maintained by oneself is not possible, provided that the practitioner follows the same ritual procedure.

When the *liṅga* has been worshipped by another, one should perform at least the brief offering of eight flowers; or, in the case of a fixed *liṅga*, one should perform the worship with the common mantras.
The Praṇava, Mātṛkā, Māyā, Vyomavyāpin, the six-syllabled mantra,
Prāsāda, and the Aghora mantra— these seven are considered common [to all].

Having thus worshipped Śiva in whatever manner possible, when wishing to eat at the proper time, one should set aside the very best portion from all the cooked food; having offered half of that to Śiva, one should perform with the other half the Vedic and Śaiva fire-sacrifices (*homa*) according to one's qualification. Regarding the Vedic [sacrifice]:
The Vaiśvadeva oblation; the Śaiva oblation on the hearth.
This is the procedure for the *cullī-homa*:
having purified the hearth by means of inspection and other rites, one [places] the fire therein.

Having unified the three fires—the elemental, the lunar, and the digestive—along with the fire located at the navel through inhalation (*pūraka*) and breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one should expel them via exhalation (*recaka*) through the *piṅgalā* channel and cast them into the hearth-fire.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer salutations: "Obeisance to Agni," "Obeisance to Soma," and "Obeisance to Sūrya."
"Salutation to Bṛhaspati; salutation to Prajāpati;

salutation to all the gods; salutation to all the Viśvedevas. Salutation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having thus worshipped Agni and the others, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending at the east (pūrva), in the fire...
Having offered oblations with those respective mantras ending in "svāhā," one should dismiss them.

One should eat the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering), or that which has been offered (*nivedita*) or its remnants. Many scriptural statements regarding the fruits of eating what is offered to Śiva are heard:
The remains of my offerings, the water from my feet, the flower, and the leaf bestow,
respectively, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus, prohibitory statements regarding that [nirmālya] are also heard, such as:
"One should never wear the nirmālya of Śambhu, nor should one eat it," and so forth.
The application of these [statements] is determined by whether or not one possesses initiation (dīkṣā) into Śiva.
The *nirmālya* is stainless, pure, and because of its purity, it is beyond reproach;
therefore, this *nirmālya* must not be consumed by those who are impure and of inauspicious nature.
One who is addicted to the fickleness of the tongue, devoid of the purificatory rites of Śiva,
yet eats the remains of Śiva’s offerings (nirmālya), shall go to the Raurava hell.

Some maintain this is because of such statements from the *Śiva Purāṇa*. In the Siddhānta Tantras, such as the *Kāmika*, it is said that for those who have been initiated, according to the distinctions of their respective *samaya* observances:
"One should not consume the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), nor should one revile a devotee of Śiva."

Such are the prohibitory statements; furthermore, prescriptions for atonement are heard, such as: "In the case of consuming *nirmālya*, one should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times if done through negligence," and so forth. Therefore—
Whatever hard foods, chewable foods, and other drinks there may be, those indeed should be offered to Śambhu; one should eat them only out of the state of being His servant.

(316) According to such statements from the Purāṇas, the *nirmālya* of Śiva is to be accepted only by those who have been initiated through the Śiva-consecration (*śivasaṃskāra*) prescribed in the Vedic, Paurāṇika, and Pāśupata traditions, and not by those initiated through the Siddhāntatantras such as the Kāmika.
Some [say]: "In the Kāmika [Tantra] itself:
'An impure soul who, out of greed for purity, consumes the supreme purifying [substance], meets with destruction by consuming it, just as a twice-born [Brahmin] who consumes [forbidden] meat.'"
In this world, those who bear my liṅga, who are spiritual guides, and who are devoted to me alone—
taking me as their sole refuge— it is only among them that [my grace] is appropriate, and not among other beings.
From this statement:
"Thousands of fasts and hundreds of *prājāpatya* penances are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of a mere fragment of Śiva’s grace."

This is also evident from such statements as those found in the *Vātula-tantra* and other scriptures. In the Siddhānta Tantras, even for those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*), that which is offered to Śiva is indeed highly commended. As for the scriptural injunctions regarding penance for the prohibition of using Śiva’s *nirmālya* (remnants), they refer to the property of the deity, the materials belonging to the deity, the food offering (*naivedya*), and what has been offered, but not to that which has been cast outside after being consumed by Caṇḍa.

Thus end the topics concerning the five kinds of *nirmālya*. In the *Kāmika*: "The property of the deity, the substance belonging to the deity, the food offering (*naivedya*) that has been presented, and the substance [offered to] Caṇḍa—*nirmālya* shall be of six kinds."

The property of a deity belonging to the lord of a village and so forth, such as cloth and other items, is *devadravya* (the property of a deity); that which is prepared as an offering for him is *naivedya* (food offering), and that which has been presented [and consumed] is *devocchiṣṭa* (the leavings of the deity).
"However, that which is given as *caṇḍadravya* is cast outside as *nirmālya*.

Thus, following the enumeration of the sixfold classification of *nirmālya*, the faults of consuming *nirmālya*, and the instruction on the atonement (*prāyaścitta*) for those [faults], [the text continues] with: "Now..."

Because the two verses beginning with "aśuddhātmā śuddhilobhāt" were recited for the purpose of obtaining permission to accept the *nirmālya* (remnants) known as *nivedita*, others maintain that the prohibitions regarding *śiva-nivedita* found in the Siddhānta Tantras refer specifically to those who have not received the aforementioned Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*).
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) of Sadāśiva are not food for humans;
one should cast them into water for animals and elephants."

Alternatively, "the wise man should burn it with fire or bury it in the ground"—by thus establishing that the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva is unfit for consumption by all human beings alike, and by describing its ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) only in earth, fire, cows, elephants, and so forth; and because it says: "The food of a Jaina is not
The *nirmālya* (remains) of Sadāśiva is indeed not to be consumed even by those who lack initiation (*dīkṣā*).

However, statements declaring that their *śivanirmālya* is praiseworthy refer specifically to the *nirmālya* of the *sakala* (manifested) form. Furthermore, in all [other] images, the deity Caṇḍa is not authorized.
Thus, because there is a prohibition against the office of the *caṇḍa* for those who possess all [the powers] (*sakala*),

and because it is described as an authorization for the offering of food (*naivedya*) for all *sakalas*— stating that "the food offering of the *sakalas* shall be for the meal of everyone"— that too [is permitted] only by those initiated by Śiva who serve him.
It should be consumed. In the *Suprabheda*, after stating, "The *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva," and so forth, it continues:
"But the *nirmālya* of those who possess parts (*sakala*) is food for the attendants;
if that were eaten by other people, it would cause fault."

Others say this because it has been so stated. Furthermore, even regarding the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Sadāśiva, the prohibition applies only to those offered at Śiva-liṅgas installed by humans and the like; it does not apply to *cara*-liṅgas and the like, because the authority over those belongs to Caṇḍa.
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile liṅga, one made of metal, a jewel-liṅga, a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga,
and in all images, Caṇḍa is not authorized.
In a self-manifested (svāyambhuva) linga, one made of stone (bāṇa), one born of jewels, one fashioned from metal,
or a linga consecrated by a perfected being (siddha), Caṇḍa is not authorized.
Some say this because of such statements. Furthermore, statements asserting that there is no authority for Caṇḍa in the Caraliṅga and other [texts] pertain to the Vaidika,
Paurāṇika, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other Tantras, but they do not pertain to the statements of the Siddhānta such as the Kāmika.
Whether the arrow is made of wood, stone, clay, or fashioned from metal, or whether it is adorned with various materials, the fierce Niyanaka remains stationed within it.
"In the Siddhānta, [the rites are performed] not in other Tantras, neither in the Left nor in the Right. (p.

318) [This applies] to unmanifest and manifest lingas, in a mandala, on a sacrificial mound, in fire, as well as in mobile and immobile [lingas], and likewise in jewels, jeweled mosaics, and so forth."
In a linga produced from fragrant substances or food, in one fashioned from earth, ashes, or wood,
and likewise in a linga made of flowers, the worship of Caṇḍa is mandatory.

And because such specific distinctions are observed in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures, the rules regarding the acceptance and rejection of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) are not established on the basis of whether they concern mobile (*cara*) or immobile (*sthira*) objects; rather, they are established on the basis of the specific nature of the *nirmālya* itself.
Betel, ashes, oil, perfumes, flowers,
cakes, fruits, and other substances used for consumption are called *nirmālya*.
Some say this is because of such a statement. In the *Kāmika*:
"Whatever is offered to one's own chosen *liṅga* is like an offering of sacrificial porridge (*caru*); of this there is no doubt.
One should cause that food offering (*naivedya*) to be given to brothers, sons, and indeed to yogins."
Thus, from the description of the analogy of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*): "Whether a crystal *bāṇaliṅga* or a *caru*-liṅga has been installed as the cause [of worship],
one should not consider the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) presented to it to be mere refuse."
"Food [offered] to children and young women increases strength.
Because this establishes that such food is not *nirmālya* (remnant of an offering), even food offered to mobile *liṅgas* (*caraliṅga*) and the like is indeed fit to be eaten;
however, it must not be eaten by the worshiper himself. As it is said: "The *naivedya* is for brothers and sons," and so forth.
Because of the specific statement; some maintain that the statement regarding the acceptability of mere betel and such refers specifically to the *liṅga* installed by humans and others.
Having prepared the food offering, he says "To Śiva" and offers it above that;
then, every day with devotion, he eats my remains.
"He who is like me is said to be one who eats the sacrificial oblation (caru) in that manner.

Thus, in the *Kāmika*, it is stated that "having offered, he should eat," which establishes that even the one who performs the offering must eat the remains of that [offering]. Therefore, what has been offered to Śiva is indeed fit to be eaten by the worshipper as well.

Some, however, maintain that the statements prohibiting the offering of food to him should be interpreted as referring to offerings made to Saṃhārarudra and others; for it is precisely at the conclusion of the description of his worship— following the invocation of Paramaśiva into the form of Sadāśiva— that [the prohibition occurs].
Since it is heard many times in the divine scriptures that there is a prohibition against what has been offered [to another deity],
it is indeed proper that all kinds of *śivanirmālya* (the remains of offerings made to Śiva), even when interspersed with thousands of injunctions and prohibitions, must be avoided.
A great fault is heard of, and great strength is also heard of;
in such a case, the fruit should be abandoned, for the fault is indeed more powerful.
Because of this statement; and also because it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"One should never consume a leaf, flower, fruit, water, food, water for the feet, or medicine without first having offered it to the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva."
It should be stated that the prohibition against eating without having announced [the meal] is heard [in scripture];
for, like the prohibition against eating without honoring a guest,
that rule can possibly be intended as a mandate to eat only what remains from that [offering].
The wise person should eat as food the remnants of whatever has been offered to Śiva— be it grain, medicine, water, leaves, flowers, fruits, or the like.

Thus they describe it, because it is established in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* in exactly that manner. In this way, nine positions have arisen upon examining the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions regarding the use of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings). [The view is that] only those who possess initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the form of the purification by Śiva are permitted to use the *nirmālya* of Śiva; for others, [it is forbidden].

The first position is that there is a prohibition of that [practice]. Even among those who possess Śiva-initiation (*śivasaṃskāra*), permission for it is granted only to those such as the *atyāśramins* who have received Vedic initiation and the like, but not to those who have received initiation according to the Siddhāntatantras such as the *Kāmika*. As for them...
The second position is that [the prohibition] is based on the observation of rules regarding the prohibition of those [flowers] and the penance for consuming them.

The third position is that the instruction regarding the prohibition and the penance applies only to the five kinds of *nirmālya* other than what has been offered (*nivedita*), whereas even for them, that which has been offered is to be accepted. Furthermore, even among those that have been offered...
The fourth position is that because of the prohibition against what has been offered to the Śiva-liṅga, only that which is offered to a *sakala* [manifest] deity is to be accepted.

It is not all offerings to the Śiva-liṅga that are prohibited; rather, it is specifically what has been offered to a fixed (*sthira*) liṅga installed by humans and others, whereas what is offered to a mobile (*cara*) liṅga and so forth is not.
The fifth position is that [the offering] is to be accepted, because there is no provision for a fierce (caṇḍa) officiant in that context.

There is no fixed rule regarding the prohibitions and permissions concerning the "offered" (nivedita) found in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, as these pertain to the realm of moving and stationary beings;
this applies even to the worship of moving beings and so forth on the path of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the *Kāmika* and other tantras.
Because of the presence of a fierce nature [in the ascetic], however, there is the established rule that the prohibition concerns food and the like,
while the permission concerns fruits, cakes, betel, and so forth; for there exist specific statements regarding other matters.

The sixth position is as follows: food and other offerings presented by wandering ascetics (*caraliṅgin*) and others should indeed be accepted; however, they must be given to one’s brothers and kin, and not consumed by the officiant (*pūjaka*). This is the seventh position.
The eighth position is that, with the understanding of it being an offering to Śiva (*śivārpaṇa-buddhi*), what is offered to Śiva may be consumed even by the officiant.

The ninth position is that, because a prohibitive statement carries greater weight than a descriptive one regarding injunctions and prohibitions, it is proper to avoid all *śivanirmālya* (remnants of offerings to Śiva). Among these, the ninth position is utterly untenable; for in the acceptance of *śivanirmālya*...

Because it would follow that the many words of divine scriptures, Purāṇas, and so forth, which establish great fruits, would lack authority; for the words of scripture cannot tolerate even a single syllable being unauthoritative, much less so in the case of the words of Śiva, among which there are those [that might be considered] mere explanatory praise (arthavāda).

The proclamation from the bell of all the divine scriptures is that even the attempt to establish the authority [of such a view] leads to great transgression. Furthermore, the statement "a great fault is heard" and so forth applies to those cases where there is scope for the authority of both injunction and prohibition elsewhere. In such instances, regarding those two...
In some cases, the prohibition regarding a conjunction is more powerful; this is intended to mean that, for example,

while the authority of the statement praising the consumption of *āmalaka* on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) finds its scope on a *dvādaśī* that is not conjoined with Sunday, the authority of the statement prohibiting it on Sunday prevails.

On a Sunday devoid of conjunction with the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), there is scope for the rite; however, when a Sunday does coincide with the twelfth lunar day, two prohibitive statements regarding the consumption of *āmalaka* fruits apply, and among these, the prohibitive statement is more authoritative.
This is because the prohibitive statements override those stating the fruits [of the rite], which would otherwise lead to their total lack of authority.

However, those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge do not respect mere relative strength; therefore, in this case, it is more appropriate to demonstrate the determination of the respective domains of the injunctions and prohibitions.
We shall, however, demonstrate that [system] by means of the path previously shown,
in accordance with all scriptures and in a manner pleasing to all followers of Śiva.

The meal for the Śaivas is threefold. One [type] is based on the intention that after the completion of the worship of Śiva, following the performance of the fire-ritual (*śivāgnikārya*) in the external sacrificial pit (*bāhyakuṇḍa*), there is the self-meal immediately thereafter. Another is at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), consisting of the substances being offered.

The first [type of offering] consists of the mere commencement of the offering to Śiva, wherein one’s own food—consisting of the transfer of form—is offered; however, the second [type] is preceded by an offering consisting of the transfer of that very arrangement for the sake of Śiva, through the contemplation [of it as such].
At the very moment of the first offering, [the food exists] in a subtle form, like the sacrificial oblation (havis) used in the sacrifice to another deity.

The third [type of worship] consists of offering one’s own food together with *rucī* and then consuming it only after it has been enjoyed by Śiva, with the realization that "this is the duty of a servant of Śiva, consisting of the acceptance of his leftovers" (p. 321). Among these, the first is described in the *Suprabheda*, in the chapter on the fire-ritual (*vahnikāryapaṭala*).
It has been explained: "At the conclusion of the fire-rite (agnikārya), one should perform the oblation (homa) in the fire of the vital breath (prāṇāgni).
Beside that, in the fire-hall, the place for eating is prescribed."
Or else, the supreme sacrifice to the fire of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra) should be performed even at home;
having especially made that place pure by smearing it with cow dung.
Having adorned it with ancestral powders, provided with a canopy and lamps,
[the vessel] should be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or a plantain leaf.
One should take a single vessel, having purified it as is appropriate;
having placed all [the offerings] together in the vessel, one should worship Śiva for the sake of one's own self.
The self is this sacrificer, and the intellect is known as his wife;
the hair of the head and body are the darbha grasses, and the tongue and other organs are the sacrificial vessels.
One should worship him within the fire situated inside the altar of the heart-lotus,
having strewn the darbha-grass of the body's hairs, while reciting the Praṇava conjoined with Śiva.
Having recited [the mantra] and sprinkled [water], the knower of mantras should then consecrate with the Śiva-mantra;
having muttered the Śiva-mantra over the water, he should [mutter] the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (aṅgas) in their proper order.
Having meditated upon Śiva and having drunk water with the mantra "To Śiva" while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra,
one should again offer oblations to Śiva with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with the *Īśāna* mantra.
Having slowly taken up the food with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb,
one should especially drink water while reciting the mantras beginning with "yad vā amṛta."
The practitioner should offer five oblations with the five vital breath mantras;
having touched the vessel, he should thereafter eat.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, standing facing the sun,
he should then touch his abdomen with the left hand while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
While recollecting Śiva and uttering the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), one should cause water to flow from the right thumb onto the right big toe.
This would be like a mere handful of water at the feet of one's own self;
thus has this "Prāṇāgnihotra" been described as eternal.
This fire-ritual has been proclaimed; now hear the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Thus [it is said].

This meal must be performed with food that has not been offered [to the deities]. To that end, the existence of unoffered food is demonstrated by scriptural statements found in the section on the *cullī-homa* (stove-oblation), such as: "One should offer with half of the food; and its procedure is now declared. Second, [the method of eating].
Regarding the food offering, it is shown in the *Vātulottara*:
"O Śivā, having offered the form of the substance, one should also offer its flavor;
if the offering is devoid of the offering of both, it shall be fruitless."
The offering of food (naivedya) is said to culminate in the enjoyment of that specific grace;
if it is devoid of the granting of grace, even the offering of food is fruitless.
By such [statements], this [offering] must be performed with food for which the act of offering has been commenced but not yet completed.

At the time of the ritual service (*upacāra*) of the food offering (*naivedya*), the act of offering— which was begun by placing the food offering before the Deity— is continued until the point of the offering of delight (*ruci-arpaṇa*), through the projection of the form (*rūpārpaṇa*) of that food offering which was then placed there.

That very food, whose act of offering has been commenced but not yet completed, is "praśasta" (recommended) when intended for the gods, ancestors, and so forth; the worshipper should eat that food offered with intent for them, with the very thought of dedicating it to Śiva.
The third provision for sustenance:
"In this world, those who bear my insignia, who are spiritual guides devoted to me,
and who have me as their sole refuge— for them alone is there that which is to be enjoyed, and not for other beings."
Whatever is fit to be tasted, whatever is fit to be chewed, and whatever else is fit to be drunk—
all those should indeed be offered to Śambhu and consumed with the mindset of a servant.
Those who have entered the path of the Dāsa and are established in the Śaiva Pāśupata [tradition]—
by them alone should food, drink, and even scent be consumed by those seeking liberation.
Thus, it is well known in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures that this meal must be performed with food that has already been offered (*nivedita*).

At the time of the offering of the *naivedya* (food offering) before the Deity, that which is placed there is said to be "offered" because it is consumed at that very moment by Śiva along with *ruci* (the goddess of taste) in a subtle form. That very [food]...

A Brāhmaṇa who has entered into service for the sake of attending to Śiva’s remains [the *ucchiṣṭa*] should eat that which is the *ucchiṣṭa* of Śiva; a Śūdra who has entered into this service should likewise eat it. And thus, those general prohibitory statements regarding the *nirmālya* of Śiva [are to be understood in this specific context].

There are two established rules: first, those [prohibitions] which concern mere human beings who are of the nature of bound souls (paśu) and lack the realization of being servants of Śiva; and second, those scriptural statements prohibiting various things which refer specifically to those who have been initiated and possess the realization of being servants of Śiva, and which concern the five kinds of ritual offerings (nirmālya), with the exception of that which has already been offered [to the deity].

This has been demonstrated by the ancients themselves. Here, the second arrangement—that among the six kinds of *nirmālya*, only one is fit for consumption—is well-known from the scriptures (*āgama*).
The first arrangement is clearly elaborated in the *Śiva Purāṇa*; for therein it says:
"My food offering, water for the feet, flower, and leaf are unworthy"—
thus some great sages have reported that the Lord himself has said.
"They say that; O Lord, how is it so? Tell me the truth.
To this question of Jaimini, [the Lord replied]: "O Jaimini, that is the subject matter of the words of the God of gods."
Those who have been cursed by Vīrabhadra are averse to devotion to Śiva.
Those who are devoted to other gods than Śambhu, those who have not been initiated,
those whose actions are impure, and those whose minds are equanimous toward others rather than toward Śambhu— [these are excluded].
"It is not fitting for them [to receive] those four types of grace from the Lord"—

such is the statement of Vyāsa that is observed. Furthermore, there are statements well-known in the Kāmika and other scriptures to the effect that the *nirmālya* of Śiva is fit for initiated devotees (*dīkṣita-bhaktas*).
These have been cited previously.

(324) Now, it is proclaimed by those who know the Śiva-śāstras that the *nirmālya* of Śiva removes all sins, wards off all diseases, bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, is equal to bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and is the sole means for both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*); yet, it must not be consumed by those who lack devotion and initiation.

It is also called "the tangible"; how is this logically consistent? Likewise, by virtue of being endowed with the power to avert all sins and so forth, it must indeed become common to all, just like the recitation of the name of Śiva or like all forms of expiation.

For how could that which is fit [for consumption] be something to be avoided by some? Therefore, why should it not be the case that the *nirmālya* of Śiva was considered inferior and thus to be avoided by some? Even Haradattācārya has stated this very point in a manner that is general, without specifying whether the excellence or inferiority is absolute: [The text continues with the citation: "Even a lowly person, having attained the state of being a *liṅgin*, becomes worthy of worship through the grace of the Lord; what then need be said of one who is the very embodiment of the Supreme Lord? (Haradatta on *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* 1.20.5) Thus, since he has spoken in a way that accommodates both the superiority and inferiority of those who are confused [about the matter], there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the venerable Vidyāraṇya has also stated: "Whether it be the *nirmālya* of Viṣṇu, the *nirmālya* of Śiva, or even the *nirmālya* of the Goddess, it is the supreme medicine for those whose minds are afflicted by the disease of worldly existence. (Vidyāraṇya, *Śataśloki*) Therefore, the prohibition against consuming the *nirmālya* of Śiva is merely intended for those who are ignorant of the true nature of the Lord. It is not, however, a prohibition based on the inherent impurity of the substance itself. As it is said: "The *nirmālya* of Śiva is not impure; rather, it is the supreme purifier. It is like the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), and it bestows liberation upon those who consume it with devotion. (Unspecified source) Consequently, the *nirmālya* of Śiva is indeed the most excellent of all substances. It is not at all inferior. This is established by the fact that even the venerable Śaṅkarācārya has declared: "Obeisance to you, O Śambhu, whose *nirmālya* is the supreme medicine for the world, which destroys the poison of worldly existence and grants the fruit of liberation. (Śaṅkarācārya, *Śivamahimnaḥ Stotra*) Thus, the *nirmālya* of Śiva is the most excellent of all things. It is not to be avoided by anyone. It is the supreme means for attaining the highest goal. Whether by way of excellence or by way of deficiency,
we do not know what kind of latent impression (vāsanā) there could be, or for whose sake it exists;
since that which belongs to one who has been initiated and that which belongs to one who has fallen are of an identical form.
The sages reject even the most desirable food.
By what kind of mental impression (*vāsanā*) is contact with a Caṇḍāla, a Caṇḍilī, a funeral pyre, a liquor-seller, or with cows, Brahmins, fire, or women consecrated for a vow, prohibited?
Or, when touched, purification is effected by the recitation of auspicious stories.
They say that even one who has been initiated and is like fire himself must avoid food;
yet once he has received his royal fee, he may eat.
A conch shell is purifying, but the bone of humans is impure.
"In this matter, the established statement is our ultimate authority.

Therefore, this must be explained after careful discernment: is the *nirmālya* of Śiva to be avoided by some because of its excellence (*utkarṣa*), or rather because of its inferiority (*apakarṣa*)? It is said: the *nirmālya* of Śiva...

There is no room for dispute regarding the fact that [He] possesses all the most excellent qualities, such as being the remover of all sins; for even in those Purāṇas and Āgamas where a prohibition of Him has been made, it is established therein that He nonetheless possesses such qualities. Indeed, [these qualities] are heard of in the Purāṇas and Āgamas.
The scriptural statements:
"The water for washing the feet and the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) should be worn with devotion and great effort;
sins born of mind, speech, and body do not touch such a person."
The man who, out of devotion, eats that which is praised as pure becomes a pure-souled Brahmin; his sin is swiftly destroyed.
Those who have taken refuge in me should always wear the water and flowers from my grace;
this should be done with special care by the sick and those afflicted by poison.
And whatever is given to one's own chosen liṅga, it is like the offering of sacrificial porridge (caru); of this there is no doubt.
O Nārada, one obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
The water from the feet is a great sacred ford, as are the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers,
the Narmadā, the Sarayū, O brahmins, and likewise the Godāvarī river.
O sage, these [deities] are always present in the bathing water of Śambhu;
indeed, that bathing water of Śambhu, which contains all sacred fords (tīrthas), is worthy of being utilized.
Whoever gives ten thousand cows to a Śrotriya who maintains the sacred fires shall obtain that same fruit by bathing in the water at my feet.
And so forth. Furthermore, in the medical treatises (Vaidyaśāstra):
"By drinking the water of the floral offerings (nirmālya) of the trident-bearing God of gods, one is liberated from consumption, leprosy, fever, asthma, and even from sins."
In the Rāmāyaṇa also: "There, the celestial sages, Gandharvas, and those dwelling on the surface of the earth,
touched the water fallen from the body of Bhava, thinking it to be pure."
In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as well:
"Or rather, do not others besides you— such as Brahmā and the rest— know that the one called Śiva is inauspicious, having scattered his matted hair in the cremation ground?"

"Having purified that [water], they bear upon their heads what has been cast from his feet by the ashes, the skull-bowl, and the Piśācas dwelling there. Thus, regarding the touch of even the supremely purifying *śivanirmālya* (the remains of offerings to Śiva):
The prohibition for certain individuals regarding the touching of the Śivaliṅga is indeed due to their lack of qualification, just like the prohibition [against touching] the Śivaliṅga itself.

For instance, although the Śivaliṅga was previously a particular worldly stone, through the purificatory rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā-saṃskāra*), its impure form— which is a transformation of *māyā*— is cast off, and it becomes composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*).
Just as that which has been "born" immediately thereafter becomes untouchable for those who have not been initiated (p.

326), so too the *nirmālya*— having become such through the multitude of purificatory rites such as inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and others— is thereafter consumed by Śiva as being fit for His own enjoyment.
Consequently, it became utterly pure, and therefore it was untouchable for them. With this intention, it is stated in the *Vātulottara*:
"In the case of well-established *liṅgas*, the former mental disposition [of impurity] no longer applies."
"Likewise, one should not recall the former name of Śivaprasāda.

Thus, such *śivanirmālya* (the remains of offerings to Śiva) is to be touched only by those devotees of Śiva whose impurities have been shaken off through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and whose bonds (*pāśa*) have been severed; for them, it is like the *liṅga* of Śiva itself.

And by his command, they were to be fed; for those devotees of Śiva, through the initiation of Śiva and by means of the daily practice of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the ritual placement of the staff and the tonsure (*daṇḍamuṇḍakalānyāsa*),
had attained a non-material form like that of the Śiva-linga and the sacred remains of Śiva (*śivanirmālya*).
Considering those who possess bodies composed of Rudra to be merely ordinary beings due to their similarity in having hands, feet, and so forth,
the wise person does not hold them in contempt.

This is because of the statement in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*. As for the objection raised—that despite possessing qualities such as the removal of all sins, why has this [practice] not become common to everyone like a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)—that too is refuted by this very point: [it is because of its connection with] touching the extremely pure remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) to Śiva.
For it has been stated that others lack the qualification [for this].

Indeed, Vedic hymns such as the Aghamarṣaṇa, which remove great sins like the killing of a Brahmin, do not become common to those outside the three higher castes who lack the qualification even for hearing the Vedas. Not so.
There is no deficiency whatsoever in the Vedic hymn by that much; rather, there is indeed an excellence.
With this very intention, the Lord spoke in the Purāṇas:
"The impure soul, out of a desire for purification, [should partake of] my supreme, purifying food."
"By consuming it, one meets destruction, just as a Śūdra does by [studying] Vedic recitation and the like.
As for the doubt raised— that since the offering to Śiva (śivanirmālya) is as utterly pure as the chanting of Śiva’s names, why has it not become common to all?— to that we reply:

Even though the name of Śiva is exceedingly pure and non-worldly (aprākṛta), by the command of Śiva it has become common to all; so too has the five-syllabled Vedic jewel of a living being (jīvaratna) composed of that [name]. For instance, it is said in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
In this Kali age, turbid and difficult to overcome,
when the world is shrouded by the darkness of demerit and turned away from dharma;
When the conduct of the castes and stages of life has declined, when social confusion has arisen,
when all authority is in doubt, or when there is a certain perversion [of that authority].
When the instruction of the Guru has not been imparted and the lineage of teacher and disciple has passed away,
by what means, O Maheśvara, are Your devotees liberated?
To this question of Ambikā, Śiva replied:
"By taking refuge in my supreme and heart-pleasing five-syllabled mantra (vidyā),
men born in the Kali age, whose souls are purified by devotion, are liberated."
For those who are corrupted by faults born of mind, speech, and body—beyond the reach of description or recollection;
for those who are ungrateful, merciless, and deceitful in nature.
Even for those who are greedy and crooked-minded, if their hearts are inclined toward me,
my five-syllabled Vidyā removes the fear of saṃsāra.
"O Goddess, I have made this vow many times upon the surface of the earth:
even one who has fallen may be liberated if he is my devotee by means of this vidyā.
And again:
