If a mortal has fallen, he becomes entirely unfit for ritual action;
indeed, whatever rite is performed by one unfit for action leads only to hell.
Then, regarding Ambikā’s question, "How can one who has fallen [into sin] be liberated by this knowledge?", Śiva spoke these words:
"What you have said is true; nevertheless, listen, O beautiful one."
Thinking this to be a secret, I previously concealed it;
yet, if out of delusion one should worship me while fallen [in status], accompanied by the mantra.
"Without my five-syllabled mantra, one will undoubtedly become a denizen of hell.
Thus, because it was brought about for the common benefit of all by the command of Śiva, it is also designated therein as "accomplished through command" (ājñāsiddha).

"Therefore, this statement—which consists of few syllables, is rich in meaning, is the essence of the Vedas, bestows liberation, is established by the Command (ājñā), is free from doubt, and has Śiva as its soul—is [authoritative]. Thus, the greatness of the name 'Śiva' is inconceivable. (p. 328) Therefore, the majesty of his name is beyond the reach of logic.
It is indeed appropriate that [the status of] outcasts, Caṇḍālas, and so forth is common to all; enough with this elaboration. Let us return to the subject at hand.

As for the statement cited that "the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva is not food for human beings" and so forth, that refers specifically to the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva that has been offered to Caṇḍa. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having brought the *nirmālya*, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa."
That from which one attains purity is proclaimed as *nirmālya*.
Having given water for rinsing the mouth to Caṇḍa, one should discard the floral remains (nirmālya);
one should offer it either into deep water, into fire, or even to cows.
Because the rule for the ritual disposal [of the offering] in water and so forth is prescribed immediately after the offering to Caṇḍa, and because it is stated therein:

"The food of Caṇḍa, which is difficult to overcome, must be avoided with great effort," and because it is said that property belonging to a deity or the food of Caṇḍa is not fit for the enjoyment of others, such is the case regarding the substance of Caṇḍa.

This is because, by establishing that [the offering] is entirely unfit for consumption, it follows that only that much [of the substance] requires such treatment regarding water and other elements. Now, if this were the case, it would follow that everything offered to Śiva (*śivanirmālya*) is indeed unfit for consumption.
Liquids to be licked, foods to be sucked, edibles, drinks, and so forth, as well as betel, garlands, and ointments—
all these remains of your offerings are given to you by the command of Śiva.

If it is argued that, according to the indicative marks of the mantra for the offering to Caṇḍa, it is understood that all *śivanirmālya* (the remains of Śiva’s worship) must be offered to Caṇḍa— this is not so; for in the *Kāmika* [Tantra],
regarding worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), it says:
One should worship Caṇḍa in the northeast with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order;
one should offer to him all the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) that have been prepared.
Having thus stated that all *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) must be offered to Caṇḍeśa, [the text continues]:
"Some say it should be placed on the top of the *liṅga*; others, on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*);
or one should take what is on the pedestal to the northeast, or outside to the chamber of Caṇḍa."

Since it has been stated that there is even a position of offering only a single portion of the perfumes, flowers, and remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), by that same logic one may infer the acceptance of a position of offering only a single portion of the food presented (*niveditānna*). As it is said elsewhere: "The garlands, perfumes, food, drink, and so forth, when enjoyed by Śiva..."
It is declared that what has been thus offered is supreme and removes all sins.

(On page 329: "Among the six kinds of *nirmālya*, only the food (*bhojya*) is offered. This is because it is explicitly established that the true nature of what is offered is distinct from the substances [intended for] Caṇḍa. Furthermore, in the case of worship performed for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*), there is no room for such doubt; for it is stated in the Kāmika itself:

After the description of the worship of Śiva, having begun with the statement "at the end, one should worship Caṇḍeśvara," [the text] prohibits the worship of Caṇḍa by stating: "Caṇḍeśa is not [worshipped] in the case of an image made of stone, metal, wood, or one that is consecrated (*siddha*), nor in the case of a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) [liṅga]. Furthermore, even in the *Ajita*, regarding worship for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*): [it states the same prohibition].
No worship of the gateway should be performed, nor the offering to Caṇḍeśa; there should be no invocation or sacrificial oblation there, nor even a daily festival.

Thus, because of that prohibition; however, if the worship of Caṇḍa is performed according to the previously cited statement from the Kālottara, there is still no fault. And in the Aṃśumatī, in the chapter on the worship of Caṇḍeśa:
"It is considered to be threefold: purely innate (sahaja), and independent (svatantra)."
It is taught that for one's own sake alone, one should perform worship within the mandala.
The limb of Yama is to be known as innate (sahaja) and established in its fierce form;
if the limb of Yama were independent, the worship of Caṇḍeśa would be threefold.
Thus, having introduced the threefold worship of Caṇḍeśa, regarding the worship of Caṇḍa at the conclusion of the sacrifice for one's own sake, [it is said]:
"Having offered ointment and a garland with its root mantra,
one should likewise cause the food offering and betel to be given with that very same root mantra."
Having thus described the worship of the incense, flowers, and so forth as distinct [from the preceding], it is said: "The worship of the Kevala has been declared; now hear the worship of the Sahaja.
It is performed within the region of the inner mandala and within the range of the mandala."

"The wise one should install Caṇḍeśa and worship him with the *nirmālya* alone," because it is stated that the offering of the *nirmālya* occurs specifically in the worship of Caṇḍeśvara, who is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of Yama.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*, in the section on the worship of Caṇḍa:
Having offered the food oblation as prescribed in the ritual manual, together with betel leaf,
one should also present that which was consumed by Śiva, including the remnants of his limbs.
And because it has been stated thus: "One should offer the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva to Caṇḍeśa.
Furthermore, in accordance with the subtle statement found in the section on worship for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*), there is no fault even in the view that the *nirmālya* is offered to Caṇḍeśa.
(p. 330) Because, according to the method described for worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), it is possible to offer even a single portion of that [offering];
and in the *Smṛtinibandhas* it is said:
"A hundredth part of the food offering (*naivedya*) should be given to Viṣvaksena."
And he offered water for washing the feet and the prasāda to Caṇḍeśvara at the liṅga.
This is because it is established that [the portion] consisting of a hundredth part is indeed the portion for Caṇḍa. Thus,

in accordance with the statements of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, regarding the statement in the *Suprabheda* that "this is the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva," that which is the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva is offered to Caṇḍeśa.
The meaning is that it is not to be consumed by ordinary humans. Alternatively, this is its intended sense:

the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Śiva is not to be consumed by mere humans who are like animals (*paśu*) and devoid of the realization of being servants of Śiva. Therefore, [it is not to be used] for the sake of worldly desires.

Whether in worship for the sake of others or in worship for one's own sake, when a great abundance of sacrificial offerings has been presented, [one should provide for] those temple attendants who are unable to eat that much, as well as for the householders of the priests and others who have received Śiva-initiation.
If Śiva-devotees are not available, one must not give what remains after offering to them to just any ordinary person; rather, it should be given to cows or elephants,
or else thrown into deep water, into fire, or buried in the ground— this is the ultimate rule.

Just as in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, when the officiating priests lack the capacity to consume the remnants of the oblation, the remaining oblation given to those priests must not be given to members of other castes who have not been initiated; rather, it should be given only to those who have been initiated.
It should be given to Brahmins and others, or else thrown into the fire; this is the primary rule:
if the officiating priests are unable to consume the remnants of the oblation, they should either bestow them upon other Brahmins or cast them into the sacrificial fire.
Such is the statement. Or, for example, just as the rule that "in the absence of a Śūdra who is a slave or one who eats the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa,

it should be thrown into water or buried in the ground" is intended to apply specifically to cases of incapacity— as expressed in the statement, "one should bury it in the ground or cast it into water"— it is with this very intention that it has been said.
Haradattācārya says:
"They record in the Smṛti that when it is said, 'You are a Brāhmaṇa,' food is declared unfit to be eaten for you among the assembly of those who dwell in heaven."
"O Lord, even the leavings of the twice-born, though excellent,
must be cast upon the ground or submerged in water.
According to this verse, even when a servant exists who eats the leavings, those leavings [must be disposed of] on the ground...
The intended meaning is not that one should immerse oneself in water; rather, it is stated [in the scripture]:
"Only the leavings and worn-out garments should be given" (p.
331) to one who has entered into service and desires to perform attendance.

Because of the traditional teaching that one should give the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*) to a Śūdra, and because of the Smṛti texts stating that service consists of giving worn-out sandals, umbrellas, clothing, and brooms, as well as eating the leavings and following the profession of an artisan—
this [duty] belongs to the Śūdra. In this very same way, to you...

Regarding the statement "that which is offered [to another] is unfit for consumption," the intended meaning here is that even for one who is worthy of eating what has been offered to Śiva and has surrendered to the state of being a servant of Śiva (śivadāsya), if such a person is not available, it must not be given to just anyone; rather, it should be disposed of by means of digging it up or similar methods. Thus, by this verse, the Teachers have expressed [this matter] with the highest excellence.
It has already been clearly established that the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) should be discarded by those other than [Śiva’s] servants, and not taken away; however,

in order to demonstrate— through the bold assertion (*prauḍhi*) in the subsequent verses beginning with "utkarṣate"— that the description of the excellence of Śiva’s grace (*tatprasāda*) is not relevant to the present treatise which defines the excellence of Śiva himself.
An obscure method has been adopted.

However, those [texts] which establish that even what is offered to one's own chosen *liṅga* must be given specifically to brothers, sons, sisters, and so forth, refer to the case of the worshipper of Śiva who performs the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) as his meal; for by that [rite], he himself [partakes].

It is impossible to consume [it] [in the ordinary sense], because by the very act of one's own eating—which consists of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) dedicated to Śiva—the purpose of one's own self, namely satisfaction, is also accomplished as a matter of course. However, giving it to those who are uninitiated is prohibited;
rather, like the remnants of sacrificial oblations (*havis*) from rites such as the *iṣṭi*, it must be consumed according to the proper rule in order to avoid the fault of neglect.
This must be established: for those who have been initiated, the eating of that [food] bestows great fruit.

Therefore, in response to the inquiry as to "to whom it should be given," these [scriptural passages] are intended to mean that it should be given even to women, children, and others who, though not initiated, are nonetheless ineligible for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) within one's own home. As for that which...
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having stepped over the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Stepping over it is equal to touching it; touching it is equal to selling it or eating it."
Thus, just as in the case of leaping over [a sacred fire], there is a prescription for expiation even for the initiated upon touching the *nirmālya* (the remains of offerings), as it is said:
"Whatever has been touched by the *nirmālya*, or by a person who has eaten it..."
In that regard, the previously mentioned [penance] is reduced by one-quarter for touching, crossing over, or eating [the forbidden substance].

Thus is the prescription for penance upon touching one who has touched the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) or its consumer; in all these instances, the term *nirmālya* refers specifically to the *nirmālya* that has been cast outside. In that section on penance:
The property of the deity (*devasva*), the substance belonging to the deity (*devatādravya*), the offering already presented (*naivedya*),
and the substance for Caṇḍa (*caṇḍadravya*), as well as the *nirmālya*— thus the *nirmālya* is of six kinds.
This is because the specific designation *nirmālya* is applied particularly to that which has been cast outside.
"Even that which has been offered to the deity [and] remains on the pedestal is not *nirmālya* (remains of an offering) once the deity has been dismissed.
Thus, even after the dismissal of the deity, until the point of casting it outside,
[the text] refers to "the property of the deity" (*devasva*) in the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*) in order to avoid the need for expiation regarding its touch.

This is because the absence of the status of *nirmālya* (remnant offering) is described by the words "devāta-dravyam" (the substance of the deity). Otherwise, if the word *nirmālya* occurring in the injunctions for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) were to refer to all *nirmālya* without exception,
it would follow that the specific designation of *nirmālya* as "cast outside" (*bahiḥ-kṣipta*) would be rendered redundant.
Furthermore, it would lead to the absurdity of describing the absence of impurity (*nirmālya*) even after the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), up until the point of casting [the offerings] outside;
for there is no fault in touching the ground of the deity or those things touched by them.

Furthermore, because the terms *sparśa*, *prāyaścitta*, and *nirmālya* occurring therein must necessarily refer to specific objects: that which is called "cast outside" refers to what remains after being given to the attendant devotees during the great offerings of sacrificial food (*mahāhaviḥ-nivedana*) and so forth.

Whatever has been led out from the cow, elephant, and so forth; whatever has been thrown into water and the like; or whatever has been given away for the purpose of an external offering—all that, by the force of the scriptural injunction, becomes as untouchable as the sacrificial post (yūpa) immediately after the consecration of the post.

If it is argued that, in that case, since the instructions regarding penance for consuming *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) and so forth would apply only to those [substances] merely cast outside, then the prescription of penance for the consumption and so forth of *devasva* (the property of the deity), *devatā-dravya* (the substance belonging to the deity), and *nivedya* (the offered food), as well as *caṇḍa-dravya* (substances dedicated to Caṇḍa), would not be obtained—[we reply]: no; because it is precisely in that very context [that they are addressed].

Following the prescription of penances for the eating, neglecting, giving away, selling, stepping over, and touching of *nirmālya*, as well as for the eating, stepping over, and touching of that which has been touched by one who has eaten or stepped over the *nirmālya*—

[The text continues: "In the case of eating, stepping over, or touching *nirmālya*, or [the food] eaten, stepped over, or touched by one who has consumed or stepped over *nirmālya*, after the rules for expiation have been stated— "

Taking other objects belonging to a temple—such as those arising from a village of deities or the like—as well as rice and so forth, by whatever means or pretext, and then consuming them; [this is theft].
"He who does so is deluded; he is considered a stealer of what belongs to us [the deity] due to his impurity.

By such statements, the scriptures describe distinct expiations for the consumption or giving away of the property of the deity, the materials offered to the deity, and the *caṇḍa* (discarded) substances. Thus, it is stated in the *Sūkṣmāgama*:

For stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) or the food presented to the deity (nivedya), or for giving them away, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; furthermore, one should cast [the transgressor] out from among cows and elephants.

Thus, because the offering (nivedya) is taken separately from the remains of the offering (nirmālya), the specific application of the term *nirmālya* to those items mentioned in the instructions for expiation indicates that it refers exclusively to those things that have been merely cast outside.

Otherwise, if those [six items] were intended solely as the six kinds of *nirmālya*, then since the *nivedana* would also be included therein, the separate mention of the *nivedya* would be redundant. As for that which is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"If he has been sprinkled with the water used for bathing, milk, and so forth..."
One should bathe, or otherwise wash, both above and below the navel.
This same principle is prescribed even for the mobile liṅga (caraliṅga) in the sacrificial hall;
thus,
at the time of Śiva’s consecration, [the rite is performed] by sprinkling substances such as consecration water, milk, and curd from above.
The procedure for bathing and washing by means of dividing the body with curd is not intended to imply that the drops of water from the consecration of Śiva are impure for the worshipper;
for the excellence of the water used in the consecration of Śiva and so forth has already been elaborated upon previously, but rather [this is said] immediately thereafter.

It is improper for one whose body is moistened by the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) to perform the anointing with perfumes and other services for Śiva that are to be performed by the priest; likewise, it is improper for a disciple whose body is stained by drops of oil after having performed the massage and bathing of his guru.

This is said with the intention that it is like the application of fragrant ointments and so forth for the Guru. In this manner, other similar plausible statements should also be interpreted accordingly. Thus, those who eat with the thought that it is the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*) should consume the remains of what has been offered. For those who eat with the thought that it is service (*dāsya*), [they should consume] what has been offered.
The rule that "one should eat" is faultless; and this has also been shown in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:
"Then one should oneself eat pure food as one pleases, or what has been offered to the Lord of Gods, for the sake of one's own purification."
One who has faith should not offer [it] out of greed, nor that which has been presented to a fierce person;
this same rule applies to perfumes, garlands, and whatever else may be offered there.
But a wise person should not form the notion "I am Śiva" therein. Thus [it is said].
While eating the offered food, one should contemplate Śiva as residing within the fire in the center of the lotus of one's own heart;
intending thereby that one is performing the worship of Śiva in the form of the Śiva-agnikārya (fire-rite), one should maintain the realization: "I am Śiva."
One should act; however, the meaning is that one should cultivate only the consciousness of being a servant of Śiva.
Thus, by one who eats the food offered [to the deity], even the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis) must be performed with that very same offered food.
The man who performs the Prāṇāgnihotra by the grace of Śiva alone shall obtain the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices for every single grain of rice offered.
Thus, according to the statement in the Śiva Purāṇa.
(p. 334) The Procedure for Eating:
Next is the procedure for eating—(having offered oblations with the mantras prescribed in one's own Sūtra ending in *svāhā*, one should dismiss them;
having thus completed the fire-ritual,) with hands washed and having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*).
Accompanied by Śiva-devotees of virtuous conduct, avoiding those of low birth and the uninitiated from sharing the same row,
he reaches the place for eating and sits upon a seat facing east;
[the area] marked with four, three, two, or one line according to the sequence of the Ācārya, Putraka, Sādhaka, and Samayika, measured by a square hand-span.
On the ground adorned with a mandala marked by lines of ash on all sides,
there should be a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or bell-metal, purified seven times with ash and consecrated with the Aghora mantra; or, in its absence, [another suitable vessel].
Having placed a vessel made of blameless leaves such as those of the plantain, palāśa, lotus, mango, or madhūka tree,

and having spread ghee therein, one should sprinkle with water using the Astra-mantra the pure food that has been served— doubly anointed with ghee and presented with side-dishes— and [place it] in three [parts].
Having consecrated [the food] seven times with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having performed the sprinkling and other rites according to the respective colors,
one should offer food in the measure of half a morsel to Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.

One should offer [the oblation] on a circle smeared with cow dung on one's own right side, saying, "Svāhā to the secondary vital airs (upaprāṇavāyu). Then, having offered a handful of water to the Nāgas and others using the *sruva* ladle with the little finger of the left hand, [one should prepare] water sufficient for the immersion of a black gram (*māṣa*).

Having sipped the remaining water with the *amṛta-mantra*, one should perform the five oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*). By means of that, one should contemplate the satisfaction of the vital breaths— *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*— in their respective order, as well as the selves dependent upon them, the sources of the elements, the ancestors dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, and the gods.

Then, after eating as much as one desires, one takes the leftover food and gives it to the inhabitants of hell on the ground with the formula "svāhā. Following the *uttarāpośana* (the final sipping of water), one pours out the remainder of that water using the little finger, and performs the subsequent rites beginning with the wiping of the hands and ending with the pure *ācamana*.

Having performed [this] (for the purpose of purifying the fault of eating, one should sprinkle Kālāgnirudra, who resides at the tip of the big toe of the right foot, with water from the big toe of the right hand),
one should sprinkle Kālāgnirudra with water from the tip of the big toe. However, regarding the eating of those who eat what has not been offered:
The distinction has already been shown by the example from the *Suprabheda*.

Regarding those who eat what has been offered and those who eat what has not been offered, apart from the time of eating, whatever else there may be— whether food such as medicine, betel, or water, or objects of enjoyment such as perfumes and flowers— [is to be understood accordingly].
One should offer all that [one receives] to the Deity with the mind and then consume it. (p.
335) One should never eat a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, drink, or medicine without having first offered them to the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva.
Thus, from the *Kāmika*:
"Whatever object is present before one for the sake of enjoyment,
having offered that to the Deity, one should perform it with self-devotion."
This is also because of the statement in the Vātula-tantra:
"The wise man, having offered food, medicine, water, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth to Śiva, should eat the remainder of that."

Thus, the rule for consuming the remnants of medicines and other items that have been offered pertains specifically to those medicines and such things that are to be taken during the course of a meal by one who is performing the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and is therefore eating what has not been formally offered. However, in other cases, only the remains of what has been offered to Śiva (*śivocchiṣṭa*) should be consumed by the servants of Śiva. Furthermore, by the devotee...

Whatever worldly or Vedic action one intends to perform with a view toward any particular fruit, all of that should be performed with the realization that it is of the nature of worshiping Śiva. Furthermore, the pleasure arising from those various actions is also enjoyed by Śiva as its enjoyer; thus, one should think: "I am merely enjoying that very pleasure which has already been enjoyed by Śiva."
One should enjoy with a state of being. Thus, even without one's own effort,

the objects known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell that present themselves should be experienced by one’s own senses, preceded by their dedication to Śiva and with the thought that they are His leftovers (ucchiṣṭa).
Even the pleasure arising from the experience of various objects should be enjoyed only with the understanding that it is their leavings.
Whatever action is to be performed and arises again,
the wise person should perform each of those with the thought of offering them to Mahādeva.
Whatever pleasure has arisen from the senses, having offered that to Śiva and obtained his grace, it should be enjoyed through the medium of the senses.
Thus it is heard in the Vātula [Tantra]. And for that purpose, the devotee must always remain vigilant:
"In unions and in separations, he who would constantly and vigilantly offer even atom-sized pleasures to his chosen liṅgas."
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse, he whose mind is dedicated to Śiva is a devotee; he is not otherwise.
Thus, because it is heard in the *Bṛhatkālottara*: "In this way, for one who performs an action preceded by the offering of the action itself,
who experiences objects preceded by the offering of the objects, and who experiences pleasure preceded by the offering of the pleasure produced by each [object]," [pleasure is attained].
And for one who eats with mindfulness, even if by virtue of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous births he occasionally commits a forbidden act through negligence,
or experiences forbidden objects, or enjoys forbidden pleasures, there is no staining by sin.

It happens; however, for one who contemplates that everything is the propitiation of Śiva, even everything becomes solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva. In that regard, [one should avoid] those forms of play intended for one's own enjoyment, such as watching dances, or sporting in palaces, gardens, and ponds.
When undertaking an action, at the time of that specific action, there are [results] to be accomplished through the operations of the organs of action— speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—
as well as those to be accomplished through the respective objects produced by the organs of cognition— ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
And for the purpose of bestowing pleasures, [the Lord] [bestows] the ears and so forth,

as well as the organs of action such as speech, upon Īśāna and the other [faces], who are respectively present as presiding deities over His own five cognitive faculties beginning with hearing and the five organs of action beginning with speech.
Having unified one's own ears and other senses with speech and the rest,

and having contemplated those very pleasures— which are accomplished through the operations of each respective sense— as being experienced by Śiva, the presiding lord of the forms [of the deities] such as Aiśāna, one should regard them as the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) of Śiva.

One should enjoy [the offerings] oneself. Being unable to remain vigilant at every moment of encountering those various objects—which effortlessly present the pleasures of the sense-objects—one may do so either in the morning or at the conclusion of the Śiva-pūjā, thinking: "Until this time tomorrow..."

Thinking, "I offer to Śiva the pleasures born from the experience of objects consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are presented with effort yet effortlessly," one should offer them all simultaneously.
In this way, there is the simultaneous offering of objects, either in the heart and other centers, or for that which is contemplated within the locations such as the heart.

This [offering] should be performed either in the ears and other sense organs of Sāmbaśiva; or in the ears and other sense organs located in the faces of Īśāna and the others, who constitute Sadāśiva as manifested in locations such as the heart; or in the ears and other sense organs of Īśāna and the others, which are unified with one's own ears and other sense organs. In all cases, this applies to the act of offering.

The mantra "namontaḥ śivamantra eva mantraḥ" (the mantra ending in *namaḥ* is indeed the Śiva-mantra). Its meaning should be meditated upon as: "This is for Śiva, not for me. And that meaning is obtained by the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) of the word *mama*, which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, all of this is a supreme secret. In this manner, every day at dawn—
Having performed worship preceded by contemplation of Śiva, ritual bathing, and the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
one should worship Śiva at three times, two times, or once a day, using forty, sixteen, ten, or five offerings— or even merely with eight flowers— as the occasion permits.

Worshipping the Śiva-scriptures, studying them, listening to discourses on Śiva, and at the time of eating, either accepting the remnants of what has been offered to Śiva with the intent of performing the Śiva-fire-rite, or accepting what has been offered to Śiva with the intent of serving Śiva; (p. 337) [he attains liberation].
Having offered all other objects of enjoyment— such as betel, water, perfumes, flowers, and the like— to Śiva, one should consume them;

and while performing whatever actions one intends to do, one should contemplate that the resulting pleasures are for the enjoyment of Śiva, and thus perform those acts with one's own effort through the mindset of worshipping Śiva.

Even when objects of the senses present themselves spontaneously at their respective times of appearance, one should offer them simultaneously to Śiva; experiencing all pleasures with the thought that they are the remnants of Śiva (śivocchiṣṭa), even during the time of deliberating on external worldly affairs, ultimately...

He contemplated the line of bliss (*ānandalekhā*), which consists of the nectar of unsurpassed light, moving through the internal path by means of its inward and outward movements and bringing it to fruition through constant reflection upon the names and forms of Śiva, while also perceiving it during the [five] moments (*samaya*).

The supreme deity of the five syllables, whose lotus feet are sought after by many Upaniṣads, the sovereign of all goddesses, an ocean of boundless compassion, the bearer of the burden of protecting those who have taken refuge in him,
sporting together with Ambikā within the hollow of the lotus of his own heart— the embodiment of a mass of bliss.
Constantly beholding the Supreme Śiva with his inner vision, he may dwell in happiness together with his beloved kinsmen.

On this point, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: even all this taught in the Āgamas— namely, bathing, the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*), the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads according to Vedic tradition, the recitation of the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*), and the worship of the door-keepers during the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*)— belongs to Śiva alone, yet it is internally contradictory regarding its preceding and succeeding parts.

The inclination toward the worship of other deities such as Viṣṇu; the specific mudrās mentioned in the secondary (upacāra) rites which are accomplished through the activity of both hands; the installation of a *liṅga* in Vedic and other traditions; the showing of lamps preceded by the ringing of a bell with the left hand; and in some cases, the fire sacrifice (*homa*)—all such things [are excluded].
Regarding how this is established, the essential point here is as follows:
"Devotion to Śiva arises in those men who have perfected themselves through many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, and whose sins have been exhausted."

Through the consideration of numerous such authorities (*pramāṇa*), the excellence of Vedic rites is described; since even the Vīraśaivas must accomplish Śiva-bhakti— which is of the nature of a goal— by means of ritual actions as its instruments, the worship of any deity other than Him is not [permitted].

We accept this as the primary view; however, describing all deities as specific manifestations of the Supreme Lord in the form of the Consort (Śakti), and thus as being useful for the worship of Śiva, is the supreme joy of gold. There is no room for any suspicion of contradiction whatsoever.
These categories of reality, which were taught in the *Dvātriṃśad-upadeśa*, have been heard;
for they are all included within the worship of Śiva and must be described individually.
The one hundred and one stages, beginning with the *piṇḍa* and ending with the *jñānaśūnya*, are likewise contained within the six stages; such are the thirty-two instructions.
They are included within the worship of Śiva; thus it is described as follows: worship is of two kinds, namely worship with attributes (saguṇopāsanā) and worship without attributes (nirguṇopāsanā).
Although the thirty-two subjects of instruction constitute the limbs of worship with attributes, [they are nevertheless included].

According to the Tantra, it should be understood that the meaning of the first four instructions is primarily intended as an auxiliary to the worship of the Attributeless (Nirguṇa), just as the deities to whom oblations are offered in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice serve as auxiliaries to the Soma sacrifice by means of completing the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* rite itself.

(The state of being a means of accomplishment) is the door [to the goal], because the Soma sacrifice alone is the intended object. And in the present context, the fourfold teaching on the means which are limbs of the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is also useful for the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa); for even in the meditation on the qualified...

Because the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) alone is the intended goal, the other instructions are also, through a traditional lineage, merely limbs of the worship of the attributeless. These twenty-eight forms of worship appear as worship with attributes (saguṇa); and this is indeed authorized by the Vedic system, not merely Tantric.

Because the Vedic-Tantric system is superior to the purely Tantric system, the Vedic Vīraśaiva doctrine— beginning with "One only, without a second"— is authoritative. All dualistic and other systems, being purely Tantric, are to be disregarded as lacking authority, since they contradict the unified harmony of the Tantras and Āgamas.
The practices mentioned in both the Tantras and the Vedas have been collected and established without contradiction.

Just as by worshipping the King alone, or by honoring the entire circle of his ministers with offerings such as garments, it is through the King's own pleasure that great satisfaction arises for the King himself; so it is in the case of [the Lord] endowed with qualities.

The worship of that gatekeeper brings about the exaltation of Śiva himself; however, it has been described in the Āgamas that the worship of another deity— whether by regarding them as equal to Śiva or as superior to him—
leads to falling into hell, just as [offending] a king through equality with a king or superiority over a king [leads to punishment].

If there is anger from the king regarding service to another [deity], then the king’s traitor, marked with the seal of a dog and so forth, must be expelled from the country; likewise, creating opposition through equality with or superiority over Śiva leads to hell—let the details suffice. In the *Vātulottara*, Śiva speaks these words to the Goddess:
O Goddess of the gods, the very meaning of the Vedas has been clearly described by me to you in due order, out of affection for you, through the Kāmika and other Āgamas.
He who reviles the meaning of the Vedas, he who reviles my scripture, and he who contradicts my scripture— even if he be a follower of the Vedas— falls away in an instant.
Conformity with the Vedas and the Āgamas is obtained through my grace; my devotee is equal to one who follows the Vedas and the Āgamas, without a doubt.
Therein, I shall likewise tell you the secret known as Vīraśaiva:
one should contemplate that everything has been attained simply by hearing the word "Śiva."
Aversion toward those things opposed to it is the primary cause of my pleasure;
even by sacrificing one's life, one should become preeminent in the dharma of Śiva.
Both the one who harbors secret malice and the one who acts openly hostile are destined for hell;
yet so too is he who, though himself a knower of all scriptures, is diligent in the rites of Śiva.
One who converses with those bearing other sectarian marks, who dwells together with them, and who is filled with affection for my enemies is called an "internal traitor" (antardrohī).
He who harms others externally and bears other marks should be known as such;
he may be liberated at the end of a kalpa, but one who harbors internal malice is not liberated.
This alone is the conduct of the community; this alone is the worship of Śiva;
this alone is spiritual practice—the total avoidance of those who harm me.
O Goddess, those who are marked with ashes, those who are adorned with rudrākṣa beads,
and those who mutter the five-syllabled mantra— one should perceive them as my very form.
For devotion alone, O Goddess, brings about the fruit for all in the Vedas and the Āgamas; yet in the presence of doubt, it perishes.

Whether he be a non-devotee or a devotee, by recognizing those who are proficient in the meaning of what I have spoken as being my very own form, he shall place his trust in them and attain liberation.
Trust is the supreme liberation; trust itself bestows all goals. Even a wise man perishes through lack of trust in the scriptures.
The patron who is capable should perform worship, especially with faith, toward those mobile liṅgas,
or toward the prāṇaliṅga or the stationary (sthāṇu) liṅga.
In those various teachings, the clear meaning is as follows:
it was spoken by Śiva; therefore, all Vīraśaivism is indeed Vedic.
(340) All men whose minds are defiled by the impurities of the Kali age, not knowing the primordial Vīraśaiva doctrine which is higher than the highest, fall into delusion.
In whom Śambhu’s grace resides, his mind shall flow toward this [path].
Śiva alone is the supreme truth; worship of him bestows liberation.
I shall now briefly proclaim the explanation of the ritual procedure for worship,
as it was taught by Śiva himself to Śivā within the Śiva-śāstra.
Having performed the internal sacrifice (aṅgayāga), which concludes with the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
one may or may not subsequently perform the external sacrifice (bahiryāga).
There, having mentally conceived the substances and purified them,
and having meditated upon the god Vināyaka and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite;
Having properly worshipped Nandīśa in the south and Suyaśas in the north with his mind, he should then prepare the seat.
The lion’s posture (siṃhayoga) joined with the infinite support (ādhārānantasaṃyukta),
or the pure lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with the three principles (tattvatraya).
Above that, one should meditate upon Śiva, accompanied by Ambā, enchanting to all,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and beautiful in every limb.
Endowed with every excellence, adorned with all ornaments,
with red face, hands, and feet, and a countenance with a gentle smile like a kunda flower.
Resembling pure crystal, with three eyes like blooming lotuses,
four-armed, with noble limbs, and bearing the beautiful crescent moon.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding a deer and an axe, auspicious,
the abode of all that is beneficial, with a beautiful blue throat.
Then, one should contemplate Maheśvarī on his left side, who is beyond all comparison and surrounded by her devoted retinue.
Her wide and long eyes had the luster of the petals of a full-blown blue lotus;
her face possessed the splendor of the full moon, and her hair was dark and curled.
Resembling the petals of a blue lotus, with a crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
she possesses exceedingly round, thick, lofty, smooth, and plump breasts.
She had a slender waist and broad hips, wore very fine yellow garments,
was adorned with all ornaments, and was radiant with a tilaka on her forehead.
Adorned with a mass of hair strewn with various flowers, her form was graceful in every respect, and her face was slightly downcast with bashfulness.
Holding a blooming golden lotus in her right hand,
with her other hand resting like a staff, she is seated upon a throne.
Having thus meditated upon the God and the Goddess upon their auspicious and excellent throne, one should,
with devotion and all ritual offerings, present the flower of one's inner being.
Alternatively, one may indeed conceptualize any one of the forms of the All-pervading Lord—
whether that of Śiva known as Sadāśiva, or the supreme form of Maheśvara.

Or else, having performed the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth upon one's own body according to the procedure for that which is called the *Ṣaḍviṃśaka* or likewise for that named *Śrīkaṇṭha*, [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon Śiva, who transcends both being and non-being, as embodied within that image,
one should invoke Him in the proper sequence and perform the worship mentally.
Thereafter, one should perform the oblation at the navel with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and other materials;
and one should meditate upon Śiva between the eyebrows, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp.
Thus, whether in the subsidiary rites, the independent sacrifice consisting of meditation,
or at the conclusion of the fire-ritual, the procedure is everywhere exactly the same.
Then, having completed the entire sequence of propitiation consisting of reflection,
one should worship the Lord in this manner either in a *liṅga*, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or in the fire.
One should sprinkle the place of worship with the root mantra to purify it;
one should then scatter flowers there with water scented by sandalwood.
Having dispelled obstacles with the Astra-mantra and protected [the site] with the Varma-mantra,
and having assigned the Astra-mantra to the directions, one should worship the auspicious officiant.
There, having spread darbha grass around and having purified all the vessels by means of washing, sprinkling, and so forth, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.
The sprinkling vessel, the arghya vessel, and after that the pādya vessel,
and then the vessel for the ācamanīya— this is the tetrad.
Having washed, sprinkled, and inspected them, one should then pour auspicious water upon them;
one should arrange all the articles of worship as they are available.
Jewels and the like, silver, gold, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata),
fruits, sprouts, and darbha grass— these are the various kinds of meritorious substances.
One should especially place cool and pleasing flowers and other offerings into the bathing water and the fragrant scented water.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with *uśīra* and sandalwood; likewise, one should include *jātī*, *takkola*, camphor, *bahumūla*, and *tamālaka*.
One should especially cast the powder into the water for sipping (ācamanīya),
and likewise add cardamom, camphor, and sandalwood to all the vessels.
Kusha grass tips, unbroken rice grains, barley, paddy, sesame seeds, clarified butter, white mustard seeds, flowers, and sacred ash should be placed in the arghya vessel.
One should sequentially place kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, tamālaka, and sacred ash into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having placed the mantra everywhere and having enveloped it on the outside with the armor-mantra (varman),
one should thereafter protect it with the weapon-mantra (astra) and display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Having sprinkled all the articles of worship with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using the root mantra, one should then purify them according to the prescribed rule.
In the absence of a single *prokṣaṇī* vessel for all ritual acts, the best of practitioners say that one should prepare the *arghya*; they call this the "general" [procedure].
Then, having worshipped the god Vināyaka according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, one should do so at the southern side of the door.
One should properly worship Nandin himself as the lord of the inner apartments—
resembling a mountain of gold and adorned with all ornaments.
The Lord is gentle, crowned with the crescent moon, three-eyed, and four-armed;
he holds a blazing trident, a deer-horn, and a golden staff.
One with a face like the orb of the moon, or else with the face of a monkey;
and on the side of the northern gate, the wife of Marut, who is his daughter.
Having honored Suyaśā, who was observant of her vows and devoted to adorning the feet of her mother,
he entered the inner apartment of the Supreme Lord.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* or the image (*bera*), one should remove the floral remains (*nirmālya*).
Having washed it, one should place the flower upon one's head for the sake of its purification.
Holding flowers in his hand, he should recite the mantra according to his ability for the purification of the mantra;
having worshipped Caṇḍa in the northeast, he should offer him the remains of the floral offerings (nirmālya).
Afterwards, one should fashion the seat and the supporting base (ādhāra) and so forth in due order;
one should meditate on the auspicious Ādhāra-śakti as dark-complexioned and facing downwards.
In front of her was an endless white serpent with five hoods, coiled in the shape of an earring, its neck uplifted as if licking the very sky.
Upon that is an auspicious four-legged seat strewn with flowers;
its feet are indeed Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
According to their colors— white, yellow, red, dark-blue, and so forth, starting from the southeast (Āgneya)—
the factors beginning with Adharma and ending with Viśeṣaguṇa are situated in order from the east to the north.
One should contemplate his limbs as resembling the lapis lazuli gem (rājāvarta-maṇi).
Then, there is a vast and auspicious lotus seat with its petals facing upward.
They say its eight petals are the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*;
the filaments and so forth are the Rudras, Vāma and the rest, together with the Śaktis, Vāmā and the rest.
The seeds are also those very powers within Manonmanī;
above the pericarp is the stalk of dispassion, which is knowledge whose essence is Śiva.
The one whose self is the dharma of Śiva should place the *kanda* at the end of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) as a triple mandala;
the seat consists of the triad of principles beginning with Ādi, situated within that triple mandala.
One should prepare a divine seat, the face of the offering, spread with various coverings, radiant with pure knowledge.
One should perform the invocation, the installation, the confinement, the inspection,
and the prostration, each time forming the respective mudrā individually.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, and thereafter incense,
a lamp, and betel leaf, one should then bathe the two Śivas.
Alternatively, having thus mentally constructed the seat and the form itself,
one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa by means of the root mantra, as well as by the Brahma-mantras and other mantras.
Likewise, one should invoke Śiva, the supreme cause,
the deity who resembles pure crystal, partless and imperishable.
The supreme cause of all gods, consisting of all worlds,
abiding both within and without, pervading all, subtler than the atom and yet greater than the great.
The immutable Lord is visible to his devotees without effort,
yet he remains beyond the reach even of the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra.
And it is remembered by the learned as the essence of the Vedas, beyond the reach of [ordinary] perception;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, and is the medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
Known as the Śiva-tattva, which exists for the sake of the world as Śiva,
one should worship it with devotion upon the top of the liṅga by means of the five-fold offerings.
At the time of bathing the Liṅgamūrti of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self, one should perform auspicious rites such as the utterance of the word "Victory! (jaya).
With the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) preceded by curd, milk, ghee, honey, and so forth;
with fruits, the essences of fruits, sesame, mustard, and parched grain flour.

Having bathed [the image] with auspicious seeds such as barley and having smeared it with powders derived from black gram and other grains, one should bathe it with warm water after anointing it with flour and similar substances.
One should rub [the image] with bilva leaves and other substances to remove the applied fragrance;
then, having bathed it again with waters according to the ritual protocol for a universal monarch (cakravartin), [one proceeds].
One should offer fragrant garlands and turmeric in the proper sequence;
then, having sprinkled water upon the liṅga or the image (bera), one should proceed.
One should bathe [the deity] with fragrant water and water mixed with *kuśa* grass and flowers,
and then with water containing gold and jewels empowered by mantras, in their proper sequence.
But in the absence of these materials, one should bathe Śiva with faith using whatever materials are available, or even with mere mantras and water.
Then, one should perform the ritual bath preceded by mantras, using either a water-pot, a conch shell, a vardhanī vessel, or even the hand, provided it holds kuśa grass and flowers.
With the Pavamāna, the Rudra, and the Anilamantra,
with the sūtras beginning with the Liṅgasūkta, and with the Śiras from the Atharvaveda;
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the Rig verses, the Saman chants, the five Brahma-mantras, and with the auspicious Praṇava.
Just as one should perform the bathing and other rites for the god, so too for the goddess;
there is no distinction whatsoever between them, since they are equal.
First, one should perform the rites such as bathing for the God of Gods;
afterwards, by the command of the God of Gods, one should perform them for the Goddess.
When Ardhanārīśvara is worshipped, there is no distinction of priority or sequence regarding the mantras, tantras, or ritual services, whether performed at the linga or elsewhere.
Having performed the consecration of the liṅga with pure and fragrant substances,
and having wiped it with a cloth, one should offer a garment and a sacred thread.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers,
ornaments, incense, a lamp, food offerings, drinking water, and water for cleansing the mouth.
Then follows water for sipping and mouth-perfume;
thereafter, a beautiful and auspicious crown adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Various ornaments and diverse garlands,
as well as a fan, a chowrie, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan, and a mirror.

Having made the offering, one should perform the *nirājana* rite amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments, accompanied by songs, dances, and the like, along with the resonant cries of "Victory! (jaya).
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, adorned with auspicious flowers such as lotuses, along with seeds, curd, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
With tridents, pairs of conchs, lotuses, and *nandyāvarta* designs made from cow-dung,
and with variegated *svastikas*, mirrors, and vajras marked by the directions beginning with fire (the southeast), [one should draw the mandala].
Having placed eight lamps around [the central area] and one in the middle,
the nine Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, are to be visualized and worshipped within them.
Having covered it with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and protected it on all sides with the weapon-mantra (astra),
and having displayed the cow-seal (dhenumudrā), one should lift up the vessel with both hands.
Alternatively, one should place five lamps in the vessel in due order—
in the intermediate directions as well as in the center— or else just a single lamp.
Then, having lifted that vessel, one should rotate it three times in a clockwise direction above the *liṅga* and other objects, using the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon the head and fragrant ashes;
afterwards, having made a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should present the offering (*upahāra*).
Then, having offered water for drinking, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana);
thereafter, one should present betel-leaf accompanied by the five fragrant spices (pañcasaugandhika).
One should sprinkle the items to be sprinkled and perform singing, dancing, and so forth;
having meditated upon the two Śivas within the Liṅga and other icons, one should chant the name of Śiva according to one's ability.
One should perform circumambulation, prostration, praise, self-surrender,
and the presentation of one's tasks with humility.
Having offered the *arghya* and a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and having formed the mudrās according to the ritual rule,
one should afterwards ask the deity for forgiveness, dismiss (*udvāsya*) him, and contemplate [the deity] within oneself.

One should perform the rites beginning with the water for the feet and ending with the mouth-perfume, or ending with the arghya offering; however, in times of extreme distress, one may simply scatter flowers while being preceded by sincere devotion.
At that very moment, the supreme Dharma becomes well-performed through one's being;
one should not eat without having first honored Śiva until the movement of the vital breaths has ceased.
If one should eat [forbidden food] at will out of wickedness, there is no expiation for him;
but if it has been eaten through negligence, then having diligently vomited it up, [he is purified].
Having bathed, worshipped the God and the Goddess twice as much, and observed a fast,
one should recite the ten-thousand-name hymn of Śiva while observing celibacy.
On the following day, having given gold or other gifts according to one's ability to Śiva or to a devotee of Śiva,
and having performed a great worship, one shall become pure.
Furthermore, whatever has not been mentioned here— whether due to fear of violating the sequence of worship or for other reasons—
I shall explain that elsewhere in brief, but not in detail.
One should perform the worship of the retinue (āvaraṇābhyarcā) prior to the offering of the oblation, after the offering of the lamp, and likewise when the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) has arrived.
There, in the first enclosure, one should worship the deities of Śiva and Śivā, starting from Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta, and likewise from Hṛdaya (Heart) to Astra (Weapon).
In the northeast, or in the eastern part, as well as in the south and the north;
likewise in the west, in the southeast, in the northeast, and in the southwest.
Then, in the northwest and northeast, and subsequently in the four cardinal directions, the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) is declared; [one should recite] the mantra ending with "sadyojāta."
Alternatively, one may worship [the deities] beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon-mantra;
outside of that, one should worship Śakra in the east and Yama in the south.
One should worship Varuṇa in the western quarter, Dhanada (Kubera) in the northern,
Īśa (Īśāna) in the north-eastern, Agni in the south-eastern, and Nirṛti in the south-western quarter.
In the northwest, one should place Māruta; in the southwest, Viṣṇu; in the southeast, Vidhi (Brahmā); and in the northeast, Īśvara.
Outside the lotus, one should also arrange the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt and ending with the lotus in their respective positions.
One should worship the world-protectors in their well-known forms in the directions in due order;
having consecrated the god and the goddess, as well as all the deities of the surrounding enclosures.
They should be meditated upon as seated at ease with their palms joined in the añjali gesture;
[this applies] to all the deities of the enclosures by means of their names followed by the word "namaḥ."
One should perform worship with flowers, along with prostrations and recollection, in due order;
one may also worship the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) alone, without the other enclosures.
O Goddess, in sacrifice, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering—whether external or internal—the oblation is of six kinds: pure [substances] and rice mixed with mung beans.
Milk-rice mixed with curd, and ghee from a tawny cow;
of these, one or several, combined with various side dishes.
One should offer excellent churned curd mixed with pieces of jaggery,
as well as various foods, primarily cakes, and delicious fruits.
Water that is exceedingly cool, scented with cardamom, sandalwood, flowers, and other fragrances;
and soft betel nut-leaf smeared with the essence of oil and sugar.
The leaves of the nāgavallī plant should be pale and auspicious;
likewise, the powder of white stone should be neither too dry nor too parched.
One should also use natural camphor, auspicious sandalwood paste from species such as *jāti* and others grown in the forest, and an ointment made from the powder of black agallochum (*kālāguru*).
Musk, saffron, and the essence consisting of deer-musk;
fragrant flowers and auspicious leaves.
They were made of fine linen, silk, and celestial cloth;
they were well-proportioned, inlaid with the nine precious gems, and fashioned entirely of refined gold.
In particular, all these ornaments, resembling circles of lightning,
were treated with camphor, resin, agaru, and sandalwood.
Well-perfumed with flowers and other offerings, they were scented on all sides with powders of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and guggulu resin.
Incense prepared with ghee and honey is highly praised,
especially with the exceedingly fragrant ghee produced from a tawny cow (kapilā).
Lamps that are perpetually lit, made with camphor wicks, are recommended;
likewise, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—curdled milk, fresh milk, curds, and clarified butter—as well as churned milk.
The milk of a tawny cow is desired by Śambhu for bathing as well as for drinking;
likewise, auspicious seats made of ivory are favored.
There were variegated coverlets, adorned with gold and jewels,
provided with soft pillows and made of fine cotton.
One should give high and low, beautiful and comfortable beds, or water collected from a river flowing to the ocean.
Cloth-filtered and cool, it was excellent for bathing and drinking;
there was also a parasol, moon-like and smooth, resplendent with strings of pearls.
There were two divine white chowries, adorned with nine gems, captivating with their golden handles,
and embellished with refined gold.
Having the form of a royal swan, adorned with a jeweled handle,
there was also a mirror that was very glossy and anointed with divine perfumes.
Covered all over with jewels and adorned with excellent garlands,
the conch emits a deep resonance; it resembles a swan, jasmine, or the moon,
and its mouth, back, and other parts are embellished with gems and gold.
And there were delightful trumpets that produced various sounds.
There were drums such as the bherī, mṛdaṅga, muraja, timila, and paṭaha, fashioned entirely of gold and adorned with pearls.
One should diligently prepare vessels that resound like the ocean,
as well as all kinds of beautiful containers and bowls.
One should construct all the supports for that [temple] out of gold alone,
as well as the abode of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
It should be constructed like a royal residence, possessing the characteristics described in the Śiva scriptures,
with high walls and a gateway shaped like a mountain peak.
Covered with many jewels, with golden doors and panels,
it was made of refined Jāmbūnada gold and surrounded by hundreds of jeweled pillars.
It was enriched with canopies of pearl necklaces, featuring coral door-arches,
and adorned with radiant golden crowns marked by the sign of the water-pots.
Its upper portion was adorned with the king of weapons as its insignia,
and it was beautified by dwellings worthy of royalty and royal thoroughfares.
It was protected on all sides by palaces with lofty peaks,
and by the foremost officials stationed in the assembly hall throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The perimeter was exquisitely adorned with inner enclosures,
as if by thousands of excellent women skilled in dance and song.
It was filled with many men skilled in the flute and lute,
and guarded by heroic protectors accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots.
It was surrounded on all sides, in every direction and intermediate point, by many flower gardens, numerous lakes, and many oblong ponds.
By those who know the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who are experts in the Śiva scriptures,
who delight in the Śiva way of life, who are devoted, and who possess the characteristics prescribed in the Śiva scriptures;
It was inhabited by illustrious twice-born men— Śaivas and Māheśvaras— who were peaceful, smiling-faced, dignified, and ever devoted to virtuous conduct.
Thus, whether internally or externally, in a place constructed according to one's capacity— be it made of stone, ivory, wood, or brick—
Whether it be in a place made entirely of clay, or in a sacred forest, or on a mountain,
by a river, in a temple, or in another auspicious place or house;
Whether wealthy or poor, one should worship the God with devotion using only wealth acquired through righteous means, without deceiving one's own capacity.
Moreover, even if one worships Śiva with devotion using wealth acquired through improper means,
there is no transgression for him, because the Lord is subject to the power of one’s inner disposition.
Even if one worships with wealth acquired through righteous means, if it is done without devotion, one does not obtain the fruit thereof; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Whatever is performed with devotion according to one's means, dedicated to Śiva—
whether it be small or great— the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor.
Impelled by devotion, even a man of meager means should perform [the rite];
one who is devoid of devotion would not perform it, even if he possessed the wealth of great opulence.
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions while devoid of devotion to Śiva, one would not partake of the fruit thereof; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Neither by those most fierce austerities nor by all the great sacrifices would one go to the divine city of Śiva, were it not for devotion whose essence is Śiva.
For this is the most secret of secrets regarding the Supreme Lord Śiva everywhere;
there is no doubt that through devotion to Him, one who is endowed with it is liberated.

The recitation of Śiva-mantras, meditation, burnt offerings, sacrifice, austerity, sacred learning, charity, and study—all these have their true purpose in the underlying state of being; of this there is no doubt.
A man devoid of right intention is not liberated even after performing everything;
conversely, one endowed with right intention is liberated even without having performed anything at all.
What is the fruit for a devotee of Śiva through thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa penances, hundreds of Prājāpatya penances, and vows such as monthly fasts?
In this world, men who are not devotees perform austerities in mountain caves for the sake of meager enjoyments; however, the devotee is liberated through his devotion.
Yogis established in sattva perform sattvic action which bestows liberation; those enveloped by rajas perform rajasic actions which bestow supernatural powers.
The Asuras and Rākṣasas, endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas),
worship the Lord for the sake of worldly ends, as do other men of a similar nature.
Whether resorting to a tamasic, rajasic, or even a sattvic disposition,
one who acts with devotion for the sake of the City attains auspiciousness.
Since devotion was fashioned like a boat to rescue one from the ocean of sin,
what use then have those endowed with devotion for passion (rajas) or darkness (tamas)?
Whether he be an outcaste or even a low-born person, whether he be a fool or even a scholar—
if he has attained the state of Śiva, he is worthy of worship by all gods and asuras.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śiva through devotion alone;
for there is no fruit whatsoever for those who lack devotion.
I shall speak to you this supreme secret; listen to these words of mine, which have been thoroughly ascertained after deliberation by the Vedas, the Shastras, and those who know the Vedas.
Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed;
or even a killer of his mother, a killer of his father, a killer of a hero, or a killer of an embryo.
Having worshipped Śiva, the supreme cause, with devotion through mantra,
they are gradually liberated from those various sins over the course of twelve years.
Therefore, with every effort and endowed with devotion, one should worship Śiva;
for if one is a devotee, it matters not what else one has, provided one subsists on alms and has conquered the senses.
Even after committing a very great sin, if one worships the Lord of Gods with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra, one is liberated from that sin.
Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by vows—
even with these observances, they do not attain union with the world of Śiva.
Whoever worships Śiva even once with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra alone shall go to the abode of Śiva, owing to the majesty of the Śiva-mantra.
Therefore, all austerities and sacrifices, even those with the gift of one's entire possessions as the fee,
are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-sūtras.
Whether bound or even liberated from the noose by means of the five-syllable mantra, the devotee who worships [the deity] is released; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether one is non-Rudra or indeed Rudra, whoever— be they fallen or even deluded— worships Śiva with the thread [mantra], that person is liberated.
One is liberated by constantly [reciting] either the six-syllabled mantra, or likewise the five-syllabled one, or that [mantra] together with its Brahma-aṅga and the *saṃhaṃsa*.
Therefore, a devotee should worship Śiva with devotion using the *sūtra-mantra*.
Indeed, a devotee of Śiva who has conquered anger is as good as having attained his goal, whether he has already attained it or not.
In this matter, that which is obtained from one who has not obtained [it] is indeed superior; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, having obtained the Lord of Gods, one should worship him with the thread and the mantra.
Those who worship Mahādeva once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or at all times, should be known as lords of the Gaṇas.
He who, having been born, does not worship the Blessed Lord Śiva— being a self-harmer—
wanders for a very long time in this saṃsāra, which is an ocean of suffering.
Having obtained the human state, which is so difficult to attain, the fool does not worship Śiva;
therefore, his birth is fruitless, as it will not lead to liberation.

Having obtained this human birth which is so difficult to attain, those who worship the wielder of the Pināka bow—verily their birth is fruitful; they are the best of men who have achieved their life's purpose.
Those who are devoted to Bhava, whose minds are inclined toward Bhava,
and who are intent on the constant remembrance of Bhava— they do not partake in suffering.
Delightful mansions, graceful amusements, playful women,
and wealth whose end is never seen— these are the fruits of the ritual of worshiping Śiva.
Those who desire great enjoyments and the status of being accepted in the abode of the thirty gods always worship the lotus feet of Hara.
Good fortune, a radiant form, truthfulness, generosity, majesty, valor,
and renown in the world shall accrue to one who worships Śiva.
Therefore, having renounced everything and fixing one's mind solely on Śiva,
one should perform the ritual for the worship of Śiva if one desires one's own welfare.
Life passes swiftly; youth passes swiftly;
disease approaches swiftly; therefore, Śiva should always be worshipped.
As long as death has not arrived, as long as old age has not overtaken you,
and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long worship Śaṅkara.
There is no other dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in the three worlds;
having realized this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort.
If one should perform worship in the temple, one should carry out the door-sacrifice, the curtain-rite, the offering of oblations to the retinue, and the daily festival.
After the offering of the oblation, either the officiant himself or his attendant should present the *bali* offering to the surrounding structures of the temple in the proper sequence.
Having gone out, standing before the faces of Bali, the gods, and others,
one should offer flowers, incense, and a lamp, as well as food along with water.
Then, standing upon the great seat (mahāpīṭha) and facing north, one should offer the bali-oblation.
Then, that food and so forth which was previously offered to the deity—
One should offer all of that, whether with remainder or not, to Caṇḍa;
and having performed the oblation according to the rule, one should afterwards complete the remainder of the worship.
Having performed the ritual application according to the rules up until the recitation of the mantra,
one should then conduct the daily festival as prescribed in the teaching of Śiva.
Having invoked the divine Pāśupata weapon into a stainless, radiant vessel adorned with red lotuses, one should worship it there.
Having placed that vessel upon the head of the adorned twice-born man,
whose body was divested of weapons and who held a staff over which he had muttered prayers;
Outside the palace precincts, there were auspicious sounds,
as well as dances, songs, and the like, accompanied by lamps, banners, and other such items.
Having performed three circumambulations— neither too fast nor too slow—
and having gathered [the essence] at the great seat (mahāpīṭha) through the practice of three circumambulations;
Having entered again and standing at the door with palms joined in reverence, the patron (yajamāna) should lead him into the interior of the palace and then cause him to marry her that very day.
Having performed the circumambulation and other rites in the sequence previously described,
and having offered the eight flowers, one should then conclude the worship.
(Upamanyu: (Vāyavīya Uttarabhāga 28) Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of occasional rites for those who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva, according to the path taught in the Śiva-śāstra.
And in all months, during both fortnights,
on the eighth and fourteenth days, as well as on the festival days (parvan) in due order.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and especially during eclipses, a great or even more extensive worship should be performed with devotion.
Having prepared the *brahmakūrca* according to the rule every month,
and having bathed Śiva with it, one should drink the remainder while fasting.
For even the most grievous faults, such as the killing of a Brahmin,
there is no atonement superior to the drinking of the *brahmakūrca* mixture.
On the Puṣya day, under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for the Lord.
On the Maghā day, under the asterism called Maghā, one should offer a "butter-blanket" (*ghṛtakambala*).
One should indeed commence the great festival at the end of Uttaraphalgunī in the month of Phālguna;
then, on the full moon day of Citrā in Caitra, one should prepare the swing according to the prescribed rite.

In the month of Vaiśākha, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform the Puṣpa-mahālaya rite; in the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the asterism called Mūla, one should cause a cool white pitcher to be offered.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, during the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation, one should likewise perform the consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
In Śrāvaṇa, one should arrange the primary mandalas and other rites.
Thereafter, under the constellation named Śraviṣṭhā, on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, [these should be performed].
And one should perform the sprinkling ritual and water-sports on the day when the moon is situated in Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Then, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should offer milk-rice and fresh rice;
and on the day of the Śatabhiṣaj asterism, one should perform the fire-rite with that very same [offering].
On the full moon day of Kārttika, when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās, one should offer a thousand lamps;
likewise, in Mārgaśīrṣa, on the day of Ārdrā, one should bathe Śiva with ghee.
If one is unable during those times, one should instead perform a festival,
or a formal assembly, or a great worship, or an especially extensive ritual adoration.
Even when auspiciousness has turned away, even regarding praiseworthy deeds,
in the case of dejection, misconduct, bad dreams, or the sight of the wicked;
During such inauspicious events as portents and the like, or when a disease is severe,
one should perform rites such as bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and charity.
The rites should be performed according to the specific signs, preceded by the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa);
and if the temple of Śiva is damaged, one should perform the re-consecration.
To him who thus abides constantly in the most auspicious dharma, ever striving,
Maheśvara grants liberation within a single birth.
He who performs these rites in successive order during the regular and occasional ceremonies goes to the divine, primordial abode of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for hundreds of millions of eons, that person,
passing away from that state at the end of time, [attains] the stage of Āuma and likewise the stage of Kaumāra.
Having reached the worlds of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and especially that of Rudra,
and having dwelt there for a long time, he enjoys pleasures according to his desires.
Furthermore, having reached those five locations situated above him and having obtained knowledge from Śrīkaṇṭha, he shall proceed once more to the city of Śiva.
And even one who delights in half-observance, having likewise repeated it twice,
shall afterwards attain knowledge and reach union with Śiva.
But that embodied being who has practiced for half of a half, after the destruction of the body,
transcends the two worlds up to the end of the cosmic egg and beyond the unmanifest (avyakta).
Having attained the fierce abode of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain King through his manly prowess,
he enjoyed manifold pleasures for many thousands of yugas.
When his merit is exhausted, having reached the earth, he is born into a great family;
even there, by the power of his former impressions, he possesses great intelligence.
Having abandoned the ways of the beasts, one should be devoted to the way of Śiva;
by virtue of that very reverence for his dharma, one shall go again to the city of Śiva.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, one shall go to the city of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara);
there, together with the Lords of Knowledge, one shall enjoy many pleasures in succession.
Whether within or outside the cosmic egg, he then returns once more;
thereafter, having obtained the knowledge of Śiva and attained supreme devotion, he [proceeds].
Having attained the state of similarity with Śiva, he does not return again,
even if he is a devotee of Śiva whose mind remains attached to sense objects.
Whether performing or not performing the duties of Śiva, he is liberated;
[he may be] one who turns once, twice, or thrice, or one who turns back.
Furthermore, one shall not become a universal monarch (cakravartin) who holds authority over the dharma of Śiva;
therefore, having taken refuge in Śiva for whatever reason, [one should act accordingly].
If one has exerted oneself for the sake of the highest good, one should direct the mind toward the *Śivadharmas*;
we shall not obstruct anyone here by any means whatsoever.
By its very nature, this does not please those who are intent on stubbornness and excessive disputation;
yet it may please others due to the weight of their meritorious mental impressions.
Therefore, having reflected upon this entirely in accordance with one's own nature, [one should act] so that the cause of saṃsāra may not be able to sprout within them.
One should apply oneself to the Śivadharmas if one desires one’s own welfare.
(If one has exerted oneself for the sake of the highest good, one should direct one’s mind toward the Śivadharmas.
(Kṛṣṇa)—(Vāyu Purāṇa, Uttara-khaṇḍa 29).
"O Blessed One, from your own lips I have heard that which is equal to the Vedas, as proclaimed by Śiva regarding those who take refuge in you— namely, the obligatory and occasional rites. Now,
I desire to hear the authoritative source concerning the duties of Śiva-dharma."
If there is also action performed for the sake of desired results, you should explain it now.
(Upamanyu:
There is that which has results pertaining to this world, and likewise that which has results pertaining to the next world;
