and there is also that which has results pertaining to both this world and the next, and that, moreover, is of five kinds.
Some action consists of ritual performance, some action consists of austerity;
some consists of recitation and meditation, and likewise, some consists of all these combined.
Likewise, ritual action is divided according to the sequence of fire-offerings, gifts, and worship;
all of this yields fruit only for those possessed of power (śaktimat), and not for others.
And Śakti is the primordial power of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self;
therefore, the wise one who upholds the command should perform all duties.
Now I shall explain the rites for specific desires, which yield fruit both in this world and the next;
these should be performed by the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, both internally and externally, in due order.
Śiva and Maheśvara do not differ here at all;
just as they do not differ, so too the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras do not differ.
For those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are known on earth as Śaivas; those who are devoted to the sacrifice of ritual action are called Māheśvaras.
Therefore, the Śaivas should perform [the rites] inside and the Māheśvaras outside;
however, the application of the ritual action to be described hereafter must not differ.
Having examined the ground according to rule by its scent, color, taste, and other qualities,
[one should perform the rite] upon a site desired by the mind, covered with a canopy of jewels and spread with cloth.
When the surface of the earth is well-illuminated and resembles the interior of a mirror,
one should first dig up the eastern line according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
One should prepare a mandala measuring one cubit or two cubits;
there, one should draw a radiant eight-petaled lotus together with its pericarp.
With powders of jewels, gold, and other materials, gathered as were available,
it was provided with elephant-figures and endowed with great splendor.
The Siddhis are to be assigned to the petals,
and the Rudras, beginning with Vāma, accompanied by their Śaktis, are to be placed on the filaments in order, starting from the eastern petal.
In the pericarp is detachment; in the seed-syllables are the nine powers;
in the bulb is dharma whose nature is Śiva; and in the stalk is knowledge which has Śiva as its refuge.
Above the pericarp are the mandalas of Fire, the Sun, and the Moon;
beyond these is the triad of principles known as Śiva-tattva, Vidyā-tattva, and Ātman-tattva.
Having mentally fashioned upon all the seats a comfortable throne adorned with various flowers—
and [the supreme space of the sky, exceedingly radiant through the Vidyā]—
one should invoke the Supreme Lord into that form.
One should worship [the deity] together with Ambā, accompanied by the five obscurations.
Resembling pure crystal, serene, and possessing a cool radiance,
he is adorned with a crown of matted locks that resemble a circle of lightning.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a slightly smiling lotus-face,
his hands, feet, and lips resembling the petals of a jewel-adorned lotus,
endowed with all the auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament.
He was endowed with divine weapons and ornaments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents;
he had five faces and ten arms, with a crescent moon as the crest-jewel upon his head.
His eastern face is gentle, with a radiance like that of the rising sun;
it is enriched by three lotus-eyes and has the crescent moon as its crest-ornament.
The right [face] has a beautiful luster like a dark blue cloud;
it is terrible with a frowning brow and possesses three red, circular eyes.
His fangs were formidable and difficult to withstand; his sprout-like lower lip quivered;
it was exquisite, resembling coral, and adorned with dark locks of hair.
The western [face] is playful, three-eyed, with the crescent moon as its crest-ornament; it possesses the luster of the full moon and is radiant with three eyes.
The fifth [face] bears the crescent moon; it is gentle, charming with a soft smile, resembling crystal, and radiant like a streak of lightning.
Extremely serene, radiant with three wide-open eyes,
and blazing on the right side with a trident, axe, thunderbolt, sword, and fire.
And on the left [hand], it is radiant with the elephant-goad, bell, noose, and goad;
[the body] extends to the knees by means of Nivṛtti, and to the navel by means of Pratiṣṭhā.
Likewise, [the body] up to the throat is [pervaded] by Vidyā, and up to the forehead by Śāntā;
above that, it is likewise pervaded by the supreme Kalā called Śāntyatītā.
The ancient God known as Puruṣa, who pervades the five paths, who is the manifest embodiment of the five kalās, and who bears Īśāna upon his crown.
Likewise, the Aghora-heart, the Vāma-secret organ of Maheśvara,
and the Sadyojāta-foot— this is His form, consisting of thirty-eight kalās.
Īśāna consists of the Mātṛkās, as well as the five Brahmans;
he consists of that which is called Oṃkāra and is endowed with the power of Haṃsa.
(The deity consisting of five syllables, or indeed consisting of six syllables,
endowed with the six limbs and accompanied by the six classes [of mantras]; likewise,
the maṇḍala of the lap ascended by the power whose nature is will.)
By that which is called Knowledge on the right, and by that which is called Action on the left.
Having visualized Sadāśiva— who is composed of the three principles (tattvas) and is the manifest embodiment of Vidyā—
by means of the root-mantra of the form, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order;
And having worshipped according to the rule with the *arghya* offering using that root-mantra,
[he should worship] Śiva himself in embodied form, together with his supreme Śakti.
Having invoked Mahādeva there— He who is devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence— one should worship the Supreme Lord by performing the five-fold service (pañcopacaraṇa).
Then, one should proceed in sequence with the Brahma-mantras, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), together with the Mātṛkā, the Praṇava, and Śiva conjoined with Śakti.
One should worship the supreme deity either with the *sāṅga* [mantra], or with other divine mantras in their entirety, or with the *kevala-śiva* alone.
Having performed the rites beginning with the water for the feet and ending with the mouth-perfume, and excluding the dismissal,
one should commence the worship of the five enclosures in their proper sequence.
(Vāyavyottara 30):
Therein, first, one should worship the two deities Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings on the right and left sides of Śiva and Śivā respectively.
Then, one should worship the Brahmās, beginning with Īśāna and proceeding in order around [the center], together with their Śaktis, ending with Sadyojāta, in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
One should also worship the six limbs, beginning with the heart and following their sequence,
as well as those of Śiva and Śivā, starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and so forth.

There, one should worship the eight Rudras, beginning with Vāma, together with their respective Śaktis, Vāmā and the others, either subsequently or not, in order, surrounding [the central deity] starting from the east.
The first enclosure has been described by me to you, O delight of the Raghus;
out of affection, the second enclosure is now being told—listen with faith.
One should worship Ananta on the petal of the eastern direction and his Śakti to his left;
one should worship Sūkṣma together with his Śakti on the petal of the southern direction.
Then, one should worship Śivottama together with Śakti on the petal of the western direction,
and likewise worship Ekanetra on the petal of the northern direction.
One should worship Ekarudra and his Śakti on the petal in the northeast direction (Īśāna), and Trimūrti and his Śakti on the petal in the southeast direction (Agni).
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha on the southwestern petal and his Śakti to his left; likewise, one should worship Śikhaṇḍīśa on the northwestern petal.
In the second enclosure, the universal monarchs (cakravartins) are to be worshipped on all sides;
in the third enclosure, the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis) together with their powers (śaktis) are to be honored.
In the eight directions, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise,
there are Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Rudra, and Paśupati.
Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva—these are the eight forms in sequence;
and within each interval, Mahādeva and the others follow in order.
There, the eleven forms should be worshipped together with their Śaktis:
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita.
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava,
and Kapālīśa are likewise declared to be the eleven forms (mūrtis).
Therein, eight [deities] are to be worshipped first, in sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya):
the God of Gods on the eastern petal, in the northeast (aiśānī), and in the southeast (agnigocara).
Between those two is Bhavodbhava, and beyond that is Kapālīśa;
in that enclosure, one should again worship Vṛṣendra in front.
One should place Nandin to his right and Mahākāla likewise to the north;
the Teacher on the petal in the southeast direction, and the Mothers on the petal in the southern direction.
Then, one should place Gajāsya on the petal in the southwest, Ṣaṇmukha in the west,
Jyeṣṭhā on the petal of the northwest, Gaurī in the north, and Caṇḍa in the northeast.
Between the Teacher (Śāstṛ) and Nandīśa, one should worship the Lord of Sages (Munīndra), that is, Vṛṣabha;
to the north of Mahākāla, however, one should worship Piṅgala.
One should worship Bhṛṅgīśvara in the midst of the assembly of the Teacher and the Mothers;
one should worship Vīrabhadra between the Mother and Vighneśa.
One should worship the goddess Sarasvatī between Skanda and Vighneśa,
and Śrī, who is worshipped by Sāmbaśiva, between Jyeṣṭhā and Kumāra.
One should worship Mahāmoṭī between Jyeṣṭhā and Gaṇāmbā;
one should worship the goddess Durgā between Gaṇāmbā and Caṇḍa.
In this very enclosure, there is furthermore an assembly of Śiva’s attendants,
known as the Rudras, Pramathas, and Bhūtas, diverse and accompanied by their Śaktis.
One should worship the circle of Śivā’s female companions, visualizing them all around;
thus, when the third enclosure has been arranged and worshipped, [the rite is complete].
Having meditated upon the fourth enclosure, one should worship outside of it:
Bhānu is to be worshipped on the eastern petal, and the four-faced Brahmā on the south.
Rudra is on the petal in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), and Viṣṇu is on the petal in the northern direction;
thereafter, there are separate enclosures for each of these four deities.
Immediately after that worship, one should perform [the rite] according to the method prescribed in its own scripture;
or else, having worshipped the Sun, one should sacrifice in the first enclosure. First, its six limbs [should be worshipped], along with the powers (śaktis) beginning with Dīptā.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and Vimalā, in sequence.
Amoghā and Vidyutā are situated around the east and the other directions;
these four forms are to be worshipped in sequence in the second enclosure.
Beyond that are the powers (śaktis) beginning with the east and ending with the north;
then, in successive order, Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi.
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are the sons of Vivasvat;
Vitārā is in the eastern quarter, and likewise Sutārā is in the south.
Having placed Bodhinī in the western part and Āpyāyanī in the north,
and then Uṣā, Prabhā, Prājñā,
and Sandhyā in the [directions] beginning with the northeast (aiśāna), one should worship them in the second enclosure.
Soma, Aṅgāraka, and Budha, the best among the wise;
Bṛhaspati of vast intellect, Bhārgava the treasury of splendors,
Śanaiścara, as well as Rāhu, Ketu, and the smoke-colored, terrifying [Ketu].
One should worship these all around in the third enclosure in due order;
alternatively, one may worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure,
and likewise worship the twelve zodiac signs in the third enclosure.
And outside of it, on all sides, were the hosts of the seven horses (the sun),
as well as sages, gods, Gandharvas, serpents, throngs of Apsaras, village chiefs, Yakṣas, Yātudhānas, and horses.
One should also worship the Saptacchandomayas and the Vālakhilyas;
thus, having worshipped the Sun-god in the third enclosure.
Thereafter, one should worship Brahmā along with the three Āvaraṇas;
Hiraṇyagarbha in the east, and then Virāja in the south.
One should worship Kāla in the western quarter and Puruṣa in the north;
Hiraṇyavarṇa is the first, Brahmā, who resembles a lotus.
Time is like collyrium for the eyes; the Puruṣa is like a crystal.
He consists of the three qualities: the rajasic, the tamasic, and likewise the sāttvic.
These four are situated sequentially in the first enclosure;
in the second enclosure, they are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east and proceeding around.
One should then worship Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana, the Prajāpatis, in the third enclosure.
In the east and other directions, there were eight ancestors; first three in the east and then [the others] in sequence:
Dakṣa, Ruci, Bhṛgu, Marīci, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Kāśyapa,
and Vasiṣṭha— these are renowned as the lords of progeny.
Their wives, Prasūti, Ākūti, Khyāti, and Saṃbhūti, should also be worshipped together with them in due order.
Dhṛti, Smṛti, Kṣamā, Sannati, Anasūyā, Devamātā, and Arundhatī— all of them were indeed devoted to their husbands.
One should worship the four Vedas in the first enclosure— those who are constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, illustrious, and of pleasing appearance.
Furthermore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are in the second enclosure;
in the third enclosure, those preceded by the Dharmaśāstras are to be worshipped.
All Vedic sciences are indeed to be honored on all sides;
the Vedas are foremost in the east and other directions, while the others are according to one's preference.
Having performed worship everywhere, either eightfold or fourfold,
one should thus honor Brahmā together with his three enclosures.
One should subsequently worship Rudra with his enclosures in the south, west, and behind;
his six Brahma-aṅgas are known as the first enclosure.
In the second enclosure, it likewise consists of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras);
in the third enclosure there is a division, which shall now be described.
His four forms are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east:
the three-fold, manifest God in the east is known by the name Śiva.
In the south is the Rajasic Brahma, the creator of the universe, who is worshipped as Bhava;
in the west is the Tamasic Agni, the destroyer, who is worshipped as Hara.
Sāttvika, the bestower of happiness, the gentle one, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe,
and Mṛḍa— thus is Śambhu, the twenty-sixth, Śiva, in the western quarter.

(The residence is surrounded by the east and other directions, while others [the deities] are according to one's preference. Having worshipped [them] thoroughly, one should then worship Vaikuṇṭha in the northern part.
Having placed Vāsudeva at the forefront, one should worship him in the first enclosure;
then Aniruddha to the south, and Pradyumna to the west.
In the north, one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa, and in the west, these two [deities] either in their normal or reversed order.
This is declared to be the first enclosure; now hear about the second enclosure.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana,
Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and you yourself as the horse-headed one (Aśvavaktra).
In the third enclosure, one should worship the wheel in the eastern quarter;
in the south, one should worship the one named Nārāyaṇa, and elsewhere, the Unobstructed (Avyāhata).
In the west is Pāñcajanya, and in the north is the Śārṅga bow;
thus, with these three enclosures, one beholds directly the supreme Hari known as Viṣṇu.
One should worship Mahāviṣṇu and Sadāviṣṇu by manifesting them in embodied form;
thus, through the sequence of Viṣṇu’s fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), there is a quartet of forms.
And having worshipped Him, one should worship His four powers in sequence:
Prabhā in the south-eastern quarter, and Sarasvatī in the south-west.
One should worship Gaṇāmbikā in the northwest and Lakṣmī in the northeast;
likewise, immediately after [the worship of] the forms beginning with Bhānu, one should worship their respective Śaktis.
Having performed the worship, one should sacrifice to the Lords of the World (Lokeśas) right there in that enclosure:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa.
One should worship Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and Īśāna in the west;
thus, having worshipped the fourth enclosure according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the weapons of Maheśa outside the lotus:
the glorious trident (triśūla) in the northeast (aiśāna), and the thunderbolt (vajra) in the direction of the lord of the great region (māhendra).
One should worship the axe in the south-eastern quarter, the arrow in the southern quarter,
the sword in the south-west, and the noose in the region of Varuṇa (the west).
One should worship Aṅkuśa in the northwest quarter and Pināka in the north.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla facing west in the northeast (raudra) quarter.
Having thus worshipped the fivefold enclosure, one should thereafter worship outside.
Or outside [the city], for all the gods of the obstructions, or else in the fifth [layer].
One should worship a great bull in front, together with the five Mother-cows;
thereafter, all those of divine origin are to be worshipped on every side.
The sky-faring sages, the Siddhas, the Daityas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the lords of the Nāgas beginning with Ananta and the Nāgas born of their respective lineages.
Śākinīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, and the leaders of the bhairavas,
as well as others dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla) who have arisen from various wombs.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes;
beasts, birds, trees, insects, and other beings of lowly birth.
There are humans of various forms and animals of lowly birth;
these are the worlds within the cosmic egg, and from them arise millions of such cosmic eggs.
Outside, there are innumerable cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) along with their presiding deities;
the Rudras who support these cosmic eggs are stationed in the ten directions.
Beyond that [are the systems] which are Gauḍa, Māyeya, and Śākta.

Whatever exists that is denotable by words, consisting of both conscious and unconscious principles— all that, having understood it as being at the side of Śiva and Śivā, one should worship in a general manner.
All of them, with palms joined in reverence, were to be meditated upon with smiling faces,
always gazing with affection upon the God and the Goddess.
Having thus performed the worship of the enclosure for the sake of pacifying distractions,
one should again worship the Lord of Gods and recite the five-syllabled mantra. Thereafter, one should offer to Śiva and Śivā that which is like nectar.
The great sacrificial oblation (mahācaru) should be pure, beautiful, and well-prepared with fine ingredients;
the best consists of thirty-two āḍhakas, while the lowest is less than one āḍhaka.
Having prepared it according to the prescribed method, one should offer it with faith;
then, having offered water, betel-leaf, and various side dishes.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites, one should complete the remainder of the worship;
one should procure specifically those substances suitable for ritual enjoyment.
One who possesses devotion should not practice stinginess regarding wealth when resources are available;
for even toward one who is deceitful, negligent, or performs defective rites, [one should remain steadfast].
"It is the teaching of the virtuous that desirable ritual acts do not necessarily bear fruit;
therefore, having abandoned deceit and indifference, one should practice with all one's faculties."
If one desires the attainment of results, one should perform rites for specific wishes.
Having thus completed the worship and having prostrated before the God and the Goddess, [one should proceed].
Having concentrated the mind with devotion, one should thereafter recite the hymn;
then, at the conclusion of the worship, the hymn should be recited at least one hundred and eight times.
Eagerly, one should recite the five-syllable mantra more than a thousand times,
after having performed the worship of the vidyā and the worship of the guru in due order.
One should also honor the members of the assembly according to one's means and according to their faith;
then, having bid farewell to the Lord of Gods along with all his retinues, [one should perform the concluding rites].
One should present the mandala to the guru along with the ritual implements,
or one may give everything accordingly to those who have taken refuge in Śiva.
Alternatively, one should offer that very [object] for the sake of Śiva in a sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra),
and worship the Lord in the Śiva-fire with the seven substances for the fire-oblation (homa).
Having duly worshipped all the deities of the enclosure,
he who is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Yogeśvara [should be honored].
There is no yoga superior to that anywhere in the world;
indeed, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by means of it.
Whether the fruit be some worldly one or even one pertaining to the next life,
it cannot be definitively determined that "this is its fruit" and "that is not."
This which is the supreme means for attaining the entirety of that which constitutes the highest good cannot be described by a person according to what each individual desires.
Just as from a wish-fulfilling gem, that fruit is obtained by him;
nevertheless, one should not employ this for the sake of a trivial result.
Since one who seeks a small result would himself become smaller than the great task,
whether the fruit be large or small, the action must be performed for it to succeed.
For those who employ the rite performed with Mahādeva in mind,
there is therefore success in matters unattainable by other means, such as the conquest of enemies and death.
A wise person should perform this rite regarding fruits, whether their results are seen or unseen,
even in the face of great calamities or the fear of severe diseases and the like.
By means of this, one shall bring about absolute peace during famines and other such calamities;
what is the use of much talk? It wards off great misfortunes.
Maheśvara has declared this weapon of his own to belong to the followers of Śiva;
therefore, there is no protection for oneself greater than this.
Thinking thus, one who applies this rite attains auspiciousness;
he who, having become pure and being well-composed, recites even just the hymn alone.
He too shall obtain an eighth part of the fruit from his most cherished object,
provided he recites it with a concentrated mind while keeping that object in view.
One obtains half and half again of the fruit; there is no need for deliberation here.
Having focused on each successive half, one should recite while fasting on the festival day.
On the eighth and fourteenth days, one shall obtain half the fruit;
likewise, he who observes the vow on festival days and other such occasions while keeping his purpose in mind.
If one recites this hymn for one month, one shall obtain the complete fruit.
Thus ends the section on the worship of the five enclosures.
The Hymn of the Five Enclosures.
(Upamanyu: (Vāyu-uttara-31) O Kṛṣṇa, I shall declare to you a hymn of praise according to the path of the five coverings;
this is the meritorious [hymn] for the Lord of Yoga, by which [all] action is brought to completion.
Victory, victory to you, O Śambhu, sole lord of the world, eternally beautiful by nature, whose essence is eternal consciousness,
who has transcended the speech of the defiled phenomenal world!
O You whose true nature transcends the path of even the minds of the wise!
Victory to you, O one of beautiful conduct, whose effortless exertion is naturally stainless!
Victory to you, ocean of pure qualities, whose great power is equal to your own self!
Victory to you, endowed with infinite splendor, whose form is peerless;
victory to you, the repository of inconceivable majesty, the source of unagitated auspiciousness!
Victory to you, the stainless and supportless one, who arises without cause!
Victory to you, the boundless supreme bliss, the cause of liberation!
Victory to you, O supreme sovereign! Victory to you, O abode of exceeding compassion! Victory to you, O independent one, the essence of all! Victory to you, O one of incomparable majesty!
Victory over the great universe that encompasses all; victory unassailable by anyone;
victory superior to everything; victory that is ultimately unsurpassed.

Victory to you, O Wondrous One! Victory to you, O Free from Meanness! Victory to you, O Uninjured! Victory to you, O Imperishable! Victory to you, O Immeasurable! Victory to you, O Devoid of Illusion! Victory to you, O Unborn! Victory to you, O Stainless!
O mighty-armed one, O great essence, O possessor of great virtues, O you of great renown! O you of great strength, O master of great illusion, O you of great flavor, O great chariot-warrior!
Homage to the supreme deity; homage to the supreme cause;
homage to Śiva, the peaceful one; homage to you, the most auspicious one.
For this entire world, including the gods and asuras, is dependent upon you;
therefore, who would dare to transgress the command ordained by you?
Furthermore, these people always rely solely upon you;
therefore, having shown them favor, please grant what they have requested.
Victory to you, O Mother Ambikā! Victory, O Mother of the world! Victory, O you who consist of the entire universe! Victory, O you of infinite sovereignty! Victory, O you of incomparable form!

Victory to you who transcend speech and mind! Victory to you, the shatterer of the darkness of insentience! Victory to you who are free from birth and old age! Victory to you, the highest of all time!
Victory to you who abide as many treasures! Victory to you whose nature is many gods!
Victory to you who possess many great beings! Victory to you who are exalted by many virtues!
Victory to you who abide as the Self transcending the universe! Victory to you, beloved of the Lord of the Universe!
Victory to you, worshipped by all the gods! Victory to you, who manifest throughout the entire universe!
Victory to you, O goddess of divine and auspicious limbs! Victory to you, the lamp of auspiciousness!
Victory to you, whose conduct is auspicious! Victory to you, the bestower of auspiciousness!
Salutations to you, the embodiment of a multitude of supremely auspicious qualities!
Salutations to Śivā, the power of Śiva who transcends the universe;
from you indeed the world is born, and into you alone it dissolves.
Without you, even the Lord himself would not be able to bestow the fruit [of his grace] from this point on;
O Queen of Gods, from birth onwards, this person has relied solely upon you.
Therefore, fulfill the desire of you, your devotee:
[be] five-faced, ten-armed, and resembling pure crystal.
The Lord whose body consists of the Brahma-phonemes and the Kalās, who is both with parts and without parts,
who is fully established in devotion to Śiva, is Sadāśiva, who transcends even the state of peace (śāntyatīta).
May the Power named Icchā, who has ascended the lap of Sadāśiva, grant me the welfare requested by me, as she has been worshipped by me with devotion.
May the Mother of all the worlds grant our heart's desire;
may the two gods Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha, the beloved sons of Śiva, [bestow it].
Possessing the power of Śiva, they are omniscient and consume the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva;
proud yet affectionate toward one another, they are eternally honored by the two Śivas.
They were always honored by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā,
and were ever intent upon effecting the protection of all the worlds.
p. 371) These two, who manifest their descent by their own will through manifold divisions of their own parts, have thus been constantly worshipped by me at the side of Śiva and Śivā.
Honoring their command, may you two grant me what I have requested:
Sadāśiva, known as Īśāna, who resembles pure crystal.
This is the form of Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is characterized by the pride of being the summit;
he is devoted to the worship of Śiva, tranquil, beyond the sphere of tranquility, and established in the void.
The seed-syllable at the end of the five syllables, joined with the five digits (kalās),
was previously worshipped together with Śakti in the first enclosure.
May the supreme Brahman, the sacred purifier,
who is ancient, known as Puruṣa, and resembling the rising sun, grant my prayer.
And there is the conceit of being the eastern face of Śiva, the Supreme Lord;
it consists of the nature of peace (śānti), resides in the wind, and is devoted to the worship of the feet of Śambhu.
First, in the seed-syllables of Śiva and among the Kalās, that which consists of four Kalās was worshipped by me with devotion and according to my ability in the eastern quarter, together with Śakti.
May the supreme Brahman, the purifier, grant me that which I have requested—
the one who resembles the mountain of collyrium, who is non-terrible yet possesses a terrible form.
The right face of the God, which worships the feet of the God of gods,
is mounted upon the Vidyāpāda and resides in the center of the circle of fire.
The second [form] is among the seeds of Śiva, endowed with the eight kalās;
it is worshipped together with Śakti on the southern side of Śambhu.
May the pure, middle Brahman, who resembles powdered saffron and wears the attire of an excellent bridegroom, grant me that which is requested, known as Vāma.
The face of the Lord is situated in the north, established upon the foundation;
it stands in the midst of the water-mandala, intent on the worship of Mahādeva.
The third [seed-syllable] among the Śiva-bījas, endowed with thirteen kalās,
is worshipped together with Śakti in the northern direction of the Lord.
May the supreme Brahman, the purifier, grant my prayer—
He who is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, who is known as Sandhyā, and who possesses auspicious characteristics.
The western face of Śiva is devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet;
it is established upon the earth and is intent on the state of cessation (nivṛtti).
The fourth [letter] among the seeds of Śiva, joined with eight kalās,
is worshipped together with Śakti in the western part of the deity.
May the first Purifier, the Brahman, grant my prayer;
may it reside within the heart-forms of Śiva and Śivā, which are permeated by the nature of Śiva.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire;
for the two forms of the crest [of Śiva] are devoted to Śiva and Śivā.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire;
[I take] the armor of Śiva and of Śivā, which are infused with auspiciousness.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire;
for the two forms of the eyes of Śiva and Śivā are centered upon Śiva.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire; and may you two, who are the very embodiments of their weapons, remain eternally devoted to their worship.
Honoring their command, let them grant my desire:
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, as well as Rudra, Kāla, and Vikaraṇa.
Bala, Vikaraṇa, Balapramathana, Para,
Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Tādṛśī— these are the eight Śaktis.
"By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant what I have requested.
Then Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and Ekanetraka [spoke].
The form named Ekarudra, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śaśikhaṇḍaka,
as well as their eight Śaktis, are worshipped in the second enclosure.
By the command of Śiva and Śivā alone,
let Bhava and the other eight forms, as well as their respective powers (śaktis), grant whatever is desired.
Mahādeva and the others, as well as the eleven forms (mūrtis),
all accompanied by their Śaktis, are worshipped in the third enclosure.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant the desired fruit;
[may] the King of Bulls, of great splendor and a voice like a massive cloud, [bestow it].
He resembles the peaks of Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and the Himālaya;
he is resplendent with a hump shaped like the summit of the White Mountain.
He is adorned with a tail resembling the lord of great serpents,
with red faces, horns, and feet, and eyes that are predominantly red.
With all his limbs full and elevated, he was radiant with a most beautiful gait;
endowed with auspicious marks, glorious, and adorned with blazing jewel-ornaments.
He was beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and bore the banner and vehicle of the two;
likewise, his other body was purified by the placement of their feet.
The illustrious cow-king, whose excellent weapon is the glorious trident,
honoring their command, may he grant my desire.
Nandīśvara, of great splendor and son of the daughter of the mountain king,
is eternally worshipped and saluted by the gods, including Nārāyaṇa.
He stood at the gate of Śarva’s inner apartments together with his attendants,
resembling the Lord of All in splendor and crushing all the Asuras.
He was consecrated as the presiding authority over all the Śiva-dharmas;
beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, he bore the glorious and excellent trident as his weapon.
Devotedly attached to those who have taken refuge in Śiva and likewise beloved by them,
may he, having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire.
Mahākāla, the mighty-armed one, like another Mahādeva,
is the eternal protector of those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva.
Devoted to Śiva, attached to Śivā, and always a worshiper of Śiva’s feet, may he—
who honors the command of the two, Śiva and Śivā— grant my desire.
He who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, the teacher, the supreme body of Viṣṇu,
the son of Mahāmoṭī, and one who is fond of honey, meat, and liquor.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent upon the worship of the two, may he,
placing their command foremost, grant my desire.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍī of fierce prowess.
These indeed are the seven mothers, the mothers of the entire world;
by the command of the Supreme Lord, may they grant me my request.
He has the face of an elephant in rut; he is the son of Gaṅgā, Umā, and Śaṅkara;
his body is the sky, his arms are the directions, and his eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
He is eternally honored by the divine elephants of the quarters, such as Airāvata;
moistened by the intoxication of the knowledge of Śiva, he creates no obstacles for the gods.
May Vighneśa, who creates obstacles for the Asuras and others, yet is himself permeated by Śiva,
grant my desire after having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā.
The six-faced one, born of Śiva, the lord who wields the spear and the thunderbolt,
is the son of Agni and likewise the son of Aparṇā.
He was likewise surrounded by Gaṅgā, Gaṇāmbā, and the Kṛttikās,
as well as by Viśākha, Śākha, and Naigameya.
He was the conqueror of Indra, the commander of Indra’s army, and the victor over the asura Tāraka;
furthermore, by his own splendor, he was the piercer of even the mountains, of which Meru is the foremost.
Resembling molten gold, with eyes like the petals of a hundred-petaled lotus,
Kumāra is the supreme exemplar of beauty among all delicate beings.
Devoted to Śiva, attached to Śivā, and always a worshiper of Śiva’s feet,
may he honor the command of Śiva and Śivā and grant our desire equally.
Jyeṣṭhā, the most excellent, the bestower of boons, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva and Śivā—
placing their command foremost, may she grant my desire.
The Mother of the Gaṇas, who is directly like a meteor and is worshipped by the three worlds,
was entreated by Brahmā through Śiva for the sake of the creation and expansion of the universe.
Śivā, when divided, is Dākṣāyaṇī, Satī, Gaurī, Haimavatī, and Umā, having emerged from between her eyebrows.
She was the mother of Kauśikī and likewise of Bhadrakālī;
she was also the mother of Aparṇā and likewise of Pāṭalā.
May Rudrāṇī, who is ever devoted to the worship of Śiva and is beloved by Rudra,
grant my desire after having duly honored the command of Śiva and Śivā.
May Caṇḍa, the lord of all the Gaṇas, who was born from the mouth of Śambhu,
having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant our desired wish.
May the leader of the Gaṇas named Vṛṣabha, who has a bull as his vehicle and is the knower of the true nature of reality,
having duly honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire. May the illustrious Piṅgala, the leader of the Gaṇas, who is devoted to Śiva and beloved by Śiva, [grant it].
By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant my desire.
May the leader of the Gaṇas named Bhṛṅgīśa, who is ever intent on the worship of Śiva,
grant my desire in accordance with the command of his Lord.
Vīrabhadra, of great splendor, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon,
is eternally dear to Bhadrakālī and the protector of the Mothers.
He was the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and of the evil-minded Dakṣa,
and he was the protector of the limbs of the gods, including Upendra, Indra, and Yama.
The glorious attendant of Śiva, the protector of Śiva’s command—
by the very command of the two Śivas, may he grant my desire.
Sarasvatī, born from the lotus-like mouth of Maheśa, is intent upon the worship of Śiva and Śivā; may she grant my desire.
Lakṣmī, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu and is devoted to the worship of Śiva and Śivā—
may she, by the very command of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire.
Mahāmoṭī is devoted to the worship of the feet of the Great Goddess;
by her very command, may she grant my desire.
Kauśikī is mounted upon a lion; she is the supreme daughter of Pārvatī, the sleep of Viṣṇu, the Great Māyā, and the slayer of the great buffalo-demon.
May she, the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, who is fond of honey, meat, and wine,
grant my desire after honoring the instruction of her mother.
The Rudras, equal in splendor to Rudra; the Pramathas, renowned for their prowess;
and those called Bhūtas, possessed of great heroism and radiance equal to Mahādeva.
They are eternally liberated, incomparable, free from dualities, and undisturbed;
they possess their powers and are accompanied by their attendants, being honored by all the worlds.
They are capable of creating and destroying all the worlds;
they are mutually affectionate and devoted to one another.
Exceedingly affectionate toward one another and mutually honoring each other,
they are eternally the most beloved of Śiva and are marked by the characteristics of Śiva.
They are gentle, terrible, and likewise mixed, consisting of two intermediate types;
they are deformed, beautiful, and likewise bearers of various forms.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they indeed grant my desire;
[so too] the group of the Goddess’s dear female friends, distinguished by divine marks.
Accompanied by many Rudra-maidens and Śaktis,
he is constantly worshipped with devotion in the third enclosure of Śambhu.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness;
for Divākara is a form of Maheśa, possessing a radiant and beautiful orb.
The first is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet it is likewise mixed with qualities (guṇasaṅkīrṇa) and consists solely of qualities (guṇakevala);
it is unchanging by nature (avikārātmaka) and is the one whose modification is universal (sāmānyavikriya).
And he possesses uncommon karma through the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
thus he is divided threefold, fourfold, and again fivefold.
In the fourth enclosure, he was worshipped along with the attendants of Śambhu;
he was dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent upon the worship of Śiva’s feet.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness;
[so too may] the six limbs of the Sun and the eight powers beginning with Dīptā.
(Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi in their respective order;
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are the forms of Āditya.)

Even today, the wielder of the thunderbolt remains on Mount Aruṇa tasting nectar; likewise, the Fire-god remains there after having consecrated Sadāśiva.
Having worshipped him along with many riches, he obtained these boons:
sovereignty over the fires and lordship over the southern and eastern quarters.
Having been consecrated by the Lord, [he received] the goat as his supreme vehicle,
weapons such as the spear (śakti), and his auspicious beloved, Svāhā.
Likewise, by the command of Īśa, this lord of the southeastern quarter,
the wonderful Agni, stands here as the presiding deity of the fires.
In the great sacred field known as Kedāra, even Yama, the foremost among those who practice self-restraint,
propitiated the Lord of the gods and obtained numerous boons.
Furthermore, [he gave] the lordship over the southern quarter, the buffalo as his supreme vehicle,
and the weapons such as the staff of death (kāladaṇḍa) for all of them once again.
Having led them forth by means of their equal rotation and having deliberated upon their merits and demerits,
he assigns to them the path to heaven through merit and residence in hell through sin.
And there are also torments in hell corresponding to each respective sin,
as well as toward the highly fortunate members of the assembly, who are impartial and possessed of great majesty.
And Śiva himself appointed Citragupta, who was engaged in his duties, to this task;
from that time forth, by the command of Śiva, the Lord of Dharma remained in Saṃyaminī as an enjoyer of his office.
Having experienced such immeasurable prosperity, the powerful Nirṛti still resides today at Gokarṇa, the abode of Śiva, serving the Supreme Lord.
Having worshipped him thoroughly, he then received from the gracious Lord of the World the status of the guardian of the southwestern quarter according to the prescribed rites.
He was consecrated with the power to grant the fruits of sacrifices and with the sword, the supreme of weapons,
as the sovereign ruler over all the Rākṣasas.
Even today,
Pracetas remains experiencing the prosperity bestowed by the Lord after he had worshipped the Supreme Lord in the Jambū forest.
He attained sovereignty over both the aquatic creatures and the waters of the ocean,
as well as the sea-monster Makara as his vehicle, following his formal consecration.
And he likewise obtained the lordship of the western quarter, together with weapons such as the noose,
all of that through his great majesty.
Even today, the highly effulgent and powerful Vāyu remains contented at Dakṣiṇa-Kailāsa in the great city of Kālahasti.
Having worshipped Mahādeva with ritual offerings with undivided mind,
he obtained a boon from Maheśāna, the gracious Lord of lords.
He was consecrated as the sovereign of the northwest quarter;
he became the lord of the winds, accompanied by banners and other weapons.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara at the Siddhavaṭa tree named Siddheśvara, he obtained a deer as his vehicle; even today, he remains peerless on this earth.
Through supreme devotion, Kubera obtained boons from Maheśvara and was invested with the ceremonial turban of office as the lord of the northern quarter.
He also attained lordship over the nine treasures, the Puṣpaka chariot,
the power of measurement, lordship over the Yakṣas from the Lord of Gods, and a celestial vehicle.
Even today, his friend Īśāna, endowed with great majesty,
remains devoted to Mahādeva, who dwells in the abode of Kamalā.
Having worshipped him in many ways with offerings such as leaves and flowers, the wielder of the Pināka bow then asked him, being well-pleased: "What is your desire?"
Having prostrated, he whose mind was fixed on no other chose as his bride the foremost of excellent women,
who possessed a name identical to his own and whose body and weapons were equal to his.
Whatever mark belongs to Śiva, even though it be common [to others],
the lord of the eastern and northern directions likewise has the bull as his vehicle.
Having himself mastered his own self, he obtained all this after praying to the Lord;
and at the conclusion of his office, the supreme lord attained union with the Supreme.
Having granted [the boon] and vanished, that powerful one even today remains in Kāñcī itself;
formerly, the Sun worshipped the Lord of Lords with lotuses.
Having worshipped with single-minded devotion, he obtained a boon from the gracious one:
a permanent residence within the mandala of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
And he obtained a chariot worthy of that, adorned with seven horses,
as well as sovereignty over the planets and the entire circle of luminaries.
Having been consecrated by the Lord, he became the sovereign of the days;
and having reached Kumbhakoṇa, Candra became beloved of Śaṅkara.
Having worshipped Mahādeva there with devotion using auspicious pearls,
he obtained from the gratified Śiva the wonderful boon of lordship over the constellations.
He attained the state of being the moon, the lord of the twice-born, and the sovereign of medicinal herbs;
indeed, he obtained the status of being the Lord’s ornament, which is exceedingly difficult to achieve.
Every day, both of them joyfully performed circumambulations of Meru,
which is the constant abode of Śiva, along with other planets dear to Śiva.
Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—
these five [planets] were present with joy at Madhyārjuna, Hālāsya, Setu, and Vaṭavana.
In the forest of Vedāraṇya, these five [sages] propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow with supreme devotion in all five places, and from him, being well-pleased, they obtained boons.
Above the mandala, it abides over the moon and the sun.
And there will be very great sovereignty over the happiness and suffering of the worlds,
as well as the state of being honored by all for the sake of pacifying every calamity.
Then Guru and Śukra were appointed as the preceptors of the gods and the asuras.
O lords of sages, it was by the grace of the Lord himself,
the God of gods, that the seven ṛṣis in former times [attained their status] as the presiding lord of the assembly.
Having worshipped the Lord in the midst of the assembly hall within the cloudless sky of consciousness (cidambare),
they obtained from Īśāna the boon of remaining situated above all the planets.
Furthermore, having attained liberation in another body, they reach the supreme state;
and by His command, they become skilled in understanding the meaning of all the scriptures.
The high-souled ones, Vasiṣṭha and the others, possess great splendor even today.
Sūta said: Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, [worshipped] Śiva as Viśveśvara in Kāśī. (Śaṃkara Saṃhitā, Upodghāta 63)
Having worshipped Maheśāna, he obtained from the gracious Lord the supreme boon of a station above the mandala of the foremost stars and sages.
Having become the central pivot for the planets,
he remains even today, dwelling unperturbed above them all while joyfully causing them to revolve.
In ancient times at Kumbhakoṇa, Śeṣa, the best among all serpents,
having propitiated the Lord of the gods, indeed bore the burden of the earth.
Endowed with great majesty, he still supports the earth today in all these places—
upon the ground and on the summits of mountains.
On the banks of the rivers dwell gods, sages, asuras, siddhas,
garuḍas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas.
And the Kinnaras, O best of sages, as well as the Kiṃpuruṣas and others,
and human beings, having propitiated Mahādeva Sadāśiva with devotion—
Having each attained their own respective station, the Nāgas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas rejoiced in happiness.
From the supreme Lord, those Kinnaras, humans, and Kiṃpuruṣas everywhere attained their own unimpeded sovereignty.
And others who are the lords of the clouds, as well as any of the elephants of the quarters;
the eight great nāgas and also the seven mountains.
O best of sages, those who are established as lords over various things should be understood to have attained that lordship through the grace of the gods, and not otherwise.
Therefore, all those seeking the highest good, the best among men,
should always perform the worship of Śiva, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By the power of the worship of Śiva, some became perfected beings (siddhas);
indeed, nine renowned yogins, such as Kapila and others, also attained perfection.
Indeed, many creators of the world have attained eternity;
some went to the realm of Śiva, while other people attained sālokya (residence in the same world).
Through the power of worshipping Śiva, the wise attain proximity, similarity of form, and even union among gods, asuras, and humans.
Endowed with superior sovereignty and renowned throughout the three worlds,
some, having attained such power, fell under the sway of delusion;
yet, having fallen from their state, they sought liberation once more from the cycle of existence, just as before.
And many who desired victory, having worshipped the Lord of the World, [proceeded].
Having conquered their enemies in battle, they ruled the earth once more;
and many who sought power obtained very great strength.
Those desiring sons obtained sons, others obtained beautiful wives,
those desiring cattle obtained cattle, and those desiring horses obtained horses.
They obtained good fortune, a beautiful form, generosity, truthfulness, valor, renown in this world, and everything else that is desirable.
Among these many subjects, including those accompanied by historical narratives, certain matters, O fortunate ones, shall now be described in brief; listen!

Sūta: (Śaṃkara Saṃhitā Udyoga Khaṇḍa 64)— In ancient times, Viṣṇu, having propitiated the Supreme Puruṣa, the enemy of Tripura, [sought deliverance] from the numerous calamities arising from the curse of the sages.
Having shaken off [worldly attachments], he attained his desired sons, wife, and kingdom;
I shall relate to you some of those highly meritorious historical narratives.
(p. 396) (The Arising of the Flame-Liṅga) Bhairavaraktabhikṣāsūta:
Once, when a quarrel had arisen between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [they fought] with one another.
"I am the creator of the worlds, not you; I am not you"—thus [he spoke] out of wrath.
Bringing about the pacification of their egoism, the Lord of the lords of all lords created Bhairava, who was himself established within the solar mandala by him.
With the tip of his fingernail, the Lord effortlessly plucked off the fifth head of that Creator, which rose high above the others,
as easily as a tender cucumber fruit.
Having severed that [skull] and held it aloft in his terrifying form,
he brought about the pacification of Viṣṇu’s ego through the pretext of begging for blood.
Desiring to divert him, Viṣṇu incited Bhairava;
having cut a vein from the top of his forehead, he gave his own blood.
Due to the loss of blood, Puruṣottama fell into a swoon;
yet once again, through the touch of Bhairavendra’s hand, he was freed from his pain.
Suddenly regaining consciousness after his fainting fit, Hari said:
"We have indeed displayed arrogance, and for that reason we have been chastised."
For the sake of turning back from that evil, we perform the worship of Śiva,
having reached Madhyārjuna and having fully honored the Teacher of the World.
He considered himself to have achieved his purpose and purified by the worship of the Lord of All,
through the grace of the gracious Pinākin, the God of gods.
Viṣṇu went to his own world with Garuḍa as before;
yet once again, Viṣṇu became arrogant and intoxicated by pride.
Competing with Brahmā and thinking "I am the Lord," he rose up again in anger without having seen the base of the great linga-form.
Having bowed down, he listened to the beneficial words of the gods;
for the sake of averting that sin, he took refuge at Aruṇācala.
There, having propitiated Īśvara and being freed from his offense by the grace of that All-pervading Lord, he went to his own abode.
Viṣṇu once again brought about liberation from Bhṛgu’s curse, and on another occasion,
he suppressed the Asuras during the great battle between the gods and the Asuras when the gods were defeated.
Then, having been severely slaughtered by Viṣṇu in that tumultuous battle,
they reached the hermitage of Bhṛgu and the ascetic wife of Bhṛgu.
Terrified by Hari, the asuras sought refuge with Khyāti;
then Viṣṇu himself, bearing the discus, arrived at that hermitage.
While he was destroying the asuras there, he was stopped by the wife of Bhrigu:
"The hermitage must not be entered by you while the sage is absent."
They must not be slain, they must not be slain—the sons of Diti who are my devotees!
I have granted them all freedom from fear; do not harm them, O Janārdana!
Seeing her, he was overcome with agitation and, out of wrath toward those who [oppose] the worlds,
he then severed that head while destroying the Daityas with his discus.
And when Madhusūdana had departed from that hermitage of Bhṛgu’s wife, who grants fearlessness to them, Janārdana left that place.
Bhrigu, having approached, saw his own beloved wife together with the Daityas;
and having perceived through the vision of his knowledge that Mādhava had severed her head, he [understood the situation].
She became exceedingly enraged at Hari, the slayer of her women by the Daityas;
she cursed Viṣṇu, saying, "May he have millions of births upon this earth."
In every place, let there also be for her a separation from her husband that causes extreme suffering;
and let those who are his devotees in this world be heretics.
Having thus cursed his wife and then restored her to life by means of the perfected mantra "Mṛtasañjīvinī" (the Life-restorer) received from the Supreme Lord;
Then Viṣṇu, the destroyer of demons, having heard this, became terrified;
for the sake of averting that curse, he went to Kāñcī, the bestower of desires.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods and beheld the God upon his bull,
he bowed down and, with a terrified heart, prayed for release from the curse.
O Viṣṇu, whatever has been done by my devotees must be done by them;
otherwise, I shall certainly not fulfill it, for this is the vow I have made.
Having thus addressed Keśava,
Mahādeva, whose hair is tawny, spoke to the sage Bhṛgu, who had appeared before him by mere thought, as if smiling.
O Bhṛgu, deliver Hari from the curse that causes many births;
O best of sages, know him to be a devotee who is intent upon my worship.
May he have ten lifetimes; in one of those births, may he be separated from his wife for a very long time and suffer, and not otherwise.
"By my command, act in this manner as the foremost among my devotees.
"So be it," the sage replied, bowing down to the Supreme Lord.
Then, having bowed again to that Lord of Umā, the Lord of Ramā made this request:
"O Blessed One, throughout all ten of my births..."
For the sake of removing my ignorance, bestow both restraint and grace;
you alone, O Lord of the gods of gods, are compassionate and kind to your devotees.
Having heard that, the Blessed One said, "So be it," and vanished;
the Blessed Nārāyaṇa also returned to his own hermitage.
Furthermore, on one occasion, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a Śapharī fish, suppressed the Matsyāvatāra-nigraha in order to recover the Vedas and to destroy that thief.
Having effortlessly subdued the Daitya Somaka and restored the Vedas to Brahmā exactly as they were before, Janārdana—
With that very same ego-sense, Mādhava split the oceans; drawing them all together, he devoured them.
Then Viriñca and the others, being terrified, propitiated the god Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world who dwells on Kailāsa, and addressed him thus:
Commanded by the god and acting under his order, the Teacher, the Yogi,
assumed the state of a fisherman and [caught] Mādhava in the form of a fish.
Restraining her pair of eyes, which possess the luster of kuruvinda gems,
she took hold of them with the tips of her nails and offered them before Śiva.
Having set this down and offered salutations, the yogi stood with palms joined in reverence;
then Brahmā and the other gods worshipped Mahādeva.
O Lord, we were greatly oppressed by that terrible fish;
now it has been captured for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
"Let this pair of eyes of his become a jewel upon your ornament"—
thus entreated by the gods, he [gave] that pair of eyes as a jewel.
The ocean of compassion, the friend of Umā, who is free from delusion, held the headless trunk upon his garland; likewise, Viṣṇu Janārdana, having meditated upon the Lord, [did the same].
Formerly, by the power of his worship of Śiva, he crushed Soma;
thereafter, however, being shrouded in darkness, he deluded the worlds through sheer infatuation.
"I have been instructed by the Sustainer of the World, and thus I have been made one who has fulfilled his purpose;
for the sake of ending this state of sin, I shall worship Śaṅkara."
Having thus reached the city of Kāñcī, he worshipped Him there;
and the wielder of the Pināka bow was indeed pleased with him for his form as a fish.
The Lord of the World offered a boon to him who had taken the form of a fish; and he too chose a boon: "Let this very restraint be my favor."
O God, by Your grace, may You assume the form of a fish for me; O twice-born ones, become the bestower of desired boons upon those who worship You in this world.
"O Lord of gods, O Maheśvara, by your grace I am a granter of boons;
O Lord of the world, you must be patient with me for what I have done.
Thus was the Lord previously entreated by Viṣṇu in his form as a fish.
Having granted this, he vanished out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
and Viṣṇu, having reached the world of Vaiṣṇava, protected his own domain. This concludes the subduing of [Hiraṇyakaśipu] during the Kūrma incarnation.
Furthermore, in another age, Viṣṇu indeed assumed the form of a tortoise;
having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope, he [performed the churning].
Together with the hosts of gods and asuras, he churned the ocean of milk;
and having obtained the nectar, he became deluded by pride.
The Tortoise agitated the gods along with the oceans;
thereupon, all the gods and asuras went to the Lord and made their report.
Then that God of gods, desiring the welfare of the deities, spoke to Vighnarāja, the subduer of enemies, for the purpose of restraining him.
Then, taking the tortoise with the tip of his trunk, Gaṇanāyaka turned it over completely and pressed its shell firmly.
While even the gods were looking on, he placed it before Śiva;
then the Lord, having gazed upon the gods, spoke this:
"Tell me now, what will become of this tortoise bone of mine?
Then, having prostrated before the Lord, Brahmā and the other lords of the gods spoke.
O Lord, since you have protected us by means of this valor,
let it remain as an ornament upon your body, serving as a signifier of that very protection.
Let this tortoise bone attain the status of the central bead in the garland of skulls;
even upon seeing this belonging to Viṣṇu, let there be no pride again.
Thus petitioned by the gods, the Lord of the Universe then accepted that bone;
and Viṣṇu, his delusion dispelled by the power of the ritual for the worship of the Lord of the Universe,
became free from sin and was thereafter honored by the lord of heaven.
The subduing of Hiraṇyākṣa through the Varāha incarnation: Once the gods were oppressed by their enemy Hiraṇyākṣa;
they approached Viṣṇu for refuge and reported their fear to him.
Having granted them freedom from fear, the enemy of the asuras and leader of the gods assumed the form of a boar and stood before the tip of Brahmā’s nostril.
Having slain Hiraṇyākṣa, he raised up the submerged earth;
out of pride for that deed, he [performed] the churning of the oceans by Hari.
And he assumed a truly massive body equal to seven mountain ranges;
seeing Viṣṇu in such a state, the gods, including Brahmā, were then [struck with awe].
They informed Maheśa that danger had arisen from Varāha;
thereupon, even the God of gods [prepared] for the subjugation of this Varāha.
The Lord commanded his son, the youth Subrahmaṇya;
and by his command, Kumāra likewise [assumed] the form of a boar as large as a mountain.
He seized it by the horn with both hands and, whirling it around as if in play,
he broke off one of its horns and placed it near the Lord.
Śaṅkara bore as an ornament the second [digit], which was a portion of the moon residing in his matted locks, even as the gods looked on.
Placing that son upon his lap, he cherished him with a joyful mind;
then Brahmā and the other gods, having offered salutations in their respective order, [departed].
They went to the god; likewise, Viṣṇu, freed from delusion, arose, and having again propitiated the god as before, he attained liberation.
The subduing of Nṛsiṃha:
On one occasion, Viṣṇu again [assumed his form] against Hiraṇya, the lord of the Dānavas.
Desiring to withdraw the world and having worshipped Śiva, the powerful one obtained a boon;
then, assuming the form of Narasiṃha, he again tore open the chest with his claws and,
having destroyed the hosts of asura soldiers, drank that blood in fury.
With that very same ego-sense, he prepared to annihilate everyone;
thereupon, the gods, overcome by fear, sought refuge with the Lord.
Then the Lord commanded Vīrabhadra for his suppression;
assuming the form of a Śarabha, the powerful Vīrabhadra [set forth].
Having seized that Narasimha and divided him into two parts by his own effortless play,
he split his exceedingly clear skin and offered it as a gift.
From that time forward, this god came to wear the skin of a man-lion (nārasiṃha);
and he too, having propitiated the god, became free from sin.
The subduing of Vāmana:
Once again, while performing the subduing of Bali,
this Madhusūdana became Vāmana, the son of Kaśyapa.
Having arrived at the sacrificial hall, the Lord, who had received the boon,
requested three paces of land for his own dwelling.
Then, having stepped onto the earth with one foot and then toward heaven with the other,
he placed Bali within the prison of his own stride because no further step could be found.
Having entrusted the kingdom once more to the Lord of the Gods, Trivikrama gave this broken egg back to him so that he might cause it to grow again.
Then the gods, having learned this news from him,
commanded Bhairava, who possessed a terrifying form, to subdue him.
He too, having approached with haste, struck Acyuta on the chest with his hand as he stood within the circle of the elders, felled him, and tore away his skin.
He wore his own soft, dark-blue skin as a cloak;
even his great, long bone, known as a skeleton, he held in his hand.
Then all the gods, free from fear, went to heaven;
Upendra also, having propitiated Mahādeva, returned to his former state.
His offense pacified, he departed as he had come;
thus was he subdued by the wielder of the Pināka bow during his five incarnations.
"Endowed with the five [faculties], I shall speak; let them hear that discourse.
The Grace of Paraśurāma" (Sūta: Śaṅkara-saṃhitā, Upodghāta-pāda 65).
Then the blessed Rāma, the Supreme Person,
became the son of Jamadagni through that very curse of Bhṛgu, born of his wife Reṇukā.
His father gave that Rāma the name Arindama because of his form;
and in due time, Rāma was invested with the sacred thread by his father, the great seer.
Always intent on service with faith and no other thought in mind,
he was once, for some reason, urged by his father.
Rāma indeed performed the decapitation of his mother Reṇukā;
thereafter, with a pleased mind, Rāma was addressed by the great seer.
"O son, know that I am pleased by your service; choose now a boon.
Whatever desired boon you wish for, I shall grant it all to you."
Having heard these words of his father, Rāma chose these boons;
first, he chose as his boon the restoration of his mother to life, just as before.
The abandonment of anger by his father, who was prone to wrath; the excessive devotion to the sage;
and his own constant faith in the worship of Śiva.
Then, having received three boons from his father, Rāma went to the forest to perform austerities, devoted solely to the worship of Śiva.
When he had departed, Arjuna, the son of Kṛtavīrya, approached the lord of sages, who had abandoned his anger,
and requested the cow adorned with the prefix "Kāma."
(Praying thus, that king, blinded by pride, endeavored to seize [the sage] by force;
when he was refused by the sage, the son of Kṛtavīrya,) p. 404) the king, was rejected by the muni.
Having severed his head with an axe, he went to Māhiṣmatī;
and Reṇukā, the beloved wife of Jamadagni, entered the fire.
Then, by that very great rain, the fire on the funeral pyre was extinguished;
yet Reṇukā, who considered herself a rishi’s wife, remained with her garments burnt.
Overcome by great suffering and shame,
the beautiful woman covered her naked thighs and buttocks with nimba leaves.
Having reached the guild of the Caṇḍālas, he lived there for some time. There was a certain man named Potra and a beloved woman named Mātaṅgī.
And they protected her— who was severely afflicted by being heated with fire and ground with flour and other substances—
having heard all of this in its entirety, Rāma departed for the forest.
Having obtained a battle-axe from the Lord, who was pleased by his worship,
he indeed became a submarine fire for the ocean of the Kṣatriyas.
Having slain Kārtavīryārjuna and other kṣatriyas as well,
he then offered them funeral libations with his own blood.
Having led [his father] with faith to Lake Bindu for the sake of his own father,
and having approached his mother who was staying in the hamlet, he bowed down to her.
He spent some time with her outside the village;
and having again satisfied his mother with such service, he remained there.
For the sake of atoning for the slaughter of warriors,
he worshipped Kṣayadvīra and gave this entire earth, acquired through his prowess, to Kāśyapa.
He reached the wonderful Vaikuṇṭha abode from Kerala.
Formerly, King Daśaratha, desiring a son, sought the grace of Rāma [Viṣṇu] from Maheśvara.
He performed the sacrifice for the desire of a son, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and other ascetics.
Then, by the power of Maheśvara’s command, Madhusūdana was born as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, from Kausalyā, the king’s wife.
Having gone to the forest with Sītā at his father’s command and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [abducted] Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, there.
Having deceived Rāma who was there with Lakṣmaṇa, he carried her away;
tormented by the fire of separation from her, Rāma remained joined with Lakṣmaṇa.
Having approached the sage Agastya, he wept, deeply afflicted by grief;
then, he was instructed by Agastya regarding the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
Having worshipped Śiva and obtained divine weapons, he built a bridge with the monkeys;
then, having defeated Rāvaṇa along with his hosts in battle by means of the leaders of the monkey troops.
Having purified his beloved Sītā in the fire, he brought her back to Ayodhyā;
there, having been consecrated with the royal fillet, he ruled a kingdom free from all obstacles.
Out of fear of public censure alone, he abandoned Sītā once more in the forest;
when she had vanished into the earth, he grieved intensely, overcome with distress.
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, with a horse sacrifice, Rāma,
the descendant of Raghu, cast off his body in the Sarayū river along with his brothers.
Acyuta returned to his own abode, the Ocean of Milk, as before;
that incarnation, however, was said in former times to bring suffering to women.
Because he was enveloped by darkness, he did not know himself through his own self; yet,
through the grace of Balarāma,
he is that very same Puruṣottama in another age, the Dvāpara Yuga.
The son of Vasudeva was born to Rohiṇī under the name Rāma;
there, having slain a host of Rākṣasas and performed a great deed once again.
Having propitiated the Lord Mahādeva together with Ambikā,
the powerful Rāma, devoted to the path of Yoga, attained Vaikuṇṭha.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu, the immeasurable self, assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa, was born to Vasudeva and Devakī, constrained by the curse of Bhṛgu.
Having worshipped Śiva, the lord of the gods, there and thereby conquering his enemies,
he approached Upamanyu and was initiated by him according to the prescribed rite.
Having propitiated Śaṅkara with supreme devotion as the foremost of the devotees of Śiva,
he then removed the burden of the earth and departed for the world of Viṣṇu.

Furthermore, at the end of the Kali age, Viṣṇu Adhokṣaja himself, having become Hayagrīva, will bestow grace through the incarnation of Kalki; he will personally annihilate the wicked beings born of the Kali age.
Having worshipped Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods, there in his form as a *liṅga*,
