When Mahādeva was pleased, Vidhi indeed made this request:
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, [grant] Viṣṇu and all the worlds."
I have the power to swallow it, to carry it even within my belly,
and furthermore, to expel it through the path of excretion.
Having thus petitioned Mahādeva and obtained that supreme boon,
Vidhi formerly challenged Viṣṇu and the worlds and quickly licked him up.
Then, entreated by the worlds, he released Viṣṇu from the path of his exit; by the command of the Lord, he created the worlds as they were before.
"That which was previously stated by Viṣṇu— that 'I have seen the upper portion of Maheśa, who exists in the form of the Great Liṅga'— "
To avoid those faults, he previously worshipped the Lord of the Universe, Śiva, with devotion at the holy Aruṇācala.
Purified by his worship of Śambhu, he was freed from that terrifying sin and,
remaining unwearied, created the entire universe just as it was before.
In ancient times, indeed, the Creator performed worship of Śiva on Śrīparvata;
then he beheld Śiva, the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Cause, who was well-pleased.
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, he, Brahmā, made this request:
"O Lord, grant me the great seat, the lotus, and the swan as my vehicle."
"O Maheśvara, in former times, after your hosts had been burnt in the great fire at the Dakṣa-sacrifice,
they were consumed by Tārkṣya in that blazing flame;
therefore, O Lord, grant me this lotus-seat with its swan-vehicle."
O Lord of the Universe, having reflected thus, I now bow down before you.
Saying "So be it," Śambhu granted that boon to Svayambhū and quickly vanished; Vidhi too remained there, dwelling in happiness.
Having reached the world of Brahmā together with the gods,
the Grandfather once again propitiated the Lord of Teachers, Vidhi.
Then, having received the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs from Maheśvara in the city of Śruti,
and having brought into being the ritual acts prescribed therein, he created all things moving and unmoving.
Once in ancient times, that Grandfather (Brahmā), having returned from the world of Brahmā,
reached Hemakūṭa and [worshipped] Maheśvara there in the form of a liṅga.
He worshipped the immutable Lord of Ambikā according to the prescribed rites;
Brahmā, beholding his father, the Lord of Brahmās, with a gracious countenance.
Afflicted by the fear of birth and death, Brahmā chose this boon:
"At the time of the final end, may the Blessed One [withdraw] this world, both moving and unmoving."
Having withdrawn [the world] together with Viṣṇu and having consumed Viṣṇu, O you who are overflowing with compassion,
he took the bones, ashes, and certain skull-fragments produced from that body.
O Mahādeva, you indeed perform the *tāṇḍava* dance by wearing [the world] as an ornament; tell me, what will you do now that this great end has arrived?
Having withdrawn this final body by means of your manifold play,
[take] the ashes from the bones born of my body, as well as the skull-caps and the hair.
O Śambhu, O ocean of compassion, perform your dance while wearing this very ornament;
by that alone I shall have attained my life’s purpose, and for me there will be no further rebirth thereafter.
O Lord of beings, having come to the great cremation ground,
who else could possibly have a rebirth, once they have received the ashes from Your eye-fire as an ornament for their body?

If even one whose bones and ashes have been cast into the Gaṅgā— obtained through the touch of your matted locks— attains liberation, what need is there to mention you, who are present within that very body?
"Let it be so for him, consisting of mere representation," saying this, Brahmā vanished; with a satisfied mind, he remained there awaiting the appointed time.
In the same way, when his end had arrived, Śambhu,
having withdrawn the cosmic order along with Hari, was adorned with a garland of his bones.
Remembering his own supreme state of absolute freedom, the Lord danced;
having thus bestowed grace upon Brahmā, he liberated him.
Thus Brahmā propitiated Śiva and obtained various boons;
who indeed can know their number? Whatever has been uttered by me is but a small portion.
The Worship of Śiva by Mahendra—
Sūta: (Śaṅkara-saṃhitā, Upodghāta-pāda 69) Hereafter, whenever the worship of Śiva was performed by Mahendra...
Among those [works], some are described as having been composed for the sake of one's own desired goal.
In ancient times, the powerful Śakra, desiring to slay Bala,
propitiated Kālahastīśa and obtained an excellent boon.
Having withdrawn his power from the Daitya in battle for the sake of pacifying that transgression,
the Lord of Śacī propitiated him there once more and thus achieved his purpose.
Again, on one occasion, by the curse of Durvāsas himself,
[the power] was transferred to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) regarding his elephant Airāvata, his excellent horse, and his wish-fulfilling jewel.
When all the wish-fulfilling trees and the Surabhi cow had fallen from heaven into the midst of the ocean,
the Lord of Śacī became utterly terrified.
Tormented by the suffering of poverty, he propitiated the illustrious Lord of Vṛddhācala and, having made his petition, obtained [his boon] through the Lord's grace as before.
And furthermore, [he took] Airāvata, the elephant, and Uccaiḥśravas, the horse from the ocean.
O Lord, he likewise obtained wish-fulfilling trees, the cow of plenty, the thought-gem, and prosperity at all times, just as before.
Again, once, due to the very curse of Gautama upon Indra,
when he was born from a thousand wombs, he felt shame even in all his limbs.
Having propitiated Viśveśvara at Kāśī, he became the thousand-eyed Indra;
however, O lords of sages, on one occasion, by the touch of Mahendra’s foot—
Some cursed him, saying, "Let this body of yours become another!
By that curse, he too became possessed of another body and was exceedingly distressed.
Having spent much time there and having worshipped the Supreme Lord in Kedāra,
he then regained his former body.
Even that sovereignty over heaven was lost through the grace of Śambhu;
and in former times, the slayer of Vṛtra propitiated Śambhu in Kāñcī for the sake of a son.
Having obtained Jayanta as her son, the daughter indeed became joyful in heart;
then, on another occasion, Maghavan approached the abode of Kamalā.
Having propitiated the Lord of Gods, he obtained the cloud as his own vehicle and,
through the grace of the Supreme Ruler, the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
In ancient times, having worshipped Maheśvara in the holy city of Puṇḍarīkapura,
Śatakratu attained the unsurpassed status of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
The beloved of Śaṅkara reached the vicinity of glorious Kailāsa,
and likewise, another, Indra, having worshipped the destroyer of cities (Śiva).
In the meritorious field of Aruṇācala, he obtained his beloved and excellent wife Śacī,
and he attained the delightful pleasure-garden frequented by Rambhā and other celestial courtesans.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, Śatakratu obtained manifold fruits there; I have described only a few of them, not all.
Thus I shall describe the worship of the Wielder of the Trident performed by the gods, as well as by others. (p.
425) Regarding the worship of Śiva beginning with the Sun:
once, a certain Arka was worshipping Īśāna in the sacred fields of Śiva.
One's own body is like a jarjhara drum; even its mouth is utterly contemptible.
Having cast off his supreme divine form, he who was beloved of the Lord became another—
the Sun— just as Bhadra formerly regained his eyes when they were plucked out.
Having worshipped Mahādeva, who is praised by many, at Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the supreme Ravi likewise obtained his broken teeth here in this sacrifice.
Another, the Sun, abandoned his fault while honoring Śiva; he had formerly committed a transgression born of passion toward the wife of a sage due to his being her lover.
The supreme Sun attains liberation from the defects born of association with shadows;
likewise, other Ādityas, having likewise dispelled their respective defects, [attain the same].
And they attained their own desires as well as the beauty of their bodies;
likewise, Candra, having propitiated the ancient Lord Īśāna along with Ambā.
Immediately after obtaining release from Dakṣa’s curse,
he cast off the pain in his body caused by Vīrabhadra’s assault.
In this way, Candra too joyfully cast off many misfortunes and attained all happiness through his worship of Śaṅkara.
All the lords of the quarters, having worshipped the Supreme Lord,
obtained sons as well as all their desired sovereignty.
Having abandoned all sins through the power of the grace of the Lord of All, they attained [liberation];
likewise, the eight Vasus performed worship of the trident-bearing God of Gods.
Having performed their respective rites, they attained their desires, freed from all sins;
likewise, the two Aśvin deities worshipped Maheśvara.
Upon becoming purified of all sins, they attained their own desired goal;
and the eleven Rudras, as well as the high-souled ones, [attained] Maheśvara.
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the seven ṛṣis, their sins destroyed, attained all their desires by honoring him completely.
Pure and free from sin, they attained every desire;
pure and free from sin, the two of them attained all their desires.
Sūta: (Śaṃkara Saṃhitā Upodghāta 70)—The son of Uttānapāda was the prince named Dhruva;
[so too were] the nine planets beginning with the Sun, and the twenty-seven lunar mansions.
The zodiac signs beginning with Aries, the yogas beginning with Viṣkambha, and the gods of the earth (the lunar mansions).
All seven instruments, as well as the stationary birds,
the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Garuḍas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas [were present].
Yakṣas, Siddhas, Guhyakas, as well as Kimpuruṣas and others,
Kinnaras, Piśācas, and Daityas headed by Prahlāda.
Humans, beasts, birds, and those beginning with trees—
the stationary, the moving, and whatever other living beings there may be.
The mountains and the oceans, as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā;
the Brahman-sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, and the celestial sages beginning with Nārada.
And having worshipped all the cosmic eggs, together with all their enclosures,
he worshipped the eternal Lord of the gods in the form of the Liṅga.
Having each attained their respective stations and whatever was desired therein,
and having shaken off all misdeeds, they obtained supreme bliss.
Having propitiated each deity individually, I have declared those by whom their desired objects were attained.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim how those who, having gathered together and worshipped Śaṅkara,
shook off all that was undesirable and obtained their own cherished desires.
I shall relate them to you; listen with careful attention.
Long ago, in the destruction of Tripura, there were three cities made of silver, iron, and gold.
They dwell upon the earth, in the midst of the sky, and in the triple heaven;
among them, three great asuras born from the stars were the most eminent.
Vidyunmālī, Tārakākṣa, and the powerful Kamalākṣa dwell there together with sixty-six crores of asuras.
Oppressing the three worlds and easily conquering the gods,
they formerly performed austerities directed toward the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
Having undertaken a rigorous discipline out of a desire for the eternity of the self,
their asceticism has scorched the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then the eternal Brahmā appeared before them,
mounted upon a swan, his presence surrounded by Indra and the other lords of the gods.
Having worshipped that god, the asuras chose a boon:
"O Lord of the immortals, grant us truly eternal status."
"O God of gods, have mercy! O Four-faced One, salutations to you!
Then Brahmā said to them: "If there is indeed permanence for us..."
"Therefore, O best of asuras, we are indeed able to give;
for even a giver, O dānavas, is not able to give what does not exist."
Neither I, nor Viṣṇu, nor any other excellent beings, nor anyone else whatsoever—except for Śiva—is eternal; all are indeed impermanent, even those who are enlightened.
"He alone is declared to be eternal in this world, the conqueror of death;
therefore, O you who are other than my sons, choose another boon."
Having heard these words of the Creator and having consulted with one another,
they bowed down to him and chose a boon worthy of his eternity.
"O Lord of the Gods, we three brothers indeed have three cities,
fashioned from gold, silver, and iron, located on the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven."
At the end of those thousands of years,
O Unborn One, let them attain union with him who was then heard of as having no second for even a single moment.
If the three cities were destroyed by him with that single arrow alone, then let death not come to us; grant us this boon today.
Furthermore, let there be very great sovereignty and incomparable valor,
and let the dwellings of all the asuras be once again in their cities.
"O Lord, may we have the freedom to roam through cities according to our own will.
Having granted all this, when Brahmā had departed for the world of Brahmā, [the Lord remained].
Wherever the Asuras were hiding out of fear of the gods, all those sons of Tāraka, having heard the news, immediately gathered together from there.
And with various gifts in their hands, they gave their own daughters to them;
and having reported their own suffering to them, the non-gods attained happiness.
Then Maya, who was skilled in illusion, was summoned by them in an instant;
having assembled and consulted with them, he did so with great satisfaction.
He constructed for them a city made of silver and gold,
as well as houses enriched with the nine jewels and great gate-towers.
And having beheld those three cities along with their various streets adorned with jeweled archways, together with the non-gods, they [remained] there.
And they praised Maya further, having attained incomparable satisfaction;
they also questioned him regarding what was beneficial and what was harmful for themselves.
With a joyful heart, he said to them, headed by Vidyunmālin:
"O Asuras, you have obtained a boon that is equal to eternity."
That the best of gods is one alone, yet the giver of death with a single arrow at the end of a thousand years— this indeed is the skill of his intellect.
In this matter, O non-gods, listen to what I have said here:
the Supreme Lord is remembered in the world and in the Veda as the foremost of gods,
the one with swift arrows, the one with a steady bow, the one whose nature is self-sustained, and the lord of the universe.
Āṣāḍha, the subduer, is devoted to his devotees;
he is recited everywhere in the Vedas as Tigmāyudha (the one with sharp weapons).
His worship must always be performed according to the rule by all who are the self of everything.
(429) Adversities, enemies, diseases, and malevolent planets come to an end;
the mind attains clarity when Maheśvara is worshipped.
This Rudra, the three-eyed one who increases prosperity, should always be worshipped by you along with your kinsmen in his form as a *liṅga*.
While Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was being worshipped in that manner,
those who were indeed your assailants were slain by him.
That Śiva is the bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for all living beings;
therefore, you should worship that very Lord day after day.
O you of noble vows, through devotion and worship, the asuras constantly attained sovereign power from Jagannātha in his linga-form.
"Victory shall always remain in the palm of your hand.
Having thus received his word, he replied to him, "So be it."
Those Asuras requested lingas presided over by Maya,
and he indeed fashioned a linga for each of them in an instant.
In every house, the Asuras worshipped Īśa; adorned with ashes, they were equipped with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered their anger.
Having heard these words of his, those three— Vidyunmālī, Tārakākṣa, and Kamalākṣa— acted accordingly in every house.
Having received from him their respective emblems, they, filled with joy, each worshipped them with an elaborate display of great opulence.
All were devoted to sacred study, their sins burnt away by austerity;
their bodies were adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, and they had conquered their senses.
As they worshipped in this manner, increases in prosperity and power came to them.
In both the world and the Veda, it is well known that for those whose souls are devoted to the worship of Śiva,
even trees become wish-fulfilling kalpa-vṛkṣas, whether they grow in houses or in gardens.
In his cow-pen stood cows that were joyful and like wish-fulfilling cows;
in their courtyards were established slabs of the thought-gem (cintāmaṇi).
p. 430) As these enemies of his were thus worshipping for their own welfare, the treasures, such as Śaṅkha and the others, manifested their presence there.
Singing, laughing, and dancing, those best of Asuras experienced perpetual festivals, constant prosperity, and eternal auspiciousness.
The foremost of the asuras sported upon chariots, elephants, horses, and the like,
as well as in diverse gardens, ponds, and lakes.
They spent their years playing everywhere in rivers and streams,
constantly and intensely devoted to their own duties, like those who subsist on ambrosia.
Accompanied by their wives and honored by celestial bards, they took delight;
wherever they desired, there they rejoiced together with those cities.
In the mandala of the thousand-rayed sun, in the midst of the stars of the moon,
in the world of Brahmā, in the world of Viṣṇu, on the earth, and in the intermediate space;
They rejoiced everywhere— in the world of the Lord of Gods and in the world of the Guardians of the Quarters—
and those people who were below them began to move about once again.
And on that path, all those foremost of gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, perished, oppressed by fear, having abandoned their respective worlds.
Having reached Mount Mahāmeru and consulted with one another, they said:
"How can these people, who are proud of their boons, be slain by us here?"
Then Viṣṇu said to them: "O Asuras, those who worship Śiva and are devoted to the worship of the Liṅga in this world cannot be conquered by you."
And their wives were devoted to their husbands, regarding their husbands as deities;
therefore, the Asuras became invincible and exceedingly powerful.
All the gods said to him: "These enemies of the gods, devoid of devotion, are performing the worship of Śiva at the word of Maya and Takṣaka."
Worship of Śambhu devoid of devotion is certainly not pleasing to Him;
yet we have all propitiated the Lord Sadāśiva.
Thereupon, those [gods], thinking "We shall be the eldest" because they were born from the command of Īśvara, spoke to him again.
Hari said to them: "O gods, you do not know their boons;
their destruction will come by a single arrow, and not otherwise through the sacrifices."
"O gods, why do you prattle in vain about things that have become subordinate?
They replied to him: "We are indeed composed of those very elements produced from sacrifice."
If we suppress and afflict our enemies within their own cities,
then we shall be capable of remaining established in our respective worlds.
Having thus deliberated, all those gods, led by Viṣṇu, summoned all the deities;
and Janārdana, together with the gods, [proceeded].
Then, meditating upon the Lord who bestows victory, he praised Him with the Upasad hymns;
at that moment, great and powerful beings arose.
And they commanded them with joy: "Devour those cities;
go along with the Asuras and all living beings!"
Having approached those beings who dwell in the cities,
he saw them radiant with ashes and rudrākṣas, devoted solely to the worship of Śiva.
Beholding all the Asuras, alas, they were not capable of conquering them;
instead, like a troop of monkeys, they merely retreated back toward the garden.
Those Asuras, having seen them eating fruits such as jackfruit, mangoes,
and others, struck them with clods of earth and sticks.
Then a battle broke out between them, the spirits and the enemies of the gods;
by the command of Śiva, those spirits perished, even though they were great.
Then those Asuras, having recognized such behavior on the part of the gods,
arrived in the celestial realms and carried out a violent plundering.
Those superior in strength struck down the gods stationed here and there;
then, those gods who were there were severely assailed by the asuras.
Having quickly reached Mount Meru, they reported this in the presence of the gods;
thereafter, the deities, afflicted by intense grief, remained within the caves of Meru.

The other gods remained there out of affection and likewise continued to dwell in their respective cities. Then, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, they went to Kailāsa to present a petition to Maheśa regarding the account of the gods.
Having bowed at the gate of the god, Janārdana respectfully inquired of the gatekeepers along with the gods regarding the opportunity for an audience with the deity.
"O gods, this is not your time; depart," said those hosts.
Hearing that, the deities replied, "Our course cannot be otherwise."
"Let us remain right here in this very presence for as long as the opportunity lasts," they said, consulting one another loudly, "Alas, alas, O Lord!"
Then, raising their arms, they cried out to the Supreme Lord with voices choked by distress: "O Śaṅkara, O Īśa, O Maheśāna, O Śiva!"
As those leaders of the Gaṇas, headed by Hari and Brahmā, were crying out,
they struck them severely with staffs, standing as if they were the very guardians of the gates.
Being struck thus, those gods were utterly overwhelmed on all sides;
slowly they approached the great and wonderful Lake Mānasa.
There the gods said to Hari: "How will the task be accomplished?
How shall we be able to make our petition in the presence of the Lord?"
"The gatekeepers here, possessed of great majesty, will not tolerate our staying.
To those who were thus deeply distressed, Hari spoke to the gods headed by Brahmā.
They do not strike us while we sit here in silence;
rather, such as they are, they strike only upon seeing us shouting at them.
"The gatekeepers at the door will certainly not tolerate their master being reviled.
Having heard these words of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the gods then [acted].
Then, threatening one another, they questioned Hari again:
"O Hari, tell us what our course of action should be hereafter."
Hari said to them: "All of you are indeed wise;
speak your minds, for at this time nothing pleases me."
Then, for a long time, they each expressed their own respective opinions;
and having reached a decision, they quickly spoke to Acyuta in the assembly.
The Asuras were devoted to the worship of Śiva;
they were adorned with sacred ash, wore ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, and were intent upon the worship of the Liṅga.
All were devoted to their Vedic studies and kindled the sacrificial fires;
O Janārdana, the wives among them were especially devoted to their husbands.
Those whose wives are devoted to their husbands cannot be slain at all;
nor can those in this world who are devotees of Śiva, adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
However, O Viṣṇu, even if those born of Diti were to abandon their emblems and worship through your illusory power (māyā),
Śiva will still destroy them.
"If Mount Meru does not become our certain dwelling place," while the gods were saying this, Hari spoke to them again.
"O gods of the thirty-three, I shall strive; this is indeed appropriate for me. And you, by my word, should worship the auspicious Lord Śiva through austerity."
"The Supreme Lord, the God, will surely withdraw them all.
Having spoken thus to Nārada, the illusory one reached Tripura.
There, the Buddha was born of his own accord, and Viṣṇu’s disciple was Nārada;
both of them deluded the race of the Asuras in an instant.
By means of a deceptive treatise, with sweet speech,
with various costumes, and with such things as food and drink, those two [tried to entice them].
Having displayed various jewels and divine ornaments, they showed themselves as women devoted to their husbands, skilled in manifold arts.
And those two destroyed their devotion to their husbands with their words.
(Sūta: Śaṃkara-saṃhitā, Upodghāta-pāda 71)—Seeing them thus, the former gods were deluded by that illusion.
The enemies of the gods became utterly infatuated with those two and lost their senses; they then sent Nārada, the disciple of that [preceptor], to them.
Having summoned him, they asked him in private: "Who is he, and from where has he come?
By the power of our good fortune, what is the purpose of his arrival today?"
He said to them joyfully, "This Lokāloka mountain is his dwelling place;
out of a love for surveying the worlds, he wanders there at times."
Wherever his own mind finds delight, there this self-controlled one abides;
staying there, he demonstrates the majesty of the knowledge of the Self.
All those who were instructed by him attained their desired goals;
some, having heard [his teachings], stood around him, surrounding him.
The master of illusion, having given them whatever they desired— various garments, ornaments, wealth, grain, and excellent women— deluded them.
Seeing him as he went along, carrying the riches produced by that greatness,
other people watched him again and again and stood there, turning back themselves.
The Buddha-teacher joyfully granted their heart's desire;
and again, the Daityas respectfully summoned Nārada in private.
When those who were his disciples asked him, "Do such wonderful supernatural powers (siddhis) arise for us in this way, or not? he [replied]:
Nārada replied to them: "I am a fool among disciples;
yet I too possess supernatural powers—behold them this very moment!"
Taking water from his water-pot and remembering with his mind those who have mastery over themselves,
he [realized that] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the gods were indeed present there.
They then came into being and bowed respectfully to the Teacher,
having caused the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to vanish in a mere moment.
He bestowed abundant nectar upon the Asuras, which had been attained through his own majesty;
furthermore, his disciple Nārada granted whatever was desired by their minds.
Furthermore, he deluded the intellect of the Daityas through his illusory power (māyā);
at that time, the sons of Diti did not request him to become their disciple.
Nārada, having joyfully informed his teacher of all that,
repeatedly entreated the teacher and caused those disciples to perform it.
He instructed those who had immediately abandoned the worship of Śiva,
and he taught them, "O Asuras, worship me alone."
"I am indeed the Buddha by name; let there be the recitation of my name for you. Through the worship of me alone, may your desired fruits be accomplished."
In this world, however, that which is seen is the very same as that which is false in the next;
therefore, Śiva-pūjā should certainly not be performed, nor should the sacred ashes (vibhūti) be worn.
The words of the entire Veda do not speak falsely regarding the seeds of the rudrākṣa;
those by whom all of this has been rejected are not disciples, nor anyone else.
"Furthermore, their worldly accomplishments will not succeed in any way whatsoever.
By these words of his, they all abandoned the worship of Śiva.
Likewise, those women who were devoted to their husbands— having abandoned their rudrākṣa beads, sacred ash, and the teachings of Śiva— were utterly deluded by Nārada.
Out of constant delusion, you lived as you pleased, attached to paramours,
through your longing for the garments and ornaments produced by his illusory power.

Having abandoned the conduct of Śiva, they devoted themselves to household walls and such things; being unchaste women, day and night they were intent on sweeping and the worship of [domestic objects].
Then Viṣṇu, in the form of the Buddha, asked Nārada:
"Is the entire host of the asuras truly under the power of our māyā?"
"Are women indeed attached to paramours, their inner selves deluded by illusion?
Thus questioned, Nārada then bowed to him and replied.
O Lord, deluded by your māyā, these lowest of asuras have each occupied one of the three cities, O Madhusūdana; today, leave them behind.
One is known as Paramayogya, another as Śīlapara, and another as Virakta;
these three yogins are the most excellent among the Pāśupatas.
They are superior even to Upamanyu, Bhṛgu, and Dadhīca;
they are more excellent even than Agastya, being solely devoted to devotion to Śiva.
And these three high-souled ones have become recipients of Śiva’s grace;
our māyā does not bind them, just as a lotus fiber does not bind elephants.
Hearing the words spoken by Nārada and reflecting upon them within his heart, Hari said to those others: "These three are not to be conversed with."
O disciples, my dear ones who desire prosperity, do not engage in quarrels with those three who are devoted to the worship of Śiva by means of my words.
Thus, having deluded everyone by means of his own māyā, Mahāviṣṇu established another portion of himself as the Buddha, who deludes the intellects of men.
Having summoned Nārada, he departed from the triple city;
then, desiring to ascend Mount Kailāsa, he drew near to it.
The sinless Garuḍadhvaja, together with the gods and sages, was unable to ascend that best of mountains, which is difficult for those of unrefined self to reach.
"For the sake of the gods' work, we have rendered these atheists into Asuras;
(we have deprived them of their ash, rudrākṣas, and worship of Śiva).
Because of that, a very great fault has arisen here, there is no doubt."
Śrī Kailāsa cannot even be remembered by those whose minds are possessed by defects.
Thus, for the sake of pacifying that fault, Keśava,
meditating upon the Lord who dwells within the heart, performed intense penance directed toward Īśa at the bidding of Nārada.
Then the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, being pleased,
spoke to Viṣṇu and Nārada with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"Alas! Shame, shame upon you two fools! Even for the sake of the gods' mission, this path has been cleared by my devotees without any hesitation on your part."
Therefore, it is not possible for you two to ascend Kailāsa;
hence, you should approach Lake Mānasa together with the gods.
"Accomplish the task of the lords of the gods," Śiva said, and vanished while speaking.
"So be it," they replied; and having propitiated him, they were greatly honored by the deities.
They both related the entire account concerning the three cities of the asuras:
"The asuras have abandoned the conduct of Śiva through our illusory power."
By a method favorable to us, Maya and Bhārgava were made to quarrel with one another and were caused to be cursed by the command of Śiva.
Desiring to perform great penance for the sake of that peace, directed toward Īśa,
those two best of gods reached the Himavat mountain and began their practice.
Therefore, since the non-gods are bound by my great net of illusion,
let us all now indeed come together here with faith.
"Let us propitiate the Lord of Gods, the imperishable husband of Pārvatī.
Having thus addressed Brahmā and all the others, the one whose banner is Garuḍa [spoke].
Having plunged into the waters of that Lake Mānasa,
he remained within the water and recited extremely fierce mantras.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, surrounded the Slayer of Madhu and performed intense,
great penance within the waters with their arms raised upward.
Then the Blessed One, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon, being pleased,
appeared before the gods, the goddess, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
And they all, with the hair on their bodies standing on end from joy, praised Mahādeva;
and beholding those foremost of gods, the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament spoke to them.
"O gods, you have gratified me with your asceticism while remaining self-controlled;
from now on, practice the Pāśupata vow without delay."
"Without doubt, that which is desired by your mind will indeed be fulfilled before long," said the Lord of Gods, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon.
Then Śarajanman, sitting on her lap, suddenly began to dance before the God of gods, Tryambaka, the mother of the worlds.
Having struck the arm of the god with a blue lotus, she was amazed and said:
"O best among those who possess sons, behold Kumāra as he dances!"
Having thus raised his own chest while dancing at the word of the Goddess,
Śambhu, delighting in the rhythm of hand-claps, said, "O child, dance!"
Then the child, the abode of play, danced upon the chest of the Wielder of the Trident;
at the word of the Lord of All, "Dance," everything there began to dance.
By whom in the three worlds can the command of the Lord of the Universe be transgressed?
Even the gods, headed by Viṣṇu and Brahmā, dance while remaining under his control.
The parents, being satisfied, embraced their son;
Śiva, having smelled his head with both hands, took him to his own chest.
O gods, he entered the inner apartments with his son with supreme joy;
then the gods, together with Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, were present there.
Distressed, the gods said to one another: "Now we are unsuccessful;
even though we have seen the Lord of All Worlds, our task has not been accomplished."
"We shall observe the Pāśupata vow proclaimed by the God.
Having thus propitiated Śiva, they undertook the Pāśupata vow.
The gods, adorned with stainless ashes, [worship] with supreme faith;
therefore, having fixed this in the mind, the Supreme Self is gratified by the vow.
The Teacher of the World commanded Nandin, the foremost of his attendants:
"There is no means whatsoever today to destroy the three cities."
"Tell the gods quickly: 'Let them provide everything necessary for battle, including the chariot, the arrows, and the bow.'"
Saying "So be it," Nandin departed and related all the words of Śambhu; gladdening the gods with his speech, he returned once more to the inner apartments.
When [the chariot] had emerged from the mountain and other [sources], the gods provided Śambhu with a chariot for the means of battle,
as well as a charioteer, horses, and a great bow with arrows.
Having meditated there for a very long time and consulted with one another, they said:
"The great Meru, made of gold, is indeed worthy of the Lord; it is here that he shall dwell."
Here, the king of serpents became the bowstring, while Vāyu, Agni, the Moon,
and Keśava made the leaves and the tips of the fruits for the supreme gods.
The Vindhya mountain was its axle-pin and Mount Kesarācala its support;
the earthly realm was the seat of that most magnificent chariot.
Space became her open expanse, and the moon and sun were in her wheel;
the stainless Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvan, and others—were her streets.
The foremost sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, were intent on reciting benedictions;
so too were the panegyrists, kinnaras, yakṣas, siddhas, and other kiṃpuruṣas.
The Gandharvas, Garuḍas, and others such as the Cāraṇas and lords of poets;
the eight mountains, the great serpents, the oceans, and the rows of clouds.
Canopies, jewels, and ornaments became his;
likewise, sacred mantras, the arts, cows, treasures, and all forms of prosperity were his.
Sacrifices, ritual acts, and duties; time, cosmic cycles, and the ritual stakes; days, months, seasons, and solstices; as well as yogas and karaṇas.
The moments, the muhūrtas, and the kāṣṭhas became the great chariot-rims;
thus was the chariot constructed, and Brahmā became its charioteer.
The Praṇava is its whip; the Vedas are fashioned as the chariot-poles, with the waters as the reins;
Viṣṇu, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk, is the arrow of great splendor.
He whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha, who wields the Śārṅga bow, the great attendant of Śiva;
on Mount Meru he is Manovatī-Brahmā, the charioteer, and the Praṇava is his whip.
Brahmā, the lord of Satyaloka, is an attendant of Śiva;
and all the gods, beginning with Śakra, who are the commanders of armies, are his soldiers.
Then the ascetics and yogis became chanters of auspicious blessings;
at that time, Viṣṇu, having approached from Kailāsa, came into the presence of Nandin.
And having prostrated before him, Nandin reported this event to him;
and at that time, having bowed with joined palms, he spoke to the Lord.
Then the Lord Śruta-vijñapti, a treasury of compassion, together with the Goddess,
mounted a brilliant white bull and approached the vicinity of the chariot.
Having seen him, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, then praised Sāmba;
delighted by that hymn of praise, the god who was born from the ocean raised him up from his bull.
Taking up his bow along with an arrow, he set foot upon the chariot;
while that Lord of Gods was thus placing his foot, the chariot—composed of the worlds—[proceeded].
Then, unable to bear the weight, it fell downward with a loud crackling sound;
at that moment, the gods, including Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, were struck with fear.
The great yogi Nārāyaṇa, having become a bull, drew the chariot;
yet, overwhelmed by the excessive burden, he fell down with his eyes gouged out.
Terrified, Hari praised Śiva with his mouth vomiting blood;
Brahmā and the others also praised the Lord of Gods with their arms upraised.
Then Śambhu, the ocean of compassion, bestowed his strength upon Viṣṇu;
in an instant, the great bull Kakudman bore the chariot of the gods.
Just as before, by the command of the Supreme Lord, the chariot was prepared;
then Mahādeva took his place in the chariot for the welfare of the universe, accompanied by the Goddess.
Then Nārāyaṇa, standing at the front together with the immortals, offered praise.
Then Śiva, adorned with the cool-rayed moon, spoke to Viṣṇu:
"O Mahāviṣṇu, choose the boons you desire; I am pleased with those that reside within your heart."
And quickly, without hesitation, by my command,
perform today the great sacrifice for my sake, O Mahāviṣṇu, which has been undertaken by you.
While Īśāna was speaking thus, Hari requested a boon:
"Just as I am the root-śakti when the śakti exists within one's power."
"O Lord, O Master of the World, may I likewise become a bull among bulls;
this alone is the praiseworthy boon for me, and no other, O Teacher of the World."
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, may I always have devotion unto you.
Then Śiva granted him the status of a bull and devotion to Hari.
Beholding that, all the gods attained incomparable joy;
then the deities worshipped the elephant-faced one who had risen to remove their obstacles.
With various kinds of foods, edibles, fruits, and other offerings, the Lord Brahmā, the master, urged his charioteer, saying, "O God, drive the horses! thus did the Lord speak.
At his command, Brahmā spoke and urged on the horses;
the leaders of the Gaṇas struck the kettledrums, tabors, and ḍiṇḍimas.
(From gomukhas, conchs, horns, timilas, paṇavas and other drums,
as well as delightful kāhalas and various insignia,) there arose a great sound of musical instruments at the departure, which surpassed the roar of the ocean.
Making the quarters deaf, it yawned unrestrainedly throughout the directions.
The god joyfully commanded the gods, the lords of the hosts, and the Pramathas who travel on foot, to mount their respective vehicles.
At your command, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, together with his attendants, mounted Garuḍa, his own vehicle, preceded by Hari and Brahmā.
Brahmā attended [the assembly] mounted upon a swan, and the Lord of Śacī [Indra] attended mounted upon an elephant;
the lords of the quarters likewise attended, each relying upon their own respective vehicle.
Vighneśvara and Mahāsena, together with various lords of the Gaṇas,
are mounted upon a peacock and a mouse on the right and left sides respectively.
At the forefront, the glorious Nandīśvara, taking up a golden staff,
cleared away all those who were obstructing the path from his presence.
With a joyful mind, the god Śaṅkara set out in his chariot together with Ambā,
intending to destroy the three cities of the Daityas.
The gods, sages, and others— such as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas—
[beheld] the Lord accompanied by Ambā, mounted upon his chariot and adorned with the ornaments of that chariot.
Having seen Śiva seated upon his great chariot, we have attained the fruitfulness of our birth and the great fruit of our sight; we have achieved our purpose.
They spoke thus, wishing to see the merit acquired by the Goddess in the past and what else it might be;
hearing the words of those speaking, which were sweet to the ear, the Lord proceeded.
Then the Lord of the heaven-dwellers set out to destroy the three cities of his enemies;
at that time, the gods, the foremost sages, the yogins, and the lords of the Gaṇas, such as Tumburu, Nārada, and others [approached] the God.
And their wives, eager to perform service,
uttered blessings and sang auspicious songs.
(Śaṃkara Saṃhitā, Upodghāta 72) Then the Daityas, utterly deluded by the Māyā of Mahāviṣṇu,
abandoned the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa beads, the worship of Śiva, as well as the Śruti and Smṛti.
Constantly devoted to the conduct of the Buddha and desiring direct perception,
the women, seeking visible results, were [instructed] by the words of Nārada as they grew in understanding.
Thus, in all these three cities, along with their women, and likewise in every single house, ill omens appeared.
The fragrant scents, the wish-fulfilling gems, and the trees of paradise have perished;
for the time of their conjunction occurs only at the end of a thousand years.
When Śambhu was pleased, a favorable moment arose; for what indeed is difficult when Śambhu is gratified?
Having witnessed the union of those three cities, the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, [prepared for action].
Seeing their joy and agitation as they, with contented minds, swiftly sought to discharge their arrows, the wielder of the trident [Śiva] observed them.
Gazing at the face of Girijā, he quickly offered a slight smile,
causing the arrows of the gods, headed by Mahāviṣṇu, to tremble.
Standing on the tip of Mount Meru’s bow, with his left hand held nonchalantly,
he then gazed upon the three cities with the corners of his three eyes;
in the brilliance of the sparks of fire produced by his gentle smile, [the worlds were consumed].
At that time, the foremost of the gods, caressed by the swaying hands of the goddesses, became like moths to the fire of his eye, even as Manmatha had been to the fire of his eye in the past.
Vāyu, Agni, Śaśin, and Govinda, having seen their cities previously consumed by his smile while they were fighting against the Asuras in their minds, now prayed for their own liberation.
Saying "So be it," he stringed the bow of Meru with indifference,
making it resound with the greatness of its bowstring and stroking it with the tip of his finger.
Having strung the bow and taken up the arrow consisting of the gods,
the fire of that arrow and the fire of his smile incinerated Tripura in an instant.
The enemies of the gods, their bodies scorched by the sparks of his smile,
were first subdued by the words of the Buddha, because they were subsequently devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Thereupon, they all attained the status of leaders of the Gaṇas;
delighted by the Pramathas, they took their place at the side of Śambhu.
Those three best of asuras did not fall into delusion at all,
for they had not abandoned their worship of Śiva, nor their sacred ash, nor their rudrākṣa beads.
Even as their own homes were burning, they remained pure;
like those within the ocean amidst the fire, they praised the Lord.
By the power of our fortune, we have not today been deluded by the Buddha’s illusion;
had we been like these others, there is no doubt that we would have become exactly as they are.
O Śambhu, they spent that time chanting "Śiva, Śiva";
then, having approached Śiva, the three, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise.
Bowing down to the Lord of All with their hair standing on end from joy,
Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, spoke to those devotees as he stood upon his chariot.
"You are exceedingly devoted to me, long-lived and illustrious.
O Asuras, tell me what you desire; I shall grant it to you."
p. 444) They chose this unsurpassed boon from the Lord who speaks:
"O ocean of compassion, we [wish to dwell] at your door on the peak of Kailāsa."
"We shall become gatekeepers, leaders of the door in the inner apartments.
Thus entreated by them, the Lord, the Master, made them the guardians of the gates.
Indeed, such a boon as this is extremely difficult to obtain in the world for all beings, including the gods; yet, O Lord, you have granted our desire and then vanished once more.
Then those gods, headed by Viṣṇu, made this agreement:
"From this day forward, in this world—including gods, asuras, and humans—"
Those gods and even sages who do not perform the worship of the Liṅga—
whether they be humans, Siddhas, Gandharvas, or whoever they may be— are the lowest of men.
Those who are devoid of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads have entered the path of heretics;
they are not to be spoken with by us, even though we are intensely devoted to dharma.
Those who engage in conversation, establish social ties, or perform Vedic and Smārta rites together with such persons have no atonement whatsoever.
Having then sworn, "This is indeed the truth, not a falsehood," the gods remained right there for a very long time, performing supreme worship of the Liṅga.
Having performed [the rites] and chanting once more, they all departed as they had come;
having reached their respective worlds, they worshipped the Lord.
In the past, the Asuras worshipped Śiva unintentionally;
for a long time they were indestructible, but later they abandoned their worship of Śiva.
Slain by Śiva himself at the end, they attained the status of attendants of Gaṇeśa;
those who did not abandon the path of Śiva became his gatekeepers once more.
Those twice-born ones were present in person at the abode of Śaṅkara on Kailāsa;
thus, having assembled with the gods for the sake of victory over the enemies of the deities.
For it was by worshipping him that his enemies were indeed conquered by those led by Viṣṇu;
therefore, worship of Śiva must be performed with every effort.

p. 445) Thus, having united with the gods who had obtained bliss through the worship of the station of Paramaśiva, they attained valor, happiness, victory, glory, and all manner of supreme enjoyments as well as liberation.
Therefore, by mortals, immortals, hosts of asuras and sages, and the foremost of the Siddhas and Gandharvas—
With devotion and faith, the worship of Śiva in the *liṅga* should be performed daily according to the prescribed rules by those who possess conviction.

Action that yields fruit in this life (*aihikaphaladakarman*)—(Upamanyu): "O Kṛṣṇa, I have thus described to you this action which grants success both here and in the hereafter. (Vāyusaṃhitā, Uttarabhāga 32).

The supreme [path] consists of the combination of ritual action, austerity, recitation, and meditation. Now, I shall describe here the great [practice] of the Śaivas, which bestows fruit upon men even in this very life, and which consists of worship, fire-offerings, recitation, meditation, austerity, and charity.
Therein, one who is most proficient in the meaning of mantras should first accomplish the mantra;
for a rite that brings about visible success yields fruit in no other way.
Even if a mantra has been mastered, a wise person should not hastily perform an action whose fruit might be obstructed by some unseen force or by a sudden flare-up.
However, a remedy for that obstacle can be performed here;
having examined it through omens and other means, one should first perform the remedial rite.
If a man, out of delusion, performs an action intended for results in this life in a manner other than prescribed,
he shall not partake of its fruit and will instead incur ridicule.
One should never perform an action with visible results without confidence;
indeed, one should not be lacking in faith, for one who lacks faith does not attain the fruit.
There is no fault on the part of the Lord, even when an action is fruitless,
because we observe the manifestation of results in this very world for those men who act exactly as prescribed.
The practitioner who has mastered the mantra, who has dispelled all obstacles,
and who is confident and full of faith, attains that fruit by performing [the rite].
Alternatively, for the sake of attaining that fruit, one should be devoted to celibacy;
at night, one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), or milk-rice (pāyasa), or fruits.
One should not commit even in thought that which is forbidden, such as violence and the like;
always having one's limbs smeared with ashes, one should be well-attired and pure.
Having thus become possessed of proper conduct, on an auspicious day favorable to himself,
in a location endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and adorned with garlands of flowers and other ornaments;
Having smeared the ground with cow dung to a size of at least one cubit,
he should draw an auspicious lotus that shines with its own luster.
It consists of refined gold, has eight petals and filaments,
is provided with a pericarp in the center, and is adorned with all kinds of jewels.
It was provided with a stalk exactly resembling its own form,
and was firmly established within a bulb made of gold of a corresponding kind.
There, having again mentally conceived all [the features] beginning with *aṇimā*,
[one should fashion the seat] made of jewels, or gold, or crystal, endowed with the proper characteristics.
Having installed the *liṅga* there together with its pedestal according to the prescribed rite,
one should invoke and worship the imperishable God there, accompanied by Ambā and his attendants.
There, the form of the embodied Lord Maheśvara is to be fashioned,
having four arms and four faces, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in a tiger skin, her face slightly smiling,
she holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and carries the antlers of a deer.
Alternatively, she may be visualized with eight arms according to the preference of the meditator;
likewise, the trident, axe, sword, and vajra are held in her right hands.
In her left hands she likewise holds a noose, a goad, a shield, and a serpent;
she has the brilliance of the rising sun and possesses three eyes in each face. Her eastern face is gentle, with a radiance corresponding to its own form.
The right [face] resembles a dark blue cloud and is terrible to behold;
the left resembles coral and is adorned with dark locks of hair.

The western face has the luster of the full moon; it is gentle and bears the crescent of the moon. Seated upon its lunar disc is the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara, renowned as Mahālakṣmī, dark-complexioned and enchanting.
Having thus fashioned the form and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order,
one should then invoke the embodied [deity] and worship the Supreme Cause.
For the purpose of bathing there, one should prepare the five products of the cow from a tawny-colored specimen.
Having prepared the maṇḍala in front, adorned with jewel-dust and the like, one should place the five nectars and, in particular, the seed-syllables within the full vessels.
One should then place the pitcher of Īśāna upon the pericarp;
thereafter, one should arrange the pitchers of Sadyojāta and the others around it.
Then, having filled eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa) with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) starting from the east in sequence, and having wound them with thread as before;
Having placed the meritorious substances along with the mantras and the ritual procedures,
he should completely cover them on all sides with a cloth such as fine silk (dukūla).
Having assigned the mantra everywhere, preceded by each respective mantra,
when the time for bathing has arrived, amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments;
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the five products of the cow and other substances;
thereafter, with water containing kuśa grass and the like, as well as water containing gold and gems.
Having successively extracted perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as those perfected by mantra,
one should bathe Maheśvara with each of these while reciting the respective mantras.
One should perform the ritual of worship beginning with perfumes and flowers and ending with lamps;
the unguent should consist of at least one pala, or more than eleven palas.
Gold and jewel flowers, fragrant blossoms,
blue lotuses, white lotuses, and numerous bilva leaves.
And lotuses, both red and white, should be available;
the incense should be derived from black aloe-wood, along with camphor, clarified butter, and guggulu resin.
Lamps fed with tawny ghee and made with camphor wicks,
as well as the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the enclosures, are to be worshipped.
Having offered the great caru-oblation, prepared with milk, jaggery, and ghee,
as well as fragrant water scented with pāṭala flowers, leaves, and so forth.
Well-prepared betel-leaf accompanied by the five fragrant ingredients,
and especially ornaments fashioned from gold and jewels.
Garments that are most variegated, fine, new,
and beautiful should be given, along with singing, instrumental music, and other such offerings.
The recitation of the root mantra should be one hundred thousand times according to the supreme count; the worship here may be one, three, or more, depending on the desired fruit.
The oblation for each substance should consist of at least ten offerings, increasing by one for each subsequent item;
Śiva should be visualized in his terrible form during rites such as killing and bewitching.
Śambhu, whose form is gentle, should be meditated upon in the Śiva-linga, in the Śiva-fire, in other images as well, during rites for pacification and nourishment.
For rites such as killing, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of iron;
however, for all other peaceful rites, they should be made entirely of gold.
With dūrvā grass mixed with ghee and cow’s milk, as well as with honey;
or with sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with ghee, or even with milk alone.
One should perform oblations with sesame seeds for victory over death,
and with ghee, milk, or even lotuses alone, for the pacification of disease.
One who desires prosperity should offer oblations for the pacification of great poverty;
one who seeks subjugation should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers together with clarified butter.
A twice-born man should perform attraction (ākarṣaṇa) with ghee and karavīra flowers;
he should perform expulsion (uccāṭana) with oil, and immobilization (stambhana) with honey.
Stambhana (paralysis) is achieved even with mustard seeds, and pātana (bringing down) with garlic alone.
Tāḍana (striking) occurs with the blood of both the donkey and the camel.
For the purpose of causing death or eradication, one should employ rohi seeds mixed with sesame.
One should effect inciting enmity with the oil of the lāṅgalaka plant,
and likewise achieve the binding [of enemies] and the immobilization of an army with the seed of the rohiṇī plant.
With all the sacrificial substances mixed with red mustard seeds.
In rites of sorcery (ābhicārika), one should perform oblations with oils produced from hand-presses,
combined with *kaṭukī*, chaff, and even cotton seeds.
In rites of malevolent magic, one should offer oblations of mustard seeds mixed with sesame seeds.
Milk brings about the pacification of fever as well as the fruit of good fortune;
likewise, a fire-oblation (homa) performed with honey, clarified butter, and curd brings about all accomplishments.
With milk, rice, or even plain sacrificial porridge (caru),
as well as with the seven types of fuel-sticks and so forth, one performs the rites for pacification and nourishment.
Through specific substances, there is likewise the accomplishment of the fire-oblation (homa), as well as subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa);
these bring about subjugation and attraction, and especially bestow prosperity.
An oblation performed with bilva leaves likewise grants victory over enemies;
for rites of pacification, one should use fuel-sticks made of palāśa, khadira, and other such woods.
Flowers from the *karavīra* and *arka* are for acts of cruelty, and thorny plants are for suppression;
one who is tranquil should perform rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and especially those of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
One whose mind is merciless and enraged may perform rites of malevolent magic (ābhicārika) if there is no other remedy in an extremely dire situation.
One may perform malevolent rites (ābhicārika) directed against an assassin;
however, one must not perform malevolent rites directed against the ruler of one's own kingdom.

Whether he be a believer, one of excellent virtue, a person worthy of honor, or whoever else he may be— one who has taken refuge in Śiva, whether by thought, deed, or word— against him one should not act, even if he be an assassin.
Having performed a malevolent rite (*abhicārika*) directed against the ruler of one's own kingdom, or even against one who has taken refuge in Śiva, a man shall fall into ruin immediately.
Therefore, if one desires one's own happiness, one should not harm even a protector of one's own kingdom or any devotee of Śiva by means of malevolent rites or other such acts.
Having performed an act such as killing directed against anyone else,
one who is possessed by remorse should perform an expiation.
Whether one is poor or wealthy, one may perform [this rite] even at a Bāṇaliṅga,
or at a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, or at one made by sages (ārṣaka), or even at one of divine origin (daivika).
In the absence of gold and jewels, or if one lacks the capacity for their worship,
one should perform this rite with the mind alone, or with substitute materials.
And even one who is capable in some respect but incapable in another respect,
if he acts according to his capacity, attains the fruit.
Even when this rite has been performed, if the result is not seen, one should repeat it two or three times; then the result will certainly be seen.
Whatever unsurpassed materials used for worship— such as gold, gems, and the like—
one should give all of that to the guru, and thereafter offer a separate sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If he does not desire it, he should offer all of that to Śiva;
otherwise, he should bestow it upon the devotees of Śiva and not upon others.
Even one who might personally accomplish [the rite] with devotion, independent of the guru and others, should likewise perform it here; however, he himself must not take [the substance].
If, out of greed, one personally takes the excellent materials intended as offerings, that fool shall not obtain what he desires; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
One should worship that consecrated liṅga for as long as one lives;

Since the fruit would not otherwise deviate [from its cause], what need is there for further encouragement?
Nevertheless, I shall describe the supreme accomplishment of rites by way of brief enumeration.
Even if one is assailed by enemies or by manifold diseases,
or even if one has entered the jaws of death, one is liberated from all harm.
An excessively miserly man acts like a king; one who is destitute acts like Vaiśravaṇa; even one who is ugly acts like a god of love, and even an old man acts like a youth.
An enemy immediately becomes a friend, and an adversary becomes a servant;
nectar turns into poison, and even poison turns into nectar.
Even the ocean acts as dry land, and even dry land acts as the ocean;
a chasm acts as a mountain, and that mountain acts as a chasm.
Fire acts like a lotus-pool, and the lake acts like the fire Vaiśvānara;
the garden acts like a forest, and that forest acts like a garden.
The small deer acts like a lion, while the lion acts like a toy deer; women act like women going to meet their lovers, and Fortune acts like one of virtuous conduct.
Speech acts like a self-willed servant, but fame acts like a courtesan;
intelligence acts like one who follows her own whims, while the mind acts like a diamond needle.
Power acts like a great wind, strength like an elephant in rut,
and action directed toward the enemy faction becomes paralyzed despite all efforts.
To enemies, every single person on their side acts as an adversary;
even while living with their kinsmen, enemies act like corpses.
Even when afflicted by disease, he is himself like an immortal, his life-threatening perils having vanished; even that which is unwholesome, when consumed by him, acts as a perpetual elixir.
Even though it is being practiced incessantly, delight becomes ever new;

Even the supernatural powers, such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest, result in fruits that are merely accidental;

[He was worshipped] by the world-protectors such as Indra, by the nine planets beginning with the Sun,

Having each attained their respective station, this was performed by all;

And Gaṇeśa attained the status of Gaṇeśa by this very rite,
having bathed Śiva and Śivā with white sandalwood water upon their lingas.
Having worshipped with white, blooming lotuses and having prostrated,
he arranged there a beautiful lotus seat endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
When wealth is available, one should install a small *liṅga* in the center of the network of filaments, using offerings such as oblations or flour-cakes according to one's own capacity.
Having placed a beautiful and auspicious image of the size of a thumb, composed of all fragrances,
on the right side, one should worship it with bilva leaves.
One should place agallochum on the right side, realgar on the west,
sandalwood on the north, and yellow orpiment on the east.
One should worship with fragrant, beautiful, and diverse flowers;

Kṛṣṇa:

Upamanyu said:
The unmanifest (avyakta) is declared to be the subtle body (liṅga), the source and dissolution of the three guṇas;

hanging from the tip of the trident, he praised the God with a joyful mind.
Delighted by that hymn of praise, the Lord endowed him with a boon;
and that Daitya chose as his boon the unsurpassed office of the Lord of the Ganas.
Then the Lord, with a gracious mind, granted the leadership of the Gaṇas to the Daitya,
and the Master, from within his own belly, released Śukra who had been swallowed.
Śukra, having worshipped Īśāna, then entered his own mandala;
thereafter, the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, propitiated Śiva along with Ambā.
Having completely cast off their female forms, they then went to their respective abodes;
even the sinful asura Andhaka, having beheld the wielder of the trident at the end, [attained his own state].
He attained the leadership of the immortals, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
(Sūta)— (Śaṃ- Saṃ- Upa 74)—
Once again, the Lord, together with his beloved, the daughter of the mountain, [dwelt there].
Accompanied by his inner circle of lords of the Gaṇas, Śiva resorted to the Śṛṅgāra forest;
there, in that grove of passion, Śiva took the hand of the Goddess.
He slowly beheld those thickets, creepers, and other trees, adorned with blossoms and new shoots, pointed out to him by the Queen's glance as they gazed together upon them.
Having seen there in the center a wonderful banyan tree with massive branches, he, together with Umā, reached the middle of the altar at its base.
There,
having gazed upon the banyan tree and the God of gods, the Goddess sat with a smile upon a seat with a divine covering.
The tree said, "O Mahādeva, she has not been seen anywhere.
He said to her as she was speaking thus: "Even from here, at the end of this age, he [will appear]."
When the dissolution of Brahmā arrives, this great hundred-fold [kalpa] will then become but a single leaf upon the waters of the ocean.
Mahāviṣṇu will fall there and lie down in the form of a child;
Janārdana will remember me for the purpose of Brahmā’s creation.

(466) "By means of him, I shall bring forth Hiraṇyagarbha from his mouth" (as the Śruti says: "One [being] was established upon the navel of the Unborn). Subsequently, this world proceeds in creation just as it did before."
"O King, having summoned the garden-keepers together with their wives,
you shall have the two birds brought from the middle of the pond."
The Lord whose crest is the charming moon said to those two,
"Go," and they, taking a swan and a parrot, departed immediately.
